questions.expl: Magnesium is highly active and ALWAYS requires protective coatings — special chemical and electrochemical treatments plus paint finishes.

questions.q: Anodizing is the most common surface treatment used to protect which metal?
questions.expl: Anodizing (an electrolytic oxide coating) is the most common surface treatment for non-clad aluminum. It is then primed/topcoated for full protection.

questions.q: Per AC 43-4B Table 3-1, MAGNESIUM is highly susceptible to which attack, and how does its corrosion appear?
options: Pitting; white, powdery, snow-like mounds and white spots
questions.short: Pitting; white powdery snow-like mounds/white spots.
questions.expl: Table 3-1 lists magnesium as highly susceptible to pitting, with white powdery snow-like mounds and white spots. Worksheet Q7's answer is 'pitting.'

questions.q: Magnesium is susceptible to what TYPE of corrosive attack (worksheet Q7)?
questions.expl: Magnesium, the most chemically active aircraft metal, is highly susceptible to pitting-type corrosion that appears as white powdery snow-like mounds and lifts the paint film.

questions.q: Per Table 3-1, how does corrosion on STAINLESS steels (300/400 series) typically appear (worksheet Q8)?
options: Classic red rust like carbon steel
A rough surface, sometimes with a uniform red, brown, or stain
questions.short: Rough surface; sometimes a uniform red, brown, or stain.
questions.expl: Stainless does NOT show classic red rust. Table 3-1 describes a rough surface, sometimes with a uniform red, brown, or stain. It is prone to crevice/pitting (marine) and intergranular (300 series).

questions.q: Per Table 3-1, the corrosion product appearance for ALUMINUM is:
questions.expl: Aluminum corrosion appears as white-to-gray powder. Reddish-brown is low-alloy steel rust; blue/blue-green is copper-based; green is nickel.

questions.q: Per Table 3-1, copper-based BRASS and BRONZE corrosion appears as:
options: No visible product below 700 deg F
questions.expl: Brass/bronze (copper alloys) show surface and intergranular corrosion appearing as a blue or blue-green powdery deposit.

questions.q: Per Table 3-1, low-alloy STEEL corrosion appears as:
questions.expl: Low-alloy steel shows the classic reddish-brown oxide (rust). This is distinct from aluminum's white-gray powder or copper's blue-green deposit.

questions.q: Per Table 3-1, TITANIUM produces 'no visible corrosion products at low temperature,' but colored surface oxides develop above:
questions.expl: Titanium is highly corrosion resistant; colored surface oxides develop above 700 deg F (370 deg C). Repeated contact with chlorinated solvents can degrade it at high temperature.

questions.q: Per Table 3-1, CADMIUM is described as 'used as sacrificial plating to protect steel,' and its corrosion ranges from a white powdery deposit to:
options: Brown or black mottling of the surface
questions.short: Brown or black mottling of the surface.
questions.expl: Cadmium gives uniform surface corrosion ranging from white powder to brown or black mottling. The mottling SIGNALS that sacrificial protection is working — do not remove it for appearance.

questions.q: WHEEL WELLS and landing gear are among the MOST corrosion-prone areas on an aircraft primarily because they:
options: Are always painted with the thinnest coatings
Are exposed to mud, water, salt, gravel and runway debris, with complex shapes hard to coat
questions.short: Runway debris exposure + complex shapes hard to coat.
questions.expl: Wheel wells/landing gear receive more punishment than any other area: mud, water, salt, gravel and debris thrown from runways, plus complicated shapes/fittings that make complete paint coverage difficult.

questions.q: Why is complete protective-paint coverage difficult on the landing gear / wheel well area (worksheet Q9)?
options: The area is too hot to paint
Paint is banned there by regulation
Their complicated shapes, assemblies, and fittings
questions.expl: Beyond debris exposure, the complicated shapes, assemblies, and fittings of the landing gear/wheel well make complete protective-coating coverage difficult — leaving bare spots for corrosion.

questions.q: ENGINE FRONTAL areas and cooling-air vents are corrosion-prone mainly because (worksheet Q10):
options: Constant abrasion by dirt/gravel/rain removes protection while moist salt/pollutant-laden air flows over unpainted surfaces
They are sealed from all airflow
questions.short: Abrasion strips protection; contaminated air flows over bare surfaces.
questions.expl: Constant abrasion by airborne dirt, gravel and rain strips protective surfaces, and unpainted areas (cooling fins, machined mounting bases) are continuously exposed to moist, salt- or pollutant-laden air.

questions.q: Exhaust trail areas are a known corrosion trouble spot mainly because exhaust deposits combine with moisture to form:
options: Mildly corrosive acids that attack the surface
questions.short: Mildly corrosive acids on the surface.
questions.expl: Exhaust gas deposits trap and hold other corrosive agents and, with moisture, can form mildly corrosive acids — making the exhaust trail a high-priority corrosion control point.

questions.q: Battery compartments and vents are corrosion-prone because the electrolyte and its fumes:
options: Spread corrosive agents to nearby metal and trapped areas
questions.short: Spread corrosive agents to nearby metal.
questions.expl: Battery acid (or alkaline) fumes and electrolyte spills corrode the battery box and nearby structure; vents can carry corrosive fumes downstream. Spills must be neutralized promptly.
questions.cite: AC 43-4B p. 4-29, para. 4.13.2.8 (cleaning agents); see also areas guidance

questions.q: A protective coating that corrodes ITSELF to protect the underlying base metal is called a:
questions.expl: Sacrificial coatings (cadmium, zinc, aluminum) corrode preferentially to protect the base metal. Non-sacrificial coatings protect by barrier action.

questions.q: Which group lists ONLY sacrificial protective coatings (worksheet Q11)?
questions.expl: Sacrificial coatings are cadmium, zinc, and aluminum. Hard chromium/nickel plating, conversion coatings, primers/sealants, and topcoats are non-sacrificial.

questions.q: Hard CHROMIUM plating and NICKEL plating are examples of:
questions.expl: Hard plating (chromium, nickel) protects by forming a hard barrier, not by sacrificing itself — so it is non-sacrificial. Cadmium/zinc/aluminum are the sacrificial coatings.

questions.q: Which of the following is a NON-sacrificial protective finish per worksheet Q11?
questions.expl: Non-sacrificial finishes include hard plating (chromium, nickel), chemical conversion coatings, sealant/primers, and topcoat. Cadmium, zinc, and aluminum are sacrificial.

questions.q: Primers, sealants, and the topcoat protect the base metal by:
options: Forming a barrier that keeps electrolytes off the metal (non-sacrificial)
questions.expl: Sealant/primers and topcoat are non-sacrificial: they shield the metal from moisture and electrolytes by barrier action, rather than corroding in its place.

questions.q: Which cleaning agent is correctly matched to neutralizing an electrolyte spill from a SULFURIC-ACID (lead-acid) battery?
questions.expl: Sodium bicarbonate neutralizes acidic (lead-acid/sulfuric) spills. Monobasic sodium phosphate and boric acid are for nickel-cadmium (alkaline) spills.

questions.q: Monobasic sodium phosphate and boric acid are used to neutralize electrolyte spills from which battery type?
questions.expl: Nickel-cadmium electrolyte is alkaline, so it is neutralized with an acidic agent (monobasic sodium phosphate and boric acid). Sodium bicarbonate handles acidic lead-acid spills.

questions.q: Per worksheet Q12, a MILD ABRASIVE used to polish out scratches in canopy/transparency materials is:
questions.expl: The miscellaneous cleaning agents in para. 4.13.2.8 include plastic polish (a mild abrasive to polish out scratches in canopy materials), alkaline chemicals, sodium bicarbonate, and monobasic sodium phosphate/boric acid.

questions.q: Per worksheet Q12, ALKALINE chemicals among the miscellaneous cleaning agents are used to:
questions.expl: Alkaline chemicals are listed as miscellaneous cleaning agents used to neutralize specific acidic soils on the aircraft surface.

questions.q: In addition to routine maintenance, an aircraft operating in a MODERATE corrosive environment should be inspected for corrosion every:
questions.expl: Suggested intervals: severe = 15 days, moderate = 45 days, mild = 90 days. The 45-day moderate interval is the worksheet Q13 answer and a classic exam number.

questions.q: Per AC 43-4B suggested intervals, an aircraft in a SEVERE corrosive environment should be inspected every:
questions.expl: Severe = 15 days, moderate = 45 days, mild = 90 days. Severe zones get the shortest interval.

questions.q: Per AC 43-4B suggested intervals, an aircraft in a MILD corrosive environment should be inspected every:
questions.expl: Mild zones = 90 days, moderate = 45 days, severe = 15 days. Milder environment, longer interval.

questions.q: Before performing a corrosion inspection, the aircraft should be (worksheet Q14):
questions.expl: AC 43-4B directs that the aircraft be washed prior to ANY inspection for corrosion, so contaminants do not hide developing corrosion. Worksheet Q14 answer = True.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the nondestructive inspection (NDI) methods listed in AC 43-4B?
questions.expl: NDI methods include visual/fiber-optic, liquid (dye) penetrant, magnetic particle, eddy current, X-ray (radiographic), ultrasonic, and acoustic emission. Tensile/hardness-file are destructive/mechanical.

questions.q: Which NDI method uses a dye drawn into surface-breaking flaws, then a developer to make the flaw visible, and is LIMITED to flaws open to the surface?
questions.expl: Liquid penetrant reveals only surface-breaking flaws (the dye must enter an opening). Eddy current and ultrasonic find some subsurface flaws; X-ray sees internal/volumetric defects.

questions.q: Which NDI method can ONLY be used on ferromagnetic (magnetizable) materials such as steel?
questions.expl: Magnetic particle inspection requires a ferromagnetic material; it cannot be used on aluminum or other nonmagnetic metals. Penetrant, eddy current, and ultrasonic work on nonmagnetic metals too.

questions.q: Which NDI method uses penetrating radiation to reveal internal (subsurface/volumetric) defects?
questions.expl: Radiographic (X-ray) inspection sees internal/volumetric defects, including hidden corrosion and inclusions. Penetrant and magnetic particle are limited to surface or near-surface flaws.

questions.q: Which NDI method uses high-frequency SOUND waves to detect subsurface flaws and measure remaining thickness?
questions.expl: Ultrasonic uses high-frequency sound to find subsurface flaws and measure remaining thickness (useful for hidden corrosion). Penetrant/magnetic particle are surface methods.

questions.q: Which inspection method uses a borescope/fiber-optic device to look inside areas the eye cannot directly reach (worksheet Q15 'A')?
questions.expl: Visual inspection, aided by fiber-optic borescopes, lets the inspector see hidden cavities and ducts. The worksheet Q15 list begins with visual/fiber-optic then the six AC methods.
questions.cite: AC 43-4B p. 5-12, para. 5.4.1.2 (fiber optics also p. 4-14, para. 4.11.6)

questions.q: Which NDI method induces eddy currents in a conductive part and detects flaws by changes in those currents (works on nonmagnetic metals like aluminum)?
questions.expl: Eddy current inspection works on conductive metals (including nonmagnetic aluminum) and can find surface and near-surface cracks and corrosion thinning.

questions.q: When mixing acid and water, the correct and safe procedure is to:
options: Never add water to acid - always add acid to water
Heat the acid first, then pour in water
questions.short: Add acid to water; never add water to acid.
questions.expl: Never add water to acid - the violent exothermic reaction can spatter acid. Always add acid slowly to water. Worksheet Q16(a) = True.

questions.q: When MIXING ALKALIS with water, AC 43-4B requires that the containers used:
options: Be made to withstand the chemical heat generated
questions.short: Be made to withstand the heat generated.
questions.expl: Mixing alkalis with water generates heat; use containers made to withstand the chemical heat generated. Worksheet Q16(b) = True.

questions.q: When using solvents, cleaners, strippers, etchants, or conversion coatings, AC 43-4B requires that you:
options: Apply with bare hands and rinse afterward
Work without gloves for better feel
questions.expl: Rubber or plastic gloves are required when handling solvents, cleaners, strippers, etchants, or conversion coatings. Worksheet Q16(d) = True.

questions.q: If a paint stripper, etchant, or conversion-coating material contacts your skin or clothing, you should:
options: Wash it from the body/skin/clothing immediately
Let it dry, then brush it off
questions.expl: Wash any paint stripper, etchant, or conversion coating material immediately from body, skin, or clothing - these are corrosive to tissue. Worksheet Q16(c) = True.

questions.q: Pits remaining after removal of corrosion products must be blended out when they are found in:
questions.expl: In critical and highly-stressed areas, remaining pits must be blended out to prevent stress risers that cause stress-corrosion cracking. Worksheet Q17 answer.

questions.q: When reworking a corrosion dish-out, AC 43-4B specifies blending the depression using a length-to-depth ratio of:
questions.expl: Rework depressions with a smoothly-blended dish-out using a length-to-depth ratio of 20:1. NOTE: AC 43-4B specifies only this 20:1 ratio; it does NOT state any separate 10:1 width ratio.

questions.q: Blending out remaining pits in critical/highly-stressed areas is required mainly to prevent:
options: Stress risers that lead to stress-corrosion cracking
questions.short: Stress risers that lead to stress-corrosion cracking.
questions.expl: Sharp pits act as stress risers (concentrators) and can initiate stress-corrosion cracking or fatigue cracks in loaded structure, so they are blended smooth.

questions.q: Why does AC 43-4B require a smoothly blended dish-out (20:1) rather than a sharp gouge when removing corrosion?
options: To make it look better only
To avoid creating a sharp stress concentration in the structure
questions.short: To avoid a sharp stress concentration.
questions.expl: A gradual 20:1 blended contour spreads load smoothly; an abrupt edge would concentrate stress and could initiate cracking. The ratio controls the smoothness of the cleanup.

questions.q: Before resorting to chemical testing, the PRIMARY reference used to identify an aircraft metal is the:
questions.expl: AC 43-4B: the primary method of identifying metal is the aircraft SRM. Chemical testing is used only after other methods are exhausted. Worksheet Q18 answer.

questions.q: Chemical testing to determine an aircraft metal's composition should be used:
options: Only when all other identification methods are exhausted
questions.short: Only when all other methods are exhausted.
questions.expl: The SRM is primary; chemical testing is a last resort used only when all other identification methods have been exhausted.

questions.q: Which of the following must NEVER be used to remove corrosion from an ALUMINUM surface?
options: Steel wool or a steel wire brush
questions.short: Steel wool or steel wire brush.
questions.expl: Steel wool, steel wire brushes, copper alloy brushes, and severe abrasives must never be used on aluminum - they embed dissimilar particles that start galvanic corrosion. Worksheet Q19.

questions.q: Per worksheet Q19, which of these is on the 'never use on aluminum' list?
questions.expl: The four prohibited items for aluminum are: steel wool, steel wire brushes, copper alloy brushes, and severe abrasive materials.

questions.q: Using a steel wire brush on aluminum is harmful chiefly because it:
options: Embeds steel particles that set up dissimilar-metal (galvanic) corrosion
questions.expl: Steel (or copper) particles embedded in aluminum become future corrosion sites by forming galvanic couples. That is why steel/copper brushes and steel wool are prohibited on aluminum.

questions.q: Which materials are ACCEPTABLE for removing corrosion from aluminum?
options: Copper alloy brushes and crocus cloth
Aluminum wool, fiber (Tampico) bristle brushes, and mild abrasives
questions.short: Aluminum wool, fiber bristle brushes, mild abrasives.
questions.expl: Acceptable choices are aluminum wool, fiber (Tampico) bristle brushes, and mild abrasives. Steel/copper brushes, steel wool, and severe abrasives are prohibited on aluminum.

questions.q: Austenitic (300-series) stainless steels resist corrosion because of a tightly adhering oxide (passive) film. If that film is broken, re-passivation does NOT restore it, and serviceability is affected, AC 43-4B says you must:
questions.expl: If corrosion occurs on austenitic steel and the part's structural integrity or serviceability is affected (film not restored by re-passivation), the part must be removed. Worksheet Q20.

questions.q: Austenitic 300-series stainless steels are protected from corrosion primarily by:
options: A tightly adhering passive oxide film
questions.short: A tightly adhering passive oxide film.
questions.expl: Non-magnetic austenitic (300-series) stainless relies on a tight, self-healing passive oxide film. If that film is broken and cannot re-passivate, active corrosion can begin.

questions.q: Stainless steel that shows a brown/tea-colored stain on the surface is best assessed as:
options: A rough/stained surface — evidence of corrosion attack on the passive film
questions.short: Rough/stained surface = corrosion of the passive film.
questions.expl: Stainless does not show classic red rust; tea-staining/brown discoloration indicates the passive film has been attacked (crevice/pitting). Table 3-1 describes a rough surface, sometimes red/brown/stained.

questions.q: Cadmium- and zinc-plated parts must NEVER have their coatings cleaned with a:
questions.expl: AC 43-4B: under no condition should a cadmium (or zinc) coating be cleaned with a wire brush - it would remove the thin sacrificial layer. Worksheet Q21.

questions.q: Why must a cadmium-plated part never be wire-brushed?
options: The wire brush removes the thin sacrificial cadmium layer that protects the steel
questions.short: It removes the sacrificial cadmium layer.
questions.expl: The cadmium layer is thin and sacrificial. A wire brush would strip it, exposing the base steel to corrosion. Clean with non-abrasive methods instead.

questions.q: Properly functioning cadmium plating may show white-to-brown-to-black MOTTLING on its surface. This mottling indicates (worksheet Q22):
options: The plating has failed and must be stripped
Sacrificial protection is taking place - do not remove it for appearance
questions.short: Sacrificial protection working - leave it alone.
questions.expl: Mottling (white to brown to black) shows the cadmium is sacrificially protecting the base metal; under no condition should it be removed merely for appearance.

questions.q: Cadmium-plate mottling ranges in color from white to:
questions.expl: The sacrificial-protection mottling on cadmium plate ranges from white through brown to black spots. It signals the coating is working and should not be removed for appearance.

questions.q: Before applying soap and water to a plastic (transparent) surface, you should FIRST (worksheet Q23):
options: Polish it with a dry cloth
Flush it with fresh water to dissolve salt deposits and wash away dust
questions.expl: Flush plastic surfaces with fresh water first to dissolve salt and remove grit, then wash with soap and water, preferably by hand. Dry cloths and solvents scratch or craze plastic.

questions.q: To remove oil and grease from a plastic windshield/window, you should (worksheet Q24):
options: Rub gently with a cloth wet with soap and water
questions.short: Rub gently with a soap-and-water-wet cloth.
questions.expl: Remove oil and grease by rubbing gently with a soap-and-water cloth. Solvents like carbon tetrachloride, lacquer thinner, and gasoline soften the plastic and cause crazing.

questions.q: Which of the following must NOT be used on aircraft plastics because it softens the plastic and causes crazing (worksheet Q25)?
questions.expl: Acetone, benzene, carbon tetrachloride, lacquer thinners, window-cleaning sprays, gasoline, fire-extinguisher fluid, and deicer fluid all craze plastic. Soap, water, and a chamois are safe.

questions.q: Worksheet Q25 lists three solvents NOT to use on plastics. They are acetone, benzene, and:
questions.expl: The worksheet's three blanks are acetone, benzene, and carbon tetrachloride (first three of the full FAA list). All soften the plastic and cause crazing.

questions.q: Crazing of an aircraft plastic windshield refers to:
options: A network of fine cracks/clouding caused by solvent attack or stress
questions.short: A network of fine cracks/clouding in the plastic.
questions.expl: Crazing is fine cracking/clouding of plastic, commonly caused by incompatible solvents (acetone, benzene, carbon tetrachloride, etc.). It is unrelated to metal corrosion.

questions.q: To avoid scratching a plastic windshield, you should NOT:
options: Rub it with a dry cloth
Wash it by hand with soap and water
Dry it with a clean chamois
questions.short: Rub it with a dry cloth.
questions.expl: Because the surface is soft, do not rub plastic with a dry cloth - it scratches and builds static that attracts dust. Wash by hand and dry with a chamois or absorbent cotton.

questions.q: Which of the following IS safe to use when drying a cleaned plastic transparency?
options: A clean, damp chamois or absorbent cotton
questions.short: A clean, damp chamois or absorbent cotton.
questions.expl: Dry plastic with a clean damp chamois or soft absorbent cotton - never a dry/abrasive cloth and never solvents, which scratch or craze the surface.

questions.q: Per AC 43-4B, which cleaning method is specifically noted to CRAZE plastic and should not be used on transparencies?
questions.expl: AC 43-4B notes that steam cleaning crazes plastic. (The detailed solvent list that crazes plastic is in FAA-H-8083-30B p. 8-24.)

questions.q: A mechanic finds a worm-like trail of corrosion under the painted skin of a stored aircraft kept in a humid hangar (~85% RH). The MOST likely corrosion and a good prevention step are:
options: Filiform corrosion; store below 70% RH and use low-diffusion coatings
Galvanic corrosion; add a sacrificial anode
questions.expl: A worm-like trace under paint at 78-90% RH is filiform corrosion. Prevention includes storing below 70% RH, low-diffusion coatings, and washing off acidic contaminants.

questions.q: During a corrosion inspection a mechanic plans to clean an aluminum panel using a power wire brush from the steel-parts bench. What is wrong with this plan?
options: Aluminum cannot be cleaned at all
A steel wire brush embeds steel particles into aluminum, causing galvanic corrosion; use aluminum wool or a fiber brush
Nothing - wire brushing aluminum is preferred
questions.short: Steel brush -> embedded steel -> galvanic corrosion.
questions.expl: Never use a steel wire brush (or steel wool/copper brush) on aluminum; embedded steel particles start dissimilar-metal corrosion. Use aluminum wool, fiber (Tampico) brushes, and mild abrasives.

questions.q: A lead-acid battery has leaked electrolyte into its box. The correct neutralizing agent, and the reason cadmium mottling on the box plating should be left alone, are:
options: Monobasic sodium phosphate; mottling must be wire-brushed off
Sodium bicarbonate; mottling shows the cadmium is sacrificially protecting the steel
questions.short: Sodium bicarbonate; mottling = sacrificial protection working.
questions.expl: Sodium bicarbonate neutralizes acidic (lead-acid) electrolyte. Cadmium mottling (white-to-brown-to-black) shows sacrificial protection is working and must not be removed for appearance.

questions.q: A 7075 aluminum fitting was improperly heat-treated and then exposed to salt air. Which corrosion is it now MOST susceptible to, and what advanced form could follow?
options: Intergranular corrosion, which can advance to exfoliation
questions.expl: Improperly heat-treated 2014/7075 are prone to intergranular corrosion along grain boundaries, which can advance to exfoliation (lifting/swelling of surface grains).

questions.q: A mechanic finds tiny holes under a white powdery deposit on a magnesium gearbox housing. The corrosion form is ___ and magnesium is described as ___ to it.
questions.expl: White/gray powder over tiny holes is pitting, the most common corrosion of aluminum and magnesium. Table 3-1 lists magnesium as highly susceptible to pitting.

questions.q: To repair a shallow corrosion pit in a highly-stressed wing spar cap, the mechanic should blend the area to a smooth dish-out with a length-to-depth ratio of:
options: No blending - just paint over it
questions.expl: In critical/highly-stressed areas, pits must be blended out (not left as stress risers) using a smoothly contoured 20:1 length-to-depth dish-out.

questions.q: In 1966 the agency was placed under a new department and renamed the FAA. What department took it over?
questions.expl: Correct answer: Department of Transportation (DOT).

questions.q: The FAA's single primary goal is:
questions.expl: Correct answer: Safety.

questions.q: The FAA's primary mandatory tools — the rules it enforces — are called:
questions.expl: Correct answer: FARs (the 14 CFR parts).

questions.q: Which statement is TRUE about CFRs vs FARs?
options: CFRs cover the entire body of U.S. federal regulation; FARs are the 14 CFR aviation parts
questions.short: CFRs cover the entire body of U.S. federal regulation; FARs are the 14 CFR aviation parts
questions.expl: Correct answer: CFRs cover the entire body of U.S. federal regulation; FARs are the 14 CFR aviation parts.

questions.q: 'Regulatory' means ____ and 'non-regulatory' means ____.
questions.expl: Correct answer: Mandatory / non-mandatory.

questions.q: The correct 'Order of Maintenance' is:
options: Something is broken -> fix it -> document it
Inspect it -> sell it -> document it
Fix it, find it, ignore it
questions.short: Something is broken -> fix it -> document it
questions.expl: Correct answer: Something is broken -> fix it -> document it.

questions.q: Which FAR part contains Definitions and Abbreviations?
questions.expl: Correct answer: Part 1.

questions.q: Per the FAA handbook, 'airworthy' means an aircraft:
options: Conforms to its type design AND is in a condition for safe operation
questions.short: Conforms to its type design AND is in a condition for safe operation
questions.expl: Correct answer: Conforms to its type design AND is in a condition for safe operation.  EXAM CORRECTION: The handbook quotes this definition under PART 3, §3.5 (not Part 1). Part 1 is Definitions/Abbreviations generally; the verbatim 'airworthy' definition lives in §3.5.

questions.q: 'Product' is defined as:
options: An aircraft, aircraft engine, or aircraft propeller
questions.short: An aircraft, aircraft engine, or aircraft propeller
questions.expl: Correct answer: An aircraft, aircraft engine, or aircraft propeller.

questions.q: A 'record' is any writing, drawing, map, recording, tape, film, photograph, or other documentary material by which information is:
questions.expl: Correct answer: Preserved.

questions.q: Per Matthew's notes, FAR Part 3 Subpart A covers General Requirements and Subpart B covers:
questions.expl: Correct answer: Security Threat Disqualification.  EXAM CORRECTION: Heads up: in current 14 CFR, the 'Security Threat Assessment / disqualification' language for AIRMEN lives in Part 65 (§65.14) and TSA's 49 CFR Part 1540, not 14 CFR Part 3. Keep your instructor's 'Part 3 = General Requirements (§3.5 definitions)' framing for the worksheet, but expect Part 3 = 'General Requirements' on the written. [verify exact Subpart B label with instructor]
questions.cite: 14 CFR Part 3 (General Requirements); cf. Part 3 structure

questions.q: Part 21 covers:
options: Certification Procedures for Products and Parts
questions.short: Certification Procedures for Products and Parts
questions.expl: Correct answer: Certification Procedures for Products and Parts.

questions.q: Part 23 (general aviation airplanes) historically applied to airplanes weighing:
questions.expl: Correct answer: Less than 12,500 lb takeoff weight.  EXAM CORRECTION: Two corrections for the written: (1) Part 23's full title is 'Airworthiness Standards: Normal, Utility, Acrobatic, AND COMMUTER Category Airplanes' — your notes left COMMUTER off. (2) The 2017 rewrite (Amdt 23-64) replaced the category list with a single 'normal category' performance-based standard, so the strict 12,500-lb line is legacy. Seating is 9 or fewer except commuter (up to 19).

questions.q: Part 25 covers Transport Category Airplanes — generally those weighing:
options: More than 12,500 lb takeoff weight (major airlines)
questions.short: More than 12,500 lb takeoff weight (major airlines)
questions.expl: Correct answer: More than 12,500 lb takeoff weight (major airlines).

questions.q: Airworthiness standards for aircraft ENGINES are in:
questions.expl: Correct answer: Part 33.

questions.q: Airworthiness standards for aircraft PROPELLERS are in:
questions.expl: Correct answer: Part 35.

questions.q: Airworthiness Directives (ADs) are issued under:
questions.expl: Correct answer: Part 39.

questions.q: Part 43 covers:
options: Maintenance, Preventive Maintenance, Rebuilding, and Alteration
questions.short: Maintenance, Preventive Maintenance, Rebuilding, and Alteration
questions.expl: Correct answer: Maintenance, Preventive Maintenance, Rebuilding, and Alteration.

questions.q: In Part 43, which appendix lists Major Alterations, Major Repairs, and Preventive Maintenance?
questions.expl: Correct answer: Appendix A.

questions.q: Which Part 43 appendix covers the Recording of major repairs and major alterations?
questions.expl: Correct answer: Appendix B.

questions.q: Which Part 43 appendix gives the Scope and Detail of items in an Annual and 100-Hour inspection?
questions.expl: Correct answer: Appendix D.

questions.q: The Altimeter System test and inspection requirements are in Part 43:
questions.expl: Correct answer: Appendix E.

questions.q: The ATC Transponder test and inspection requirements are in Part 43:
questions.expl: Correct answer: Appendix F.

questions.q: Part 45 covers:
questions.expl: Correct answer: Identification and Registration Marks ('N#').

questions.q: Part 47 covers Aircraft Registration — which Matthew likens to:
questions.expl: Correct answer: A title.

questions.q: Part 65 covers Certification of Airmen OTHER THAN flight crewmembers. Per his notes, the difference between a Repairman and a Maintenance Technician is:
options: Repairman holds an A&P; the tech does not
Repairman is not A&P-certificated; the maintenance tech holds an A&P
questions.short: Repairman is not A&P-certificated; the maintenance tech holds an A&P
questions.expl: Correct answer: Repairman is not A&P-certificated; the maintenance tech holds an A&P.
questions.cite: 14 CFR Part 65 (Subpart E Repairmen, Subpart D Mechanics)

questions.q: General Operating and Flight Rules — pilots, owners, lessees — are in:
questions.expl: Correct answer: Part 91.

questions.q: Replacement tubing must be of the same size and material as the original tubing. The PRIMARY reasons are:
options: Weight and compatibility with the substance going through the line
questions.expl: Notes: replacement tubing must be same size & material as original because of weight and compatibility of the substance going through the line. FAA: replacement tubing should be of the same size and material as the original.

questions.q: Copper tubing becomes hard and brittle from vibration. To restore it to a soft condition it must be __________.
questions.expl: WORKSHEET Q1. Anneal brass, copper, and aluminum by heating to a dull red and cooling rapidly in cold water. Annealing restores the soft (workable) condition.

questions.q: Which aluminum alloy tubing is used for GENERAL PURPOSE lines of LOW or NEGLIGIBLE fluid pressure (e.g., instrument lines, ventilating conduits)?
questions.expl: Notes: 1100 H14 (1/2 hard) or 3003 H14 (1/2 hard) = general purpose, low/negligible pressures.

questions.q: Which aluminum alloys are used for general-purpose LOW and MEDIUM pressure systems (hydraulic/pneumatic 1,000–1,500 psi, fuel and oil lines)?
questions.expl: Notes & FAA: 2024-T3, 5052-O, and 6061-T6 aluminum alloy = low and medium pressure systems.

questions.q: How is the alloy designation shown on SMALL aluminum tubing (vs. large tubing)?
options: Stamped on the surface (same as large)
By a painted color code (large tubing is stamped)
questions.expl: Notes: large aluminum tubing — designation stamped on tubing; small tubing — designation by color code (band not more than 4" wide, at the ends and midway).

questions.q: CRES stands for:
questions.expl: Notes: CRES = Corrosion Resistant Steel. Use CRES when exposed to the elements / risk of FOD (landing gear, wheel wells).

questions.q: Corrosion-resistant steel (CRES 304, 321, or 304 1/8-hard) is used in HIGH-PRESSURE hydraulic systems of what pressure, for landing gear, flaps, brakes, and fire zones?
questions.expl: Notes & FAA: CRES used in high-pressure hydraulic systems (3,000 psi or more) for landing gear, flaps, brakes, and fire zones. NUMERIC: 3,000 psi.

questions.q: Titanium 3AL-2.5V tubing is used in transport-category/high-performance hydraulic systems at pressures ABOVE what value?
questions.expl: Notes & FAA: titanium used for pressures above 1,500 psi. NUMERIC: 1,500 psi.

questions.q: Compared to steel, titanium 3AL-2.5V is approximately:
questions.expl: Notes & FAA: titanium is 30 percent stronger than steel and 50 percent lighter than steel. NUMERIC: 30% / 50%.

questions.q: Which fittings are used with TITANIUM tubing?
questions.expl: Notes & FAA: Cryofit fittings or swaged fittings are used with titanium tubing.

questions.q: True or False: Titanium tubing and fittings may be used in an oxygen system as long as the system is clean.
questions.short: FALSE — never use titanium in any oxygen system
questions.expl: Notes (!!!) & FAA: DO NOT use titanium tubing or fittings in any oxygen system assembly. Titanium is oxygen-reactive; a freshly formed surface can spontaneously combust in gaseous oxygen even at low pressure.

questions.q: Rigid metal tubing size is determined by its __________ diameter.
questions.expl: WORKSHEET Q2. Metal tubing is sized by outside diameter (OD), measured fractionally in sixteenths (1/16) of an inch. (Wall thickness, in thousandths, is also specified.)

questions.q: To find the INSIDE diameter of rigid tubing, twice the wall thickness is subtracted from the __________ diameter.
questions.expl: WORKSHEET Q3. ID = OD − 2(WT). Notes formulas: ID = OD − 2(WT); OD = ID + 2(WT); TWT = OD − ID; one WT = (OD − ID)/2.

questions.q: CALCULATION: A No. 10 tube (OD = 0.625") has a wall thickness of 0.063". What is its inside diameter?
questions.expl: ID = OD − 2(WT) = 0.625 − 2(0.063) = 0.625 − 0.126 = 0.499". This is the exact example in the handbook.

questions.q: CALCULATION: A tube has OD 0.500" and ID 0.402". What is ONE wall thickness?
questions.expl: One WT = (OD − ID)/2 = (0.500 − 0.402)/2 = 0.098/2 = 0.049". (Total wall thickness TWT = OD − ID = 0.098".)

questions.q: Outside-diameter tube sizes are given in increments of:
questions.expl: Notes & FAA: OD sizes are in 1/16" increments — e.g., No. 6 = 6/16" (3/8"), No. 8 = 8/16" (1/2"). (Wall thickness is printed in thousandths.)

questions.q: When cutting SOFT tubing, the preferred tool is the roll (wheel) cutter. If a hacksaw is used instead, how many teeth per inch are preferred?
questions.expl: Notes: roll cutter best for soft material; fine-tooth hacksaw OK, prefer 24–32 teeth per inch. FAA specifies preferably 32 teeth per inch. A saw reduces work-hardening of the tube.

questions.q: A new piece of replacement tubing should be cut about how much LONGER than the tube being replaced, to allow for bending variations?
questions.expl: Notes & FAA: cut a new piece approximately 10 percent longer than the tube to be replaced to provide for minor variations in bending. NUMERIC: 10%.

questions.q: When cutting and deburring tubing, the burr should be removed toward the __________, and the objective is a square end free of burrs.
questions.expl: Notes: always burr toward the open end; objective is a square end free from burrs. Deburr carefully so the wall thickness at the end is not reduced (prevents defective flares).

questions.q: All runs of rigid tubing must have at least how many bend(s) between the fittings, to absorb strain / vibration and allow for expansion?
questions.expl: WORKSHEET Q13 & notes. Never select a straight path: bends are necessary to absorb strain and vibration and to allow expansion/contraction with temperature. At least ONE bend between fittings.

questions.q: Tubing UNDER what diameter can usually be bent by hand without a bending tool?
questions.expl: Notes & FAA: tubing under 1/4" in diameter usually can be bent without a bending tool. NUMERIC: 1/4".

questions.q: A small amount of flattening in a bend is acceptable, but the small (flattened) diameter must NOT be less than what percent of the original OD?
questions.expl: Notes & FAA: the small diameter of the flattened portion must not be less than 75% of the original outside diameter — i.e., flattening of not more than 25%. NUMERIC: 75% / 25%.

questions.q: How many basic tube END FINISHES are there?
options: Four: single flare, double flare, flareless, beading
Three: single flare, double flare, beading
questions.short: Four: single flare, double flare, flareless, beading
questions.expl: Notes: 4 end finishes — single flare, double flare, flareless, beading. Double flares are more resistant to damage.

questions.q: True or False: A double flare is more resistant to damage (shearing/torque) than a single flare.
questions.expl: Notes & FAA: a double flare is smoother and more concentric, seals better, and is more resistant to the shearing effect of torque. Used on soft aluminum tubing 3/8" OD and under.

questions.q: What is the flare cone angle for AVIATION fittings?
questions.expl: WORKSHEET Q4 & notes. Aircraft flaring dies are ground to 35°–37° (commonly stated/labeled 37°). EXAM TRAP: the automotive flaring tool makes a 45° flare and is NEVER permitted on aircraft tubing.

questions.q: Match the flare standard to its angle. Which is CORRECT (per the class notes)?
questions.expl: Notes flare-angle table: AN = 37°, AC (Air Corps) = 35°, MS = 0° (flareless — no flare), AUTO = 45°. Only 'AC = 35°' is correct as written.

questions.q: An AN FLARED fitting is made up of which two parts?
questions.expl: Notes & FAA: a flared (AN) tube fitting consists of a sleeve and a nut (AN819 sleeve + AN818 nut). The nut draws the flare against the male cone to seal.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The flare and the heel of a bend must be free from cracks, dents, nicks, scratches, or any other __________.
questions.expl: Notes & FAA: the flare and tubing must be free from cracks, dents, nicks, scratches, or any other defects. Any crack or deformity in a flare is cause for rejection.

questions.q: Although flareless fittings eliminate flaring the tube, another operation referred to as __________ is necessary prior to installing a NEW flareless tube assembly.
questions.expl: WORKSHEET Q5 & notes. The correct term is PRESETTING, not swaging. 'Another operation, referred to as presetting, is necessary prior to installation of a new flareless tube assembly.' Presetting forms a tight seal between sleeve and tube without damaging the connector. ⚑ Don't confuse with swaging (a permanent fitting process).

questions.q: An MS FLARELESS fitting consists of which three parts?
questions.expl: WORKSHEET Q19-related & notes. MS flareless fitting = body, sleeve, nut. The body's internal design causes the sleeve to cut into the tube OD when body and nut are joined. Designed for 3,000 psi systems with severe vibration.

questions.q: MS (flareless) fittings are usually tightened by:
questions.expl: Notes: MS fittings usually tightened by number of turns. FAA flareless install: run the nut down, then at first bottoming turn 1/6 turn (one flat); never beyond 1/3 turn (two flats). AN flared fittings, by contrast, use specific torque values.

questions.q: Which wire material is used with MS (flareless) fittings?
questions.expl: Notes: CRES wire is used with MS, known as flareless. Swaged or MS flareless fittings are used with corrosion-resistant tubing.

questions.q: AN fittings usually have a specific __________ value (unlike MS flareless, which use turns).
questions.expl: Notes: AN fittings usually have a specific torque value. See Figure 9-20 flared-fitting torque table. Always use a torque wrench to avoid over/under-tightening.

questions.q: What COLOR DYE identifies STEEL fittings of AN or MS design?
questions.expl: WORKSHEET Q12 & notes. AN steel fittings = BLACK; AN aluminum fittings = BLUE. EXAM TRAP: steel = black, aluminum = blue.

questions.q: Per the class color-code table, ALUMINUM ALLOY tube fittings are colored:
questions.expl: Notes color-code table: Aluminum Alloy = BLUE, Carbon Steel = BLACK, CRES = NATURAL, Aluminum Bronze = CADMIUM plate, Titanium = GREY. ⚑ FAA handbook explicitly names black (steel), blue (aluminum), and cadmium/natural (aluminum bronze); the CRES=natural / titanium=grey rows are AIM-deck additions — use the AIM table for the worksheet.

questions.q: Per the class color-code table, ALUMINUM BRONZE fittings are:
questions.expl: Notes: Aluminum Bronze = CADMIUM plate. FAA: aluminum bronze fittings are cadmium plated and natural in appearance.

questions.q: Per the class color-code table, TITANIUM fittings are:
questions.expl: Notes color-code table: Titanium = GREY. (AIM-deck value; FAA handbook does not list a titanium fitting color explicitly — use the AIM table on the worksheet.)

questions.q: True or False: You may apply thread/sealing compound to the FACES of the fitting or the flare to improve the seal.
questions.expl: Notes & FAA: NEVER apply compound to the faces of the fitting or the flare — it destroys the metal-to-metal contact needed to produce the seal and creates a bad seal.

questions.q: CAUTION: If an ALUMINUM-ALLOY FLARED tube assembly still leaks after being tightened to the required torque, you should:
options: Keep tightening past torque until it stops
Apply sealant to the flare faces
Disassemble it for repair or replacement (do NOT overtighten)
questions.expl: Notes CAUTION & FAA: do not pull the joint tight with torque. If a flared aluminum-alloy assembly leaks after correct torque, disassemble for repair or replacement. Overtightening cuts off the flare or ruins the sleeve/nut.

questions.q: If a FLARELESS tube assembly leaks after being torqued, by how much may the nut be further tightened?
options: Up to a full additional turn
It may never be tightened further
Up to 1/6 turn beyond the noted torque (max total 1/3 turn)
questions.short: Up to 1/6 turn more (1/3 turn max total)
questions.expl: Notes & FAA: if a flareless connection leaks, it may be tightened an additional 1/6 turn (total of 1/3 turn). Never beyond 1/3 turn (two flats) — that is the max without permanently damaging the sleeve and nut.

questions.q: Are SWAGED (Permaswage) fittings reusable?
options: No — they are permanent (remove by cutting the tube)
questions.expl: WORKSHEET Q11 & notes. Swaged fittings create a PERMANENT, virtually maintenance-free connection. If they must be disconnected, cut the tubing with a tube cutter. Therefore swaged fittings are NOT reusable.

questions.q: A popular repair system for connecting/repairing hydraulic lines on transport-category aircraft uses permanent (Permaswage) fittings because they create a connection that is:
questions.expl: Notes & FAA: Permaswage permanent fittings create a permanent connection that is virtually maintenance-free; used where routine disconnections are not required; often used with titanium and CRES tubing.

questions.q: Permanent (swaged) fittings are installed with:
options: Portable hydraulically-powered tooling (compact for tight spaces)
questions.expl: Notes & FAA: permanent fittings are installed with portable hydraulically-powered tooling, compact enough to be used in tight spaces.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Cryofit fittings are standard fittings with a __________ sleeve.
questions.expl: Notes & FAA: Cryofit fittings are standard fittings with a cryogenic sleeve made of shape-memory alloy (Tinel). Made 3% small, frozen in liquid nitrogen and expanded 5% larger, then it contracts onto the tube during a 10–15 second warm-up. Removed only by cutting the tube.

questions.q: Scratches or nicks in ALUMINUM-ALLOY tubing may be repaired by burnishing if they are no deeper than what percent of the wall thickness (and not in the heel of a bend)?
questions.expl: WORKSHEET Q16 & notes. Scratches/nicks not deeper than 10% of the wall thickness in aluminum-alloy tubing, not in the heel of a bend, may be repaired by burnishing with hand tools. NUMERIC: 10%.

questions.q: A DENT in a tube is acceptable if it is LESS than what percent of the tube/line diameter (and not in the heel of a bend)?
questions.expl: WORKSHEET Q17 & notes. A dent of less than 20% of the tube diameter is not objectionable unless it is in the heel of a (short-radius) bend. NUMERIC: 20%. ⚑ Don't confuse with the 10% scratch/nick limit.

questions.q: How are dents removed from soft tubing?
options: Draw/push a 'bullet' (ball or slug) through the tube
questions.expl: FAA: remove dents by drawing a bullet (ball bearing/slug) through the tube with a cable, or pushing it through with a dowel. For soft aluminum, a hardwood slug may be used.

questions.q: Lines carrying physically dangerous materials such as OXYGEN, NITROGEN, or FREON may be marked:
questions.expl: WORKSHEET Q15 & notes. Physically dangerous materials (oxygen, nitrogen, Freon) = PHDAN. Compare: fuel = FLAM, toxic materials = TOXIC.

questions.q: A line marked FLAM indicates the line carries:
questions.expl: Notes & FAA: if you see a line marked FLAM there is fuel in that line. Toxic = TOXIC; physically dangerous = PHDAN.

questions.q: Per the notes, FUEL lines are identified by which color and geometric symbol?
questions.expl: Notes line-ID code: Fuel = RED, symbol STAR.

questions.q: Per the notes, HYDRAULIC lines are identified by which color and symbol?
questions.expl: Notes line-ID code: Hydraulics = BLUE & YELLOW, symbol CIRCLE.

questions.q: Per the notes, OXYGEN lines are identified by which color and symbol?
questions.expl: Notes line-ID code: Oxygen = GREEN, symbol RECTANGLE.

questions.q: Per the notes, FIRE PROTECTION lines (rigid lines) are identified by which color and symbol?
questions.expl: Notes line-ID code: Fire Protection (rigid lines) = BROWN, symbol DIAMOND.

questions.q: Where are tapes/decals identifying a fluid line normally placed?
options: On both ends and at least once in each compartment the line runs through
questions.expl: FAA: tapes and decals are placed on both ends of a line and at least once in each compartment, plus adjacent to each valve, regulator, filter, or accessory. Manufacturer installs originally; the mechanic replaces them.

questions.q: Deep, permanent impressions in a hose caused by over-tightened hose clamps (or supports) are known as:
questions.expl: WORKSHEET Q6 & FAA. 'Cold flow' describes the deep, permanent impressions in a hose produced by the pressure of hose clamps or supports. It is a sign of deterioration / reason for replacement.

questions.q: Which flexible hose liner is compatible with PHOSPHATE ESTER based hydraulic fluid (Skydrol)?
questions.expl: WORKSHEET Q7 & FAA. Butyl is excellent with phosphate ester (Skydrol) but must NOT be used with petroleum. Buna-N and Neoprene are the opposite — good for petroleum, NOT for Skydrol. (Teflon is also Skydrol-compatible.) ⚑ Your relayed note said 'Teflon for Skydrol' — Butyl is the rubber-liner answer the worksheet pairs with Skydrol.

questions.q: Which flexible hose liner is compatible with NEARLY EVERY liquid/substance used in aircraft?
questions.expl: WORKSHEET Q8 & FAA. Teflon (tetrafluoroethylene) 'is compatible with nearly every substance or agent used,' range −65°F to +450°F, practically unlimited shelf life. ⚑ CORRECTION: your relayed note said 'Buna-N/Butyl' for nearly every liquid — that is WRONG. Buna-N is petroleum-only and must NOT touch Skydrol. The universal liner is TEFLON.

questions.q: Buna-N and Neoprene hose liners have good resistance to petroleum products but must NOT be used with:
questions.expl: FAA: Buna-N has excellent resistance to petroleum products; do not use for phosphate ester (Skydrol). Neoprene is similar (better abrasion resistance, slightly less petroleum resistance); also not for Skydrol.

questions.q: Teflon hose has what broad operating TEMPERATURE range?
questions.expl: FAA: Teflon operating range is −65°F to +450°F. NUMERIC.

questions.q: The stripe running the length of a flexible hose that contains identifying information is called the __________ line.
questions.expl: WORKSHEET Q9 & FAA. The lay line indicates the natural lay (no twist) of the hose and carries the identification markings. A twisted lay line means the hose was installed with a twist (a defect).

questions.q: A MEDIUM-pressure flexible hose has what kind of outer cover (vs. the fabric-braid cover of low-pressure hose)?
questions.expl: WORKSHEET Q10. Medium-pressure rubber hose has ONE wire-braid reinforcement and a smooth (non-cloth) rubber outer cover; low-pressure hose has a fabric-braid (rough/cloth) cover. ⚑ Confirm the exact word your slide uses if it differs.

questions.q: LOW-pressure flexible hose is rated below what pressure, with fabric-braid reinforcement?
questions.expl: FAA: low pressure = below 250 psi (fabric braid). Medium = up to 3,000 psi (one wire braid; larger sizes up to 1,500 psi). High = all sizes up to 3,000 psi operating.

questions.q: Flexible fluid lines must have between what two percentages of SLACK between fittings?
questions.expl: WORKSHEET Q14. The FAA handbook does not give a number here; AC 43.13-1B Par 9-30 states the hose length should provide about 5 to 8 percent slack. A hose stretched tight will overstress and fail. NUMERIC: 5–8%.

questions.q: True or False: REUSABLE end fittings for flexible hose normally have THREE pieces.
questions.expl: WORKSHEET Q19. Reusable (detachable) MS-type hose end fittings are normally TWO pieces — a socket and a nipple. (Three pieces — body, sleeve, nut — describes the MS FLARELESS rigid-tube fitting, not the hose end fitting.) ⚑ If your slide deck calls flareless the '3-piece reusable' answer, flag it.

questions.q: When a flexible hose with SWAGED (factory) end fittings fails, what must be done?
questions.expl: FAA: when failure occurs in a hose with swaged end fittings, the entire assembly must be replaced. Hose with reusable end fittings can be re-fabricated using new hose.

questions.q: The proof-pressure test medium for all tube assemblies EXCEPT oxygen should be:
options: A liquid medium such as hydraulic fluid, water, or oil
questions.short: Liquid: hydraulic fluid, water, or oil
questions.expl: Notes: proof-pressure testing of all tube assemblies (except oxygen) uses a liquid medium such as hydraulic fluid, water, or oil. Air/instrument lines may be tested with dry oil-free air or nitrogen; gas tests are done underwater.

questions.q: OXYGEN tubing must be proof-tested using:
questions.expl: Notes: oxygen tubing should be tested using DRY NITROGEN only. (Oxygen reacts with petroleum/oil — never use oil-based media or petroleum lubricants on oxygen systems.)

questions.q: A repaired/overhauled flexible hose should be tested to at least how many times system pressure before installation?
questions.expl: FAA: when a flexible hose is repaired/overhauled with existing hardware and new hose, test it to at least 1.5 times system pressure before installing. NUMERIC: 1.5×.

questions.q: True or False: The workability, resistance to corrosion, and light weight of aluminum are major factors in its adoption for aircraft plumbing.
questions.expl: WORKSHEET Q18. Aluminum alloy tubing is widely used for low/medium-pressure fuel, oil, hydraulic, and pneumatic lines precisely because of its workability, corrosion resistance, and light weight.

questions.q: Rigid tube is / is NOT limited to use only in areas where a long straight run is possible. Which is correct?
options: It may only be used in the cabin
It IS limited to long straight runs only
It may only be used on the engine
It is NOT limited to long straight runs
questions.expl: WORKSHEET Q20. Rigid tubing is USED where long, relatively straight runs are possible, but it is NOT LIMITED to only those areas — it is bent and routed throughout, and must have at least one bend between fittings. ⚑ If your slide framed it as 'rigid tube IS used where straight runs are possible,' the intended word may flip to 'is' — read the slide wording.

questions.q: AN flared and MS flareless fittings are NOT interchangeable. How do you tell them apart by sight?
options: AN has a straight end; MS has a cone
AN has a cone at the end; MS flareless has a straight end
AN is grey; MS is blue
questions.short: AN = cone end; MS flareless = straight end
questions.expl: FAA: AN flared fittings have a cone at the end (matches the tube flare); MS flareless fittings have a straight end. They are different and not interchangeable.

questions.q: How long is a temporary airman's certificate good for?
questions.expl: Worksheet answer: Not more than 120 days.  —  A certificate and ratings effective for a period of NOT MORE THAN 120 DAYS may be issued to a qualified applicant, pending review of the application and the issue of the permanent certificate.

questions.q: What is the duration of an A&P (mechanic) certificate?
options: No expiration — effective until surrendered, suspended, or revoked
It is good for 120 days, then must be renewed
It expires on March 31 of each odd-numbered year
questions.short: Effective until surrendered, suspended, or revoked
questions.expl: Worksheet answer: No expiration — effective until surrendered, suspended, or revoked.  —  Except for repairman certificates issued under §65.101, a certificate or rating issued under Part 65 is EFFECTIVE UNTIL IT IS SURRENDERED, SUSPENDED, OR REVOKED. An A&P (mechanic) certificate therefore has no expiration date.

questions.q: How many days do you have to notify the FAA of a change in your permanent mailing address?
questions.expl: Worksheet answer: 30 days.  —  Within 30 DAYS after any change in his permanent mailing address, the holder of a certificate issued under Part 65 must notify the FAA Airman Certification Branch, in writing, of his new address.

questions.q: May an A&P mechanic return to service work which he/she has NEVER done before, under supervision?
options: Yes — any other A&P may supervise, experience is not required
Yes — under the DIRECT SUPERVISION of a certificated, appropriately rated mechanic (or repairman) who has experience in that specific operation
No — he may never return to service unfamiliar work under any circumstances
Yes — but only after the FAA tests him on it first
questions.short: Yes — under direct supervision of someone experienced in that operation
questions.expl: Worksheet answer: Yes — under the DIRECT SUPERVISION of a certificated, appropriately rated mechanic (or certificated repairman) who has had previous experience in that specific operation.  —  A mechanic may NOT supervise the maintenance, preventive maintenance, or alteration of, or approve and return to service, any aircraft or appliance for which he is rated UNLESS he has satisfactorily performed the work concerned at an earlier date. If he has NOT done it before, he may show the ability to do it by performing it to the satisfaction of the Administrator OR under the DIRECT SUPERVISION of a certificated and appropriately rated mechanic (or certificated repairman) who HAS had previous experience in the specific operation concerned.  ⚑ Nuance: 'under supervision' is the key. He CANNOT return it to service solo if he's never done it; he can do/return it under the direct supervision of someone experienced in that exact operation. Strictly, the supervisor's prior experience is what makes the RTS valid.

questions.q: How many months out of each 24 months must a mechanic exercise the privileges of his/her rating to maintain currency?
questions.expl: Worksheet answer: 6 months (within the preceding 24 months).  —  A certificated mechanic may not exercise the privileges of his certificate and rating unless, within the PRECEDING 24 MONTHS, the Administrator has found him able to do that work, OR he has, FOR AT LEAST 6 MONTHS, served as a mechanic under his certificate and rating, technically supervised other mechanics, supervised maintenance/alteration in an executive capacity, or any combination of these.

questions.q: May an 'A' (airframe) rated mechanic perform the 100-hour inspection of an AIRFRAME?
options: No — only an IA may perform a 100-hour inspection
No — he needs both A and P ratings
Yes — and approve the airframe for return to service
Only if a powerplant mechanic supervises him
questions.short: Yes — and approve the airframe for return to service
questions.expl: Worksheet answer: Yes.  —  A certificated mechanic with an AIRFRAME rating may perform the 100-hour inspection required by Part 91 on an AIRFRAME, or any related part or appliance, and approve and return it to service.

questions.q: May a 'P' (powerplant) rated mechanic perform the 100-hour inspection of a POWERPLANT?
options: No — only an IA can inspect a powerplant
Yes — and approve the powerplant for return to service
No — only an A&P with both ratings can
questions.short: Yes — and approve the powerplant for return to service
questions.expl: Worksheet answer: Yes to BOTH — a 'P' mechanic may perform the 100-hour inspection of a powerplant AND of a propeller.  —  A certificated mechanic with a POWERPLANT rating may perform the 100-hour inspection required by Part 91 on a POWERPLANT OR PROPELLER, or any part thereof, and approve and return it to service. The propeller falls under the powerplant rating, NOT the airframe rating.  ⚑ Exam trap: the propeller goes with the POWERPLANT (P) rating, not the airframe (A) rating. §65.87 names 'a powerplant OR propeller.' Many students wrongly put the prop under 'A'.

questions.q: Follow-up to the previous question: a PROPELLER 100-hour inspection falls under which rating?
options: Neither — only an IA may inspect a propeller
It requires a separate propeller rating
questions.expl: Worksheet answer: Yes to BOTH — a 'P' mechanic may perform the 100-hour inspection of a powerplant AND of a propeller.  —  A certificated mechanic with a POWERPLANT rating may perform the 100-hour inspection required by Part 91 on a POWERPLANT OR PROPELLER, or any part thereof, and approve and return it to service. The propeller falls under the powerplant rating, NOT the airframe rating.  ⚑ Exam trap: the propeller goes with the POWERPLANT (P) rating, not the airframe (A) rating. §65.87 names 'a powerplant OR propeller.' Many students wrongly put the prop under 'A'.  §65.87 names 'a powerplant OR propeller' — so a P mechanic CAN do the 100-hour inspection of a propeller. The propeller does NOT go with the airframe rating.

questions.q: Must an A&P mechanic have his certificate available while exercising the privileges of his rating?
options: Yes — he must keep it within the immediate area where he works and present it on request
No — it stays filed with the FAA
No — only when applying for an IA
Yes — but only a photocopy is required
questions.short: Yes — keep it within the immediate work area and present it on request
questions.expl: Worksheet answer: Yes — he must keep it within the immediate area where he normally exercises the privileges, and present it on request.  —  Each person who holds a mechanic certificate must KEEP IT WITHIN THE IMMEDIATE AREA where he normally exercises the privileges of the certificate and must present it for inspection upon the request of the Administrator, an authorized NTSB representative, or any Federal, State, or local law enforcement officer.  ⚑ Wording trap: the reg says 'keep it within the immediate area' / 'display,' NOT 'carry it on his person.' Available in the work area is the standard.

questions.q: Could an 'A' rated mechanic perform the airframe 100-hour inspection WHILE a 'P' rated mechanic performed the powerplant 100-hour inspection on the same aircraft?
options: No — only an A&P holding both ratings may sign any part of it
Only if both also hold an Inspection Authorization
Yes — each works within his own rating and approves only his portion
No — one person must do the entire 100-hour inspection
questions.short: Yes — each works within his own rating
questions.expl: Worksheet answer: Yes — each works within his own rating.  —  Yes. An AIRFRAME-rated mechanic may do the 100-hour inspection of the AIRFRAME (§65.85) and a separate POWERPLANT-rated mechanic may do the 100-hour inspection of the POWERPLANT/PROPELLER (§65.87) on the SAME aircraft at the same time. Each may approve and return to service only the portion covered by his own rating; together they complete the full 100-hour inspection.  ⚑ This is why an 'A&P' (both ratings) can sign off the whole 100-hour alone — but two single-rated mechanics splitting it is equally legal, each within his rating.

questions.q: How many years must one hold an A&P certificate (both ratings, currently effective) to be eligible for the Inspection Authorization?
questions.expl: Worksheet answer: 3 years.  —  To be eligible for an Inspection Authorization, the applicant must HOLD A CURRENTLY EFFECTIVE MECHANIC CERTIFICATE WITH BOTH AN AIRFRAME AND A POWERPLANT RATING, each of which has been in effect for a total of AT LEAST 3 YEARS.

questions.q: How many years of actual work experience (actively engaged in maintaining aircraft) are necessary to be eligible for the Inspection Authorization?
questions.expl: Worksheet answer: 2 years.  —  The applicant must have been ACTIVELY ENGAGED, for AT LEAST THE 2-YEAR PERIOD before the date he applies, in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained in accordance with 14 CFR.

questions.q: When does the Inspection Authorization expire (current 14 CFR)?
questions.expl: Worksheet answer: March 31 of each odd-numbered year.  —  Each Inspection Authorization EXPIRES ON MARCH 31 OF EACH ODD-NUMBERED YEAR. The holder may exercise its privileges only while he holds a currently effective mechanic certificate with both a currently effective airframe AND powerplant rating.  ⚑ AIM DIVERGENCE FLAG: Current 14 CFR §65.92(a) = 'March 31 of each ODD-NUMBERED YEAR' (a 2-year cycle since the 2007 rule change). Older AIM slides/textbooks sometimes still say 'March 31 of EACH YEAR' (the pre-2007 1-year cycle). If your instructor's slide says 'March 31 each year,' write that on the worksheet; the FAA written exam answer is 'March 31 of each odd-numbered year.' [confirm which wording your instructor wants]

questions.q: To RENEW the IA via annual inspections, how many annual inspections must the I.A. have performed?
options: At least one for each 90 days held (8 over the 2-year period)
At least one for each 30 days held
questions.short: One annual inspection for each 90 days held (= 8 over 2 years)
questions.expl: Worksheet answer: At least one annual inspection for each 90 days he held the authority (= 8 annual inspections over the 2-year period).  —  To RENEW, one renewal option is that the applicant has PERFORMED AT LEAST ONE ANNUAL INSPECTION FOR EACH 90 DAYS that he held the current authority. Over a full 24-month authorization that works out to 8 annual inspections. (Renewal may alternatively be met by 2 major repairs/alterations per 90 days, performing/supervising one progressive inspection, an 8-hour refresher course, or passing an oral test.)  ⚑ Watch the wording: the reg states it as a RATE — 'one annual inspection for each 90 days.' The '8' is the 2-year total. AIM may ask either the rate or the total.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the four additional privileges of the Inspection Authorization (§65.95)?
options: Inspect & approve for return to service after a MAJOR ALTERATION
Inspect & approve for return to service after a MAJOR REPAIR
Perform an ANNUAL inspection and approve for return to service
Issue a brand-new airworthiness certificate to a homebuilt aircraft
questions.short: Issuing a new airworthiness certificate is NOT an IA privilege
questions.expl: Worksheet answer: The IA may: (1) inspect & approve for return to service after a MAJOR REPAIR; (2) inspect & approve for return to service after a MAJOR ALTERATION (both per FAA-approved data, on FAA Form 337); (3) perform an ANNUAL inspection and approve for return to service; (4) perform or supervise a PROGRESSIVE inspection.  —  Per §65.95(a), the holder of an Inspection Authorization may — (1) INSPECT AND APPROVE FOR RETURN TO SERVICE any aircraft or related part/appliance after a MAJOR REPAIR, if done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator; (2) INSPECT AND APPROVE FOR RETURN TO SERVICE after a MAJOR ALTERATION, again per FAA-approved data (documented on FAA Form 337); (3) PERFORM AN ANNUAL INSPECTION and approve for return to service; and (4) PERFORM OR SUPERVISE A PROGRESSIVE INSPECTION per §§43.13 and 43.15. (Limitation: NOT aircraft maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program.)  ⚑ Note on counting to FOUR: the CFR lists §65.95(a)(1) (return to service after major repair OR major alteration) and §65.95(a)(2) (annual / progressive inspection) — literally TWO numbered items. AIM teaches it as FOUR by splitting (a)(1) into 'major repair' + 'major alteration' and (a)(2) into 'annual' + 'progressive.' That 4-part split is the worksheet's expected answer; just know the CFR groups them as 2 numbered paragraphs.  The four IA privileges are: major repair RTS, major alteration RTS, annual inspection, and perform/supervise progressive inspection.

questions.q: Besides approving major repairs/alterations and performing annual inspections, the fourth IA privilege is to perform or supervise a ___ inspection.
questions.expl: Worksheet answer: The IA may: (1) inspect & approve for return to service after a MAJOR REPAIR; (2) inspect & approve for return to service after a MAJOR ALTERATION (both per FAA-approved data, on FAA Form 337); (3) perform an ANNUAL inspection and approve for return to service; (4) perform or supervise a PROGRESSIVE inspection.  —  Per §65.95(a), the holder of an Inspection Authorization may — (1) INSPECT AND APPROVE FOR RETURN TO SERVICE any aircraft or related part/appliance after a MAJOR REPAIR, if done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator; (2) INSPECT AND APPROVE FOR RETURN TO SERVICE after a MAJOR ALTERATION, again per FAA-approved data (documented on FAA Form 337); (3) PERFORM AN ANNUAL INSPECTION and approve for return to service; and (4) PERFORM OR SUPERVISE A PROGRESSIVE INSPECTION per §§43.13 and 43.15. (Limitation: NOT aircraft maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program.)  ⚑ Note on counting to FOUR: the CFR lists §65.95(a)(1) (return to service after major repair OR major alteration) and §65.95(a)(2) (annual / progressive inspection) — literally TWO numbered items. AIM teaches it as FOUR by splitting (a)(1) into 'major repair' + 'major alteration' and (a)(2) into 'annual' + 'progressive.' That 4-part split is the worksheet's expected answer; just know the CFR groups them as 2 numbered paragraphs.  §65.95(a)(2): the IA may perform or supervise a PROGRESSIVE inspection per §§43.13 and 43.15.

questions.q: Who is responsible for determining whether an aircraft is in condition for safe flight?
options: The certificated mechanic who last signed it off
questions.expl: Worksheet answer: The PILOT IN COMMAND (PIC).  —  §91.7(b): 'The pilot in command of a civil aircraft is responsible for determining whether that aircraft is in condition for safe flight.' The PIC must discontinue the flight when unairworthy conditions occur. (Distinct from §91.3, which makes the PIC the final authority for the OPERATION of the flight.)  ⚑ Don't confuse the two: §91.7(b) = PIC determines CONDITION FOR SAFE FLIGHT. §91.3(a) = PIC is the FINAL AUTHORITY as to the OPERATION of the aircraft. This question is §91.7(b).

questions.q: Who is PRIMARILY responsible for maintaining an aircraft in airworthy condition (including AD compliance)?
questions.expl: Worksheet answer: The OWNER or OPERATOR.  —  §91.403(a): 'The owner or operator of an aircraft is PRIMARILY RESPONSIBLE for maintaining that aircraft in an airworthy condition, including compliance with part 39 of this chapter' (Airworthiness Directives).

questions.q: Who is responsible for seeing that maintenance/return-to-service entries are properly recorded in the aircraft records?
questions.expl: Worksheet answer: The OWNER or OPERATOR.  —  §91.405(b): the owner or operator 'shall ensure that maintenance personnel make appropriate entries in the aircraft maintenance records indicating the aircraft has been approved for return to service.' (The mechanic actually writes the entry per §43.9/§43.11 — but the OWNER/OPERATOR is responsible for SEEING THAT it gets done.)

questions.q: Who is responsible to see that all Airworthiness Directives (Part 39) are accomplished?
options: The FAA Flight Standards District Office
questions.expl: Worksheet answer: The OWNER or OPERATOR.  —  §91.403(a): the owner/operator is primarily responsible for maintaining the aircraft in airworthy condition, 'INCLUDING COMPLIANCE WITH PART 39 OF THIS CHAPTER' — Part 39 is the Airworthiness Directives part. AD compliance status is then recorded in the maintenance records per §91.417(a)(2)(v).  ⚑ AD authority lives in Part 39; the OWNER/OPERATOR responsibility to comply is §91.403(a); the recordkeeping (current AD status) is §91.417(a)(2)(v). If the worksheet wants the records cite, use §91.417; for 'who is responsible,' the answer is §91.403(a).

questions.q: What is the title of 14 CFR Part 91?
options: Maintenance, Preventive Maintenance, Rebuilding, and Alteration
Certification: Airmen Other Than Flight Crewmembers
questions.expl: Worksheet answer: "General Operating and Flight Rules."  —  14 CFR Part 91 is titled 'GENERAL OPERATING AND FLIGHT RULES.' It governs the operation of aircraft within the United States and contains the airworthiness and inspection responsibilities (Subpart E, §§91.401-91.419).

questions.q: The Airworthiness Limitations section requires an aft pressure bulkhead inspection at 5000 hours TIS. Excluding a special flight permit, may the aircraft be operated PAST 5000 hours without that inspection?
options: Only if a 100-hour inspection is current
Yes — up to 10 additional hours are allowed
No — Airworthiness Limitations are mandatory; it may not be operated past the interval
Yes — Airworthiness Limitations are only recommendations
questions.expl: Worksheet answer: NO — it is NOT legal.  —  §91.403(c): 'No person may operate an aircraft for which a manufacturer's maintenance manual or instructions for continued airworthiness has been issued that contains an AIRWORTHINESS LIMITATIONS SECTION unless the mandatory replacement times, INSPECTION INTERVALS, and related procedures specified in that section ... have been complied with.' Airworthiness Limitations are MANDATORY. So once the 5000-hour inspection comes due, you may not operate past it without doing the inspection (a special flight permit / ferry permit under §21.197 would be the only exception, which the question excludes).  ⚑ Exam trap: Airworthiness Limitations are MANDATORY (not advisory). The only way to legally fly past a due Airworthiness Limitation without doing it is a special flight permit (§21.197) — and the question excludes that, so the answer is a flat NO.

questions.q: Who is responsible to see that all required inspections are accomplished?
questions.expl: Worksheet answer: The OWNER or OPERATOR.  —  §91.403(a) makes the owner/operator primarily responsible for airworthiness, and §91.405(a) states the owner/operator 'shall have that aircraft inspected as prescribed in subpart E of this part' (annual, 100-hour, etc.). So the OWNER/OPERATOR is responsible for seeing that required inspections get done.  ⚑ Either §91.403(a) (primary responsibility) or §91.405(a) (shall have the aircraft inspected) is defensible. AIM typically wants §91.405(a) for the 'inspections' question. Write §91.405(a).

questions.q: An outboard wing section is replaced after damage. How is this work classified, and what data must be used?
options: Preventive maintenance — no special data required
A minor repair — any acceptable data may be used
An alteration — only the pilot may approve it
A major repair — it must be performed using FAA-APPROVED data
questions.short: A major repair — performed using FAA-approved data
questions.expl: Worksheet answer: It is a MAJOR REPAIR: it must be performed using FAA-APPROVED DATA, recorded on FAA Form 337, a maintenance-record entry made, and APPROVED FOR RETURN TO SERVICE by an appropriately rated person (an IA for the inspection/RTS of a major repair). If flight characteristics may have changed, an operational check flight is also required.  —  §91.407 requires that, before operating after maintenance, the aircraft has (a)(1) been APPROVED FOR RETURN TO SERVICE by a person authorized under §43.7, and (a)(2) the maintenance record entry required by §43.9 or §43.11 has been made. A wing-structure replacement after damage is a MAJOR REPAIR (Part 43 Appendix A) — so it must use APPROVED DATA, be documented on FAA FORM 337 (§43.9, §43.5), and be inspected/approved for RTS by an IA (§65.95(a)(1)). Per §91.407(b), if the work 'may have appreciably changed its flight characteristics,' an appropriately rated pilot must make an operational check flight and log it before carrying passengers.  ⚑ This blends Part 91 + Part 43 + Part 65. The Part 91 cite the worksheet wants is §91.407 (operation after maintenance). The supporting facts: major repair → approved data + Form 337 (§43.9/§43.5), IA return to service (§65.95(a)(1)), possible op-check flight (§91.407(b)).

questions.q: Follow-up: after that major wing repair, what is required before the aircraft is returned to service?
options: Nothing — replacing a wing is not recorded
Only a logbook entry by the pilot
A new airworthiness certificate from the FAA
An FAA Form 337 + maintenance record entry, approved for return to service by an appropriately rated person (IA) — and an operational check flight if flight characteristics may have changed
questions.short: Form 337 + record entry + IA return to service (op-check flight if needed)
questions.expl: Worksheet answer: It is a MAJOR REPAIR: it must be performed using FAA-APPROVED DATA, recorded on FAA Form 337, a maintenance-record entry made, and APPROVED FOR RETURN TO SERVICE by an appropriately rated person (an IA for the inspection/RTS of a major repair). If flight characteristics may have changed, an operational check flight is also required.  —  §91.407 requires that, before operating after maintenance, the aircraft has (a)(1) been APPROVED FOR RETURN TO SERVICE by a person authorized under §43.7, and (a)(2) the maintenance record entry required by §43.9 or §43.11 has been made. A wing-structure replacement after damage is a MAJOR REPAIR (Part 43 Appendix A) — so it must use APPROVED DATA, be documented on FAA FORM 337 (§43.9, §43.5), and be inspected/approved for RTS by an IA (§65.95(a)(1)). Per §91.407(b), if the work 'may have appreciably changed its flight characteristics,' an appropriately rated pilot must make an operational check flight and log it before carrying passengers.  ⚑ This blends Part 91 + Part 43 + Part 65. The Part 91 cite the worksheet wants is §91.407 (operation after maintenance). The supporting facts: major repair → approved data + Form 337 (§43.9/§43.5), IA return to service (§65.95(a)(1)), possible op-check flight (§91.407(b)).  §91.407(a): approved for RTS (§43.7) + the §43.9/§43.11 record entry. Major repair = Form 337 (§43.9). §91.407(b): op-check flight by an appropriately rated pilot if flight characteristics may have changed.

questions.q: A privately operated aircraft (under 12,500 lb max certificated takeoff weight) must have what type of inspection every 12 calendar months?
questions.expl: Worksheet answer: An ANNUAL inspection.  —  §91.409(a)(1): no person may operate an aircraft unless, within the preceding 12 CALENDAR MONTHS, it has had an ANNUAL INSPECTION in accordance with Part 43 and been approved for return to service by a person authorized by §43.7. (The annual must be signed by an IA per §65.95.)

questions.q: An aircraft's annual inspection was completed on 05/03/93. When is the next annual inspection due?
questions.short: May 31, 1994 — the last day of the 12th calendar month
questions.expl: Worksheet answer: MAY 31, 1994 (the last day of the 12th calendar month after the inspection).  —  §91.409(a) is keyed to 'the preceding 12 CALENDAR MONTHS.' A calendar-month inspection is good through the LAST DAY of the 12th month. An annual done anytime in MAY 1993 is therefore due by the end of MAY 1994 — i.e., MAY 31, 1994. The aircraft may be operated through 5/31/94.  ⚑ Calendar-month math: count 12 months forward, then go to the LAST DAY of that month. May 1993 → due 5/31/1994 (NOT 5/3/1994). The day of the month doesn't matter for a calendar-month interval.

questions.q: In addition to the annual, what inspection is required if the aircraft is operated for hire or for flight instruction for compensation?
questions.expl: Worksheet answer: A 100-HOUR inspection.  —  §91.409(b): no person may operate an aircraft carrying any person (other than a crewmember) FOR HIRE, or give flight instruction for hire in an aircraft they provide, unless within the preceding 100 HOURS of time in service it has had an annual OR 100-HOUR inspection and been approved for return to service.

questions.q: By how many hours may the 100-hour inspection be exceeded while en route to a place where the inspection can be performed?
questions.expl: Worksheet answer: NOT MORE THAN 10 HOURS (en route).  —  §91.409(b): 'The 100-hour limitation may be EXCEEDED BY NOT MORE THAN 10 HOURS while en route to reach a place where the inspection can be done. The excess time used to reach a place where the inspection can be done MUST BE INCLUDED IN COMPUTING THE NEXT 100 HOURS of time in service.'  ⚑ Exam trap: the 10 overflight hours are NOT free — they get SUBTRACTED from the next 100-hour interval (you don't get back to a full 100). The 10-hour allowance applies ONLY to the 100-hour inspection, NOT to the annual.

questions.q: You flew 8 of the allowable 10 overflight hours to reach the shop. How is that excess time treated for the NEXT 100-hour interval?
options: It doubles the next inspection interval
It is free — the next interval is a full 100 hours
