The excess time must be SUBTRACTED — it is included in computing the next 100 hours (next interval = 92 hours)
The aircraft is grounded for 8 hours
questions.short: Subtracted — the excess counts toward the next 100 hours
questions.expl: Worksheet answer: NOT MORE THAN 10 HOURS (en route).  —  §91.409(b): 'The 100-hour limitation may be EXCEEDED BY NOT MORE THAN 10 HOURS while en route to reach a place where the inspection can be done. The excess time used to reach a place where the inspection can be done MUST BE INCLUDED IN COMPUTING THE NEXT 100 HOURS of time in service.'  ⚑ Exam trap: the 10 overflight hours are NOT free — they get SUBTRACTED from the next 100-hour interval (you don't get back to a full 100). The 10-hour allowance applies ONLY to the 100-hour inspection, NOT to the annual.  §91.409(b): 'The excess time used to reach a place where the inspection can be done must be INCLUDED IN COMPUTING THE NEXT 100 HOURS of time in service.' So 8 overflight hours → next interval is 100 − 8 = 92 hours.

questions.q: Under §43.11, an inspection (annual/100-hour/progressive) record entry must include the aircraft's ____ and an airworthy/unairworthy statement.
questions.expl: Correct: TOTAL TIME IN SERVICE.

questions.q: Besides total time in service, what statement must a §43.11 inspection record entry contain?
options: A statement that the aircraft is AIRWORTHY (or a list of discrepancies / unairworthy items)
questions.short: A statement that the aircraft is AIRWORTHY (or a list of discrepancies / unairworthy items)
questions.expl: Correct: A statement that the aircraft is AIRWORTHY (or a list of discrepancies / unairworthy items).

questions.q: In maintenance recordkeeping, TTIS (Total Time In Service) refers to:
questions.expl: Correct: FLIGHT hours / flight time.  EXAM CORRECTION: by §1.1, 'time in service' for AIRFRAME logs = the time from the moment the aircraft leaves the surface until it touches down (airborne time). Your note 'flight hours/time' is right.

questions.q: TACH (tachometer) time most directly tracks:
questions.expl: Correct: ENGINE hours / engine running time.  EXAM CORRECTION: tach time is ENGINE time and is RPM-referenced — it does not equal clock time at all power settings. It's used to track engine/component times, NOT airframe time-in-service.

questions.q: A TEMPORARY maintenance record is good for how long?
options: ONLY 1 YEAR, or until the work is repeated or superseded
questions.short: ONLY 1 YEAR, or until the work is repeated or superseded
questions.expl: Correct: ONLY 1 YEAR, or until the work is repeated or superseded.  EXAM CORRECTION: §91.417(b)(1) — these temporary records (the §43.9/§43.11 entries for maintenance, preventive maintenance, and 100-hour/annual inspections) must be kept until the work is REPEATED, SUPERSEDED, or for 1 YEAR after the work is done.

questions.q: A PERMANENT maintenance record (e.g., total time in service, current AD status, major repair/alteration records, current inspection status):
options: Is kept FOREVER and TRANSFERS WITH THE AIRCRAFT when it is sold
Is filed only with the FAA
questions.short: Is kept FOREVER and TRANSFERS WITH THE AIRCRAFT when it is sold
questions.expl: Correct: Is kept FOREVER and TRANSFERS WITH THE AIRCRAFT when it is sold.  EXAM CORRECTION: §91.417(b)(2) — these records are retained and transferred with the aircraft at sale (§91.419). 'Kept forever, goes with the aircraft' is correct.

questions.q: 'ATA' stands for:
questions.expl: Correct: AIR TRANSPORT ASSOCIATION.

questions.q: The ATA standard that organizes technical data on large/complex aircraft by a classification of maintenance actions (1997, now electronic) is:
questions.expl: Correct: ATA iSpec 2200.

questions.q: A key benefit of ATA chapter numbers is that:
options: They change with every aircraft model
The SEQUENTIAL chapter numbers are CONSISTENT regardless of the aircraft
questions.short: The SEQUENTIAL chapter numbers are CONSISTENT regardless of the aircraft
questions.expl: Correct: The SEQUENTIAL chapter numbers are CONSISTENT regardless of the aircraft.

questions.q: 'AMM' is the:
questions.expl: Correct: AIRCRAFT MAINTENANCE MANUAL.

questions.q: 'CMM' is the:
questions.expl: Correct: Component Maintenance Manual.

questions.q: 'SRM' is the:
questions.expl: Correct: STRUCTURAL REPAIR MANUAL.

questions.q: Aircraft structure is classified as primary and secondary. The aircraft SKIN is an example of:
questions.expl: Correct: SECONDARY structure.  EXAM CORRECTION: be careful — PRIMARY structure carries flight/ground/pressurization loads and its failure is catastrophic; SECONDARY structure carries lighter loads. Some pressurized fuselage skin IS primary structure. Your note 'skin = secondary' is the general-case example; the classification depends on the load the part carries.

questions.q: OVERHAULED means the item was disassembled, cleaned, inspected, repaired as necessary, reassembled, and tested to:
options: CURRENT / serviceable standards approved for that item
questions.short: CURRENT / serviceable standards approved for that item
questions.expl: Correct: CURRENT / serviceable standards approved for that item.

questions.q: REBUILT means the item was disassembled, cleaned, inspected, repaired, reassembled, and tested to:
options: THE SAME TOLERANCES AND LIMITS AS A NEW ITEM (like-new), using new or used parts
questions.short: THE SAME TOLERANCES AND LIMITS AS A NEW ITEM (like-new), using new or used parts
questions.expl: Correct: THE SAME TOLERANCES AND LIMITS AS A NEW ITEM (like-new), using new or used parts.

questions.q: Who may use a NEW maintenance record with ZERO TIME for a rebuilt aircraft ENGINE?
options: The MANUFACTURER, or an AGENCY APPROVED BY THE MANUFACTURER
questions.short: The MANUFACTURER, or an AGENCY APPROVED BY THE MANUFACTURER
questions.expl: Correct: The MANUFACTURER, or an AGENCY APPROVED BY THE MANUFACTURER.  EXAM CORRECTION: the 'zero-time' authority is in §91.421 (rebuilt engine maintenance records), NOT §43.2. §43.2 only DEFINES overhauled vs rebuilt. Per §91.421, only an engine rebuilt by the MANUFACTURER or an agency APPROVED by the manufacturer may start a new record at zero time. Your star note is correct — just cite §91.421.

questions.q: FAA Form 337 is the:
questions.expl: Correct: MAJOR REPAIR AND ALTERATION form.

questions.q: A standard Form 337 is executed in duplicate. After return to service, the FAA's copy must be forwarded to the FAA within:
questions.expl: Correct: 48 HOURS.

questions.q: For a MAJOR REPAIR performed by a certificated REPAIR STATION, what may be used in lieu of FAA Form 337?
options: The customer's WORK ORDER (with a signed maintenance release)
questions.short: The customer's WORK ORDER (with a signed maintenance release)
questions.expl: Correct: The customer's WORK ORDER (with a signed maintenance release).

questions.q: Form 337 / major-repair paperwork must be kept (retained) for at least:
questions.expl: Correct: 2 YEARS.  EXAM CORRECTION: the repair-station 2-year retention is in Part 43 App. B(b). Note: the Form 337 RECORD of a major repair/alteration is itself a PERMANENT record that transfers with the aircraft (§91.417(b)(2)). The '2 years' is the repair station's duplicate-copy retention.

questions.q: The ONE-TIME exception where FAA Form 337 is done in THREE copies (triplicate) is for:
options: EXTENDED-RANGE (AUXILIARY) FUEL TANKS installed in the passenger/baggage compartment
questions.short: EXTENDED-RANGE (AUXILIARY) FUEL TANKS installed in the passenger/baggage compartment
questions.expl: Correct: EXTENDED-RANGE (AUXILIARY) FUEL TANKS installed in the passenger/baggage compartment.

questions.q: On that triplicate Form 337 for cabin/baggage-compartment fuel tanks, the THIRD copy must be:
questions.expl: Correct: Carried ON BOARD the aircraft.

questions.q: FAA Form 8010-4 is the:
options: MALFUNCTION OR DEFECT REPORT (M or D)
questions.short: MALFUNCTION OR DEFECT REPORT (M or D)
questions.expl: Correct: MALFUNCTION OR DEFECT REPORT (M or D).
questions.cite: AC 20-109 / FAA M or D program

questions.q: AC 43-16 ('General Aviation Airworthiness Alerts') is published:
questions.expl: Correct: MONTHLY.  EXAM CORRECTION: the current advisory circular is AC 43-16A; the Airworthiness Alerts were published MONTHLY. They are built from the Malfunction or Defect Reports (Form 8010-4) the field submits.

questions.q: Which of the following is REQUIRED content of a §43.9 maintenance record entry?
options: The DATE, a DESCRIPTION of the work, the person's NAME, SIGNATURE, certificate (license) TYPE, and certificate NUMBER
questions.short: The DATE, a DESCRIPTION of the work, the person's NAME, SIGNATURE, certificate (license) TYPE, and certificate NUMBER
questions.expl: Correct: The DATE, a DESCRIPTION of the work, the person's NAME, SIGNATURE, certificate (license) TYPE, and certificate NUMBER.  EXAM CORRECTION: §43.9(a) names four items — (1) a DESCRIPTION (or reference to acceptable data) of work performed, (2) DATE of completion, (3) NAME of the person (if other than the approver), and (4) SIGNATURE, CERTIFICATE NUMBER, and KIND OF CERTIFICATE held. Your six-item list (date/description/printed name/signature/license type/license number) maps onto these correctly.

questions.q: In a §43.9 entry, 'kind of certificate held' and 'certificate number' correspond to your note's:
questions.expl: Correct: LICENSE TYPE and LICENSE NUMBER.

questions.q: 'OEM' stands for:
questions.expl: Correct: Original Equipment Manufacturer.

questions.q: Service Bulletins (SBs) are:
options: Issued by the MANUFACTURER; good info, strongly recommended, but NOT mandatory unless made so by an AD
questions.short: Issued by the MANUFACTURER; good info, strongly recommended, but NOT mandatory unless made so by an AD
questions.expl: Correct: Issued by the MANUFACTURER; good info, strongly recommended, but NOT mandatory unless made so by an AD.  EXAM CORRECTION: an SB becomes MANDATORY only when the FAA adopts it into an Airworthiness Directive (Part 39). On its own a manufacturer's SB is recommended, not legally required (Part 91 operators).

questions.q: Your note says 'an aircraft operated in inclement weather must be inspected every 15 days.' Which is the CORRECT exam position?
options: It's an AD on all aircraft
There is NO general 14 CFR rule requiring a 15-day inclement-weather inspection — VERIFY this note with your instructor; required inspections are annual (12 cal. months) and 100-hour (§91.409)
questions.short: There is NO general 14 CFR rule requiring a 15-day inclement-weather inspection — VERIFY this note with your instructor; required inspections are annual (12 cal. months) and 100-hour (§91.409)
questions.expl: Correct: There is NO general 14 CFR rule requiring a 15-day inclement-weather inspection — VERIFY this note with your instructor; required inspections are annual (12 cal. months) and 100-hour (§91.409).  EXAM CORRECTION: ⚑ FLAG — no general 14 CFR section requires inspecting an aircraft 'every 15 days' for inclement-weather operation. The recurring inspection requirements are the ANNUAL (every 12 calendar months) and the 100-HOUR (§91.409). Ask your instructor what the slide meant (it may be a specific operator program, a corrosion-control note, or a transcription slip). Do NOT memorize '15 days' for the FAA written.

questions.q: The STANDARD Airworthiness Certificate is FAA Form ____ and is good for how long?
options: 8100-2; until SURRENDERED, SUSPENDED, or REVOKED (no expiration, while the aircraft is maintained airworthy)
questions.short: 8100-2; until SURRENDERED, SUSPENDED, or REVOKED (no expiration, while the aircraft is maintained airworthy)
questions.expl: Correct: 8100-2; until SURRENDERED, SUSPENDED, or REVOKED (no expiration, while the aircraft is maintained airworthy).  EXAM CORRECTION: per §21.181, a STANDARD airworthiness certificate is effective as long as the maintenance, preventive maintenance, and alterations are done per Parts 43 and 91 and the aircraft is registered in the U.S. — it doesn't 'expire' but is effective only while the aircraft stays airworthy. Your 'like an A&P license — until surrendered/suspended/revoked' analogy is the right idea.

questions.q: The SPECIAL Airworthiness Certificate is FAA Form ____ and is good for:
options: 8130-7; 1 YEAR or the period the Administrator prescribes
questions.short: 8130-7; 1 YEAR or the period the Administrator prescribes
questions.expl: Correct: 8130-7; 1 YEAR or the period the Administrator prescribes.  EXAM CORRECTION: §21.181(b) — special airworthiness certificates (e.g., experimental, special flight permit, restricted/limited categories) are effective for the duration the FAA prescribes; experimental ones are commonly issued for up to 1 year. Your '1 year or time prescribed by the Administrator' is correct.

questions.q: Your note lists TWO documents that must be aboard when operating: the Airworthiness Certificate and the Aircraft Registration. What's the FULLER exam answer?
options: ARROW — Airworthiness cert, Registration, Radio station license (if required), Operating limitations, and Weight & balance data
questions.short: ARROW — Airworthiness cert, Registration, Radio station license (if required), Operating limitations, and Weight & balance data
questions.expl: Correct: ARROW — Airworthiness cert, Registration, Radio station license (if required), Operating limitations, and Weight & balance data.  EXAM CORRECTION: ⚑ the full set is the ARROW memory aid — Airworthiness, Registration, Radio station license (only if required, e.g., flying internationally), Operating limitations, Weight & balance. NOTE the Airworthiness Certificate must be DISPLAYED at the cabin/cockpit entrance (§91.203(b)); the Registration must be ABOARD. Your 2 are the two CERTIFICATES — just know the full ARROW list for the written.

questions.q: The Aircraft Registration (the certificate carried aboard) is FAA Form:
questions.expl: Correct: 8050-3.

questions.q: FAA Form 8050-1 is the:
questions.expl: Correct: APPLICATION FOR AIRCRAFT REGISTRATION.

questions.q: FAA Form 8050-2 is the:
questions.expl: Correct: AIRCRAFT BILL OF SALE.

questions.q: An FCC Radio Station License is required when the aircraft has radios AND:
options: It will be flown OUTSIDE the boundaries of the United States (internationally)
questions.short: It will be flown OUTSIDE the boundaries of the United States (internationally)
questions.expl: Correct: It will be flown OUTSIDE the boundaries of the United States (internationally).  EXAM CORRECTION: the radio station license is an FCC requirement (not FAA), and per the ARROW list it's only carried when REQUIRED — i.e., for INTERNATIONAL flight. Purely domestic U.S. operations generally don't need it.

questions.q: FAA Form 337 (Major Repairs & Alterations) applies to which products?
questions.expl: Correct: AIRFRAME, POWERPLANT, PROPELLER, and APPLIANCE.  EXAM CORRECTION: Part 43 App. A defines major repairs/alterations for AIRFRAME, POWERPLANT, PROPELLER, and APPLIANCE — the same four products a Form 337 documents. Your four-item list is correct.

questions.q: Your note says to inspect assemblies for deterioration 'every 100 hours.' What is the exam-safe way to state this?
options: All assemblies must be replaced every 100 hours

It ties to the 100-HOUR INSPECTION (§91.409(b)) for for-hire/instruction aircraft and to manufacturer/ICA inspection intervals — inspect per the applicable schedule, not a blanket 100-hour rule for every aircraft
questions.short: It ties to the 100-HOUR INSPECTION (§91.409(b)) for for-hire/instruction aircraft and to manufacturer/ICA inspection intervals — inspect per the applicable schedule, not a blanket 100-hour rule for every aircraft
questions.expl: Correct: It ties to the 100-HOUR INSPECTION (§91.409(b)) for for-hire/instruction aircraft and to manufacturer/ICA inspection intervals — inspect per the applicable schedule, not a blanket 100-hour rule for every aircraft.  EXAM CORRECTION: '100 hours' = the §91.409(b) 100-hour inspection (only required for aircraft carrying persons for hire or used for flight instruction). A privately operated aircraft uses the ANNUAL. Inspect for deterioration on the schedule that applies to that aircraft.

questions.q: Worksheet #1 — An electromotive force (emf) appears in a conductor whenever—
options: there is relative motion between the conductor and a magnetic field
the conductor sits at rest inside a strong magnetic field
the conductor carries current with no magnetic field present
questions.short: Relative motion between conductor and field induces the emf.
questions.expl: Faraday's 1831 discovery, shown with the bar-magnet-and-coil demo: plunge the magnet in and the galvanometer kicks; hold it still and the needle sits on zero; pull it out and the needle kicks the other way. Moving the coil over a stationary magnet works just as well — it's the RELATIVE motion that does it. Lenz's Law adds the direction: the induced current's field always opposes the motion that made it.

questions.q: Worksheet #2 — A voltage passes through a series of changes, returns to its starting point, then begins the same series of changes again. One complete series is called a—
questions.short: A cycle — 'a repetition of a pattern.'
questions.expl: One cycle = zero → max positive → zero → max negative → zero, ready to repeat. Inside every cycle live TWO alternations (the positive hump and the negative hump) — each is half a cycle, so 'alternation' is the half-size trap. 'Period' is not the pattern at all; it's the TIME the pattern takes (that's worksheet #4).

questions.q: Worksheet #3 — The number of cycles of alternating current completed in one second is the wave's—
questions.expl: 'The frequency is the number of cycles of AC per second.' It answers HOW MANY per second; the period answers HOW LONG one cycle takes — they're inverses of each other (f = 1/t). Amplitude is about how TALL the wave is, not how often it repeats.

questions.q: Worksheet #4 — The time required for a sine wave to complete one full cycle is called its—
questions.expl: Period is a clock reading: how long ONE cycle takes. It is inversely proportional to frequency — the higher the frequency, the shorter the period (t = 1/f, f = 1/t). Wavelength is the DISTANCE covered during that time, not the time itself.

questions.q: Worksheet #5 — The distance a waveform travels during one period is its—
questions.expl: 'The distance that a waveform travels during a period is commonly referred to as a wavelength,' measured from any point on one wave to the SAME point on the next wave. Keep the trio straight: cycle = the pattern, period = the time, wavelength = the distance.

questions.q: Worksheet #6 — The induced voltage or current flowing at any single instant during a cycle is the—
questions.short: Instantaneous value — any point on the sine wave.
questions.expl: 'An instantaneous value of voltage or current is the induced voltage or current flowing at any instant during a cycle.' The whole sine wave is just a lineup of instantaneous values: zero at 0°, maximum at 90°, zero at 180°, maximum negative at 270°. The effective value is one specific summary number (0.707 × peak), not a point on the curve.

questions.q: Worksheet #7 — The largest instantaneous value a sine wave reaches is its—
questions.short: Peak value — the biggest single instantaneous value.
questions.expl: 'The peak value is the largest instantaneous value.' It happens twice per cycle: largest positive at 90°, largest negative at 270°. It's bigger than the RMS value, not equal to it — peak = 1.41 × effective.

questions.q: Worksheet #8 — The standard unit of frequency measurement is the—
questions.short: Hertz — one Hz = one cycle per second.
questions.expl: 'The standard unit of frequency measurement is the hertz (Hz).' The old books said 'cycles per second (cps)' — same thing. Don't grab a lookalike unit: the henry measures INDUCTANCE and the farad measures CAPACITANCE.

questions.q: Worksheet #9 — The effective value of alternating current is also known as the—
questions.expl: 'The effective value is also known as the RMS value or root mean square, which refers to the mathematical process by which the value is derived.' It's the workhorse number: most AC voltmeters display it, and any AC value you're given is assumed to be effective unless the problem says otherwise.

questions.q: Worksheet #10 — The effective (RMS) value of a sine wave is actually a measure of its—
questions.expl: The handbook's picture: put a resistor across the AC source and note how hot it gets; now put the same resistor on an adjustable DC source and turn the DC up until the resistor makes the SAME heat. That DC voltage equals the AC's RMS value. That's why RMS is called 'effective' — it does the same effective work as that much DC.

questions.q: Worksheet #11 — Two waveforms that go through their maximum and minimum points at the same time and in the same direction are said to be—
questions.expl: In phase = marching in step: peaks together, valleys together, moving the same direction. Both conditions matter — same TIME and same DIRECTION. (Two waves 180° apart hit max and min at the same time but in OPPOSITE directions, so they're still out of phase — that's the classic trap.)

questions.q: Worksheet #12 — When two waveforms go through their maximum and minimum points at different times, they are—
questions.short: Out of phase — a phase difference exists.
questions.expl: Max/min at different times = out of phase, and the gap gets stated in degrees ('90° out of phase'). Real-aircraft caution straight from the handbook: two AC busses that aren't locked in phase can do serious damage to systems and avionics if mixed.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-48 (Out of Phase Condition, Fig. 12-112B)

questions.q: Worksheet #13 — Of two out-of-phase waveforms, the one that reaches its maximum or minimum value first is said to—
options: be in phase with the other waveform
questions.expl: 'The waveform that reaches its maximum or minimum value first is said to lead the other waveform.' The one arriving later lags. In the handbook's example, source 1 starts rising at 0° and source 2 at 90° — source 1 leads by 90°, source 2 lags by 90°. Same fact, two names, depending on which wave you're standing on.

questions.q: Worksheet #14 — Aircraft AC electrical systems typically operate at a frequency of—
questions.expl: 'Airplane electrical systems typically operate at 400 cycles' (and even 24-volt DC airplanes carry equipment needing 400-cycle AC). 60 Hz is the HOUSE/commercial frequency, and 115 is a VOLTS number, not a frequency — aircraft AC is usually 115 V at 400 Hz, so the test loves swapping those two.

questions.q: Worksheet #15 — Per the FAA handbook, the direction of the emf induced in a generator conductor is found using the—
questions.short: LEFT hand for generators — because the FAA counts electron flow.
questions.expl: This is the deliberate trap. The FAA 'officially defines current flow using electron theory (negative to positive)' (p. 12-14), and with electron flow the generator rule uses the LEFT hand (p. 12-44, Fig. 12-106). Physics classes and many electronics texts use CONVENTIONAL flow (+ to −), so they teach Fleming's RIGHT-hand rule for the very same job — right answer in that book, wrong answer on this test. FAA convention to memorize: GENERATOR = LEFT hand, MOTOR = RIGHT hand (p. 12-138).
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-44 (generator left-hand rule, Fig. 12-106); p. 12-14 (electron theory)

questions.q: Worksheet #16 — When a loop conductor is rotated in a magnetic field, voltage is induced—
options: only in the side passing the North pole
only while the loop is parallel to the flux
in each side of the loop
questions.short: Both sides — cutting the field in opposite directions.
questions.expl: 'When a loop conductor is rotated in a magnetic field, a voltage is induced in each side of the loop' (Fig. 12-107). The two sides cut the flux in opposite directions, so their emfs push current around the loop in one continuous direction — and after half a turn the sides have swapped places, which is exactly why the output reverses and you get AC. (Parallel to the flux is the ZERO-voltage position, not the only one that counts.)
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-44 (Fig. 12-107, Voltage induced in a loop)

questions.q: Worksheet #17 — Which quantity tells you how MANY complete cycles occur in one second?
questions.expl: Sort the three by the question they answer: frequency = how many per second (Hz), period = how long one takes (seconds), wavelength = how far one travels (distance). If the sentence contains 'per second,' the answer is frequency, every time.

questions.q: Worksheet #18 — The period of a sine wave is—
questions.expl: 'The period of a sine wave is inversely proportional to the frequency: the higher the frequency, the shorter the period.' The formulas are a matched pair — t = 1/f and f = 1/t — so knowing either number hands you the other with one division.

questions.q: Worksheet #19 — The largest single POSITIVE value of a sine wave of voltage occurs when the wave is at—
questions.expl: Walk the wave: 0° zero, 90° maximum positive, 180° back to zero, 270° maximum NEGATIVE, 360° zero again. So 270° is a peak too — just the negative one — and 180° is a zero crossing. The written loves asking for one specific corner of that map.

questions.q: Worksheet #20 — The effective value of a sine wave equals—
options: the average of the instantaneous values over one alternation
questions.expl: 'The effective value is less than the maximum value, being equal to .707 times the maximum value.' The 1.41 factor runs the OTHER way (peak = 1.41 × effective) — same ladder, opposite direction. Climb down from peak with ×0.707; climb up from RMS with ×1.414.

questions.q: Worksheet #21 — Which formula correctly converts a sine wave's peak voltage to its RMS voltage?
questions.expl: The 0.707 ladder: standing on PEAK, multiply by 0.707 to step DOWN to RMS; standing on RMS, multiply by 1.414 to step UP to peak. Both wrong options secretly make the number BIGGER than the peak or equal to a peak conversion (÷0.707 is the same as ×1.414) — RMS must always come out SMALLER than peak, which is a free sanity check on every problem.

questions.q: Worksheet #22 — Which statement describes ALTERNATING current?
options: It flows in one direction only, but continuously rises and falls in magnitude
It flows constantly in one direction with constant polarity, changing magnitude only when the circuit is opened or closed
It changes direction at regular intervals — rising from zero to maximum positive, back to zero, to maximum negative, and back to zero
questions.short: AC periodically reverses direction AND magnitude.
questions.expl: That's the handbook's AC-vs-DC comparison almost word for word: DC 'flows constantly in only one direction with a constant polarity'; AC 'changes direction at regular intervals.' The third option — one direction but varying strength — describes pulsating DC (what comes out of a rectifier), not AC.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-44 (AC and DC Compared, Fig. 12-103)

questions.q: Worksheet #23 — AC has largely replaced DC in commercial power systems chiefly because—
options: it can be transmitted long distances more readily and economically, since its voltage can be raised or lowered by transformers
AC generators require no voltage regulation
it meets less wire resistance over long distances than DC does
questions.short: Transformers make AC easy to step up/down — the distribution advantage.
questions.expl: Step the voltage UP with a transformer and the same power travels at lower current, which slashes line losses; step it back DOWN at the far end for safe use. Transformers only work on a CHANGING current — that's AC's home-field advantage, and DC has no equally simple trick. The wire's resistance itself doesn't care which type of current flows through it.

questions.q: Worksheet #24 — Inductive reactance and capacitive reactance oppose current flow—
options: only in AC circuits, not in DC circuits
equally in AC and DC circuits
questions.expl: 'Inductive reactance and capacitive reactance, on the other hand, oppose current flow only in AC circuits, not in DC circuits.' They exist because AC constantly changes direction and intensity — steady DC gives a coil or capacitor nothing to push back against. Resistance is the one opposition that hits BOTH kinds of current, regardless of frequency.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-49 (Opposition to Current Flow of AC); also listed p. 12-44

questions.q: Worksheet #25 — The value of an induced emf depends on which three factors?
options: the frequency, the period, and the wavelength of the output
the resistance of the conductor, the polarity of the field, and the diameter of the loop
the number of wires (turns) moving through the field, the strength of the magnetic field, and the speed of rotation
questions.expl: FAA wording: '1. Number of wires moving through the magnetic field, 2. Strength of the magnetic field, 3. Speed of rotation.' Your AIM slide says the same trio as 'field strength, number of turns, rate of flux change' — no conflict, because speed of rotation IS the rate the wires cut flux. More wires cutting, stronger field, faster cutting = bigger voltage. (Use the slide's phrasing on the worksheet, the FAA phrasing here for the written.)
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-44 (The value of an induced emf...)

questions.q: An AC sine wave has a peak value of 100 volts. Its effective (RMS) value is—
questions.expl: Ladder down from peak: 100 V × 0.707 = 70.7 V RMS. Sanity check before you even multiply: RMS is always SMALLER than peak, so 141.4 (that's the ×1.414 step, used the wrong direction) is out instantly, and 50 is the halving guess — 0.707 is more than half.

questions.q: An AC voltmeter reads 115 volts (RMS). The peak voltage of that sine wave is approximately—
questions.expl: Ladder UP from RMS: 115 V × 1.414 = 162.6 V. The meter shows you the effective value (that's what AC meters display), so the wave actually swings about 47 volts higher than the reading. 81.3 is the ×0.707 step run the wrong way; 230 is the doubling guess.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-49 (Vp = 1.414 × Vrms; meters read effective)

questions.q: Household AC is rated 110 volts. Per the FAA handbook, the maximum (peak) voltage of that supply is approximately—
questions.expl: 'The 110 volt value given for AC supplied to homes is only 0.707 of the maximum voltage of this supply. The maximum voltage is approximately 155 volts.' The rating you quote is the RMS; the wire actually sees ±155 V swings. 77.8 is what you get multiplying 110 by 0.707 — stepping DOWN from a number that was already the RMS.

questions.q: The period of one cycle of 400 Hz aircraft AC is—
questions.expl: t = 1/f: 1 ÷ 400 = 0.0025 second. Hop the decimal to milliseconds (3 hops right): 2.5 ms. So each complete cycle of your aircraft's AC lasts two and a half thousandths of a second — 400 of them fit in every second, which is the definition of 400 Hz working in reverse.

questions.q: A sine wave has a period of 20 milliseconds. Its frequency is—
questions.expl: Convert first, then flip: 20 ms = 0.020 second. f = 1/t = 1 ÷ 0.020 = 50 Hz. The classic stumble is skipping the ms→s conversion and dividing by 20 — the formulas t = 1/f and f = 1/t only speak base units (seconds and hertz).

questions.q: Unless a problem states otherwise, a given AC voltage or current value — and the reading on an AC voltmeter — is assumed to be the—
questions.short: Given values and meter readings = RMS by default.
questions.expl: Two default rules from the same paragraph: 'any values given for current or voltage are assumed to be effective values unless otherwise specified,' and 'AC voltmeters and ammeters measure the effective value.' So '115 V aircraft AC' is 115 RMS — the peak is up at about 163 V.

questions.q: Voltage source 1 begins its rise at 0° and voltage source 2 begins its rise at 90°. Which statement is correct?
options: The two sources are in phase but differ in amplitude
questions.short: Earlier in time = the leader: source 1 leads by 90°.
questions.expl: This is the handbook's own Figure 12-112B scenario: 'Because voltage source one begins its rise earlier in time (90°) in relation to the second voltage source, it is said to be leading the second source.' Read lead/lag questions by asking one thing only: who moves FIRST? First mover leads; the other lags by the stated degrees.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-48 (Out of Phase Condition, Fig. 12-112B)

questions.q: Two voltage waveforms differ by exactly 180°, so they reach their maximum and minimum values at the same instants. They are—
options: in phase only if their amplitudes are equal
questions.short: 180° apart = out of phase, even with synchronized peaks.
questions.expl: The trap the handbook flags on purpose: 'If there is a 180° difference between the two signals, then they are still out of phase even though they are both reaching their minimum and maximum values at the same time.' In-phase needs same time AND same direction — at 180° one wave peaks positive exactly when the other peaks negative. (A full 360° difference, though, IS back in phase.)

questions.q: In an AC circuit containing only inductance, the current—
options: stays exactly in phase with the applied voltage
questions.short: Inductor: current LAGS — the 'ELI' half of ELI the ICE man.
questions.expl: The handbook contrasts the two directly: a capacitance-only circuit's 'current leads the applied voltage as contrasted with a circuit in which there is inductance, where the current lags the voltage.' Memory hook: ELI the ICE man — in ELI, E (voltage) comes before I (current) with L in the middle: inductor → voltage first, current lags.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-54; p. 12-62 (inductive current lags the applied voltage)

questions.q: In an AC circuit containing only capacitance, the current—
options: drops to zero once the plates first charge
questions.short: Capacitor: current LEADS — the 'ICE' half of ELI the ICE man.
questions.expl: 'In a circuit where there is only capacitance, current leads the applied voltage.' ICE: I before E with C in the middle — capacitor → current first. (Current-stops-forever is the DC story; on AC the plates charge and discharge every alternation, so current keeps flowing in the rest of the circuit even though none crosses the dielectric.)

questions.q: One reason AC is preferred over DC for aircraft electrical systems is that—
options: AC systems eliminate the need for a battery
space and weight are saved, since AC devices — especially motors — are smaller and simpler than comparable DC devices
AC circuits require no circuit-protection devices at altitude
questions.short: Smaller, simpler, lighter — the weight case for AC.
questions.expl: 'Space and weight can be saved since AC devices, especially motors, are smaller and simpler than DC devices.' Stack the rest of the handbook's list on top: most AC motors need no brushes (no commutation trouble at high altitude), and AC circuit breakers behave at altitude where DC breakers arc themselves to death. This size/weight logic is also the classroom answer to 'why 400 Hz?' — running the magnetic guts faster lets the same power come from smaller, lighter machines.

questions.q: Because aircraft systems run at 400 Hz, a 400-cycle AC motor with the same number of poles as a 60-cycle commercial motor operates at—
options: about half the speed of the 60-cycle motor
exactly the same speed as the 60-cycle motor
about seven times the speed of the 60-cycle motor
questions.expl: AC motor speed = 120 × frequency ÷ number of poles, so speed scales straight with frequency: 400 ÷ 60 ≈ 6.7 — 'about seven times the speed of a 60-cycle commercial motor.' That's why 400-cycle induction motors spin 6,000–24,000 rpm and drive small high-speed rotors through reduction gears for flaps, landing gear, and engine starting.

questions.q: Which rule determines the direction a CURRENT-CARRYING wire will MOVE when placed in a magnetic field (motor action)?
options: the left-hand rule for a coiled conductor
questions.short: Motion from current = MOTOR = RIGHT hand.
questions.expl: FAA sorting key: what are you solving FOR? Motion in, emf out = GENERATOR = left hand (p. 12-44). Current in, motion out = MOTOR = right hand: 'if the index finger of the right hand is pointed in the direction of the magnetic field and the second finger in the direction of current flow, the thumb indicates the direction the current carrying wire moves' (p. 12-138). The coil left-hand rule (pp. 12-12–12-13) is a third, different tool — it finds a field's direction around a conductor, not motion.

questions.q: Using the FAA's generator left-hand rule, the thumb, first finger, and second finger respectively indicate—
options: thumb = induced emf; first finger = motion of the conductor; second finger = flux direction
thumb = motion of the conductor; first finger = flux direction (North to South); second finger = induced emf
thumb = flux direction; first finger = induced emf; second finger = motion of the conductor
questions.short: First finger flux N→S, thumb motion, second finger emf.
questions.expl: Straight from the handbook: 'The first finger of the left hand is pointed in the direction of the magnetic lines of force (North to South), the thumb is pointed in the direction of movement of the conductor through the magnetic field, and the second finger points in the direction of the induced emf.' Hook: F-irst finger = F-lux, thu-M-b = M-otion, s-E-cond = E-mf.

questions.q: A two-pole AC generator turns at 3,600 rpm. Its output frequency is—
questions.short: 1 pole-pair × 60 rps = 60 cps — the handbook's own example.
questions.expl: F = (poles ÷ 2) × (rpm ÷ 60). Two poles = ONE pole pair; 3,600 rpm ÷ 60 = 60 revolutions per second. 1 × 60 = 60 cps. The conductor makes one full cycle each time it passes one North-South pair — so frequency counts pole PAIRS, not poles, which is exactly the trap behind the 120 answer.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-47 (frequency of a generator, worked example)

questions.q: 1. Alternating current has several advantages over DC. Name one.
options: Alternating current can produce more than one horsepower with only 746 watts of power
Alternating current's voltage and current values can be changed easily
Alternating current is safer than DC
Alternating current creates less heat in a resistor for a given current flow
questions.short: Its voltage and current can be changed easily (by a transformer).
questions.expl: The big practical advantage of AC is that a simple transformer can step its voltage and current up or down with almost no loss — something you cannot do with DC. That is why power is generated and distributed as AC. AC is not inherently safer, it does not make less heat for a given current, and 746 watts is still one horsepower whether it is AC or DC.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (advantages of AC / transformers, pp. 12-43, 12-65)

questions.q: 2. Unless otherwise specified, AC values for voltage and current are given in ______ values.
questions.expl: When an AC voltage or current is stated without any qualifier — like '115 volts AC' — it means the effective, or RMS, value. The effective value is the one that does the same heating work as an equal DC value, so it is the meaningful number for real circuits. Peak and average are only used when specifically named.

questions.q: 3. The Alternating Current waveform produced by a rotating generator is called a ______.
questions.expl: As the generator loop rotates through the magnetic field, the induced voltage rises and falls smoothly following the sine of the rotation angle — zero, up to a peak, back through zero, down to the opposite peak, and back. That smooth curve is the sine wave, the natural output of a rotating generator.

questions.q: 4. In certain circuits, the voltage and current of the AC waveform do not line up. What do we call the distance between the waveforms?
questions.expl: When reactance is present, the current and voltage waves cross zero at different times — they are out of step. The angular amount they are shifted apart is the phase angle. Its cosine is the power factor, so it directly ties into how much real power the circuit uses.

questions.q: 5. The ratio of true power to apparent power is called the ______.
questions.expl: True power (the watts actually consumed) divided by apparent power (volts times amps, in volt-amps) gives the power factor. It runs from 0 to 1 and equals the cosine of the phase angle. A purely resistive circuit has a power factor of 1; adding reactance drops it below 1.

questions.q: 6. Transformers change the values of Voltage and Current using the principle of ______.
questions.expl: The changing current in the primary makes a changing magnetic field that links the secondary winding and induces a voltage in it. That linking of one coil's field into another coil is mutual inductance — the operating principle of every transformer. No physical connection is needed between the two windings.

questions.q: 7. What do we call the resistance to AC produced by a back voltage generated in a coil of wire?
questions.expl: A coil fights any change in its current by inducing a counter-EMF (back voltage) that opposes the source. That opposition to AC is inductive reactance, XL. It grows with frequency and with inductance (XL = 2 x pi x f x L), so a coil chokes higher-frequency AC more strongly.

questions.q: 8. A capacitor's working voltage should be at least ______% over the highest voltage applied in the circuit.
questions.expl: The handbook rule is that a capacitor should be chosen so its working voltage is at least 50 percent greater than the highest voltage that will be applied. That margin covers voltage surges and the fact that an AC or pulsating source has a peak well above its RMS value, keeping the dielectric from breaking down.

questions.q: 9. What is the frequency at which a circuit's capacitive reactance and inductive reactance are equal?
questions.expl: As frequency rises, inductive reactance (XL) climbs while capacitive reactance (XC) falls. The one frequency where they are exactly equal is the resonant frequency. At resonance XL and XC cancel, so the circuit's opposition is just its resistance and the phase angle is zero.

questions.q: 10. When it is necessary to get the maximum amount of power from AC, it is typically of this type. This type of AC also makes better DC because the power pulses overlap and never drop to an instantaneous value of zero.
questions.expl: Three-phase AC is three sine waves offset by 120 degrees. Because their peaks are staggered, the combined power is far more constant than a single phase and delivers more power for a given size machine. When rectified, the overlapping phases keep the DC from ever falling to zero, giving a much smoother DC than single-phase rectification.

questions.q: 11. Vacuum tubes ushered in the age of electronics. However, they have been replaced almost entirely by solid-state transistors because:
options: Tubes are heavy, hot, consume a lot of power, and are very large
Tubes cannot be used as electron control devices
Transistors “sound better” in an audio circuit
Transistors can handle higher power levels
questions.short: Tubes are heavy, hot, power-hungry, and large.
questions.expl: A vacuum tube needs a heated filament and a bulky glass envelope, so it runs hot, draws a lot of power, and takes up space. A transistor does the same electron-control job while being tiny, cool, rugged, and efficient — which is exactly why solid-state devices replaced tubes. Tubes CAN control electron flow; that is not the problem.

questions.q: 12. Semiconductor Diodes will conduct electricity when ______.
options: They are connected in series in a circuit
Diodes should never conduct electricity, they are check valves
They are in a circuit with the P-Type material connected to Positive, and the N-Type connected to Negative
questions.short: P-type to positive, N-type to negative (forward biased).
questions.expl: A diode conducts only when it is forward biased: the P-side (anode) tied toward positive and the N-side (cathode) tied toward negative. That polarity pushes the carriers across the junction and it turns on. Reverse it and the junction blocks. The check-valve image is right in spirit — a diode passes current one way — but it does conduct in that forward direction.

questions.q: 13. What can we use to change the entire AC waveform into DC? (Not just the positive pulses)
questions.expl: A full-wave bridge uses four diodes so that BOTH halves of the AC wave are steered through the load in the same direction — the negative half is flipped up instead of thrown away. A half-wave rectifier keeps only the positive pulses. An inverter does the opposite job (DC to AC), and a transformer only changes AC voltage, it does not rectify.

questions.q: 14. Zener diodes will conduct electricity when they are reverse biased if the reverse voltage exceeds ______.
options: No diode will conduct electricity if it is reverse biased unless it is broken
questions.expl: A zener is built to break down and conduct in reverse at a precise, repeatable voltage — its Zener voltage. Below that it blocks like a normal diode; once the reverse voltage reaches the Zener voltage it conducts and holds that voltage nearly constant. This is by design (not damage), which is what makes a zener a voltage regulator/reference.

questions.q: 15. When will a PNP transistor conduct electricity?
options: When you connect the base to positive and the emitter to negative
When you connect the base and the emitter to negative
When you connect the base to negative and the emitter to positive
When you connect the base and the emitter to positive
questions.short: Base to negative, emitter to positive.
questions.expl: A PNP transistor turns on when its emitter-base junction is forward biased, which for PNP means the emitter is more positive than the base — emitter to positive, base to negative. (An NPN is the mirror image: base positive, emitter negative.) Getting the polarity backward is the classic PNP/NPN trap.

questions.q: 16. A certain transformer has an input voltage of 1000V and an output voltage of 100V. If you can get 10 amps off of the secondary coil, how many amps are going into the primary coil?
questions.expl: Power in equals power out (ideal transformer): Vp x Ip = Vs x Is. So 1000 x Ip = 100 x 10 = 1000 volt-amps, which gives Ip = 1000 / 1000 = 1 amp. Voltage stepped DOWN 10-to-1 means current stepped UP 10-to-1: 1 amp in the high-voltage primary supplies 10 amps out of the low-voltage secondary.

questions.q: 17. A transformer has more windings on the secondary side than on the primary side. What kind of transformer is this?
questions.expl: Output voltage follows the turns ratio: more turns on the secondary than the primary means the secondary voltage is higher than the primary voltage — that is a step-up transformer. (Current goes the other way: the higher-voltage secondary carries less current.)

questions.q: 18. How can we test a diode for proper operation?
options: Use a voltmeter to determine the zener voltage
Use an ohmmeter; the diode should have low resistance in both directions
Use an ohmmeter; the diode should have low resistance when forward biased, and infinite resistance when reverse biased
Use an ohmmeter; the diode should have high resistance in both directions
questions.short: Ohmmeter: low R forward, infinite R reverse.
questions.expl: A good diode is a one-way valve, so an ohmmeter should read LOW resistance one way (forward biased) and very HIGH / infinite resistance the other way (reverse biased). Low both ways means it is shorted; high both ways means it is open. Either same-both-directions result is a failed diode.

questions.q: 19. Anytime we have a conductor move through a magnetic field, we will induce a voltage. What can we do to increase the induced EMF?
options: Reduce the speed of conductor motion and increase the magnetic field strength
Increase the distance between the conductor and the magnetic field
Increase the size of the conductor
Increase the rate at which lines of magnetic flux are cut
questions.short: Increase the rate at which flux lines are cut.
questions.expl: Induced voltage depends on how fast the conductor cuts magnetic flux lines — the more lines cut per second, the more EMF. You raise that rate by moving faster, using a stronger field, or adding turns. Slowing the motion (option b) works against you, and increasing the size or the distance does not increase the rate of cutting.

questions.q: 20. Which of the following values of AC current and voltage produces the same amount of heat as a corresponding amount of DC?
questions.expl: The effective value of AC is DEFINED as the value that produces the same heating in a resistor as an equal amount of steady DC — that is exactly why it is also called the RMS value. Peak and average do not match DC heating; the effective value does.

questions.q: 21. If the voltage and current in an AC circuit are not in phase:
options: There will be a power factor of 1
True power will be less than apparent power
True power will be more than apparent power
True power and apparent power will cancel each other out
questions.short: True power will be less than apparent power.
questions.expl: When voltage and current are out of phase, some energy sloshes back and forth in the reactance instead of being consumed. So the real power used (true power) is less than the volts-times-amps product (apparent power), and the power factor falls below 1. Only when they ARE in phase do true and apparent power become equal (PF = 1).
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-64 (true power vs. apparent power)

questions.q: 22. The total opposition to current flow in an AC circuit is called:
questions.expl: Impedance (Z) is the total opposition to AC — it combines resistance with inductive and capacitive reactance. Because resistance and reactance act at right angles, they add like the sides of a right triangle: Z is the hypotenuse, Z = square root of (R squared + X squared). Resistance alone is only the DC part of the opposition.

questions.q: 23. What do we call the resistance to AC caused by capacitors in a circuit?
questions.expl: A capacitor's opposition to AC is capacitive reactance, XC = 1 / (2 x pi x f x C). Unlike a resistor, this opposition DROPS as frequency rises, so a capacitor passes high-frequency AC more easily and blocks DC (zero frequency) completely.

questions.q: 24. A certain A.C. circuit has an inductance of .005 Henries, a capacitance of .0000057 Farads, a frequency of 400 Hz, and an applied voltage of 115V. What is the Inductive Reactance for this circuit?
questions.expl: Inductive reactance uses only L and f: XL = 2 x pi x f x L = 2 x 3.1416 x 400 x 0.005. Work it in steps: 2 x pi = 6.283; x 400 = 2513.3; x 0.005 = 12.57 ohms. The capacitance, voltage, and resistance in the problem are distractors — XL does not use them. (6.28 drops the factor of 2; 56.84 is the capacitive reactance, not inductive.)

questions.q: 25. A certain A.C. circuit has a capacitance of .000007 Farads, a resistance of 225 ohms, an inductance of .03 Henrys, and a frequency of 400 Hz. What is the Capacitive Reactance for this circuit?
questions.expl: Capacitive reactance uses only C and f: XC = 1 / (2 x pi x f x C). Bottom first: 2 x pi x 400 = 2513.3; x 0.000007 = 0.017593. Then invert: 1 / 0.017593 = 56.84 ohms. Watch the trap answers: 0.0176 is the denominator before you invert, and 75.40 is the INDUCTIVE reactance of the .03 H coil, not the capacitive reactance.

questions.q: 26. If a Parallel A.C. Circuit has an XL of 25 ohms, an XC of 40 ohms, and a Resistance of 50 ohms, what is this circuit's Impedance? (Z = 1 / sqrt[ (1/R)^2 + (1/XL - 1/XC)^2 ])
questions.expl: Use the parallel-circuit impedance formula. Reciprocals first: 1/R = 1/50 = 0.02; 1/XL = 1/25 = 0.04; 1/XC = 1/40 = 0.025. The reactive part is (0.04 - 0.025) = 0.015. Square and add: 0.02^2 = 0.0004, 0.015^2 = 0.000225, sum = 0.000625. Square root = 0.025. Invert: 1 / 0.025 = 40 ohms. (50 ohms is just R — the trap for forgetting the reactive branches.)
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, pp. 12-59-12-61 (impedance in parallel AC circuits)

questions.q: 27. How can we determine the phase angle of an A.C. Circuit?
options: The ratio of True Power over Apparent Power
Use an oscilloscope to measure the phase angle of an A.C. Circuit
The cosine of the phase angle will be equal to the Power Factor
The ratio of the voltage drop across the resistor to the total voltage in a parallel circuit
questions.short: Its cosine equals the power factor.
questions.expl: The cleanest link is that the cosine of the phase angle equals the power factor, so knowing the power factor gives you the angle. Note the other choices are actually true statements too — an oscilloscope really can display the phase shift, and True Power / Apparent Power really is the power factor. The voltage-drop-ratio statement is wrong only because it specifies a PARALLEL circuit: the resistor-drop-to-total-voltage ratio gives the power factor in a SERIES circuit, not a parallel one.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-64 (power factor = cosine of phase angle)

questions.q: 28. If an A.C. circuit has more Inductive Reactance than Capacitive Reactance, then Current ______ Voltage.
questions.expl: More inductive than capacitive reactance makes the circuit net inductive, and in an inductive circuit the current LAGS the voltage. Remember ELI the ICE man: in an inductor (L), voltage E leads current I — same thing said the other way, the current lags. (A net-capacitive circuit would be the reverse: current leads.)
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-62 (inductive circuit: current lags voltage)

questions.q: 29. There are 2 instances where an A.C. Circuit will have a Power factor of 1. Name one.
options: When the circuit is purely capacitive with no resistance
When the inductive reactance is double the capacitive reactance
When the circuit is purely resistive, or when it is at resonance (XL = XC)
When the apparent power is much greater than the true power
questions.short: Purely resistive, OR at resonance (XL = XC).
questions.expl: Power factor is 1 only when voltage and current are in phase, which happens in two cases: (1) a purely resistive circuit, which has no reactance to shift the phase, and (2) a circuit at resonance, where the inductive and capacitive reactances are equal and cancel each other out. Either one leaves only resistance, so the phase angle is zero and PF = 1.

questions.q: 30. In a typical electrically-operated retractable landing gear, trace the raise-gear circuit: after the pilot selects gear UP, which switch must be closed before current can reach the gear motor to retract, and what stops the motor once the gear is fully up?
options: The down-limit switch must be closed while on the ground, and the warning horn relay stops the motor
No switch is needed — the gear handle feeds the motor directly and the motor simply stalls when the gear is fully up
The nose-gear down switch must be closed, and the throttle switch stops the motor

The gear safety (squat) switch must be closed — which happens only when the aircraft is airborne with the weight off the wheels — and the up-limit switches open to stop the motor at the full-up position
questions.short: Squat switch closed (airborne) feeds the motor; up-limit switches stop it.
questions.expl: The gear safety switch (squat / weight-on-wheels switch) sits on a landing gear strut. On the ground the compressed strut holds it in the GROUND position and the gear CANNOT retract. Once airborne the strut extends, the squat switch moves to FLIGHT, and now selecting UP lets current through to the gear motor. When each gear reaches full up, its up-limit switch opens to cut the motor so it does not keep running against the stops.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-31B, Ch. 13 (Aircraft Landing Gear Systems — gear safety/squat switch & up-limit switches, p. 13-33)

questions.q: 31. In a landing-gear warning system, under what condition does the gear-warning horn sound (an unsafe mismatch)?
options: Only when the aircraft is airborne with the gear handle in the DOWN position
When the gear handle is UP while the squat switch senses weight-on-wheels — i.e., the gear is selected up while the aircraft is still on the ground
When the red and green gear-position lights are both illuminated together in flight
Whenever the gear is fully down and locked
questions.short: Gear handle UP while the squat switch says weight-on-wheels (on the ground).
questions.expl: The squat switch tells the system whether the aircraft is on the ground or in flight. If the aircraft is on the ground (weight on wheels) and the gear handle is moved to the UP position, that is a dangerous mismatch, so the warning horn sounds to alert the pilot. (The same horn also sounds in flight if the throttle is retarded for landing while the gear is not down and locked.)
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-31B, Ch. 13 (Aircraft Landing Gear Systems — squat switch & warning horn logic, p. 13-33)

questions.q: 1. A vacuum tube built with just two elements — a plate and a cathode — is known as a ______.
questions.expl: Vacuum tubes are grouped by how many working elements they contain: two elements (plate + cathode) make a diode, three (add one grid) a triode, four a tetrode, and five a pentode. The two-element tube is the diode, and like a semiconductor diode it passes current in only one direction.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-224 (vacuum tube families: diode, triode, tetrode, pentode)

questions.q: 2. The one semiconductor device that acts as an electron 'check valve' — letting current pass in one direction only — is the ______.
questions.expl: A diode is a two-element PN-junction device that conducts in only one direction, exactly like a mechanical check valve lets fluid flow one way. Forward biased it passes current; reverse biased it blocks it. A transistor is a three-element control device, not a one-way valve.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-211 (two-element PN-junction diode; one-way conduction)

questions.q: 3. If a semiconductor diode is forward biased, electrons ______ flow through it.
options: Can only for a split second
questions.short: They CAN flow (a forward-biased diode conducts).
questions.expl: Forward bias pushes the majority carriers across the PN junction, so the junction conducts and electrons flow freely. Reverse bias would widen the depletion region and block the flow. So a forward-biased diode is the 'on' state — current can flow.

questions.q: 4. A diode is FORWARD biased (it conducts) when the battery is hooked up so that the ______.
options: N-material connects to the battery + terminal and the P-material to the − terminal
P-material connects to the battery + terminal and the N-material to the − terminal
P-material and N-material both connect to the + terminal
diode is placed across the battery with no polarity
questions.short: P-material to +, N-material to − = forward bias.
questions.expl: Forward bias means the positive terminal drives the P-side and the negative terminal drives the N-side, which collapses the depletion region and lets current pass. Reverse that hookup — P to minus, N to plus — and the diode blocks. This polarity rule is exactly what decides which of two drawn diodes is the conducting one.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-211 / 12-212 (forward vs reverse biased diode)

questions.q: 5. Two identical diodes are wired to batteries connected in opposite directions. If one diode is REVERSE biased, the other diode must be ______.
questions.short: Forward biased — the opposite battery polarity forward-biases it.
questions.expl: Bias direction is set entirely by how the battery polarity meets the P and N material. If one diode sees a polarity that reverse-biases it, an identical diode wired to the opposite polarity sees the forward-bias condition and conducts. They are complementary — one blocks, the other passes.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-211 / 12-212 (bias direction set by battery polarity)

questions.q: 6. When a specific reverse voltage is reached, a ______ diode breaks down and begins to conduct in its reverse direction.
questions.expl: An ordinary rectifier diode blocks in reverse. A zener is specially made so that at a precise reverse voltage — its zener voltage — it breaks down and conducts, then holds that voltage steady. That controlled reverse breakdown is what makes it useful as a voltage reference/regulator.

questions.q: 7. A zener diode is used as a ______-sensitive solid-state voltage regulator.
questions.expl: Once the reverse voltage across a zener reaches its zener value, it conducts and clamps that voltage nearly constant even as current changes. It responds to VOLTAGE, holding the output steady, which is exactly the job of a voltage regulator.

questions.q: 8. Identify this symbol (a diode whose cathode bar is bent into little 'Z' wings):
questions.expl: The bent cathode bar — the little Z-shaped wings on the line the triangle points to — is the mark of a zener diode. A plain diode has a straight bar; the bent bar tells you it is designed to conduct at a set reverse voltage.

questions.q: 9. A three-element solid-state device (a transistor) can be used as a ______ valve in a circuit.
questions.short: A control valve (small signal controls a large one).
questions.expl: A two-element diode is a check valve — it only passes current one way. A three-element transistor is a CONTROL valve: a small base current (or voltage) controls a much larger current between the other two electrodes, just like a small handle controls a big flow.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-223 (transistor as a current-controlling device)

questions.q: 10. On a transistor symbol, you can tell it is an NPN transistor because its emitter arrow points ______.
options: Outward, away from the base bar
questions.short: NPN = emitter arrow points OUT (Not Pointing iN).
questions.expl: The classifying arrow sits on the emitter lead. If it points OUT, away from the base bar, the device is NPN. If it points IN, toward the base, it is PNP. Handy memory: NPN = 'Not Pointing iN.'
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-223 (NPN vs PNP arrangement; emitter-arrow rule)

questions.q: 11. On a transistor symbol like this one, the electrode drawn with the arrow on it is the ______.
questions.expl: The arrow always rides on the EMITTER lead — its direction (in or out) also tells you PNP vs NPN. The flat bar in the middle is the base, and the remaining plain lead is the collector. A gate belongs to FETs/SCRs, not a bipolar transistor.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-223 (transistor electrodes; arrow on emitter)

questions.q: 12. The three electrodes of a bipolar transistor are the ______.
questions.expl: A bipolar transistor has three electrodes: the emitter (with the arrow), the base (the control element in the middle), and the collector. Anode/cathode/gate belong to an SCR; source/drain/gate to a FET; plate/grid/cathode to a vacuum tube.

questions.q: 13. For a PNP transistor's emitter-base junction to be forward biased so the transistor conducts, the emitter must be ______ relative to the base.
questions.short: Emitter POSITIVE relative to base (for PNP).
questions.expl: In a PNP the emitter is P-material and the base is N-material, so forward-biasing that junction needs the emitter more POSITIVE than the base (P to +, N to −). That is the mirror image of an NPN, which conducts with the base positive and emitter negative.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-223 (PNP operation; emitter positive relative to base)

questions.q: 14. This symbol is a silicon controlled rectifier (SCR). Terminal 1 — the flat back of the triangle where current enters — is the ______.
questions.short: Anode (current enters the flat side of the triangle).
questions.expl: An SCR is drawn like a diode (triangle into a bar) with an extra gate lead. Current enters at the anode — the flat back of the triangle (terminal 1) — and leaves at the cathode — the bar the triangle points to (terminal 2). The third lead off the cathode side is the gate (terminal 3).
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 semiconductor section (pp. 12-211…12-225) — the SCR is NOT named in the FAA handbook; standard electronics [verify with AIM slides]

questions.q: 15. The three terminals of a silicon controlled rectifier (SCR) are the ______.
questions.expl: An SCR has an anode and a cathode like a diode, plus a gate that triggers it into conduction. (Emitter/base/collector is a transistor; source/drain/gate is a FET; MT1/MT2/gate is a triac.)
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 semiconductor section (pp. 12-211…12-225) — SCR not named in the FAA handbook; standard electronics [verify with instructor]

questions.q: 16. A pulse of ______ voltage applied to the gate of an SCR causes it to start conducting.
questions.short: A positive gate pulse triggers the SCR.
questions.expl: An SCR stays off until a small POSITIVE trigger pulse hits its gate; that pulse fires it into conduction, and it then latches on (keeps conducting) until the anode current drops toward zero. The gate only needs a brief positive kick to turn it on.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 semiconductor section — SCR gate triggering not covered in the FAA handbook; standard electronics [verify with instructor]

questions.q: 17. Identify this symbol — two triangles pointing opposite ways with terminals labeled MT1, MT2 and a gate:
questions.expl: The two anti-parallel triangles mean current can pass in EITHER direction once triggered, and the terminals are named MT1 and MT2 (main terminals) plus a gate. That two-way, gate-triggered device is the triac. An SCR conducts only one way and uses anode/cathode.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 semiconductor section — the triac is NOT named in the FAA handbook; standard electronics [verify with AIM slides]

questions.q: 18. A junction field-effect transistor (JFET) controls the load current flowing through it by the ______ on its gate.
questions.short: Gate VOLTAGE controls the channel current.
questions.expl: Unlike a bipolar transistor (controlled by base CURRENT), a JFET is controlled by the VOLTAGE on its gate. The gate voltage widens or narrows the conducting channel between source and drain, throttling the load current — with almost no gate current drawn.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-225 (FET/JFET gate voltage controls channel current)

questions.q: 19. Identify this symbol — a channel bar with a source and drain on one side and a gate whose arrow points toward the channel:
questions.expl: Source and drain tie to the two ends of the channel bar, and the gate sits opposite with an arrow pointing at the channel (arrow toward the channel = N-channel). That layout — source, drain, gate on a channel — is the field-effect transistor, not a bipolar transistor (which uses emitter/base/collector).

questions.q: 20. In a magnetic amplifier, a small amount of ______ current is used to control a large amount of ______ current.
options: Direct (DC) control current … alternating (AC) load current
Direct (DC) control current … direct (DC) load current
Alternating (AC) control current … alternating (AC) load current
Alternating (AC) control current … direct (DC) load current
questions.short: A small DC control current governs a large AC load current.
questions.expl: A magnetic amplifier (saturable-core reactor) uses a small DC control current to change how deeply the iron core saturates. That changes the AC reactance of the load winding, so a tiny DC input controls a large AC output current — the essence of magnetic amplification.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-248 (saturable-core reactor / magnetic amplifier) & p. 12-119

questions.q: 21. In the magnetic-amplifier alternator control, as the DC control voltage INCREASES (saturating the core more), the alternator field current will ______.
questions.short: Increase (more saturation → less AC reactance → more field current).
questions.expl: More DC control current drives the core further toward saturation, which LOWERS the AC reactance of the load (field) winding. Lower reactance lets MORE current through, so the alternator field current rises as the control voltage rises. [Note: a regulator can be arranged for the reverse action — verify the exact circuit with your instructor.]
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-248 (saturable reactor: control current changes core permeability & reactance)

questions.q: 22. Identify this symbol — an emitter plus two bases labeled B1 and B2:
questions.short: A unijunction transistor (one emitter, two bases).
questions.expl: Having a single emitter and TWO bases (B1 and B2) is the fingerprint of the unijunction transistor. A bipolar transistor has one base; a FET has source/drain/gate; an SCR has anode/cathode/gate. Two bases = UJT.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 semiconductor section — the unijunction transistor (UJT) is NOT named in the FAA handbook; standard electronics [verify with AIM slides]

questions.q: 23. Identify this symbol — a diode inside a circle with two arrows pointing IN toward the junction:
questions.short: A photodiode (light striking it = arrows pointing IN).
questions.expl: Arrows pointing INTO the diode mean light is being received: the photodiode. Light energy frees carriers in the junction and changes its reverse current, so it senses light. An LED is the mirror image — arrows pointing OUT because it emits light.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-214 (photodiode — light produces carriers in a diode)

questions.q: 24. Identify this symbol — a diode inside a circle with two arrows pointing OUT (away from the junction):
questions.expl: Arrows pointing OUT mean the device gives OFF light: the LED. When it is forward biased, electrons falling into holes radiate energy as light. Arrows pointing in would make it a photodiode (a light receiver).

questions.q: 25. In the amplifier schematic, component #1 — the cone-shaped output device fed by the output transformer — is a ______.
questions.expl: The cone/voice-coil symbol at the very output of an audio amplifier is the loudspeaker — it turns the amplified electrical signal back into sound. It is driven through the output (matching) transformer.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-44 (loudspeaker); symbol chart Fig. 4-29 p. 4-24

questions.q: 26. In the amplifier schematic, component #2 — two coils sharing an iron core, sitting between the output tube and the speaker — is a ______.
questions.expl: Two coils drawn around a common iron core (the parallel lines between them) is a transformer. Here it is the output transformer that matches the tube's high impedance to the speaker's low impedance.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-142 (transformer turns ratio); symbol chart Fig. 4-29 p. 4-24

questions.q: 27. In the amplifier schematic, component #3 — a resistor with an adjustable arrow drawn through it — is a ______.
questions.expl: A resistor with an arrow (a movable wiper) is a variable resistor — a rheostat when used with two terminals to vary current, a potentiometer when the wiper is a third terminal used to vary voltage. Either way it is an adjustable resistance, used here for bias/volume adjustment.

questions.q: 28. In the amplifier schematic, component #4 — two parallel plates with a gap between them — is a ______.
questions.expl: Two parallel plates separated by a gap is the capacitor symbol. In this amplifier it couples the AC signal between stages while blocking the DC bias, or bypasses AC to ground.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-50 (capacitor / capacitance); symbol chart Fig. 4-29 p. 4-24

questions.q: 29. In the amplifier schematic, component #5 — a coil with an adjustable arrow drawn through it — is a ______.
questions.expl: A coil is an inductor; the arrow through it means its value is adjustable — a variable inductor. It stores energy in a magnetic field and, being tunable, is used to tune a stage. (Two such coils coupled together would form a tuned transformer.)

questions.q: 30. In the amplifier schematic, components #6, #7, and #9 — plain zig-zag lines — are ______.
questions.expl: The zig-zag (or rectangular box) line is the fixed-resistor symbol. In this amplifier they set bias, act as plate/cathode loads, and drop voltage. A plain zig-zag with no arrow is always a fixed resistor.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-24 (resistors); symbol chart Fig. 4-29 p. 4-24

questions.q: 31. In the amplifier schematic, component #8 — alternating long and short parallel lines — is a ______.
questions.expl: Alternating long and short parallel lines make the battery/cell symbol: the long line is the + terminal, the short line the −. It supplies the DC bias voltage in the circuit. (A capacitor, by contrast, is two EQUAL-length plates.)
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (cells/batteries, pp. 12-23, 12-184); symbol chart Fig. 4-29 p. 4-24

questions.q: 32. In the amplifier schematic, component #10 — a coil pair whose center-tapped secondary feeds the rectifier tube — is a ______.
questions.expl: Two windings on a common core, with the secondary center-tapped to feed the rectifier tube, is the power transformer of the supply — it steps the AC line voltage to what the rectifier needs. The center tap is the classic full-wave rectifier arrangement.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-142 (transformer); symbol chart Fig. 4-29 p. 4-24

questions.q: 33. In the amplifier schematic, component #11 — a coil sitting between two filter capacitors in the power supply — is a ______.
questions.short: An inductor used as a filter choke.
questions.expl: A single coil placed between two filter capacitors in a power supply is the filter choke (an inductor). It opposes changes in current, smoothing the pulsing DC from the rectifier into steadier DC — the L in an LC 'pi' filter.

questions.q: 34. A vacuum tube drawn with only a plate and a cathode (no grid) is a ______ — used in this schematic's power supply as the full-wave rectifier.
questions.expl: No grid means two elements — plate and cathode — which is a DIODE. In the power supply it works with the center-tapped transformer as a full-wave rectifier, converting AC to pulsing DC. Adding grids would make it a triode, tetrode, or pentode.

questions.q: 35. A vacuum tube with ONE grid (a single dashed line between plate and cathode) is a ______.
questions.short: A triode (three elements: plate, one grid, cathode).
questions.expl: One grid added to the diode's plate and cathode makes THREE elements — a triode. The grid controls the electron stream, so the triode can amplify. Two grids would be a tetrode; three, a pentode.

questions.q: 36. A vacuum tube with THREE grids (three dashed lines between plate and cathode) is a ______.
questions.short: A pentode (five elements: plate + 3 grids + cathode).
questions.expl: Count the elements: plate, three grids, and cathode = five, which is a pentode. Its three grids (control, screen, suppressor) give it high gain and stability. Two grids would make it a tetrode; one, a triode.

questions.q: 37. What do we call the opposition (resistance) to alternating current that is produced by capacitors?
questions.expl: A capacitor opposes AC by an amount called capacitive reactance, Xc = 1/(2 pi f C). It only opposes AC (not steady DC) and DROPS as frequency rises. Inductive reactance is the coil's version; mutual inductance is transformer coupling.

questions.q: #1 — Identify the schematic symbol shown (a circle with the letter V, wired in-line).
questions.expl: A meter drawn as a circle with a letter inside is named by that letter — V is a voltmeter. A voltmeter connects in PARALLEL (across) the part whose voltage you want to read. An ammeter would carry the letter A; a wattmeter, W.

questions.q: #2 — Identify the schematic symbol shown (a circle with the letter A, wired in-line, labeled 'Current').
questions.expl: The circle-with-A is an ammeter — it reads current, which is why the sheet labels it 'Current.' An ammeter is wired in SERIES so all the circuit current passes through it. A voltmeter carries a V; an ohmmeter is used on a de-energized circuit.

questions.q: #3 — Identify the schematic symbol shown (a circle enclosing a square/pulse waveform).
options: A signal (pulse) generator — a square-wave AC source
An AC generator producing a sine wave
questions.expl: A circle enclosing a waveform is a source, and the waveform tells you what it produces. A square (pulse) wave marks it as a signal or pulse generator. A plain sine wave inside the circle would mark an AC source/alternator; two straight lines would mark DC.

questions.q: #4 — Identify the schematic symbol shown (a zigzag resistor with an arrow drawn diagonally through it).
questions.expl: The zigzag is a resistor and the arrow through it means its value can be adjusted — a variable resistor. Without the arrow it would be a fixed resistor. A fuse is a single smooth S-wave, not a zigzag.

questions.q: #5 — Identify the schematic symbol shown (a plain zigzag between two wires, no arrow).
questions.expl: A plain zigzag with no arrow or wiper is a fixed resistor — its job is to limit current to a set value. Add an arrow and it becomes variable. An inductor is drawn as round humps (a coil), not a sharp zigzag.

questions.q: #6 — Identify the schematic symbol shown (a resistor with a slider tapped from a 'Current' label).
questions.short: A rheostat — a two-terminal variable resistor that controls current.
questions.expl: This is a rheostat: a variable resistor wired with two terminals (one end plus the wiper) to set how much current flows — hence the 'Current' label on the sheet. A potentiometer uses all three terminals to control voltage; a fixed resistor has no wiper.

questions.q: #7 — Identify the schematic symbol shown (a resistor tapped from a 'Voltage' label, with a third/wiper terminal).
questions.short: A potentiometer — a three-terminal variable resistor used to control voltage.
questions.expl: A potentiometer is 'a three-terminal device': both ends of the resistor plus the movable wiper. Because you pick off the wiper against the ends, it divides and controls voltage — hence the 'Voltage' label. The rheostat uses only two terminals and controls current.

questions.q: #8 — Identify the schematic symbol shown (a hinged blade lifted off a single open contact).
options: A single-pole, single-throw (SPST) switch, shown open
questions.short: An SPST switch, drawn in the open position.
questions.expl: One blade (single pole) that makes to one contact (single throw) is an SPST switch; drawn lifted off the contact means it is open. An SPDT blade would reach either of two contacts. A circuit breaker adds a resettable trip mechanism.

questions.q: #9 — Identify the schematic symbol shown (one blade that can swing to either of two separate contacts).
questions.expl: One blade (single pole) that can throw to either of two contacts (double throw) is an SPDT — a selector that routes one input to one of two outputs. SPST has only one contact; DPDT would have two blades ganged together.

questions.q: #10 — Identify the schematic symbol shown (two equal-length parallel plates with a gap, a wire to each plate).
