questions.expl: Two equal-length plates separated by a gap is a capacitor; it stores electric charge, rated in farads. The trap is the battery, whose plates ALTERNATE long and short. The FAA Fig. 4-29 chart still labels the capacitor 'condenser,' so both names are correct.

questions.q: #11 — Identify the schematic symbol shown (a solid triangle pointing into a straight bar).
questions.expl: A filled triangle (the anode) pointing at a straight bar (the cathode) is a diode — it passes current the way the triangle points and blocks the other way. A capacitor is two parallel plates; a transistor is drawn inside a circle with three leads.

questions.q: #12 — Identify the schematic symbol shown (three horizontal bars, each shorter than the one above, on a stem).
questions.expl: The shrinking three-bar 'rake' is ground — the point where the circuit returns through the aircraft's metal structure. A battery is alternating long/short plates; an antenna is drawn pointing up with a fan or T shape.

questions.q: #13 — Identify the schematic symbol shown (a wire interrupted by a double chevron).
questions.expl: The double chevron in the wire marks a connector — the plug-and-receptacle point where a harness quick-disconnects for maintenance. It is not an antenna (which points up with a fan/T) and not a plain terminal or junction (a single dot or circle).

questions.q: #14 — Identify the schematic symbol shown (a button/plunger above two contacts that are NOT bridged at rest).
questions.expl: The plunger sits above two separated contacts, so at rest the circuit is open; pressing the button bridges the contacts to make the circuit. That is a normally-open pushbutton. Its opposite, the N.C. version, is drawn with the bar resting ON the contacts. It is a momentary pushbutton, not a resettable circuit breaker.

questions.q: #15 — Identify the schematic symbol shown (a bridging bar RESTING on both contacts, plunger above).
questions.expl: The bar rests on both contacts, so at rest the circuit is made (closed); pressing the plunger lifts the bar and breaks the circuit. That is a normally-closed pushbutton — the mate to the N.O. button, which is drawn with its contacts separated. A relay adds a coil that does the switching.

questions.q: #16 — Identify the schematic symbol shown (a circle with a filament loop inside, wired in-line).
questions.expl: A circle enclosing a filament loop is a lamp or indicator light — current heats the filament and it glows. A bell or buzzer is drawn as a dome/semicircle shape, not a full circle with an internal filament.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Fig. 4-29, p. 4-24 (lamp); Ch. 12 indicator symbols

questions.q: #17 — Identify the schematic symbol shown (a single smooth S-wave between two solid terminals).
questions.expl: A single smooth S-shaped link between two terminals is a fuse — a thin metal element that melts to open the circuit on an overload, and must be replaced afterward. An inductor is several ROUND humps in a row (a coil); a resistor is a sharp zigzag.

questions.q: #18 — Identify the schematic symbol shown (alternating long and short parallel plates with + and − marks).
questions.expl: Alternating long and short plates with + and − marks is a battery; the long line is the positive terminal, and multiple plate pairs mean multiple cells. The trap is the capacitor, whose plates are EQUAL length. A bus bar is a solid heavy line.

questions.q: #19 — Identify the schematic symbol shown (a circle with the letter G and + / − terminals).
questions.expl: A circle with G is a generator — it converts mechanical rotation into electrical energy, so it is a source with + and − output terminals. Its twin is the motor (M), which does the reverse. An alternator produces AC and is labeled differently.

questions.q: #20 — Identify the schematic symbol shown (a circle with the letter M and + / − terminals).
questions.expl: A circle with M is a motor — it converts electrical energy into mechanical rotation, so it is a load fed by + and − terminals. Its twin is the generator (G), which does the reverse. A solenoid is a coil that produces straight-line pull, not rotation.

questions.q: A battery cell whose chemical reaction is NOT reversible — so once its active material is used up it cannot be recharged — is called a—
questions.short: Primary cell = one-way reaction, not rechargeable.
questions.expl: In a primary cell one of the metals is consumed as the cell discharges, and that consumption is a one-way street — the reaction cannot be run backward, so the cell cannot be recharged. A secondary (storage) cell is the opposite: its reaction IS reversible, so pushing current backward through it recharges it. Both aircraft batteries — lead-acid and nickel-cadmium — are secondary cells.

questions.q: The everyday flashlight-type 'dry cell' — the most common cell of its kind — is an example of a—
questions.short: Dry cell = the most common PRIMARY cell.
questions.expl: The dry cell is the classic non-rechargeable cell — it is the most common primary cell. 'Dry' refers to its immobilized (paste) electrolyte, not to a lack of electrolyte. Because it is a primary cell, its reaction is not reversible; trying to recharge one is dangerous and can rupture it. A storage (secondary) cell is the rechargeable kind, which the dry cell is not.

questions.q: Another name for a secondary cell — the rechargeable kind used in both aircraft batteries — is a—
questions.expl: A secondary cell is any cell whose energy-releasing reaction is reversible, so you can recharge it by forcing current backward through it — that reversibility is why it can STORE and return energy, hence 'storage cell.' A primary cell (like the dry cell) can't be recharged, so it is never a storage cell.

questions.q: The difference between a 'dry' cell and a 'wet' cell is that a dry cell uses—
options: no electrolyte at all, while a wet cell uses acid
a solid metal electrolyte, while a wet cell uses a gas
a paste (immobilized) electrolyte, while a wet cell uses a free liquid electrolyte
questions.short: Dry = paste electrolyte; wet = liquid electrolyte.
questions.expl: Both kinds have electrolyte — the difference is its form. A dry cell holds its electrolyte as a thick paste so it can't spill (a flashlight cell). A wet cell carries a free liquid electrolyte, like the sulfuric-acid solution sloshing inside a flooded lead-acid battery. So 'dry' never means 'no electrolyte'; it means the electrolyte is immobilized.

questions.q: Memory effect (and the maintenance headaches that come with it) has caused nickel-cadmium batteries to be replaced in many applications by ___ batteries.
questions.expl: The handbook notes that in many applications sealed lead-acid batteries 'are gaining in use over flooded lead acid and Ni-Cad batteries,' precisely because SLA batteries do not suffer the ni-cad's voltage-depression ('memory') trait and so need no scheduled deep-cycle maintenance. Plain flooded lead-acid is the OLD vented type SLA improves on, and a primary dry-cell isn't even rechargeable — so the replacement is specifically the SEALED lead-acid battery. (Industry also calls it valve-regulated lead-acid / VRLA; the -30B term is 'sealed lead acid / SLA.')
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, pp. 12-92-12-93 (Sealed Lead Acid batteries gaining over ni-cad)

questions.q: The nickel-cadmium 'memory effect' is best described as—
options: a permanent GAIN in capacity earned by deep-cycling the battery
a loss of usable capacity after repeated shallow (partial) discharges, so the battery seems full but really isn't
the battery electronically storing its own serial number for tracking
questions.short: Memory effect = lost usable capacity from repeated shallow discharge.
questions.expl: When a ni-cad is repeatedly recharged after only partial (shallow) discharges — the classic standby/overcharge pattern — it starts acting as if its full capacity is only the small slice it habitually uses. The handbook explains this shows up 'only when a full discharge is attempted,' so 'it is possible to believe a full charge exists, while in fact it does not.' It is a LOSS of usable capacity, never a gain, and it has nothing to do with electronic tracking.

questions.q: The handbook's technically correct name for what is commonly (and erroneously) called the nickel-cadmium 'memory effect' is—
questions.expl: The handbook states the trait 'is technically known as "voltage depression" and commonly but erroneously called "memory effect."' It comes from constant overcharge with infrequent deep discharges. Don't confuse it with thermal runaway (a heat/resistance loop) or sulfation (a lead-acid plate problem) — both are different ni-cad or lead-acid faults.

questions.q: When a nickel-cadmium battery shows voltage depression ('memory'), the standard corrective action is to—
options: deep-cycle it: fully discharge each cell, then recharge (recondition it)
add sulfuric acid to restore its lost capacity
swap its potassium hydroxide electrolyte for baking soda
questions.short: Fix memory / voltage depression by deep-cycling (reconditioning).
questions.expl: Because voltage depression comes from never fully discharging the cells, the cure is to do exactly that: run a full, deep discharge and then a complete recharge (reconditioning), which restores the usable capacity. This is why the handbook says ni-cads require 'scheduled deep cycle maintenance' while SLA batteries do not. You never pour sulfuric acid into a ni-cad (its electrolyte is an alkali, KOH), and baking soda is a neutralizer, not an electrolyte.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-93 (ni-cads require scheduled deep-cycle maintenance) — deep-cycle reconditioning is standard ni-cad practice

questions.q: The electrolyte in a lead-acid battery is—
questions.short: Lead-acid electrolyte = sulfuric acid + water (an ACID).
questions.expl: A lead-acid cell's electrolyte is sulfuric acid (battery acid) in distilled water — roughly 30% acid, 70% water in a fresh, charged cell. Potassium hydroxide is the NICKEL-CADMIUM battery's electrolyte (an alkali), the classic swap trap. Boric acid isn't an electrolyte here at all — it's what you'd use to NEUTRALIZE a ni-cad spill.

questions.q: A spill of lead-acid electrolyte, or battery acid on the skin, is neutralized with—
questions.expl: You neutralize an acid with a base: the handbook has you apply bicarbonate of soda (baking soda) to spilled sulfuric-acid electrolyte, and the battery sump pad is soaked in a sodium-bicarbonate solution. Boric acid and vinegar are themselves ACIDS — those are for the ni-cad's ALKALINE spills, not lead-acid. Matching the neutralizer to the electrolyte is a favorite exam trap.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-91 (neutralize acid with bicarbonate of soda)

questions.q: Each individual cell of a lead-acid battery produces about—
questions.short: Lead-acid cell ~= 2 V (12 V = 6 cells, 24 V = 12 cells).
questions.expl: A lead-acid cell is rated at about 2 volts (roughly 2.1 fresh off the charger). So a 12-volt battery is six cells in series and a 24-volt battery is twelve cells. The 1.2-volt figure belongs to the NICKEL-CADMIUM cell, which is why a 24-volt ni-cad needs about 19-20 cells instead of 12. Anchor it: the acid cell is the higher-voltage cell.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-89 (Battery Ratings — ~2 V per lead-acid cell)

questions.q: The state of charge of a lead-acid battery is checked with a hydrometer, which measures the electrolyte's—
questions.expl: As a lead-acid cell discharges, the sulfuric acid is used up and the electrolyte weakens toward water, so its specific gravity (its weight compared with water) genuinely tracks the charge — about 1.275-1.300 fully charged, dropping toward 1.150 discharged. A hydrometer floats higher in dense (charged) acid. This trick works only on lead-acid; a ni-cad's specific gravity barely moves, so a hydrometer can't tell you a ni-cad's charge.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-90 (hydrometer / specific gravity = state of charge)

questions.q: In the aircraft, a lead-acid battery is kept charged by the—
options: pulsed-discharge method controlled by the battery relay
constant-current method, because the generator output current is fixed
constant-voltage method, because a voltage regulator holds the generator voltage steady
questions.short: Aircraft charging = CONSTANT VOLTAGE (regulator holds voltage).
questions.expl: The handbook states the aircraft charges its battery by the constant-voltage method, 'since the generator voltage is held constant by use of a voltage regulator.' With voltage pinned, the battery draws a big current when low and almost none when full — it self-tapers. Constant CURRENT (fixed current, series-connected batteries) is the bench/fast-charge method and risks overcharge near the end; there is no 'pulsed-discharge' charging.

questions.q: The electrolyte in a nickel-cadmium battery is—
questions.short: Ni-cad electrolyte = potassium hydroxide (KOH), an ALKALI.
questions.expl: A ni-cad's electrolyte is potassium hydroxide (KOH) in distilled water — an ALKALI (a base), the chemical opposite of the lead-acid battery's sulfuric ACID. That single acid-vs-alkali split is why the two batteries need opposite neutralizers and must never share a service area. Boric acid isn't the electrolyte — it's what you use to neutralize a ni-cad spill.

questions.q: A spill of nickel-cadmium electrolyte, or the alkali on skin or clothing, is neutralized with—
options: boric acid solution or vinegar (an acid)
questions.short: Ni-cad (alkaline) -> boric acid or vinegar (an ACID).
questions.expl: The ni-cad electrolyte is a caustic alkali, so you neutralize it with an ACID — the handbook calls for vinegar or a dilute boric-acid solution, then a clear-water rinse. Baking soda is a BASE (that's for the lead-acid ACID spill), and adding more potassium hydroxide would just make the spill worse. Opposite battery, opposite neutralizer.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-92 (neutralize alkali with vinegar or boric acid)

questions.q: Each individual cell of a nickel-cadmium battery produces about—
questions.short: Ni-cad cell ~= 1.2-1.25 V (24 V needs ~19-20 cells).
questions.expl: A ni-cad cell's open-circuit voltage is about 1.25 volts — noticeably lower than the lead-acid cell's ~2 volts. Because each cell is lower, a ni-cad needs MORE cells for the same bus voltage: roughly 19-20 cells for a 24-volt ni-cad versus 12 cells for a 24-volt lead-acid. The 2-volt figure is the lead-acid cell (the swap trap).
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-91 (ni-cad cell ~1.25 V); p. 12-93 (~twenty cells matched)

questions.q: For a nickel-cadmium battery, the specific gravity of the electrolyte—
options: does NOT indicate the state of charge, because it barely changes
is read with a hydrometer to find the exact charge
falls steadily as the battery discharges, just like a lead-acid battery
questions.short: Ni-cad SG barely moves -> useless for state of charge.
questions.expl: In a ni-cad the potassium-hydroxide electrolyte only ferries ions between the plates; it isn't consumed the way sulfuric acid is, so its specific gravity stays nearly constant whether the battery is full or flat. That means a hydrometer tells you almost nothing about a ni-cad's charge — the handbook says a ni-cad's true energy can only be found by a scheduled discharge on the bench. Only the lead-acid battery's specific gravity tracks its charge.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-93 (ni-cad charge found by bench discharge, not SG)

questions.q: A nickel-cadmium battery is commonly FAST-charged by the—
options: constant-voltage method (voltage held steady, current allowed to fall)
constant-current method (current held steady, voltage allowed to rise)
questions.short: Ni-cad fast charge = CONSTANT CURRENT (voltage varies).
questions.expl: In constant-current (fast) charging the charger forces a fixed current in and lets whatever voltage is needed appear across the battery. That's the mirror image of the aircraft's constant-VOLTAGE lead-acid charging, where voltage is fixed and current tapers. Constant current fills a ni-cad quickly but must be watched near the end, since holding current after the cells are full drives heat and gassing. 'Specific-gravity' is a test method, not a charging method.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-91 (constant-current vs constant-voltage) — ni-cad fast charge = constant current is standard practice

questions.q: A nickel-cadmium hazard the sealed lead-acid battery avoids: rising cell temperature lowers the cell's internal resistance, which pulls even more current and makes even more heat — a self-feeding loop called—
questions.short: Rising temp -> falling internal resistance -> THERMAL RUNAWAY.
questions.expl: Heat lowers a ni-cad's internal resistance; lower resistance lets more charging current through; more current makes still more heat — a loop that can feed on itself until cells vent, rupture, or explode. That's thermal runaway, and it's a big reason ni-cads need careful temperature-watched charging. Voltage depression is the capacity illusion cured by deep discharge; sulfation is a LEAD-ACID plate problem.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-93 (cell reversal -> high pressure and heat) — thermal runaway is standard ni-cad behavior

questions.q: You always neutralize a battery's electrolyte with a chemical of the OPPOSITE type. So an ACID electrolyte (like a lead-acid battery's) is neutralized with a—
options: base, such as baking soda (sodium bicarbonate)
salt, such as ordinary table salt
stronger acid, such as boric acid
questions.short: Acid electrolyte -> neutralize with a BASE (baking soda).
questions.expl: Neutralizing is chemical opposites: acids are canceled by bases and bases are canceled by acids. The lead-acid battery holds sulfuric ACID, so you neutralize it with the BASE baking soda. The nickel-cadmium battery holds an alkaline base (KOH), so you neutralize IT with an acid (vinegar or boric acid). Adding another acid to acid, or salt, does nothing useful.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-91 (lead-acid -> baking soda); p. 12-92 (ni-cad -> boric acid/vinegar)

questions.q: A mechanic measures about 2 volts across a single healthy cell. That cell belongs to a—
questions.expl: Cell voltage is a quick tell: a lead-acid cell sits at about 2 volts, while a nickel-cadmium cell is only about 1.2-1.25 volts. So a 2-volt reading points to lead-acid. A common dry (primary) cell is about 1.5 volts and isn't a rechargeable aircraft cell anyway. Anchor the pair: 2 V = lead-acid, 1.2 V = ni-cad.

questions.q: Infinitely large resistance, with no current able to flow, is an example of which type of circuit malfunction?
questions.short: Infinite resistance / broken path = OPEN circuit.
questions.expl: The handbook defines an open circuit as 'a circuit that is not a complete or continuous path,' and states plainly that 'an open circuit represents an infinitely large resistance.' The path is broken, so no current flows. A short circuit is the opposite — a near-zero-resistance path with EXCESSIVE current — and a ground fault is a specific unintended path to structure. Broken path + infinite resistance = open.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-79 (open circuit = infinitely large resistance)

questions.q: A short circuit is best described as—
options: an unintentional low-resistance path that lets excessive current flow
a break in the path, so no current flows at all
a normal path carrying exactly its rated current
questions.short: Short = unintentional LOW-resistance path -> excessive current.
questions.expl: The handbook defines a short circuit as 'an unintentional low resistance path between two components... or between a component/conductor and ground,' and warns it 'usually creates high current flow, which burns out or causes damage.' Near-zero resistance means Ohm's law forces a huge current. The broken-path/no-current description is an OPEN circuit — the exact opposite fault.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-78 (short circuit = unintentional low-resistance path)

questions.q: An unintended low-resistance path from a live conductor to the aircraft structure (ground) is called a—
questions.short: Conductor-to-structure short = grounded circuit / ground fault.
questions.expl: A ground fault is a short circuit whose unintended low-resistance path runs from a conductor to ground/structure — the handbook's short-circuit definition specifically includes a path 'between a component/conductor and ground.' It causes high current, just like any short. An open circuit is a broken path (no current), and 'in-phase' is an AC waveform relationship, not a fault at all.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-78 (short circuit to ground = grounded circuit)

questions.q: The portion of a transformer's magnetic flux that escapes the core and does NOT link both windings is called—
questions.short: Flux that escapes / doesn't couple both coils = LEAKAGE FLUX.
questions.expl: No transformer is perfect: the handbook explains that not all the magnetic lines set up by the primary cut across the secondary, and 'a certain amount of the magnetic flux, called leakage flux, leaks out of the magnetic circuit.' How well the primary's flux couples into the secondary is the 'coefficient of coupling.' Eddy currents are swirling currents induced IN the core; iron loss is a heat loss — neither is the flux that escapes.

questions.q: The swirling currents induced in a transformer's iron core — reduced by building the core from thin, insulated laminations — are the—
questions.short: Swirling induced core currents = EDDY CURRENTS (cut by laminations).
questions.expl: The handbook says eddy-current loss 'is caused by electric currents (eddy currents) induced in the transformer core by the varying magnetic fields,' and 'to reduce eddy current losses, cores are made of laminations coated with an insulation, which reduces the circulation of induced currents.' Leakage flux is flux that escapes the core; copper loss is the heat from the windings' own resistance — a different loss entirely.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-67 (eddy current loss, reduced by laminations)

questions.q: In a transformer, the hysteresis loss plus the eddy-current loss together make up the—
questions.expl: The handbook splits transformer losses into 'copper' and 'iron' losses, and states 'the iron losses are of two types: hysteresis loss and eddy current loss.' Hysteresis is the energy to keep re-magnetizing the core each half-cycle; eddy-current loss is from induced core currents. Copper loss instead comes from the winding wire's own resistance, and leakage flux is escaped flux, not a heat loss.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-67 (iron losses = hysteresis + eddy current)

questions.q: A transformer will operate on—
options: either AC or steady DC equally well
alternating current (or pulsating DC), because it needs a changing magnetic field
questions.short: Transformer needs a CHANGING field -> AC (or pulsating DC), not pure DC.
questions.expl: A transformer works by mutual induction — the primary's changing magnetic field induces a voltage in the secondary. The handbook says a transformer 'can also be used with pulsating DC, but a pure DC voltage cannot be used, since only a varying voltage creates the varying magnetic field that is the basis of the mutual induction process.' Steady DC makes a steady (unchanging) field, which induces nothing in the secondary.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-65 (transformer needs a varying field; not pure DC)

questions.q: A device used to change (convert) DC into AC — for example, to run 400-cycle AC instruments from an aircraft's DC bus — is a(n)—
questions.expl: The handbook says an inverter 'is used in some aircraft systems to convert a portion of the aircraft's DC power to AC,' typically 400-cycle AC for instruments, radios, and lighting. Don't mix it up: a rectifier goes the OTHER way (AC into DC), and a transformer only changes AC from one voltage level to another — it can't change DC into AC.

questions.q: A device that transforms AC into DC — by allowing current to flow in only one direction — is a(n)—
questions.expl: The handbook states 'a rectifier is a device that transforms AC into DC by limiting or regulating the direction of current flow' (most modern ones are solid-state diodes). Remember the pair by direction: a rectifier takes AC to DC, while an inverter takes DC to AC. A transformer changes only the voltage level of AC and does not rectify.

questions.q: In a purely CAPACITIVE AC circuit, the current—
options: is exactly in phase with the voltage
questions.short: Capacitive: current LEADS voltage (the ICE half of ELI-the-ICE-man).
questions.expl: In a capacitor, current leads voltage — a capacitor draws its charging current first, before the voltage across it builds up. The mnemonic ELI the ICE man captures it: in the 'ICE' half, current comes before voltage across the capacitor, so current leads. In an INDUCTOR the current instead lags. Heads-up: FAA-H-8083-30B teaches the lead/lag concept and capacitive reactance on pp. 12-47-12-48 and 12-54 but does not print the ELI-the-ICE-man mnemonic itself — it's a standard electronics memory aid.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, pp. 12-47-12-48 (phase / lead & lag) — ELI-the-ICE-man is a standard AC mnemonic, not verbatim in -30B

questions.q: In a purely INDUCTIVE AC circuit, the current—
options: is exactly in phase with the voltage
questions.short: Inductive: current LAGS voltage / voltage leads (the ELI half).
questions.expl: In an inductor, voltage leads the current — the coil opposes any change in current, so the current is slow to build and lags behind the applied voltage. The mnemonic ELI the ICE man captures it: in the 'ELI' half, voltage comes before current across the inductor, so voltage leads and current lags. A capacitor is the reverse, where current leads. The lead/lag concept is in -30B on pp. 12-47-12-48 and 12-58; the mnemonic is a standard electronics aid.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, pp. 12-47-12-48, 12-58 (phase / inductive reactance) — ELI-the-ICE-man is a standard AC mnemonic, not verbatim in -30B

questions.q: In a purely RESISTIVE AC circuit (only resistance, no capacitance or inductance), the voltage and current are—
questions.short: Resistive: voltage and current are IN PHASE.
questions.expl: A pure resistance has no reactance to delay or advance anything, so the current rises and falls in lockstep with the voltage — they reach their peaks and zeros at the same time, which is what 'in phase' means. The 90-degree shifts belong to reactive parts (leading in a capacitor, lagging in an inductor), not to a plain resistor.

questions.q: The memory aid 'ELI the ICE man' packs in two facts: in an inductor (L) voltage (E) leads current (I), and in a capacitor (C) current (I) leads voltage (E). So the 'ICE' half of the phrase describes a—
options: inductive circuit, where voltage leads current
resistive circuit, where voltage and current are in phase
capacitive circuit, where current leads voltage
questions.short: 'ICE' = capacitive, current leads; 'ELI' = inductive, voltage leads.
questions.expl: Read the letters in order. In the word ICE, current sits before voltage with the capacitor between them — so in a capacitor, current leads voltage. In the word ELI, voltage sits before current around the inductor — so in an inductor, voltage leads current. A resistor keeps voltage and current in phase and isn't part of the phrase. The mnemonic is a standard electronics aid; -30B teaches the underlying lead/lag on pp. 12-47-12-48.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, pp. 12-47-12-48 (lead & lag) — ELI-the-ICE-man is a standard AC mnemonic, not verbatim in -30B

questions.q: A storage battery is a group of electrochemical cells. Inside a cell that is DELIVERING power, the energy conversion taking place is—
questions.expl: 'Chemical energy can be converted into electricity; the most common form of this is the battery.' A cell frees more electrons on one metal than on the other, building a voltage that pushes current the moment you close the circuit. The REVERSE — electrical → chemical — is what happens while you CHARGE a secondary cell, but a battery's own job (delivering power) is chemical → electrical. So a statement that says 'a battery converts electrical energy into chemical energy' is FALSE as a description of what a battery does.

questions.q: A primary cell differs from a secondary cell in that a primary cell—
options: cannot be recharged, because its chemical reaction is not reversible
delivers alternating current instead of direct current
can be recharged hundreds of times
questions.expl: In a primary cell one of the metals is consumed as the cell discharges, and 'because of this consumption, the charging process is not reversible.' The handbook warns that trying to recharge a primary cell 'is usually dangerous and can lead to a battery explosion.' A secondary cell's reaction IS reversible, so it recharges. Every battery makes DC, so the AC option is a throwaway.

questions.q: The type of cell used in both the lead-acid and the nickel-cadmium aircraft battery — the kind whose reaction is reversible so it can be recharged, and the most common type today — is the—
questions.expl: 'A secondary cell is any kind of electrolytic cell in which the electrochemical reaction that releases energy is reversible.' You recharge it by pushing current backward through it. Both the lead-acid and the nickel-cadmium aircraft batteries are secondary cells. The dry cell is the everyday PRIMARY (flashlight) cell — it can't be recharged.

questions.q: On the worksheet, the three primary-cell types listed are carbon-zinc, alkaline, and—
questions.expl: Your AIM sheet drills the classic primary-cell trio carbon-zinc / alkaline / mercury. Divergence to know: the FAA handbook's own examples of 'the most common primary cells today' are alkaline, silver-oxide, and lithium (plus the older carbon-zinc) — it does NOT list mercury. Lead-acid and nickel-cadmium are wrong here regardless, because both are SECONDARY (rechargeable) cells, not primary. Use the worksheet trio on the AIM sheet; know the FAA examples for the written.

questions.q: The electrolyte in a lead-acid storage battery is—
questions.expl: 'The electrolyte is sulfuric acid (battery acid)' mixed with distilled water — about 30% acid, 70% water by volume in a new, fully charged cell. Potassium hydroxide is the OTHER battery's electrolyte (nickel-cadmium), so it's the classic swap trap. Pure water alone carries no charge — the acid is what makes the ions.

questions.q: In a fully CHARGED lead-acid cell, the positive plate is made of—
questions.short: Positive plate charged = lead peroxide / PbO2.
questions.expl: In a charged lead-acid cell 'the positive electrode is lead peroxide, and the negative electrode is lead' — the negative plate is spongy lead. Lead sulfate (PbSO4) is what BOTH plates turn into as the cell DISCHARGES, so it's the trap for 'charged.' Memory hook: charged positive = the OXIDE (lead peroxide/dioxide); charged negative = plain lead.

questions.q: As a lead-acid cell DISCHARGES, both the positive and negative plates gradually change into—
options: lead peroxide, while the electrolyte gets stronger
spongy lead, while the electrolyte turns to acid
lead sulfate, while the electrolyte weakens toward water
questions.short: Discharge → lead sulfate on BOTH plates; electrolyte dilutes toward water.
questions.expl: On discharge the sulfate ions leave the acid and join the lead in both plates to form lead sulfate (PbSO4), while oxygen and hydrogen combine into water (H2O). So the acid gets used up — the electrolyte weakens toward water — and the specific gravity falls from about 1.270 down toward 1.150. Charging drives the reaction backward: sulfate goes back into solution, the acid strengthens, and the plates return to lead peroxide and lead.

questions.q: Space is deliberately left in the bottom of a lead-acid cell case, below the plates, in order to—
options: give shed material (sediment) room to collect without shorting the plates
hold a reserve of extra electrolyte for the cell
let the plates expand downward when the cell heats up
questions.expl: As a cell ages, active material sheds off the plates. The ribbed separators 'provide a path for sediment to settle to the bottom of the cell,' and the well below the plates lets that debris pile up clear of the plate edges. If sediment ever bridges the bottoms of a positive and a negative plate, it shorts the cell internally and kills its output — the empty space is what buys time before that happens.

questions.q: A lead-acid battery rated at 12 volts is built from—
options: 3 cells in series, each about 4 volts
6 cells in series, each about 2 volts
12 cells in series, each about 1 volt
questions.expl: 'A lead-acid cell is normally rated at approximately 2 volts,' so a 12-volt battery is six cells in series and a 24-volt battery is twelve. (Fresh off the charger a cell reads about 2.2 V, but it settles to ~2 V.) Contrast the nickel-cadmium cell, which is only about 1.25 V — so a 24-volt ni-cad needs about 19-20 cells, not 12.

questions.q: The state of charge of a lead-acid battery is checked with a hydrometer, an instrument that measures the electrolyte's—
options: specific gravity (its weight compared with water)
questions.short: Hydrometer = specific gravity of the electrolyte.
questions.expl: 'The state of charge of a battery is indicated by the density of the electrolyte and is checked by a hydrometer, an instrument that measures the specific gravity.' The float rides high in dense (charged) acid and sinks in weak (discharged) acid. This trick works ONLY on lead-acid: as it discharges the acid genuinely weakens, so specific gravity tracks the charge. (A nickel-cadmium's specific gravity barely moves, so a hydrometer tells you nothing about its charge.)

questions.q: A hydrometer reading of about 1.270-1.300 on a lead-acid cell indicates the cell is—
options: in a high state of charge
questions.expl: The handbook's own ranges: 1.300-1.275 = high state of charge, 1.275-1.240 = medium, 1.240-1.200 = low. A new, fully charged aircraft cell reads about 1.300 (roughly 1.270 warm); after discharge the specific gravity drops to about 1.150. So a reading up near 1.3 means charged, and a reading down near 1.15 means flat.

questions.q: The open-circuit voltage of a single lead-acid cell can be estimated from its specific gravity using the shop rule cell voltage ≈ specific gravity + 0.84. A cell reading 1.265 therefore develops about—
questions.expl: Add about 0.84 to the specific-gravity number and you land near the cell's open-circuit voltage: 1.265 + 0.84 ≈ 2.10 V, which matches the handbook's '~2 volts per lead-acid cell.' Heads-up: this SG-plus-0.84 formula is a shop rule of thumb — it is not printed word-for-word in FAA-H-8083-30B, but it lines up with the handbook's cell-voltage figure. About 1.2 V is the NICKEL-CADMIUM cell value; 12 V is a whole six-cell battery, not one cell.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-89 (~2 V/cell) — SG+0.84 is a shop rule of thumb, not verbatim in -30B

questions.q: When taking a hydrometer reading, distilled water that is needed to top off the cells should be added—
options: just before the reading, so the level is correct
only while the battery is on charge and gassing
after the reading is taken, never just before
questions.expl: 'Always take hydrometer readings before adding distilled water, never after.' Fresh water sits on top and hasn't mixed in yet, so a sample drawn right after topping off is watered-down and reads falsely low — it doesn't represent the true strength of the electrolyte. Give the charge time to stir it in, or simply read before you fill.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-91 (take readings before adding water)

questions.q: A hydrometer reading must be temperature-corrected because the electrolyte's apparent specific gravity changes with temperature. Per the FAA handbook, correction is needed when the electrolyte temperature is—
options: outside the 70 °F to 90 °F band (above 90 °F or below 70 °F)
questions.short: No correction 70-90 °F; correct outside that band (80 °F midpoint).
questions.expl: 'No correction is necessary when the temperature is between 70 °F and 90 °F... When temperatures are greater than 90 °F or less than 70 °F, it is necessary to apply a correction factor.' Hot acid reads low, cold acid reads high, so corrections are ADDED or SUBTRACTED per the manufacturer's chart. Note the AIM/industry shortcut uses 80 °F as the reference temperature — that's simply the midpoint of the handbook's no-correction band, not a separate rule.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-90 (temperature correction) — 80 °F reference is the industry midpoint of the FAA 70-90 °F band

questions.q: Spilled lead-acid electrolyte, or acid on the skin, is neutralized with—
questions.expl: Acid is neutralized with a base: 'if the acid does contact the skin, wash the area thoroughly with water and then apply bicarbonate of soda,' and the battery sump pad is soaked in a sodium-bicarbonate solution to catch acid gases. Do NOT reach for boric acid or vinegar here — those are ACIDS, used to neutralize the nickel-cadmium's ALKALINE spills. Matching the neutralizer to the electrolyte is a favorite exam trap.

questions.q: When a lead-acid battery is being charged, the gas it gives off is—
options: an explosive mixture of hydrogen and oxygen
questions.short: Charging makes explosive H2 + O2 — no sparks, loosen the caps.
questions.expl: 'When a storage battery is being charged, it generates a certain amount of hydrogen and oxygen. Since this is an explosive mixture, it is important to take steps to prevent ignition.' Loosen the vent caps and leave them in place so pressure can escape, keep open flame and sparks away, and switch the charger off with a remote switch BEFORE connecting or disconnecting leads so you don't strike an arc at the terminals.

questions.q: In the constant-VOLTAGE charging method, as the battery approaches full charge the charging current—
options: automatically tapers off, dropping to about 1 ampere
climbs steadily higher until the battery is full
stays exactly the same the whole time
questions.short: Constant voltage → current starts high, tapers to ~1 A.
questions.expl: 'In the constant voltage method... the current at the start of the process is high but automatically tapers off, reaching a value of approximately 1 ampere when the battery is fully charged.' As the cell fills, its own voltage rises to meet the fixed source voltage, so less and less current is forced through — the battery throttles itself. That self-limiting is why constant voltage 'requires less time and supervision.'

questions.q: Which charging method takes LESS time and needs less supervision, but must NOT be used to charge batteries of different states of charge together on one line?
questions.expl: 'The constant voltage method requires less time and supervision than does the constant current method.' Because it holds voltage fixed and lets current find its own level, each battery on the line draws whatever current its state of charge calls for — so batteries in constant-voltage charging are connected in PARALLEL (same voltage), and mixing wildly different states of charge lets a low battery hog current. The constant-current method instead risks OVERcharging near the end and takes longer.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-91 (constant voltage vs constant current)

questions.q: The constant-CURRENT charging method holds the current steady the entire time. Its main danger is—
options: overcharging the battery toward the end of the charge
questions.short: Constant current → overcharge risk near the end.
questions.expl: 'In the constant current method, the current remains almost constant during the entire charging process. This method requires a longer time to charge a battery fully and, toward the end of the process, presents the danger of overcharging, if care is not exercised.' Because current keeps being forced in after the cells are full, the extra energy just heats the battery and boils the electrolyte. Batteries in constant-current charging are wired in SERIES so the same current passes through each.

questions.q: In a constant-current charging setup, the batteries being charged are connected—
options: in series, so the same current flows through each one
in a series-parallel bank matched by capacity
in parallel, so each sees the same voltage
questions.short: Constant current = SERIES; constant voltage = PARALLEL.
questions.expl: Constant-current charging forces one fixed current down a single path, so the batteries sit in SERIES — the identical current passes through every cell in the string. Constant-VOLTAGE charging instead holds one voltage across the batteries, so they hang in PARALLEL and each draws its own current. Quick pair to memorize: constant CURRENT → series; constant VOLTAGE → parallel. (This series/parallel detail is standard shop practice; the handbook describes the two methods on p. 12-91.)

questions.q: In the aircraft, the storage battery is kept charged by the engine-driven generating system. That system charges the battery by the—
options: constant-current method, because the generator output current is fixed
constant-voltage method, because a voltage regulator holds the generator voltage steady
pulsed-discharge method controlled by the battery relay
questions.short: Aircraft charging = constant VOLTAGE (regulator holds voltage).
questions.expl: 'In the aircraft, the storage battery is charged by direct current from the aircraft generator system. This method of charging is the constant voltage method, since the generator voltage is held constant by use of a voltage regulator.' The regulator pins the bus at a set voltage; the battery then draws a big current when low and almost none when full — exactly the self-tapering behavior of constant-voltage charging.

questions.q: Connecting two identical batteries in PARALLEL (positive to positive, negative to negative) increases the—
options: both the voltage and the capacity together
voltage, while the capacity stays the same
ampere-hour capacity, while the voltage stays the same
questions.short: Parallel → more capacity, same voltage. Series → more voltage, same capacity.
questions.expl: 'Connecting batteries in parallel increases ampere-hour capacity. Connecting batteries in series increases the total voltage but not the ampere-hour capacity.' Think of parallel as adding more plate area / more fuel tanks at the same pressure (voltage). Series stacks the voltages but the same single current path limits capacity. This is also why constant-voltage chargers wire batteries in parallel and constant-current chargers wire them in series.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-89 (Battery Ratings — series vs parallel)

questions.q: A battery's capacity is given as an ampere-hour rating. Per FAA-H-8083-30B, the discharge time used as the basis for rating AIRPLANE battery capacity is—
questions.short: FAA handbook: 5-hour rate for airplane batteries.
questions.expl: 'For airplane batteries, a period of 5 hours has been established as the discharge time in rating battery capacity.' A 1 ampere-hour battery could supply 1 amp for 1 hour (or 2 amps for half an hour), but heavy discharge heats the battery and lowers the total output, so a standard rating time is fixed. IMPORTANT DIVERGENCE: some nickel-cadmium and industry references rate capacity at the 1-HOUR (C1) rate — but the -30B General handbook (what the written is built from) says 5 hours, so 5-hour is the handbook-supported answer.

questions.q: A battery with a capacity of 1 ampere-hour should be able to supply—
options: 1 amp for 1 hour, or 2 amps for half an hour, before being fully discharged
questions.short: Amp-hour = amps × hours it can be delivered.
questions.expl: 'A battery with a capacity of 1 ampere-hour should be able to continuously supply a current of 1 amp to a load for exactly 1 hour, or 2 amps for 1/2 hour, or 1/3 amp for 3 hours.' The rating is just current multiplied by time. Real output shrinks under heavy loads — a hard, fast discharge heats the battery and cuts the total ampere-hours you actually get.

questions.q: In a charged nickel-cadmium cell, the active materials are—
options: nickel hydroxide on the positive plate and metallic cadmium on the negative plate
carbon on the positive plate and zinc on the negative plate
lead peroxide on the positive plate and spongy lead on the negative plate
questions.short: Ni-cad charged: positive = nickel hydroxide, negative = cadmium.
questions.expl: 'Active materials in nickel-cadmium cells are nickel hydroxide (NiOOH) in the charged positive plate and sponge cadmium (Cd) in the charged negative plate.' The name tells you both: NICKEL (hydroxide) positive, CADMIUM negative. Lead peroxide/lead is the LEAD-ACID pair; carbon/zinc is the old dry (primary) cell.

questions.q: The open-circuit voltage of a single nickel-cadmium cell is approximately—
questions.expl: 'The typical open circuit cell voltage of a nickel-cadmium battery is about 1.25 volts.' That's noticeably lower than the lead-acid cell's ~2 volts, so a nickel-cadmium battery needs MORE cells for the same bus voltage — roughly 19-20 cells for a 24-volt ni-cad versus 12 cells for a 24-volt lead-acid.

questions.q: Unlike a lead-acid battery, the specific gravity of a nickel-cadmium battery's electrolyte—
options: falls steadily as the battery discharges, just like lead-acid
rises steadily as the battery discharges
does not change appreciably with state of charge, so it can't be used to judge the charge
questions.short: Ni-cad SG barely moves → useless for state of charge.
questions.expl: In a ni-cad, the potassium-hydroxide electrolyte only carries ions between the plates; it isn't consumed the way sulfuric acid is, so its specific gravity stays nearly constant whether the battery is full or flat. That means a hydrometer tells you almost nothing about a ni-cad's charge. (This SG-doesn't-move behavior is standard ni-cad knowledge; the handbook makes the same point by saying a ni-cad's true energy can only be found by a scheduled discharge on the bench, p. 12-93.)
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, pp. 12-92-12-93 (Ni-Cad operation / bench energy test) — SG-constant is standard ni-cad behavior

questions.q: The ONLY reliable way to determine a nickel-cadmium battery's true state of charge is by—
options: performing a measured discharge (a capacity/energy test)
reading the electrolyte specific gravity with a hydrometer
questions.short: Ni-cad charge = measured discharge, not SG, not voltage.
questions.expl: A ni-cad's specific gravity barely moves and its terminal voltage stays nearly flat almost all the way down, so neither reveals the real charge. The handbook notes a ni-cad's 'voltage depression' (mis-called 'memory') 'is only detectable when a full discharge is attempted,' and that 'Ni-Cads must have a scheduled energy test performed on the bench' because you can't read their energy level on the aircraft. Bottom line: to KNOW the charge, you discharge it and measure.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-93 (voltage depression / bench energy test)

questions.q: Because a nickel-cadmium cell's terminal voltage stays nearly constant through most of the discharge, its discharge voltage curve is—
options: rising the whole time it discharges
nearly flat, dropping off sharply only near the very end
a steady, even downhill slope from full to empty
questions.short: Ni-cad discharge voltage is nearly flat, then a cliff.
questions.expl: A ni-cad holds its voltage up almost all the way down, then falls off a cliff near the end. That flat curve is great for equipment (steady voltage) but terrible for a fuel gauge — the voltage doesn't sag enough to warn you the battery is nearly empty, which (together with an unchanging specific gravity) is why the real state of charge can only be found by a measured discharge. (The flat-curve trait is standard ni-cad behavior; the handbook covers ni-cad operation on p. 12-92.)
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-92 (Operation of Nickel-Cadmium Cells) — flat discharge curve is standard ni-cad behavior

questions.q: The electrolyte level in a nickel-cadmium cell is HIGHEST when the battery is—
questions.short: Level rises on charge → HIGHEST at full charge; LOWEST discharged.
questions.expl: 'During discharge, the plates absorb a quantity of the electrolyte. On recharge, the level of the electrolyte rises and, at full charge, the electrolyte is at its highest level.' So a ni-cad's level swings the opposite way you might guess: high when charged, low when discharged. This single fact drives the watering rule in the next question.

questions.q: Distilled water should be added to a nickel-cadmium battery ONLY when the battery is—
questions.short: Water a ni-cad ONLY when fully charged — else it spews on charge.
questions.expl: 'Water should be added only when the battery is fully charged,' because that's when the electrolyte is at its highest level. If you top a ni-cad off while it's discharged (low level), the level then RISES as you charge it and pushes electrolyte out the vents — messy, corrosive, and it strips the cell. So charge first, then water. (This is the exact opposite of the trap answer 'add water when discharged.')
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-92 (add water only when fully charged)

questions.q: Spilled nickel-cadmium electrolyte, or the alkali on skin or clothes, is neutralized with—
questions.short: Ni-cad (alkaline) → boric acid or vinegar (an acid).
questions.expl: The ni-cad's electrolyte is a caustic ALKALI, so you neutralize it with an ACID: 'neutralize the alkali immediately with vinegar or dilute boric acid solution... then rinse with clear water.' The sump pad is soaked in 3% boric acid, and a compartment being converted from lead-acid is neutralized with ammonia or boric acid. Do NOT use baking soda here — that's the base you use on the ACID (lead-acid) battery. Opposite battery, opposite neutralizer.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-92 (neutralize alkali with vinegar or boric acid)

questions.q: A small amount of white crystalline deposit ("white moss") found around a nickel-cadmium cell's vent caps is—
options: potassium hydroxide crystals that mean the cell is ruined
sulfate that must be neutralized with baking soda
potassium carbonate, a normal by-product that should be cleaned off with distilled water
questions.short: White moss = potassium carbonate (K2CO3) — normal; clean with distilled water.
questions.expl: 'White moss around vent cap seals is potassium carbonate (K2CO3). Clean up these surfaces with distilled water and dry.' It forms when a little KOH electrolyte creeps out and reacts with carbon dioxide in the air — a small amount is normal housekeeping, not a death sentence. It DOES matter because 'electrolyte spillage can form grounding paths,' so you wipe it off. (Sulfate/baking soda belongs to the lead-acid world.)

questions.q: Inter-cell connectors (cell links) on a nickel-cadmium battery must be kept at the correct torque because a loose or over-tight link—
options: creates high resistance at the joint, which overheats and can leave burn marks
reverses the polarity of that cell
questions.short: Wrong link torque → resistive heating → burn/scorch marks.
questions.expl: General ni-cad maintenance requires you to 'maintain inter-cell connectors at proper torque values.' A loose (or improperly made) link is a high-resistance joint, and current through resistance makes heat — enough to discolor, scorch, or burn the hardware and the cell tops, and in the worst case start the runaway chain. Correct torque keeps the joint low-resistance and cool. Torque can't change a cell's voltage or flip its polarity.

questions.q: As a nickel-cadmium cell heats up, its internal resistance falls, which lets it draw even more current and heat further. This dangerous self-feeding cycle is—
questions.short: Rising temp → falling internal resistance → thermal runaway.
questions.expl: Heat lowers a ni-cad's internal resistance; lower resistance lets more charging current through; more current makes more heat — a loop that can feed on itself until cells vent, rupture, or (worst case) explode. That's thermal runaway, and it's why ni-cad chargers watch temperature. Don't confuse it with 'voltage depression / memory' (a capacity illusion, cured by a deep discharge) or 'sulfation' (a LEAD-ACID problem). (Thermal runaway is standard ni-cad behavior; the handbook describes the heat/pressure danger of cell reversal on p. 12-93.)
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-93 (cell reversal → high pressure and heat) — thermal runaway is standard ni-cad behavior

questions.q: A nickel-cadmium battery normally emits gas—
options: only while it sits idle and self-discharges
steadily the entire time it discharges
toward the end of the charging cycle (and if overcharged)
questions.short: Ni-cad gasses toward the END of charge.
questions.expl: 'Toward the end of the charging cycle, the cells emit gas. This also occurs if the cells are overcharged.' The gas is hydrogen and oxygen from water in the electrolyte breaking down — an explosive mix, vented by the cell relief valves. A little gassing at the end of charge is normal (and uses up a little water, which is why you re-water). Heavy gassing early or all the time signals a charging problem.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-92 (cells emit gas toward end of charge)

questions.q: A common way to FAST-charge a nickel-cadmium battery is the constant-current method, in which—
options: the current is held constant while the charging voltage is allowed to vary
both current and voltage are held perfectly constant
the voltage is held constant while the current is allowed to vary
questions.short: Ni-cad fast charge = constant current (voltage varies).
questions.expl: In constant-current (fast) charging the charger forces a fixed current in and lets whatever voltage is needed appear across the battery — the voltage climbs as the cells fill. That's the mirror image of constant-voltage charging, where the VOLTAGE is fixed and the current tapers. Constant current fills a ni-cad quickly but must be watched near the end, since holding current after the cells are full drives gassing, heat, and overcharge. (The current-fixed/voltage-varies description is standard; the handbook contrasts the two methods on p. 12-91.)
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-91 (constant-current vs constant-voltage) — fast-charge = constant current is standard ni-cad practice

questions.q: Which battery uses an ALKALINE electrolyte (potassium hydroxide) rather than an acid one?
questions.expl: Straight discrimination: the nickel-cadmium battery's electrolyte is potassium hydroxide, an ALKALI. Both the flooded lead-acid and the sealed lead-acid (SLA) batteries use sulfuric ACID. That single acid-vs-alkali split drives almost every difference between them — opposite neutralizers, opposite watering rules, and the hard rule that you never service the two types in the same area.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-87 (lead-acid = sulfuric acid); p. 12-91 (ni-cad = KOH)

questions.q: A technician neutralizes a battery spill with VINEGAR or dilute BORIC ACID. The spill came from a—
questions.short: Acid neutralizer (vinegar/boric acid) → alkaline ni-cad spill.
questions.expl: You neutralize a base with an acid, so vinegar or boric acid means you're cleaning up the ALKALINE nickel-cadmium electrolyte. A lead-acid (sulfuric acid) spill is the reverse — you'd reach for the BASE, baking soda. Lock the pairs together: lead-acid ACID → baking-soda BASE; ni-cad ALKALI → boric-acid/vinegar ACID. Mixing them up is the single most-tested battery-safety trap.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-92 (ni-cad → vinegar/boric acid); p. 12-91 (lead-acid → baking soda)

questions.q: For which battery does a rising electrolyte level indicate the battery is approaching FULL charge?
questions.short: Ni-cad level RISES toward full charge — that's its watering cue.
questions.expl: The ni-cad is the odd one: its plates soak up electrolyte on discharge and give it back on charge, so 'at full charge, the electrolyte is at its highest level' — and that's exactly why you water a ni-cad only when it's fully charged. A lead-acid cell's level mainly falls from gassing and evaporation and is topped off differently, and its charge is read by SPECIFIC GRAVITY, not level. Don't let the two watering rules blur together.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-92 (ni-cad level highest at full charge)

questions.q: A hydrometer (specific-gravity check) is a valid state-of-charge test for—
questions.short: SG check works on lead-acid ONLY; ni-cad SG doesn't move.
questions.expl: Only the lead-acid battery burns up acid as it discharges, so only its specific gravity tracks the charge — that's what the hydrometer reads. A ni-cad's KOH electrolyte holds a nearly constant specific gravity full or flat, so a hydrometer is useless on it; you find a ni-cad's charge by a measured discharge on the bench instead. Match the test to the battery.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-90 (lead-acid hydrometer); p. 12-93 (ni-cad bench test)

questions.q: Why should lead-acid and nickel-cadmium batteries never be serviced or charged in the same room?
options: they would draw current from each other and self-discharge
their charging voltages are identical and would conflict
acid fumes from one destroy the electrolyte of the other (cross-contamination)
questions.short: Cross-contamination: acid kills alkaline, and vice versa.
questions.expl: Their electrolytes are chemical opposites — sulfuric ACID versus potassium-hydroxide ALKALI — so airborne acid fumes settling on a ni-cad (or alkaline mist on a lead-acid) neutralize and ruin the other's electrolyte. The handbook drives this home in the conversion procedure: a compartment must be 'clean, dry, and free of all traces of acid from the old battery,' washed and neutralized before a ni-cad goes in. Separate tools, separate areas, separate everything.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-92 (compartment must be free of all traces of acid)

questions.q: Which statement about lead-acid versus nickel-cadmium CELL VOLTAGE is correct?
options: a lead-acid cell is about 2 volts and a nickel-cadmium cell is about 1.25 volts
a lead-acid cell is about 1.25 volts and a nickel-cadmium cell is about 2 volts
questions.expl: The lead-acid cell sits at about 2 volts (12-volt battery = 6 cells); the nickel-cadmium cell is lower, about 1.25 volts, so a ni-cad needs more cells for the same bus voltage. Getting the two cell voltages backward is a classic swap trap — anchor it: the ACID cell is the higher-voltage one.

questions.q: A light general-aviation trainer most commonly carries which battery type, while turbine transport aircraft historically favored the other?
options: lead-acid in the light trainer; nickel-cadmium historically on turbine aircraft
nickel-cadmium in the light trainer; lead-acid on turbine aircraft
questions.short: Light GA = lead-acid; turbine/transport historically = ni-cad.
questions.expl: Both are secondary (rechargeable) aircraft batteries, so 'most common' honestly depends on the aircraft. Light piston trainers overwhelmingly use lead-acid (cheap, simple, and now sealed-lead-acid too). Nickel-cadmium earned its place on turbine and transport aircraft because it delivers huge starting current and takes fast charge/high-cycle service well — though the handbook notes SLA batteries are now 'gaining in use over flooded lead acid and Ni-Cad.' The handbook describes both without crowning one winner, so teach both and pick by aircraft.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, pp. 12-87-12-93 (lead-acid, ni-cad, and SLA batteries)

questions.q: A sealed lead-acid (SLA) battery avoids one troublesome nickel-cadmium trait: the false 'memory' in which a ni-cad seems fully charged but isn't. The handbook's correct name for that trait is—
questions.expl: 'This characteristic is only detectable when a full discharge is attempted... it is technically known as "voltage depression" and commonly but erroneously called "memory effect."' Constant overcharge with infrequent deep discharges causes it, so you can believe a full charge exists when it doesn't. SLA batteries don't have it, so they need no scheduled deep-cycle maintenance. (Thermal runaway is the heat loop; sulfation is a lead-acid problem.)

questions.q: 1. What is a primary cell?
options: A cell with a reversible chemical reaction
questions.expl: A primary cell uses a chemical reaction that runs one way only. Once the active chemicals are spent, the reaction cannot be reversed by pushing current back in, so the cell is discarded rather than recharged. That is exactly what makes it 'primary' — one useful life.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (primary vs. secondary cells)

questions.q: 2. What is a secondary cell?
options: A cell that cannot be recharged
A cell with a reversible electrochemical reaction
questions.short: A cell with a reversible electrochemical reaction.
questions.expl: A secondary cell can be recharged because its chemical reaction is reversible: sending current backward through it restores the original chemicals so it can supply power again. Lead-acid and nickel-cadmium aircraft batteries are secondary cells for this reason.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (secondary/storage cells)

questions.q: 3. What unit measures voltage?
questions.expl: Voltage — the electrical pressure or potential difference that pushes electrons — is measured in volts. The ampere measures current, the ohm measures resistance, and the farad measures capacitance.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (electrical units)

questions.q: 4. What unit measures current?
questions.expl: Current is the rate of electron flow, and it is measured in amperes (one ampere equals one coulomb of charge per second). The volt measures pressure, the siemens measures conductance, and the hertz measures frequency.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (electrical units)

questions.q: 5. What does resistance oppose?
questions.expl: Resistance is the property of a material that opposes the flow of current. The higher the resistance, the more it restricts how many electrons can move for a given voltage — that is the heart of Ohm's law (I = E / R).
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (resistance)

questions.q: 6. What is the unit of resistance?
questions.expl: Resistance is measured in ohms, symbolized by the Greek letter omega. One ohm is the resistance that lets one ampere flow when one volt is applied across it.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (the ohm)

questions.q: 7. Conductance is the reciprocal of what?
questions.expl: Conductance measures how easily current flows, so it is the mathematical inverse of resistance (G = 1 / R). Low resistance means high conductance. It is measured in siemens (formerly mhos — 'ohm' spelled backward).
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (conductance)

questions.q: 8. What does a capacitor store?
questions.expl: A capacitor stores energy as an electric charge held on two plates separated by an insulator (dielectric). It builds up charge when voltage is applied and releases it later — like a small, fast electrical reservoir. Magnetic energy is what an inductor stores.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (capacitance)

questions.q: 9. What does an inductor store?
questions.expl: An inductor (a coil) stores energy in the magnetic field that surrounds it whenever current flows. When the current tries to change, that stored field pushes back, which is why inductors oppose changes in current. A capacitor, by contrast, stores energy in an electric field.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (inductance)

questions.q: 10. What is the unit of frequency?
questions.expl: Frequency — how many complete cycles happen each second — is measured in hertz. One hertz equals one cycle per second, so 400 Hz means 400 cycles every second.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (frequency / AC)

questions.q: 11. What does kilo (k) represent?
questions.expl: The metric prefix kilo means one thousand, or 10³. So 1 kilovolt is 1,000 volts and 1 kilohertz is 1,000 hertz. It scales a base unit UP by a factor of a thousand.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (metric prefixes)

questions.q: 12. What does mega (M) represent?
questions.expl: Mega means one million, or 10⁶. So 1 megahertz equals 1,000,000 hertz and 1 megohm equals 1,000,000 ohms. It is the next step up from kilo (a thousand times larger).
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (metric prefixes)

questions.q: 13. What does milli (m) represent?
questions.expl: Milli means one thousandth, or 10⁻³. So 1 milliamp is 0.001 amp. Watch the capitalization: lowercase m (milli) shrinks a unit, while uppercase M (mega) enlarges it a million-fold.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (metric prefixes)

questions.q: 14. What does micro (μ) represent?
questions.expl: Micro, written with the Greek letter mu (μ), means one millionth, or 10⁻⁶. So 1 microfarad equals 0.000001 farad. It is three decimal places smaller than milli.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (metric prefixes)

questions.q: 15. What does nano (n) represent?
questions.expl: Nano means one billionth, or 10⁻⁹ — three decimal places smaller than micro. Nanoseconds and nanofarads show up constantly in electronics timing and small-value capacitors.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (metric prefixes)

questions.q: 16. What does pico (p) represent?
questions.expl: Pico is the smallest prefix in this set, meaning one trillionth, or 10⁻¹² — three decimal places smaller than nano. Picofarads are used for the tiny capacitors found in radio and timing circuits.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (metric prefixes)

questions.q: 17. 1 kV equals:
questions.expl: The prefix kilo means one thousand (10³), so 1 kilovolt = 1,000 volts. Just move the decimal three places to the right when converting kV to V.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (metric conversions)

questions.q: 18. 1 mA equals:
questions.expl: Milli means one thousandth (10⁻³), so 1 milliamp = 0.001 amp. That is a decimal point moved three places to the left. (0.000001 A would be a microamp, not a milliamp.)
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (metric conversions)

questions.q: 19. 1 MHz equals:
questions.expl: Mega means one million (10⁶), so 1 megahertz = 1,000,000 hertz. (1,000 Hz would be a kilohertz — a thousand times smaller.)
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (metric conversions)

questions.q: 20. 1 μF equals:
questions.expl: Micro means one millionth (10⁻⁶), so 1 microfarad = 0.000001 farad — the decimal moved six places to the left. (0.000000001 F would be a nanofarad.)
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (metric conversions)

questions.q: 21. When a conductor cuts through lines of magnetic force, what occurs?
questions.expl: This is electromagnetic induction — the basis of every generator. Whenever a conductor cuts across magnetic lines of force (or the field moves past the conductor), a voltage is induced in that conductor. If the conductor is part of a closed circuit, that voltage drives a current.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (electromagnetic induction)

questions.q: 22. The strength of induced voltage depends primarily on:
questions.expl: Induced voltage grows with how FAST the conductor cuts the field and how STRONG the field is (plus the number of conductors). Move faster or use a stronger magnet and you cut more flux lines per second, which raises the induced EMF. Resistance and capacitance do not set the induced voltage.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (factors affecting induced voltage)

questions.q: 23. Which are the major parts of a DC generator?
options: Field frame, armature, and brush assembly
questions.short: Field frame, armature, and brush assembly.
questions.expl: A DC generator is built around a field frame (the magnetic housing/poles), an armature (the rotating windings where voltage is induced), and a brush assembly that rides on the commutator to carry current out to the circuit. Those three are its major structural parts.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (DC generator construction)

questions.q: 24. How does an AC generator connect to the external circuit?
questions.expl: An AC generator (alternator) uses continuous slip rings and brushes to connect the rotating winding to the outside circuit. Because a slip ring is one unbroken ring per lead, it passes the current out exactly as generated — alternating — without flipping its polarity.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (slip rings vs. commutator)

questions.q: 25. How does a DC generator connect to the external circuit?
questions.expl: A DC generator uses a split-ring commutator. The commutator's gap reverses the armature connection to the brushes at the exact instant the induced voltage would reverse, so the output to the external circuit always flows in one direction — that mechanical switching is what turns AC in the windings into DC at the terminals.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (commutator action)

questions.q: 26. What are the three types of DC generators?
questions.expl: DC generators are classified by how their field windings are connected relative to the armature: series (field in series with the armature), shunt (field in parallel), and compound (both a series and a shunt field). Induction and synchronous are AC-motor terms, not DC-generator types.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (types of DC generators)

questions.q: 27. What does a DC motor convert?
options: DC electrical energy to mechanical energy
questions.short: DC electrical energy into mechanical energy.
questions.expl: A motor is the reverse of a generator. A DC motor takes in DC electrical energy and turns it into rotating mechanical energy (torque) to do work. A generator does the opposite — mechanical in, electrical out.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (DC motor principle)

questions.q: 28. What are the two principal parts of a DC motor?
questions.expl: At its core a DC motor has a field assembly (which creates the stationary magnetic field) and an armature assembly (the rotating member carrying current). The interaction between the field and the current-carrying armature produces the turning force.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (DC motor construction)

questions.q: 29. Which is NOT one of the four major parts of a practical DC motor?
questions.expl: A practical DC motor's four major parts are the armature assembly, the field assembly, the brush assembly, and the commutator (with its end frames/bearings). It uses a COMMUTATOR, not slip rings — slip rings belong to AC machines. That is why the slip-ring assembly is the odd one out here.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (DC motor major parts)

questions.q: 30. What are the three basic types of DC motors?
questions.expl: Just like DC generators, DC motors are grouped by field-winding connection: series, shunt, and compound. Each gives a different speed-versus-load behavior, which is why the type is chosen to match the job (a starter uses a series motor for high starting torque, for example).
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (types of DC motors)

questions.q: 31. In a series DC motor, the field winding is:
questions.expl: In a series motor the field coil carries the SAME current the armature does, because the two are wired in series (end to end). That means field strength rises and falls with load current, which gives the series motor its huge starting torque.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (series motor)

questions.q: 32. A series motor generally runs at what speed with a light load?
questions.expl: With little load, a series motor draws little current, so its field is weak — and a weak field lets the motor race to a very high speed. This is why a series motor should never be run completely unloaded: with no load it can overspeed to the point of self-destruction.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (series motor speed characteristics)

questions.q: 33. What happens to series-motor speed as load increases?
questions.expl: A series motor's speed varies strongly with load: add load and the speed drops. As the load grows, current and field strength rise, the motor produces more torque, and it slows down. This large speed change with load is the defining trait of a series motor.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (series motor speed vs. load)

questions.q: 34. In a shunt motor, the field winding is:
questions.expl: In a shunt motor the field is wired in parallel (shunted) across the armature, so it sees essentially the full line voltage. That keeps the field current — and the field strength — nearly constant regardless of load, which is why the shunt motor holds a fairly steady speed.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (shunt motor)

questions.q: 35. Why does a shunt motor maintain relatively constant speed?
options: Load has no effect on current
questions.short: Its field current is relatively constant.
questions.expl: Because the shunt field is connected across a nearly constant line voltage, its current and magnetic strength barely change as load varies. A steady field means the motor's speed stays relatively steady from no load to full load — the shunt motor's signature.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (shunt motor speed regulation)

questions.q: 36. When all load is removed from a shunt motor, its speed:
questions.expl: Unlike a series motor (which would dangerously overspeed), a shunt motor only speeds up a little when the load is removed, because its constant field holds the speed in check. It is safe to run unloaded — the small rise is all you get.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (shunt motor no-load behavior)

questions.q: 37. A compound motor has:
options: Both series and shunt field windings
questions.short: Both series and shunt field windings.
questions.expl: A compound motor combines the two: it carries both a series field and a shunt field. This blends the series motor's strong starting torque with the shunt motor's more stable speed, giving a compromise that suits loads needing both.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (compound motor)

questions.q: 38. What are the two general types of AC motors used in aircraft systems?
questions.expl: Aircraft AC motors are generally either induction motors or synchronous motors. Induction motors are simple and rugged; synchronous motors lock to the supply frequency. Series/shunt/compound are DC-motor categories, not AC.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (AC motors)

questions.q: 39. A three-phase induction motor is also called a:
questions.expl: The most common three-phase induction motor is nicknamed the squirrel-cage motor because its rotor is a set of conducting bars shorted at both ends by rings — a shape that looks like an old exercise cage for squirrels. It has no brushes or slip rings, which makes it very rugged.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (induction / squirrel-cage motor)

questions.q: 40. A synchronous motor makes use of a:
questions.expl: A synchronous motor's stator windings, fed by the AC supply, create a rotating magnetic field. The rotor locks onto and turns in step with that rotating field, so the motor runs at exactly synchronous speed set by the frequency and pole count.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (synchronous motor)

questions.q: 41. Unlike an induction motor, synchronous-motor torque does not depend on:
questions.expl: An induction motor MUST have its rotor slip behind the field so that currents are induced in the rotor to make torque. A synchronous motor does not rely on induced rotor currents — its rotor is separately magnetized and locks to the rotating field, so it turns in exact step with no slip.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (synchronous vs. induction motor)

questions.q: 42. AC motor speed depends on:
options: Number of poles and source frequency
questions.short: Number of poles and source frequency.
questions.expl: The synchronous speed of an AC motor is set by the supply frequency and the number of poles (RPM = 120 × frequency ÷ poles). More frequency raises speed; more poles lowers it. Voltage and current affect torque, not the basic speed.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (AC motor speed)

questions.q: 43. An electrical generator converts:
questions.expl: A generator takes mechanical energy (a spinning shaft driven by the engine) and converts it into electrical energy by electromagnetic induction. A motor is its opposite — electrical energy in, mechanical energy out.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (generator principle)

questions.q: 44. Alternator frequency depends on:
options: Rotor speed and number of poles
questions.short: Rotor speed and number of poles.
