questions.expl: An alternator's output frequency is set by how fast the rotor spins and how many magnetic poles it has (frequency = poles × RPM ÷ 120). Battery voltage, resistance, and load current do not set the frequency.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (alternator frequency)

questions.q: 45. If rotor speed increases while pole count stays constant, frequency:
questions.expl: Frequency is directly proportional to rotor speed (f = poles × RPM ÷ 120). Spin the rotor faster with the same number of poles and the poles sweep past the windings more often each second, so the frequency goes up. This is why constant-frequency AC systems need a constant-speed drive.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (frequency vs. speed)

questions.q: 46. If the number of rotor poles increases at the same speed, frequency:
questions.expl: Frequency is also directly proportional to pole count (f = poles × RPM ÷ 120). At a fixed RPM, adding more poles means more magnetic reversals pass a winding each second, so the frequency rises. More poles OR more speed both raise frequency.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (frequency vs. poles)

questions.q: 47. Which formula gives synchronous speed in RPM?
questions.expl: Synchronous speed equals 120 times the frequency divided by the number of poles. The 120 comes from 60 seconds per minute times 2 poles per pole-pair. Rearranged, it is the same relationship as f = poles × RPM ÷ 120.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (synchronous speed formula)

questions.q: 48. What is the RPM of a 4-pole motor operating at 400 Hz?
questions.expl: Plug into RPM = 120 × frequency ÷ poles: 120 × 400 ÷ 4 = 48,000 ÷ 4 = 12,000 RPM. Aircraft AC is 400 Hz, so a 4-pole machine turns at a brisk 12,000 RPM.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (synchronous speed calculation)

questions.q: 49. What is the major connection difference between an alternator and a DC generator?
options: Alternator uses a commutator; DC generator uses slip rings
Alternator uses slip rings; DC generator uses a commutator
questions.short: Alternator uses slip rings; DC generator uses a commutator.
questions.expl: The defining hardware difference: an alternator carries its output through continuous slip rings, so the current stays alternating, while a DC generator uses a split-ring commutator that flips the connection each half-turn to deliver DC. Same induction principle, different output-connection method.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (slip rings vs. commutator)

questions.q: 50. A three-phase alternator has how many phases?
questions.expl: A three-phase alternator produces three separate AC voltages from three sets of windings. 'Three-phase' literally names the count — three phases working together, which delivers smoother, more efficient power than a single phase.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (three-phase alternator)

questions.q: 51. The three phases of a three-phase alternator are electrically separated by:
questions.expl: The three windings are spaced so their voltages peak one-third of a cycle apart — 360° ÷ 3 = 120°. This even 120° staggering is what keeps three-phase power flowing smoothly, with the phases overlapping so total power never drops to zero.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (three-phase 120° separation)

questions.q: 52. Why are brushless alternators advantageous?
options: They eliminate brush wear and high-altitude arcing
questions.short: They eliminate brush wear and high-altitude arcing.
questions.expl: A brushless alternator has no brushes or slip rings in the main power path, so there is nothing to wear out and no sliding contact to arc in the thin air at high altitude. That means less maintenance and more reliable output where brushes would spark.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (brushless alternator advantages)

questions.q: 53. A brushless alternator system consists of:
options: Shunt motor, series motor, and battery
Pilot exciter, exciter, and main generator
questions.short: A pilot exciter, an exciter, and the main generator.
questions.expl: A brushless alternator is really three machines on one shaft: a permanent-magnet pilot exciter, an exciter, and the main generator. The exciter's AC output is rectified by rotating diodes right on the shaft to feed the main field — so field current gets to the rotor with no brushes at all.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (brushless alternator construction)

questions.q: 54. What is a starter-generator?
options: A generator that cannot start an engine
A device that acts as a starter during engine start and generator afterward
questions.short: A device that acts as a starter during engine start and a generator afterward.
questions.expl: A starter-generator is one machine doing two jobs to save weight, common on turbine aircraft. During start it runs as a motor to spin the engine; once the engine is running it is driven by the engine and switches to acting as a generator to power the aircraft.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (starter-generator)

questions.q: 55. What is the primary purpose of a GCU?
options: Regulate, sense, and protect the DC generation system
questions.short: To regulate, sense, and protect the DC generation system.
questions.expl: A Generator Control Unit (GCU) is the brain of the generating system. It regulates output voltage, senses conditions like overvoltage and reverse current, and protects the system by tripping the generator off line when something goes wrong.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (generator control unit / GCU)

questions.q: 56. GCUs are more commonly found on:
questions.expl: GCUs are typically found on turbine-powered aircraft, which have more sophisticated, higher-capacity electrical systems that need the automatic regulation and protection a GCU provides. Simple piston trainers often use a basic voltage regulator instead.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (GCU applications)

questions.q: 57. Which is a basic GCU function?
questions.expl: Holding the generator's output at the correct voltage is one of the GCU's core jobs, along with reverse-current sensing, overvoltage protection, and paralleling control. Tires, fuel, and cabin pressure are unrelated systems.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (GCU functions)

questions.q: 58. Overvoltage protection compares:
options: Sampled voltage to a reference voltage
questions.short: A sampled voltage to a reference voltage.
questions.expl: Overvoltage protection works by continuously comparing a sample of the generator's actual output voltage against a fixed reference. If the sampled voltage climbs above the reference by too much, the circuit trips the generator off line to protect the equipment.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (overvoltage protection)

questions.q: 59. Parallel generator operation allows:
options: Multiple generators to share the electrical load
A generator to stop producing electricity
questions.short: Multiple generators to share the electrical load.
questions.expl: Running generators in parallel lets two or more machines feed the same bus and split the total electrical load between them. This provides more capacity and redundancy — if one is lost, the others keep the bus powered.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (parallel generator operation)

questions.q: 60. If one generator fails in a parallel system, another generator may:
options: Become overexcited and carry too much load
questions.short: Become overexcited and carry too much load.
questions.expl: When one generator drops off a shared bus, the remaining generator(s) must suddenly pick up the load the failed unit was carrying. That can drive a remaining machine into an overexcited, overloaded condition — which is exactly why load-sharing (equalizing) and protection circuits are needed in parallel systems.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (parallel generator ops / load sharing)

questions.q: 61. Before a generator line contactor closes, generator voltage must be:
options: Within close tolerance of the load-bus voltage
questions.short: Within close tolerance of the load-bus voltage.
questions.expl: To connect a generator onto a live bus without a damaging surge or reverse current, its voltage must first be brought within a close tolerance of the bus voltage. Only when the two nearly match is it safe to close the line contactor and let the generator share the load.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (generator paralleling / contactor closing)

questions.q: 62. Reverse-current sensing detects when a generator:
options: Draws current instead of supplying it
questions.short: Draws current instead of supplying it.
questions.expl: Normally a generator SUPPLIES current to the bus. If its voltage falls below the bus/battery voltage, current starts flowing BACKWARD into the generator, motoring it. Reverse-current sensing watches for that backward flow so the generator can be disconnected before it drains the battery.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (reverse-current sensing)

questions.q: 63. A generator that begins drawing current instead of supplying it is experiencing:
questions.expl: When current reverses and flows into the generator rather than out of it, that condition is called reverse current. It happens when generator voltage drops below bus voltage, and it must be caught quickly because the battery would otherwise discharge back through the generator.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (reverse current)

questions.q: 64. A three-unit regulator includes a voltage regulator, current regulator, and:
questions.expl: The classic three-unit regulator has exactly three relays: a voltage regulator (limits output voltage), a current regulator (limits output current), and a reverse-current cutout relay (disconnects the battery when the generator voltage drops so the battery cannot discharge back through it).
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (three-unit regulator)

questions.q: 65. What is the purpose of the current regulator?
questions.expl: The current-regulator unit caps how much current the generator delivers, protecting it from overheating when a heavy load (like charging a low battery plus running equipment) would otherwise pull more current than the generator is rated for.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (current regulator)

questions.q: 66. What does the reverse-current cutout do?
options: Disconnects the engine from the starter
Disconnects the battery from the generator
questions.short: Disconnects the battery from the generator.
questions.expl: The reverse-current cutout relay opens the circuit between the battery and the generator whenever generator voltage falls below battery voltage. This stops the battery from discharging backward through the generator (which would waste the battery and could motor the generator).
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (reverse-current cutout)

questions.q: 67. Boolean variables have which two possible values?
questions.expl: Boolean logic deals in exactly two states, usually written TRUE and FALSE (or 1 and 0). Every Boolean variable is one or the other — there is no in-between. This two-state nature is the foundation of all digital electronics.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (Boolean logic / digital fundamentals)

questions.q: 68. Who introduced Boolean logic?
questions.expl: Boolean logic is named after the 19th-century English mathematician George Boole, who developed the algebra of TRUE/FALSE values. A century later it became the mathematical basis for digital computers and logic circuits.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (Boolean logic history)

questions.q: 69. What are the three basic Boolean operations?
questions.expl: The three fundamental Boolean operations are AND, OR, and NOT. Every more complex logic function (NAND, NOR, XOR, and so on) is built from these three building blocks.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (basic logic operations)

questions.q: 70. An AND operation is TRUE when:
options: At least one input is TRUE
questions.expl: An AND gate outputs TRUE only when every one of its inputs is TRUE — think of switches in series, where all must be closed for current to flow. If even one input is FALSE, the AND output is FALSE.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (AND logic)

questions.q: 71. An OR operation is TRUE when:
options: At least one input is TRUE
questions.short: At least one input is TRUE.
questions.expl: An OR gate outputs TRUE if any one (or more) of its inputs is TRUE — like switches in parallel, where closing any one lets current flow. It is FALSE only when every input is FALSE.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (OR logic)

questions.q: 72. What does NOT do?
questions.expl: The NOT operation (an inverter) simply flips the input to its opposite: TRUE becomes FALSE and FALSE becomes TRUE. It is the only basic operation with a single input.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (NOT / inverter)

questions.q: 73. TRUE AND TRUE equals:
questions.expl: AND is TRUE only when all inputs are TRUE. Both inputs here are TRUE, so the result is TRUE. This is the one input combination that makes a two-input AND gate output TRUE.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (AND truth table)

questions.q: 74. TRUE AND FALSE equals:
questions.expl: AND requires every input to be TRUE. One input here is FALSE, so the AND output is FALSE. A single FALSE input is enough to force an AND result FALSE.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (AND truth table)

questions.q: 75. TRUE OR FALSE equals:
questions.expl: OR is TRUE when at least one input is TRUE. One input here is TRUE, so the OR output is TRUE regardless of the other input being FALSE.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (OR truth table)

questions.q: 76. FALSE OR FALSE equals:
questions.expl: OR outputs TRUE only if some input is TRUE. Here both inputs are FALSE, so there is nothing to make it TRUE — the OR result is FALSE. This is the only input combination that makes a two-input OR gate FALSE.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (OR truth table)

questions.q: 77. NOT TRUE equals:
questions.expl: NOT reverses the logical value. Applied to TRUE, it produces the opposite — FALSE.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (NOT truth table)

questions.q: 78. NOT FALSE equals:
questions.expl: NOT reverses the logical value. Applied to FALSE, it produces the opposite — TRUE.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (NOT truth table)

questions.q: 79. A generator is spinning faster while its number of poles stays the same. What happens to frequency?
questions.expl: Frequency is directly proportional to rotor speed (f = poles × RPM ÷ 120). With the pole count fixed, spinning faster makes the poles pass the windings more often each second, so the output frequency rises.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (frequency vs. speed)

questions.q: 80. A series DC motor is given a heavier load. What happens to its speed?
questions.expl: A series motor slows down markedly as load increases. The added load raises current and field strength, boosting torque but dropping speed. This large speed change with load is exactly how a series motor behaves.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (series motor speed vs. load)

questions.q: 81. A shunt DC motor has its load removed. Its speed:
questions.expl: Because a shunt motor's field stays nearly constant, removing the load makes it speed up only a little. It does not run away like a series motor would — the steady field keeps the no-load speed in check.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (shunt motor no-load behavior)

questions.q: 82. Why is three-phase AC useful in aircraft systems?
options: Its phases are 120° apart and it is well suited to AC motors
It can only operate at zero frequency
questions.short: Its phases are 120° apart and it is well suited to AC motors.
questions.expl: Three-phase power has its three voltages evenly staggered 120° apart, so the delivered power is smooth and it naturally creates the rotating magnetic field that AC motors need. That makes it efficient and ideal for driving aircraft AC motors.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (three-phase advantages)

questions.q: 83. What is the field-winding connection difference between series and shunt motors?
options: Series is parallel; shunt is series
Series is series; shunt is parallel
questions.short: Series field is in series; shunt field is in parallel.
questions.expl: The names describe the wiring: a series motor's field is in series with the armature (same current through both), while a shunt motor's field is in parallel with the armature (across the line voltage). That single wiring difference is what gives each its distinct speed-torque behavior.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (series vs. shunt motor)

questions.q: 84. Why does a GCU need overvoltage protection?
options: To protect the electrical system from excessive voltage
questions.short: To protect the electrical system from excessive voltage.
questions.expl: If a regulator fails and lets output voltage climb too high, it can damage every piece of equipment on the bus. Overvoltage protection in the GCU senses that runaway voltage and trips the generator off line, shielding the aircraft's electrical system.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (overvoltage protection)

questions.q: 85. Why is reverse-current protection important?
options: It prevents the generator from drawing current from the system instead of supplying it
questions.short: It prevents the generator from drawing current from the system instead of supplying it.
questions.expl: Without reverse-current protection, a generator whose voltage has dropped below bus voltage would pull current backward out of the battery/bus and motor itself — draining the battery and doing no useful work. The protection disconnects it so power only ever flows the right way.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (reverse-current protection)

questions.q: 86. Which statement best describes an alternator versus a DC generator?
options: An alternator produces AC and uses slip rings; a DC generator uses a commutator
A DC generator uses slip rings and produces AC
An alternator uses a commutator and produces DC
Both produce DC and use commutators
questions.short: An alternator produces AC and uses slip rings; a DC generator uses a commutator.
questions.expl: This ties the whole comparison together: the alternator's slip rings pass the current out as generated, so its output is AC, while the DC generator's commutator flips the connection each half turn to deliver DC. Same induction, opposite output-connection scheme.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (alternator vs. DC generator)

questions.q: 87. Which statement best describes a series DC motor?
options: Its field winding is in parallel with the armature and speed changes little
Its field winding is in series with the armature and speed changes substantially with load
questions.short: Field in series with the armature; speed changes substantially with load.
questions.expl: The series motor's field is wired in series with the armature, so field strength tracks load current. That gives strong starting torque but a speed that swings widely with load — fast when unloaded, much slower when loaded.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (series motor summary)

questions.q: 88. Which statement best describes a shunt DC motor?
options: Its field is in parallel with the armature and speed varies relatively little with load
Its field is in series with the armature and speed varies greatly
questions.short: Field in parallel with the armature; speed varies relatively little with load.
questions.expl: The shunt motor's field is connected in parallel across the line, so its field current and strength stay nearly constant. The result is a motor that holds a fairly steady speed from no load to full load.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (shunt motor summary)

questions.q: 89. Which statement best describes a compound DC motor?
options: It combines series and shunt field windings
It is always an AC motor
questions.short: It combines series and shunt field windings.
questions.expl: A compound motor carries both a series field and a shunt field, blending the series motor's strong starting torque with the shunt motor's steadier speed. It is the middle-ground choice between the two.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (compound motor summary)

questions.q: 90. Which statement best summarizes electromagnetic generation?
options: A conductor must remain stationary to generate voltage
A conductor cutting magnetic lines of force induces voltage; greater speed or field strength increases induced voltage
Induced voltage depends only on resistance
Magnetic fields prevent voltage from being induced
questions.short: Cutting magnetic lines induces voltage; more speed or field strength increases it.
questions.expl: This is the core of every generator: relative motion between a conductor and a magnetic field induces a voltage, and that voltage grows with faster motion, a stronger field, and more conductors. A stationary conductor in a steady field induces nothing.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Aircraft Electrical System / Fundamentals of Electricity) (electromagnetic induction summary)

questions.q: 1. Which Bell Lab scientist invented the transistor in 1948?
options: All of them — Bardeen, Brattain, and Shockley
questions.expl: The transistor was the joint work of John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, and William Shockley at Bell Laboratories, so no single name is the answer. Heads-up: the FAA handbook teaches how the transistor works (NPN/PNP construction and biasing) but does not name its inventors — that history is AIM-lecture context, so the cite here points to the handbook's transistor section.

questions.q: 2. Electrical wiring may be made from many different types of metal. Of the four metals listed, the best conductor material is:
questions.expl: Silver has the lowest resistivity of common metals, so among silver, copper, aluminum, and steel it is the best conductor. The handbook ranks the metals directly: 'silver is the best conductor.' Copper is a close second and is used for most wiring because silver is far more expensive.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 5 (conductors — silver ranks first); resistance of conductors Ch. 12, p. 12-23

questions.q: 3. If the cross-sectional area of a conductor is doubled, the resistance to current flow will be what amount of the original resistance?
questions.expl: Resistance is inversely proportional to cross-sectional area — a fatter wire gives electrons more room to move without collisions. The handbook states it plainly: 'If the cross-sectional area of a conductor is doubled, the resistance to current flow is reduced in half.' Double the area, halve the resistance.

questions.q: 4. A lead-acid battery cell contains positive plates coated with:
questions.expl: In a charged lead-acid cell the positive electrode is lead peroxide (PbO2) and the negative electrode is spongy metallic lead, both sitting in a sulfuric-acid electrolyte. During discharge both plates convert toward lead sulfate. The positive plate's active material is the lead peroxide.

questions.q: 5. In theory, a 100-ampere battery will furnish:
options: All of these — each equals 100 ampere-hours
questions.short: All of these are equal in theory.
questions.expl: The ampere-hour rating is current multiplied by time. 100 A x 1 h, 50 A x 2 h, and 20 A x 5 h all equal 100 ampere-hours, so in theory each delivers the same total charge. (In practice a higher discharge current lowers the usable capacity a little, but the 'in theory' framing makes them equal.)

questions.q: 6. The most commonly used reversible type motor in aircraft is:
questions.expl: The series-wound DC motor has very high starting torque and is compact, which is why the reversible split-field series motor is the one used for aircraft actuators — landing gear, flaps, and trim. The handbook lists series, shunt, and compound as the three DC-motor types; the series motor is favored for these high-torque reversing jobs.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-138 (DC motor types — series motor)

questions.q: 7. The SCR (silicon-controlled rectifier) has what number of electrodes:
questions.expl: The silicon-controlled rectifier is a three-terminal device: anode, cathode, and gate. A small gate current switches it on so it conducts from anode to cathode. Note: the FAA handbook covers diodes, transistors, and FETs but does not detail the SCR by name — the three-electrode fact is AIM-lecture / standard thyristor knowledge, so the cite points to the handbook's solid-state rectifier section.

questions.q: 8. SCR (silicon-controlled rectifier) electrodes are labeled:
questions.expl: The SCR's three terminals are the anode, the cathode, and the gate — current normally flows anode-to-cathode once the gate triggers it on. 'Drain/Gate/Source' names a FET, and 'Emitter/Base/Collector' names a bipolar transistor. As with the previous item, the FAA handbook does not name SCR terminals, so this is AIM/standard-electronics content cited to the rectifier section.

questions.q: 9. The grid in a triode vacuum tube controls electron flow between the:
questions.expl: In a vacuum tube the heated cathode emits electrons and the plate (anode) collects them. The triode adds a control grid between those two; a small change in grid voltage throttles the electron stream flowing from cathode to plate. That control of the cathode-to-plate current is what lets a triode amplify.

questions.q: 10. The ratio between true power and apparent power is expressed as the power factor and may be found in a series circuit by dividing:
options: Circuit resistance by current flow in amperes
True voltage by current in the circuit
questions.short: Circuit resistance by impedance (R divided by Z).
questions.expl: Power factor is true power divided by apparent power. In a series AC circuit that ratio equals the resistance divided by the impedance (PF = R/Z), because true power is dissipated only by the resistance while apparent power is set by the total impedance. So dividing R by Z gives the power factor directly.

questions.q: 11. The formula for finding impedance (total opposition to current flow in an AC circuit) can be found by using:
options: Both the law of right triangles and the Pythagorean theorem
questions.short: Both — they are the same right-triangle relationship.
questions.expl: Impedance combines resistance and reactance at right angles, so Z is the hypotenuse of a right triangle: Z = square root of (R squared + X squared). That is exactly the Pythagorean theorem, which is the law of right triangles — the two names describe the same method, so both apply.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-49 (opposition to current flow of AC / impedance)

questions.q: 12. In a solid state diode, current flow will increase if:
questions.expl: A diode conducts when it is forward biased — the applied voltage pushes carriers across the junction. Increasing that forward bias lowers the junction's effective resistance and lets more current through. Decreasing forward bias, or reverse biasing, chokes the current off.

questions.q: 13. If an AC voltage is applied to the primary of an iron core transformer, the iron core will be magnetized and demagnetized at the same frequency as that of the:
questions.expl: The alternating primary voltage drives an alternating magnetic flux in the iron core. Because the flux follows that source, the core magnetizes and demagnetizes once per cycle of the applied AC voltage — so the core's magnetic reversal frequency equals the frequency of the voltage applied to the primary.

questions.q: 14. For all induction motors, the principle of operation is a:
questions.expl: Both single-phase and three-phase induction motors work by producing a rotating magnetic field in the stator. That moving field drags the rotor along with it, just as a rotating horseshoe magnet makes a compass needle follow. No brushes or slip rings feed the rotor — the field itself does the work.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-148 (rotating magnetic field / induction motors)

questions.q: 15. In a step-down transformer, the resistance of the secondary winding will be:
options: Twice as much as the primary winding
Less than that of the primary winding
The same as that of the primary winding
More than that of the primary winding
questions.short: Less than that of the primary winding.
questions.expl: A step-down transformer has fewer turns on the secondary than on the primary, and because the secondary carries the higher current it is wound with heavier (thicker) wire. Fewer turns of larger-diameter wire means less total wire resistance, so the secondary winding's resistance is lower than the primary's.

questions.q: 16. If a transformer winding is completely short-circuited, several things may occur if power is applied:
options: The voltage reading across the secondary is zero
questions.expl: A dead short in a winding lets excessive current flow, which drives the temperature up (overheating), collapses the output so a meter across the secondary reads zero, and cooks the insulation, giving off a strong burnt odor. Because a short can produce every one of these symptoms, the complete answer is all of them.

questions.q: 17. Microswitches are used primarily as:
questions.expl: A microswitch trips on a very small movement of its actuator, which makes it ideal as a limit switch — it senses when a moving part (landing gear, flap, door) reaches the end of its travel and signals or stops it. The handbook describes the microswitch opening or closing a circuit with a very small motion, exactly the limit-switch job.

questions.q: 18. A resistor having the value of 2700 ohms would be color coded this way:
options: First band yellow, second band violet, third band green
First band red, second band violet, third band red
First band red, second band violet, third band green
First band blue, second band brown, third band green
questions.expl: Read the bands as first-digit, second-digit, multiplier. 2700 ohms = 27 x 100, so the digits are 2 and 7 and the multiplier is 100 (two zeros). On the color code 2 = red, 7 = violet, and x100 = red. So the bands are red, violet, red.

questions.q: 19. When a storage battery is being charged, what two gases are generated?
questions.expl: Charging electrolyzes some of the water in the electrolyte, releasing hydrogen at one plate and oxygen at the other. Hydrogen is explosive, which is why battery areas must be well ventilated and kept clear of sparks and flame during charging.

questions.q: 20. A battery's state of charge is indicated by:
options: Both the electrolyte density and a hydrometer reading
questions.short: Both the electrolyte density and a hydrometer reading.
questions.expl: As a lead-acid battery discharges the sulfuric acid is used up and the electrolyte gets less dense (lower specific gravity). A hydrometer is the tool that measures that specific gravity, so the electrolyte's density and the hydrometer reading are two ways of saying the same thing — together they indicate state of charge. (A hygrometer measures humidity — the trap answer.)

questions.q: 21. To reverse the direction of rotation in a DC motor:
options: Reverse the direction of current in the armature windings
Reverse the direction of current in the field windings
Reverse the direction of current in the armature windings and field windings
Reverse the direction of current in the armature windings or the field windings
questions.short: Reverse the current in the armature OR the field — but not both.
questions.expl: Reversing the current in EITHER the armature or the field flips the torque and reverses rotation. If you reverse BOTH at once, the two reversals cancel and the motor keeps turning the same way — which is exactly why simply swapping the two supply leads does not reverse a DC motor. So the answer is armature or field, one of them.

questions.q: 22. Zener diodes are used primarily for:
questions.expl: A zener is run in reverse breakdown, where it holds a nearly constant voltage across itself even as the current through it changes. That fixed drop makes it a voltage reference/regulator. Ordinary rectifier diodes are the ones used to convert AC to DC.

questions.q: 23. Photo diodes are light-activated variable:
questions.expl: A photodiode's reverse current rises as more light strikes its junction — brighter light creates more carriers, which is the same as its resistance dropping. Because its opposition to current varies with light, it behaves as a light-activated variable resistance in a detecting circuit. (The handbook describes the light-controlled reverse current; AIM groups this behavior as a light-variable resistor.)

questions.q: 24. A bridge-type, full-wave rectifier has:
questions.expl: A full-wave bridge rectifier uses four diodes (D1 through D4). On each half-cycle one diagonal pair conducts while the other pair blocks, so both halves of the AC waveform are steered through the load in the same direction — giving continuous full-wave DC.

questions.q: 25. Rheostats and potentiometers are examples of:
questions.expl: Both are adjustable resistors. A rheostat is a two-terminal variable resistor used to control current; a potentiometer is a three-terminal version used to divide voltage. Either way, they vary resistance, so they belong to the variable-resistor family.

questions.q: G33 #1 — A wire ends in the symbol shown: three horizontal bars, each shorter than the one above. It identifies—
questions.expl: The shrinking three-bar 'rake' is the ground symbol — the point where the circuit returns through the aircraft's metal structure. An antenna symbol points UP with a T/fan shape; a fuse is a wavy line between terminals.

questions.q: G33 #2 — The zigzag symbol shown represents—
questions.expl: The sharp zigzag is a fixed resistor — 'the general use of a resistor in a circuit is to limit the amount of current flow' (p. 12-24). An inductor is drawn with round humps, and a fuse is one smooth S-wave.

questions.q: G33 #3 — Two coils separated by a pair of parallel lines (the core) form the symbol for—
options: a dual inductor with no core
questions.expl: A transformer 'consists of two coils that are not electrically connected' — energy crosses through the magnetic core, drawn as the parallel lines between the windings (p. 12-65). One coil alone would be an inductor.

questions.q: G33 #4 — Two terminals bridged by a rounded, resettable bump (amp rating printed above) is the symbol for—
questions.expl: 'Unlike the fuse, the circuit breaker can be reset; whereas the fuse or current limiter must be replaced' (p. 12-29). The bump = a reset button riding over the contacts. Fig. 12-68 is the schematic symbol.

questions.q: G33 #5 — Two parallel plates of EQUAL length with a gap between them (wire enters each plate) is—
questions.expl: Equal-length plates with a gap = capacitor; it stores charge measured in farads (pp. 12-51–12-53). The Fig. 4-29 chart still labels it 'CONDENSER' — know both names. A battery's plates ALTERNATE long/short.

questions.q: G33 #6 — A zigzag resistor with an arrow drawn diagonally through it is—
questions.expl: 'A rheostat is a variable resistor used to vary the amount of current flowing in a circuit' (p. 12-26). The arrow = the movable slider. Drawn with a third wiper terminal instead, it's a potentiometer.

questions.q: G33 #7 — A solid triangle pointing into a straight bar is the symbol for—
questions.expl: Triangle = anode, bar = cathode; conventional (+) current flows the way the triangle points and is blocked the other way. Fig. 12-218 shows general-purpose diodes; Fig. 12-219 the special-purpose family.

questions.q: G33 #8 — Two solid triangles meeting point-to-point, marked 10A, is the symbol for—
questions.short: A current limiter (this exact 10A symbol is on the Fig. 4-29 chart).
questions.expl: The current limiter 'is very much like the fuse. However, the current limiter link is usually made of copper and will stand a considerable overload for a short period of time' (p. 12-29). Symbol: Fig. 12-67B.

questions.q: G33 #9 — Two ganged switch blades (dashed link), each blade able to reach two contacts, is a—
questions.expl: Count poles = blades (2), throws = contacts per blade (2). The dashed line means both blades move together. Fig. 12-74 is the DPDT schematic symbol; Figs. 12-71–12-73 show SPST, SPDT, and DPST.

questions.q: G33 #10 — Alternating LONG and SHORT parallel lines with + and − marks is the symbol for—
questions.short: A battery — the long line is the positive plate.
questions.expl: The battery/source symbol alternates long and short plates (long = +). It sits beside the BUS symbol on the Fig. 4-29 chart. A capacitor's two plates are EQUAL length — that's the classic trap.

questions.q: G33 #11 — This transistor symbol's emitter arrow points AWAY from the base bar. It is—
questions.expl: 'The transistors are classified as either NPN or PNP according to the arrangement of their N and P-materials' (p. 12-105). Mnemonic: NPN = Not Pointing iN; PNP = Points iN Proudly. Symbols: Fig. 12-221.

questions.q: G33 #12 — This transistor symbol's emitter arrow points IN toward the base bar. It is—
questions.short: PNP — the arrow Points iN Proudly.
questions.expl: PNP = a thin N-region between two P-regions; its emitter arrow points in toward the base. NPN is the mirror image (arrow out). Same figure, opposite arrow: Fig. 12-221, p. 12-106.

questions.q: G33 #13 — A gate with a single CURVED back, curved sides meeting at a point, and a plain output is—
questions.expl: The OR gate 'has two or more inputs and one output'; a high on ANY input produces a high output (p. 12-122). Curved back + pointed nose + NO bubble = plain OR.

questions.q: G33 #14 — A gate with a FLAT back and a rounded (D-shaped) nose, no bubble, is—
questions.expl: 'The AND gate is made up of two or more inputs and a single output' — all inputs must be high for a high output. Flat back + round nose = the D-shaped AND symbol of Fig. 12-255.

questions.q: G33 #15 — An OR-shaped gate with a small circle added on its output is—
questions.expl: 'The term NOR is a combination of the NOT and OR' (p. 12-122): the bubble inverts the OR output. Single input arc (not doubled), bubble on the nose: Fig. 12-263.

questions.q: G33 #16 — CAREFUL (this is the one to fix on your sheet): an OR-shaped gate with a DOUBLED curved line across the inputs and NO circle on the output is—
questions.short: X-OR. No output bubble = no inversion — this is NOT an X-NOR.
questions.expl: The exclusive OR 'produces a 1 output when only one of the inputs is a 1' (p. 12-122). Double input arc = eXclusive; the bubble is what turns it into X-NOR (Fig. 12-265). G33 #16 has no bubble, so the answer is X-OR — not XNOR as written.

questions.q: G33 #17 — A diode symbol whose cathode bar has BENT ends (little Z-wings) is—
questions.short: A zener diode — the bent bar is the giveaway.
questions.expl: Zener diodes ('breakdown diodes') 'are designed so that they break down (allow current to pass) when the circuit potential is equal to or in excess of' a chosen reverse voltage (p. 12-103) — that's why they regulate voltage. Symbol: Fig. 12-219.

questions.q: G33 #18 — A diode symbol with two small arrows pointing AWAY from the junction is—
questions.short: An LED — the arrows are light radiating OUT.
questions.expl: In a forward-biased LED, electrons falling into holes 'radiate energy' as light (p. 12-103). Arrows OUT = emitting. A photodiode's arrows point IN (it receives light) — both are in Fig. 12-219.

questions.q: G33 #19 — A 16-pin component drawn as two parallel rows of 8 pins with a notch marking pin 1 (like your sheet's pinout diagram) is an IC in a—
questions.short: Dual In-line Package — the standard IC package. (Fix the wording on your sheet.)
questions.expl: The two-row pinout diagrams on p. 12-127 are ICs in Dual In-line PACKAGES. Heads-up: the handbook's p. 12-33 term 'Dual In-Line Parallel (DIP) switch' applies to a bank of tiny switches in that same package shape — not to an IC pinout. For an IC, say Dual In-line Package.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-127 (IC pinouts); p. 12-33 (DIP switches); AIM G33 #19

questions.q: The older name you will still see (even on the FAA's own Fig. 4-29 chart) for a capacitor is—
questions.expl: The Fig. 4-29 symbol chart literally labels the capacitor symbols 'CONDENSERS,' and Ch. 12 still works condenser problems (p. 12-55). Same device, two names — G33 #5 accepts either.

questions.q: A zener diode differs from a rectifier diode because it is designed to—
options: block current in both directions until gated on
conduct in reverse once the voltage reaches its breakdown value
questions.short: Conduct in reverse at its breakdown voltage.
questions.expl: Zeners 'break down (allow current to pass) when the circuit potential is equal to or in excess of' the design voltage (p. 12-103) — which makes them voltage regulators. A rectifier diode is chosen to never operate in breakdown.

questions.q: A light-emitting diode radiates light when it is—
questions.expl: 'In a forward biased diode, electrons cross the junction and fall into holes. As the electrons fall into the valence band, they radiate energy' (p. 12-103). In an LED that energy leaves as visible light.

questions.q: Compared with a fuse, the current limiter's link—
options: melts instantly at the slightest overload
is usually copper and stands a considerable overload for a short time
questions.short: Copper link; tolerates a brief overload.
questions.expl: 'The current limiter link is usually made of copper and will stand a considerable overload for a short period of time' (p. 12-29). Like a fuse — and unlike a breaker — once it opens it must be REPLACED.

questions.q: The FAA handbook calls the potentiometer—
questions.short: 'The potentiometer is considered a three-terminal device.'
questions.expl: Terminals 1 and 2 carry the full resistance; terminal 3 is the wiper (p. 12-27). That third wiper terminal is exactly what separates its symbol from a rheostat's.

questions.q: A rheostat is used in a circuit to—
options: vary the amount of current flowing
store a charge for the ignition system
questions.short: Vary current — it's a two-terminal variable resistor.
questions.expl: 'A rheostat is a variable resistor used to vary the amount of current flowing in a circuit' (p. 12-26). It uses two terminals; wire a potentiometer's wiper + one end and you've made one (Fig. 12-62).

questions.q: A transformer changes—
options: electrical energy of a given voltage into electrical energy at a different voltage level
questions.short: Voltage level — via two magnetically-coupled coils.
questions.expl: 'A transformer changes electrical energy of a given voltage into electrical energy at a different voltage level. It consists of two coils that are not electrically connected' (p. 12-65). Rectifying is the diode's job; converting mechanical energy is the generator's.

questions.q: After a circuit breaker trips and is reset once, it trips again. You should—
options: keep resetting it until it holds
replace it with the next-higher amp rating
troubleshoot for the cause instead of resetting it again
questions.expl: 'It is usually not advisable to continue resetting the circuit breaker, but to initiate troubleshooting' — repeated resetting risks damage 'or worse, the possibility of a fire' (p. 12-29). Also: 'Automatic reset type circuit breakers are not allowed in aircraft.'

questions.q: Per the FAA handbook, the acronym in 'DIP switch' stands for—
questions.short: Dual In-Line Parallel — for the SWITCH bank (p. 12-33).
questions.expl: 'The acronym “DIP” switch is defined as Dual In-Line Parallel switch in reference to the physical layout' (p. 12-33). But an IC in that same two-row shape (G33 #19) is a Dual In-line PACKAGE. Switch bank = Parallel; IC = Package.

questions.q: Mnemonic check: 'Points iN Proudly' tells you that the emitter arrow pointing INTO the base bar means—
questions.expl: Arrow in = PNP; arrow out = NPN (Not Pointing iN). One glance at the emitter arrow settles G33 #11 vs #12 every time (Fig. 12-221).

questions.q: Which transistor symbol has the emitter arrow pointing OUT, away from the base?
questions.expl: NPN = N-P-N sandwich, arrow out. If you remember only one thing for the written: the arrow always sits on the EMITTER, and it points in only for PNP.

questions.q: Diode family lineup — the ONE feature that marks the zener symbol apart from a standard diode is—
options: the bent (Z-shaped) ends on the cathode bar
a circle drawn around the whole symbol
two arrows pointing away from the junction
questions.expl: Fig. 12-219 lines them up: straight bar = standard diode, bent-wing bar = zener, arrows OUT = LED, arrows IN = photodiode. Answer G33 #7/#17/#18 by that one detail.

questions.q: On the LED symbol, the two small arrows point—
options: away from the diode — it emits light
into the diode — it senses light
along the wire — direction of current
questions.expl: Arrows out = LED (emitter); arrows in = photodiode (receiver). Both appear side-by-side in Fig. 12-219, and the direction of those arrows is the ONLY difference.

questions.q: A logic-gate outline with a CURVED input edge (curved back) always belongs to the—
questions.expl: Shape sorts the families: curved back = OR family; flat back + D-nose = AND family; plain triangle = buffer/NOT. Then bubbles and double arcs pick the exact member.

questions.q: The small circle (bubble) drawn on a gate's output means the output is—
options: inverted — it adds NOT (OR→NOR, AND→NAND, X-OR→X-NOR)
amplified to a higher logic voltage
questions.expl: The handbook introduces the bubble on the NOT function ('a small circle on the output,' p. 12-121), and every N-gate is built that way: 'the term NOR is a combination of the NOT and OR' (p. 12-122).

questions.q: Add an output bubble to an X-OR gate and the symbol becomes—
questions.expl: 'The exclusive NOR (X-NOR) gate is nothing more than an X-OR' with the output inverted (p. 12-122). This is exactly the G33 #16 trap in reverse: bubble = X-NOR, no bubble = X-OR.

questions.q: The DOUBLED curved line across a gate's inputs marks the gate as—
questions.expl: The X-OR 'is different from the standard OR gate' — output 1 only when the inputs DIFFER (p. 12-122) — and its symbol says so with the second input arc (Fig. 12-264). Double arc = X; bubble = N.

questions.q: Symbol trap from the Fig. 4-29 chart: how do you tell the capacitor from the battery at a glance?
options: The capacitor has more plates than the battery
Capacitor plates are the SAME length; battery plates alternate long/short
questions.short: Equal plates = capacitor; long/short pairs = battery.
questions.expl: Both are parallel-line symbols, which is why G33 pairs them. The capacitor (condenser) shows two equal plates with a gap; the battery alternates long (+) and short (−) plates. Both sit on the Fig. 4-29 chart.

questions.q: This smooth S-shaped wavy line between two terminals — often confused with the current limiter and breaker — is—
questions.expl: Protection-device lineup: S-wave = fuse, point-to-point triangles = current limiter (Fig. 12-67B), bridge bump with a reset = circuit breaker (Fig. 12-68). Fuse and limiter get replaced; the breaker resets.

questions.q: You can tell a potentiometer's schematic symbol from a rheostat's because the potentiometer—
options: shows a third (wiper) terminal connected into the circuit
questions.short: Three connections vs. the rheostat's two.
questions.expl: Rheostat (Fig. 12-58): resistor + arrow, two terminals, controls current. Potentiometer (Fig. 12-60): 'a three-terminal device' — both ends plus the wiper — used to pick off a voltage.

questions.q: A single coil of round humps on a wire — with NO second coil and NO core lines — is—
questions.short: An inductor. Add a second coil + core lines and it becomes a transformer.
questions.expl: One coil = inductor. The transformer symbol (G33 #3) is literally two of these facing each other across the core's parallel lines (p. 12-65). The resistor is pointed zigzag, not round humps.

questions.q: 1. The frequency of the alternator voltage depends upon:
options: Strength of magnetic field and number of poles
Speed of rotation and strength of applied voltage
Number of poles and speed of rotation of the rotor
questions.short: Number of poles and rotor speed.
questions.expl: Alternator output frequency is set by how many magnetic poles the machine has and how fast the rotor spins: f = (poles × rpm) ÷ 120. Field strength and applied voltage change the OUTPUT VOLTAGE, not the frequency.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — alternator frequency

questions.q: 2. The total current of a circuit is the sum of the current in all branches:
options: The current remains the same throughout
questions.expl: In a parallel circuit the current splits among the branches and the branch currents add up to the total line current (Kirchhoff's current law). In a series circuit the SAME current flows through every part, so nothing 'adds.'
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — parallel circuits / Kirchhoff's current law

questions.q: 3. Many areas of aviation have shifted their focus from eliminating error to:
questions.expl: Modern human-factors and safety-management thinking accepts that people will always make mistakes, so the goal moved from the impossible dream of ELIMINATING error to catching, preventing, and MANAGING it before it causes harm.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 14 (Human Factors) — error management / SMS

questions.q: 4. A diode that is designed to break down and allow current to pass:
options: The LRU is defective and should be replaced with a GCU
questions.expl: A zener diode is built to conduct in the reverse direction once voltage reaches its 'zener' breakdown point, and it does this without being damaged. That controlled breakdown is exactly why zeners are used as voltage regulators/references.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — zener diode

questions.q: 5. Electrons of an atom appear at certain definite energy levels, known as:
questions.expl: Electrons occupy fixed energy levels arranged in shells around the nucleus. The outermost shell — the valence shell — decides whether a material is a conductor, insulator, or semiconductor.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — atomic structure / electron shells

questions.q: 6. The dry cell is the most common type of ______ battery.
questions.expl: A dry cell runs a one-way chemical reaction and cannot be recharged, which makes it a PRIMARY cell. Lead-acid and Ni-Cad are secondary (rechargeable) cells because their reaction reverses.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — primary vs. secondary cells

questions.q: 7. The four basic categories of LC 'analog' filters — low-pass, high-pass, band-pass, and band-stop — are collectively known as:
questions.expl: Filters built only from inductors and capacitors need no power supply of their own — they shape frequencies using stored energy in the L and C, so they are called PASSIVE filters. Active filters, by contrast, add an amplifier.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — LC / passive filters

questions.q: 8. What device is used to convert DC power to AC on some aircraft?
questions.expl: An inverter changes DC into AC (battery DC → 115 V 400 Hz AC for instruments and avionics). A rectifier does the opposite job, turning AC into DC.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — inverter (DC→AC)

questions.q: 9. There are two general types of AC motors used in aircraft systems:
questions.expl: Aircraft AC motors are either induction motors (simple, rugged, rotor 'slips' behind the field) or synchronous motors (rotor locks in exact step with the rotating field). Series/shunt/compound are DC-motor categories.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — AC motors

questions.q: 10. What is the basic function of all amplifiers?
questions.expl: Every amplifier exists to produce GAIN — to make a small input signal larger at the output. Anything that shrinks the signal is doing the opposite of amplifying.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — amplifiers / gain

questions.q: 11. The factors affecting capacitance are: parallel plates ______ proportional to their area, and ______ proportional to their spacing, separated by a dielectric.
options: Selecting a capacitor at least 50 percent higher than system voltage
questions.expl: Bigger plate area holds more charge, so capacitance is DIRECTLY proportional to area. Move the plates farther apart and capacitance falls, so it is INVERSELY proportional to spacing.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — factors affecting capacitance

questions.q: 12. Where the airframe or engine manufacturer has published a recommended corrosion inspection schedule and treatment program, which publication has precedence over the recommendation of the Advisory Circular?
options: The applicable program (manufacturer's) takes precedence over the recommendation of the Advisory Circular
The Advisory Circular takes precedence over the applicable program
The FAA decides who has precedence on a case-by-case hearing
questions.expl: An Advisory Circular gives acceptable general guidance, but when the airframe or engine maker publishes its own corrosion inspection and treatment program, that manufacturer's program takes precedence over the AC's recommendation.
questions.cite: AC 43-4B Corrosion Control / AC 43.13-1B — manufacturer program precedence

questions.q: 13. In a 115 V 400 Hz SERIES circuit with a 16 Ω resistor, 30 µF capacitor, and 22 mH inductor, what is the impedance?
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — series RLC impedance

questions.q: 14. To properly seat DC generator brushes, use No. 000 or finer sandpaper and under no circumstances:
options: Inspect the brushes after the generator has run a short period for debris
Use emery cloth or similar abrasives
Rotate the armature in the direction of rotation
questions.short: Never use emery cloth or similar abrasives.
questions.expl: Emery and similar abrasives are electrically CONDUCTIVE — grit left on the commutator can short bars together and cause arcing. Only non-conductive fine sandpaper (No. 000 or finer) is safe for seating brushes.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — DC generator brush service

questions.q: 15. Each cell in a Ni-Cad battery contains nickel hydrate in the positive plate and sponge cadmium on the negative plate. The open-cell voltage is:
questions.expl: A nickel-cadmium cell rests at roughly 1.2–1.25 volts open circuit. A 2-volt-per-cell figure belongs to lead-acid, not Ni-Cad.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — Ni-Cad cell voltage

questions.q: 16. What three factors create opposition to the flow of electrons in an AC circuit?
questions.expl: In AC, three things oppose current: plain resistance, inductive reactance (XL), and capacitive reactance (XC). Combined vectorially they make up impedance (Z) — so impedance is the RESULT, not one of the three ingredients.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — impedance components

questions.q: 17. A six-cell, 12-volt lead-acid battery produces approximately ______ per cell.
questions.expl: A lead-acid cell produces about 2 volts. Six of them in series give 6 × 2 = 12 volts, which is exactly why a 12-volt lead-acid battery has six cells.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — lead-acid cell voltage

questions.q: 18. Apparent power is the power in the entire circuit, including both resistance and reactance. It is:
options: Symbolized by the letters AP and measured in watts
Symbolized by the letter S and measured in volt-amps
questions.short: Symbolized by S and measured in volt-amps.
questions.expl: Apparent power is the total voltage × current the source must supply, symbolized S and measured in volt-amps (VA). True power (watts) is only the part actually consumed by resistance, so apparent power is greater than or equal to true power.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — apparent power / power triangle

questions.q: 19. When the direction of current flow is known, the direction of the lines of force can be established by:
questions.expl: Using electron-flow (current from negative to positive), grip the conductor with the LEFT hand, thumb pointing in the direction of electron flow, and the fingers curl the way the magnetic lines of force circle the wire.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — left-hand rule for magnetic field

questions.q: 20. The third particle of the atom is the ______ and is negatively charged.
questions.expl: The three basic atomic particles are the proton (positive), the neutron (no charge), and the electron (negative). The negatively charged one is the electron.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — atomic particles

questions.q: 21. There are two types of feedback in amplifiers:
questions.expl: Feedback returns part of the output to the input. POSITIVE feedback reinforces the input (used in oscillators); NEGATIVE feedback opposes it (used to stabilize gain and reduce distortion).
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — amplifier feedback

questions.q: 22. A 'repair' as performed on an aircraft means:
options: The restoration of the airframe to a condition for safe operation after damage or deterioration
The upkeep and preservation of the airframe including components thereof
Simple and minor preservation and the replacement of small standard parts not involving complex assembly operations
questions.short: Restoration to a safe condition after damage or deterioration.
questions.expl: A repair restores an article to a condition for safe operation after it has been damaged or has deteriorated. The first choice describes general maintenance/upkeep and the third describes preventive maintenance.
questions.cite: 14 CFR Part 43 (Maintenance / Preventive Maintenance) & §1.1 definitions — definitions of maintenance/repair

questions.q: 23. ESD is defined as:
questions.expl: ESD stands for Electrostatic Discharge — the sudden dump of static charge that can destroy sensitive solid-state components, which is why technicians ground themselves before handling them.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — ESD / handling of solid-state devices

questions.q: 24. At what frequency will the effects of a capacitor and an inductor be equal?
questions.expl: At the resonant frequency, inductive reactance (XL) exactly equals capacitive reactance (XC) so the two cancel. Below and above resonance one dominates; only AT resonance are they equal.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — resonance

questions.q: 25. In a DC generator, what causes the current to always flow in the same direction through the external circuit?
questions.expl: The armature actually generates AC, but the split-ring COMMUTATOR reverses the connection to the brushes at the instant the voltage would reverse, so the output to the outside circuit always flows one way — that is what makes it DC.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — commutator action

questions.q: 26. If kilo means 1,000, milli means:
questions.expl: The prefix milli means one-thousandth (10⁻³ = 0.001). It shrinks a unit, the mirror image of kilo, which multiplies by a thousand.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — metric prefixes

questions.q: 27. A transistor may be connected as common-emitter (CE), common-base (CB), or common-collector (CC). Which is most commonly used in amplifier circuits?
questions.expl: The common-emitter configuration provides both good voltage gain and good current gain, which makes it the workhorse of amplifier circuits. Common-collector is mainly a buffer and common-base is used at high frequencies.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — transistor amplifier configurations

questions.q: 28. In a 115 V 400 Hz SERIES circuit with 20 Ω resistance, an 18 mH inductor, and an 8 µF capacitor, the impedance will be:
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — series RLC impedance

questions.q: 29. If the maximum (peak) value is 186 volts, what is the effective value?
questions.expl: Effective (RMS) value = peak × 0.707. So 186 × 0.707 = 131.5 volts.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — effective (RMS) value

questions.q: 30. The most common type of fire extinguisher on the flight line is:
questions.expl: Carbon-dioxide (CO2) extinguishers are the traditional flight-line choice: CO2 smothers fuel and electrical fires, leaves no residue, and is non-conductive. (Halon is also widely used aboard aircraft — confirm which your instructor's slide names.)
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 1 (Safety, Ground Operations & Servicing) — fire extinguisher types

questions.q: 31. In a 115 V 400 Hz PARALLEL circuit with an 8 Ω resistor, 13 µF capacitor, and 19 mH inductor, what is the impedance?
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — parallel RLC impedance

questions.q: 32. Potential difference is known as:
questions.expl: Potential difference is the electrical 'pressure' between two points that pushes electrons — that pressure is voltage, measured in volts.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — potential difference / voltage

questions.q: 33. What switch has incandescent or LED bulbs to indicate function?
questions.expl: A lighted pushbutton switch has a bulb (incandescent or LED) built into the button so it glows to show its state or function — common on annunciator and control panels.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — switches

questions.q: 34. 3 volts is how many kilovolts?
questions.expl: Kilo means one thousand, so 1 kV = 1,000 V. To go from volts to kilovolts you divide by 1,000: 3 ÷ 1,000 = 0.003 kV.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — metric conversions

questions.q: 35. The four categories or states of matter are:
questions.expl: Matter exists as solids, liquids, gases, and plasma. The other lists mix up atomic particles or unrelated components.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — states of matter

questions.q: 36. When are we as an A&P required to generate a 3rd copy of a Form 337 and place it onboard the aircraft?
options: When the aircraft has extended-range fuel tanks installed in the cargo/cabin area
When it is done by a Repair Station
When the aircraft operates under a Special Airworthiness Certificate
questions.short: When extended-range fuel tanks are installed in the cargo/cabin.
questions.expl: For an extended-range (ferry/auxiliary) fuel tank installed in a cargo or passenger compartment, a copy of the Form 337 must be kept aboard the aircraft, in addition to the copies for the owner and the FAA.
questions.cite: 14 CFR Part 43 (Maintenance / Preventive Maintenance) & §1.1 definitions Appendix B — Form 337

questions.q: 37. A bag of resistors is marked 360 ohms ±10%. What color bands are on the resistors?
questions.expl: 3 = orange, 6 = blue, and the third (multiplier) band for ×10 is brown (36 × 10 = 360). The tolerance band for ±10% is silver. Gold would be ±5%, and a 3-band resistor with no tolerance band would be ±20%.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — resistor color code

questions.q: 38. Current flowing through a coil of wire produces a magnetic field. When the wire is formed into a coil, it becomes a(n):
questions.expl: A coil that stores energy in its magnetic field is an inductor, and inductance is measured in henries. Inductive reactance (XL, in ohms) is the OPPOSITION that inductor offers to AC — a related but different quantity.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — inductor / henry

questions.q: 39. What is matter?
options: Anything that has mass and volume
questions.short: Anything that has mass and occupies volume.
questions.expl: Matter is defined as anything that has mass AND takes up space (volume). Having mass alone or space alone is not the full definition.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — definition of matter

questions.q: 40. How would you define maintenance that requires the replacing or cleaning of spark plugs?
questions.expl: Cleaning and replacing spark plugs (and setting the gap) is specifically listed as preventive maintenance in the regulations — simple, minor work that does not involve complex assembly operations.
questions.cite: 14 CFR Part 43 (Maintenance / Preventive Maintenance) & §1.1 definitions Appendix A(c) — preventive maintenance

questions.q: 41. A field of force around a charged body is called:
questions.expl: The invisible field of force surrounding a charged body — the region where its charge exerts force on other charges — is the electrostatic field.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — electrostatic field

questions.q: 42. 'The induced current caused by the relative motion of a conductor and a magnetic field always flows in such a direction that its magnetic field opposes the motion.' This best describes:
questions.expl: Lenz's law states that an induced current always opposes the change that created it — the induced field pushes back against the motion. That 'push-back' is why generators require mechanical effort to turn.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — Lenz's law

questions.q: 43. The electrolyte of a Ni-Cad battery is ______ and is neutralized with ______.
questions.short: Potassium hydroxide, neutralized with boric acid.
questions.expl: A Ni-Cad uses an ALKALINE electrolyte, potassium hydroxide (KOH), so spills are neutralized with a mild acid — boric acid. Lead-acid is the opposite: sulfuric acid neutralized with baking soda (bicarbonate of soda).
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — Ni-Cad electrolyte

questions.q: 44. The density of a substance is its weight ______.
questions.expl: Density is how much a substance weighs for a given amount of space it fills — weight per unit volume (for example, pounds per cubic foot).

questions.q: 45. In an AC motor with a rotating magnetic field, one revolution of the field occurs in one cycle. If the frequency is 60 cps, the magnetic field makes how many revolutions per minute?
questions.expl: One revolution per cycle at 60 cycles per second = 60 rev/sec. Multiply by 60 seconds per minute: 60 × 60 = 3,600 revolutions per minute.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — rotating field speed

questions.q: 46. What has largely replaced direct current in commercial power systems?
questions.expl: Alternating current replaced DC for power distribution because AC voltage can be stepped up and down with transformers, letting power travel long distances efficiently.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — AC vs. DC power

questions.q: 47. Capacitive reactance is measured in:
questions.expl: Reactance — capacitive OR inductive — is an opposition to AC current, so like resistance it is measured in ohms. Farads measure capacitance itself and henries measure inductance.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — capacitive reactance

questions.q: 48. When current flow is in one direction, it is called:
questions.expl: Current that flows steadily in one direction only is direct current (DC), like the output of a battery. Current that periodically reverses is alternating current.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — direct current

questions.q: 49. A flashing red light from the control tower means:
options: Taxi clear of the runway in use
questions.short: Taxi clear of the runway in use.
questions.expl: To an aircraft on the ground, a FLASHING red light-gun signal means taxi clear of the runway in use. A STEADY red means stop — don't confuse the two.
questions.cite: FAA light-gun signals (AIM / Pilot-Controller reference) — light-gun signals

questions.q: 50. A pictorial drawing of two or more parts that fit together as an assembly is what kind of view?
questions.expl: An exploded view pulls the parts apart along common center lines so you can see how they fit together in the assembly — ideal for parts catalogs and reassembly. An assembly drawing shows the parts already joined.

questions.q: 51. Which is the state of flight where the main rotor system is turned by the relative wind passing through the disc, rather than by engine power?
questions.expl: In autorotation the engine is disconnected or failed and upward-flowing air through the rotor disc keeps the blades spinning, letting the helicopter glide down under control.

questions.q: 52. Select the container size equal in volume to 60 gallons of fuel. (7.5 gal = 1 cu ft)
questions.expl: Divide the gallons by the gallons-per-cubic-foot: 60 ÷ 7.5 = 8.0 cubic feet.

questions.q: 53. There are two ways to connect three-phase alternators:
questions.expl: The three windings of a three-phase alternator are joined either in a delta (triangle) or a wye (Y / star) configuration. Each gives a different relationship between phase and line voltage/current.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — three-phase (delta / wye)

questions.q: 54. A thermal source of electricity is defined as a:
options: Solar cell or photovoltaic cell device
questions.expl: A thermocouple produces voltage directly from HEAT: two dissimilar metals joined and heated create a small emf. A photovoltaic/solar cell is a LIGHT source, and a battery is a CHEMICAL source.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — thermal source of emf

questions.q: 55. In a 115 V 400 Hz PARALLEL circuit with a 12 Ω resistor, 30 Ω capacitive reactance, and 40 Ω inductive reactance, what is the impedance?
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — parallel RLC impedance

questions.q: 56. Standard atmospheric pressure can support a column of mercury that is 29.92 inches tall.
questions.expl: Standard atmospheric pressure (14.7 psi at sea level) balances a mercury column 29.92 inches high — the reference figure behind barometric altimeter and manifold-pressure readings.

questions.q: 57. What is the proper formula for 'Power'?
questions.expl: Work = force × distance. Power is the RATE of doing work, so you divide that work by the time it took: Power = (Force × distance) ÷ time.

questions.q: 58. A resistor used to vary current is called a:
questions.expl: A rheostat is a two-terminal variable resistor wired in series to control CURRENT (like a simple lamp dimmer). A potentiometer is a three-terminal device used to divide VOLTAGE.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — rheostat vs. potentiometer

questions.q: 59. N-type semiconductor material is doped with elements such as phosphorus, arsenic, and antimony. This causes it to have:
questions.expl: Phosphorus, arsenic, and antimony each supply a spare (fifth) valence electron, giving N-type material extra free ELECTRONS (negative carriers). P-type material, doped the other way, has holes.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — N-type semiconductor

questions.q: 60. The universal numbering system provides a means of identifying:
questions.expl: The universal numbering system is a filing method for drawings in which the number itself identifies the standard sheet size, so drawings can be located and reproduced consistently.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B (Aircraft Drawings chapter) — universal numbering system

questions.q: 61. When using a fire extinguisher, what is the best method for extinguishing a fire?
options: Aim at the base and sweep side to side
Aim at the middle and sweep up and down
Aim at the smoke and sweep side to side
questions.short: Aim at the base and sweep side to side.
questions.expl: Aim the agent at the BASE of the flames — where the fuel actually burns — and sweep side to side (the 'S' in the PASS method: Pull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep). Hitting the smoke does nothing.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 1 (Safety, Ground Operations & Servicing) — fire extinguisher use (PASS)

questions.q: 62. Another method to reverse motor direction is called the ______ method, which changes the direction of current flow in either the armature or the field.
questions.expl: A reversing SWITCH lets you flip the current in EITHER the armature or the field (but not both), which reverses rotation. Reversing the whole supply — the battery — flips both at once and the motor keeps turning the same way.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — reversing motor direction

questions.q: 63. To prevent corrosion, operators must follow a constant cycle of:
options: Cleaning, inspection, operational preservation, and lubrication
Keeping drain holes and passages open and functional
questions.expl: Corrosion control is an ongoing cycle: clean the aircraft, inspect it, apply preservatives, and lubricate. Open drain holes and knowledge help, but the defined recurring CYCLE is clean-inspect-preserve-lubricate.
questions.cite: AC 43-4B Corrosion Control / AC 43.13-1B — corrosion prevention cycle

questions.q: 64. Three methods to increase the strength of a magnetic field are:
options: Conventional flow, electron flow, electromotive force
Increase current flow, number of loops, and type of metal in the core
questions.short: More current, more loops, better core metal.
questions.expl: An electromagnet gets stronger when you push more current through it, add more turns (loops) of wire, or use a more permeable core material such as soft iron.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — electromagnet strength

questions.q: 65. Of the three basic DC motor types — series, shunt, and compound — which is particularly suitable when constant speed is desired?
questions.expl: A shunt motor's field is across the line, so its field strength stays nearly constant and it holds a fairly steady speed from no load to full load — the choice when constant speed matters. A series motor's speed swings wildly with load.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — shunt motor speed regulation

questions.q: 66. Concerning fixed resistors, heat is typically classified as:
questions.expl: A fixed resistor's job is to oppose current, and the heat it produces is wasted energy — an unwanted loss (I²R loss), not a useful output.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — resistor power dissipation

questions.q: 67. When capacitors are connected in parallel, the effective plate area increases, and:
options: The total capacitance is less than the individual capacitances
The total capacitance is equal to the individual capacitances
The total capacitance is the sum of the individual capacitances
questions.short: Total capacitance is the sum of the individual capacitances.
questions.expl: Wiring capacitors in parallel adds their plate areas together, so their capacitances simply ADD (CT = C1 + C2 + C3…). That is the opposite of resistors in parallel.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — capacitors in parallel

questions.q: 68. Factors affecting resistance are:
questions.expl: A conductor's resistance depends on all four: what it is made of (material), how long it is (longer = more), its cross-sectional area (thicker = less), and its temperature.
