questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — factors affecting resistance

questions.q: 69. In the starting sequence of a turbine engine, the most important instrument to monitor after fuel flow is:
options: Oil pressure to prevent the engine from seizing
questions.expl: Right after fuel is introduced during a turbine start, EGT is watched closely to catch a hot start — a temperature spike that can quickly damage the engine. If EGT climbs too fast, the start is aborted.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-32B (Powerplant — engine start / fuels) — turbine engine starting

questions.q: 70. The number of cycles per second is a definition of ______.
questions.expl: How many complete AC cycles occur each second is the frequency, measured in hertz (one hertz = one cycle per second).
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — frequency / hertz

questions.q: 71. A series circuit with 110 volts at 60 cps and a capacitance of 80 µF — what is the capacitive reactance?
questions.expl: XC = 1 ÷ (2πfC) = 1 ÷ [2π(60)(80×10⁻⁶)] = 1 ÷ 0.030159 ≈ 33.157 Ω. (This is the handbook's own worked example.)
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — capacitive reactance

questions.q: 72. What is the total power of a 115 V 400 Hz series circuit containing a 1/2-hp motor at 80% efficiency, three landing lights at 1.5 amps each, and a 15-watt electric oven?
questions.expl: Motor input = (0.5 × 746) ÷ 0.80 = 373 ÷ 0.80 = 466.25 W. Lights = 3 × 1.5 A × 115 V = 517.5 W. Oven = 15 W. Total = 466.25 + 517.5 + 15 = 998.75 W. (Forgetting the oven gives the 983.75 trap.)
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — electrical power totals

questions.q: 73. Most AC voltmeters display:
questions.expl: A typical AC voltmeter is calibrated to read the RMS (effective) value — the DC-equivalent heating value — not the higher peak value. That is why '115 V' AC means 115 V RMS.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — AC meters read RMS

questions.q: 74. A 6 µF capacitor is expressed as:
questions.expl: Micro means one-millionth (10⁻⁶), so 6 µF = 6 × 0.000001 = 0.000006 farad — the decimal moved six places to the left.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — microfarad conversion

questions.q: 75. Files are usually made with two types of cutting profiles, which are:
questions.expl: File teeth come in single-cut (one row of parallel teeth, for a fine finish) and double-cut (two crossing rows, for fast material removal).

questions.q: 76. The most noticeable effect seen when a battery is turned around, reverse-biasing a diode, is:
questions.expl: Reverse bias pulls the charge carriers AWAY from the junction, so the depletion (insulating) region gets WIDER and the diode blocks current. Forward bias narrows it and lets current flow.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — reverse-biased diode

questions.q: 77. The four most common sources of electricity are:
options: Magnetic, direct current, battery, alternating current
questions.expl: Voltage can be produced by pressure (piezoelectric), chemical action (batteries), heat (thermocouples), and light (photocells) — plus friction and magnetism. The other lists mix up unrelated or duplicate terms.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — sources of electricity

questions.q: 78. Energy is defined as:
questions.expl: Energy is simply the capacity to do work — to exert a force over a distance. Everything else listed is a specific electrical phenomenon, not the definition of energy.

questions.q: 79. A combination of an iron core inside a coil of wire loops is called an:
questions.expl: Wrap a coil of wire around an iron core and pass current through it and you get an electromagnet — a magnet you can switch on and off. Reluctance and retentivity are magnetic PROPERTIES, not the device.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — electromagnet

questions.q: 80. A micrometer is read from a low-contrast scale. The barrel/sleeve shows past the 3 mark, the thimble reads near 20, and the vernier lines align to give the ten-thousandths digit. Which value is the best-supported reading?
questions.expl: Best supported reading from the (faint) scale is 0.3698 inch — barrel + thimble land in the 0.369–0.370 range and the vernier line places the ten-thousandths digit at 8. NOTE: the scan is low-contrast, so treat this ten-thousandths digit as a spot-check item against the actual gauge.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B (Materials, Processes & Precision Tools) — micrometer reading (vernier 0.0001)

questions.q: 81. The law of electromagnetic induction states that the induced emf in a closed loop of wire is:
options: Proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux through the coil of wire
questions.short: Proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux.
questions.expl: Faraday's law of induction: the induced emf equals how FAST the magnetic flux through the loop is changing. Change the flux quickly and you induce a large voltage; hold it steady and you induce none.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — Faraday's law of induction

questions.q: 82. Conventional flow is known as:
questions.expl: Conventional current is defined as flowing from the positive terminal to the negative terminal (the direction positive charge would move). Electron flow is the physical opposite: negative to positive.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — conventional current flow

questions.q: 83. Regarding helicopter weight and balance, which statement is true?
options: The moment of tail-mounted components is subject to constant change
Weight-and-balance procedures for airplanes generally apply to helicopters
Regardless of loading, lateral-axis CG control is not a major factor for helicopters
questions.short: Airplane W&B procedures generally apply to helicopters.
questions.expl: The same basic weight-and-balance math used for airplanes applies to helicopters. The other statements are false: a fixed tail component's moment does not constantly change, and LATERAL CG absolutely IS a major factor for helicopters (unlike most airplanes).
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-1 (Aircraft Weight & Balance Handbook) — helicopter weight & balance

questions.q: 84. What is the vernier scale graduation on a micrometer?
questions.expl: The vernier scale on a micrometer adds a fourth digit, reading to ten-thousandths of an inch — 0.0001 in. Without the vernier, an ordinary micrometer reads only to 0.001 in.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B (Materials, Processes & Precision Tools) — micrometer vernier graduation

questions.q: 85. An open circuit represents:
questions.expl: An open circuit is a break in the path, so no current can flow — that is the same as having infinitely large resistance. A short circuit is the opposite: near-zero resistance and very high current.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — open circuit

questions.q: 86. The magnetic field that escapes a transformer during operation is called:
questions.expl: The portion of the primary's magnetic flux that does NOT link the secondary — it 'leaks' out of the core — is leakage flux, and it represents lost coupling. Eddy currents are a different (heating) loss.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — transformer leakage flux

questions.q: 87. In a 115 V 400 Hz circuit, a 25 µF capacitor will have a reactance of:
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — capacitive reactance

questions.q: 88. One horsepower is required to move 33,000 pounds one foot in one minute, or:
options: Force times distance divided by time
questions.expl: 33,000 ft-lb per minute divided by 60 seconds = 550 ft-lb per second — the handbook's own restatement of one horsepower. (1 hp also equals 746 watts, so that figure is a true equivalent too, but the direct foot-pound restatement is 550 ft-lb/s.)

questions.q: 89. Which of the following has the greatest strength-to-weight ratio?
questions.expl: Of the three, titanium has the highest strength-to-weight ratio — nearly as strong as steel but far lighter — which is why it is used in high-stress, high-temperature aircraft structure.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B (Materials, Processes & Precision Tools) — aircraft metals

questions.q: 90. Distraction is defined as:
options: Failure to see a condition, understand what it is, and predict the possible results
Standard practices, usually undocumented, adopted by an organization or group
An unlimited number of events or conditions that interrupt one's ability to focus on a specific task
questions.short: Anything that interrupts focus on a task.
questions.expl: In human factors, distraction is any of the countless events or conditions that break your concentration on the task at hand — a leading cause of maintenance error. The second describes 'norms' and the third describes lack of awareness.

questions.q: 91. When an aircraft is weighed with full fuel, the fuel weight must be subtracted from the scale readings. What instrument is used to calculate the weight of the fuel?
questions.expl: A hydrometer measures the fuel's specific gravity (density). From the density and the known volume you calculate the fuel's actual weight so it can be subtracted. A hygrometer measures humidity — different tool.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-1 (Aircraft Weight & Balance Handbook) — fuel weight / hydrometer

questions.q: 92. A GCU is known as a:
questions.expl: GCU stands for Generator Control Unit — the box that regulates the generator's voltage and provides sensing and protection (overvoltage, reverse current) for the DC generating system.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — Generator Control Unit (GCU)

questions.q: 93. To cure the 'memory effect' of Ni-Cad batteries in standby applications, Ni-Cad batteries have been:
questions.expl: In standby uses (such as emergency lighting) Ni-Cads can develop voltage-depression 'memory,' so they have been replaced by sealed lead-acid batteries, which don't suffer the effect and need less scheduled maintenance.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — sealed lead-acid vs. Ni-Cad

questions.q: 94. To measure resistance in a circuit, the circuit must:
questions.expl: An ohmmeter supplies its OWN small current from an internal battery, so the circuit under test must be de-energized. Measuring resistance with power applied gives a false reading and can damage the meter.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — measuring resistance / ohmmeter

questions.q: 95. In a series-parallel network: ET = 124 V, R1 = 6 Ω (series, drop E1), then R2 = 4 Ω and R3 = 2 Ω in PARALLEL (drops E2 and E3), then R4 = 3 Ω (series, drop E4). What is the voltage at E2 and E4?
questions.expl: The parallel pair combines to (4 × 2) ÷ (4 + 2) = 1.333 Ω. RT = 6 + 1.333 + 3 = 10.333 Ω, so IT = 124 ÷ 10.333 = 12 A. E1 = 12 × 6 = 72 V; the parallel section drops E2 = E3 = 12 × 1.333 = 16 V; E4 = 12 × 3 = 36 V. Check: 72 + 16 + 36 = 124 V.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — series-parallel circuit analysis

questions.q: 96. When calculating capacitors in series, the total capacitance will be:
options: Less than that of the smallest capacitor
The sum of the individual capacitances
Less than the sum of individual capacitance plus the total farads
questions.short: Less than that of the smallest capacitor.
questions.expl: Capacitors in series behave the opposite of parallel ones — total capacitance drops below even the smallest capacitor in the string (1/CT = 1/C1 + 1/C2 + …), because the effective plate spacing increases.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — capacitors in series

questions.q: 97. When current and voltage pass through zero and reach maximum value at the same time:
options: The current leads the applied voltage
The current and voltage are said to be in phase
The current lags the applied voltage
questions.expl: If current and voltage cross zero together and peak together, they are IN PHASE — the mark of a purely resistive AC circuit. In inductive or capacitive circuits they are shifted, so one leads or lags the other.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — phase relationship

questions.q: 98. Maximum value is ______ times the effective value, and is called the peak value.
questions.expl: To go from effective (RMS) up to peak, multiply by 1.414 (peak = RMS × 1.414). Going the other way, from peak down to RMS, you multiply by 0.707.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — peak vs. effective value

questions.q: 99. The state of charge of a lead-acid battery is indicated by:
options: The density (specific gravity) of the electrolyte, using a hydrometer
The electrolyte being approximately 30 percent water and 70 percent acid
The level of electrolyte after a complete charge
questions.short: The specific gravity of the electrolyte (hydrometer).
questions.expl: As a lead-acid battery discharges, the acid weakens and the electrolyte's specific gravity drops. A hydrometer reads that specific gravity, giving a direct indication of the state of charge.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics) — lead-acid state of charge

questions.q: 100. Microbiological growth is commonly found in what type of aviation fuel?
questions.expl: Microbes (the 'jet fuel fungus') thrive at the water/fuel interface in turbine fuel such as Jet A, forming slime that clogs filters and promotes corrosion. AVGAS is much less prone to it.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-32B (Powerplant — engine start / fuels) — microbial growth in turbine fuel

questions.q: Worksheet #1 — The ability of a component to store an electric charge is called—
questions.short: Capacitance — a capacitor's ability to store charge (symbol C).
questions.expl: 'The measure of a capacitor's ability to store charge is its capacitance. The symbol used for capacitance is the letter C.' Picture a stretchy balloon on the end of the wire: pump charge in and it stores it, ready to give back later. Inductance is the coil's opposition to a CHANGE in current, and reactance is the AC opposition those parts create — different jobs.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-50 (Capacitance; The RC Time Constant)

questions.q: Worksheet #2 — In older electrical texts, a capacitor is referred to by what other name?
questions.short: Condenser — the old-school name for a capacitor.
questions.expl: 'Condenser' is the vintage word for a capacitor — the FAA handbook still slips into it, naming the 80-microfarad capacitor in its own reactance sample problem 'a condenser' (p. 12-54). Don't confuse it with a conductor (a wire that carries current) or a commutator (the split ring on a DC generator/motor).
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-54 (Xc sample problem — 'the capacitance of a condenser is 80 µF')

questions.q: Worksheet #3 — The opposition that an INDUCTOR (coil) offers to alternating current is called—
questions.short: Inductive reactance (XL) — a coil's opposition to AC.
questions.expl: 'This opposition is called inductive reactance, symbolized by XL, and is measured in ohms just as resistance is measured.' A coil fights any CHANGE in current, and AC is nothing but constant change, so the coil pushes back the whole time. Capacitive reactance is the capacitor's version of the same idea, and plain resistance opposes both AC and DC alike.

questions.q: Worksheet #4 — The time required for a capacitor to charge to about 63.2% of the supply voltage is one—
questions.short: RC time constant — τ = R × C.
questions.expl: 'The time constant of a series resistor/capacitor (RC) circuit... equals the product of the resistance in ohms and the capacitance in farad and is symbolized by the Greek letter tau (τ). τ = RC.' The FAA rounds it to 'charge to 63 percent of the source' (p. 12-50); your worksheet's 63.2% is the exact figure (1 − 1/e). Same milestone — after five time constants (5τ) the capacitor is ~99% full. Think of filling a surge tank through a narrow pipe: the fatter the tank (C) or the tighter the pipe (R), the longer it takes.

questions.q: Worksheet #5 — The NONCONDUCTIVE material placed between the two plates of a capacitor is the—
questions.short: Dielectric — the insulator between the plates. NOT 'diode.'
questions.expl: 'The capacitor is constructed of two parallel plates separated by a nonconductor called a dielectric.' The look-alike trap is DIODE — a one-way electronic valve, a totally different part. The dielectric's whole job is to insulate: it keeps the plates from touching so they can hold opposite charges facing each other. Air, paper, mica, ceramic, and oxide films are all dielectrics.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-50 (Capacitance — parallel plates separated by a dielectric)

questions.q: Worksheet #6 — The opposition a CAPACITOR offers to alternating current as it charges and discharges is called—
questions.short: Capacitive reactance (Xc) — a capacitor's opposition to AC.
questions.expl: As AC charges and discharges a capacitor every alternation, the capacitor builds an opposing charge that fights the current — 'the actual AC reactance Xc, which just like resistance, is measured in ohms.' Inductive reactance is the coil's version; impedance is the grand total of resistance AND reactance combined, not the capacitor's part alone.

questions.q: Worksheet #7 — The maximum DC voltage a capacitor can withstand before its dielectric is damaged is its—
questions.short: Working voltage — the max safe DC across the plates. NOT 'peak.'
questions.expl: 'The voltage rating... specifies the maximum DC voltage that can be applied without the risk of damage to the device. This voltage rating is typically called the breakdown voltage, the working voltage, or simply the voltage rating.' Push past it and 'the dielectric breaks down and arcing occurs between the plates.' The trap is PEAK voltage — that's the top of an AC sine wave, a different idea entirely; you actually pick a working voltage well ABOVE the peak the cap will see.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-51 (Voltage Rating of a Capacitor)

questions.q: Worksheet #8 — The effective value of an AC voltage — the value that differs from its peak and equals 0.707 × peak — is the—
questions.expl: The effective value is the RMS (root mean square) value — the DC-equivalent 'heating' value of the AC. It matters for capacitors because ratings are DC but AC swings higher than its RMS reading: 'An alternating voltage of 500 volts (RMS) has a peak voltage of 707 volts, and a capacitor to which it is applied should have a working voltage of at least 750 volts.' So RMS and peak are NOT the same number, and the working voltage must clear the peak with margin.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-49 (Effective Value); p. 12-51 (500 V RMS → 707 V peak)

questions.q: Worksheet #9 — A fixed capacitor that uses a mineral for its dielectric and is prized for high stability at higher voltages is the—
questions.short: Mica capacitor — metal-foil plates separated by mica sheets.
questions.expl: 'The fixed mica capacitor is made of metal foil plates that are separated by sheets of mica, which form the dielectric... Mica is an excellent dielectric and withstands higher voltages than paper without allowing arcing between the plates.' Mica (a natural mineral) is stable and moisture-sealed in molded plastic. Contrast: the electrolytic packs huge capacitance but is polarized and DC-only; the variable cap is the small tunable radio part.

questions.q: Worksheet #10 — A capacitor whose capacitance can be changed by the operator — as in a radio tuner — is a—
questions.expl: 'Variable capacitors are mostly used in radio tuning circuits, and they are sometimes called tuning capacitors.' You change the capacitance by sliding one set of plates in or out of mesh with the other, which changes the effective plate area (Factor #1 of capacitance). A fixed capacitor is locked at one value; an electrolytic is fixed AND polarized.

questions.q: Worksheet #11 — Which statement best defines a CAPACITOR?
options: a one-way device that allows current to flow in only one direction
two conductive plates separated by a dielectric, used to store an electric charge
a coil of wire that opposes any change in the current through it
questions.short: Capacitor = two plates + a dielectric = a charge storehouse.
questions.expl: 'In its most basic form, the capacitor is constructed of two parallel plates separated by a nonconductor called a dielectric. In an electrical circuit, a capacitor serves as a reservoir or storehouse for electricity.' The coil-that-opposes-change is an INDUCTOR; the one-way device is a DIODE. Only the capacitor is built as plates + dielectric to bank charge.

questions.q: Worksheet #12 — Which statement best defines REACTANCE?
options: the opposition to any current caused by the resistance of the conductor
the total combined opposition of resistance and reactance together
the opposition to alternating current caused by inductance or capacitance
questions.short: Reactance = AC opposition from inductance OR capacitance.
questions.expl: Reactance comes in two flavors — inductive reactance (XL) from coils and capacitive reactance (Xc) from capacitors — and both 'oppose current flow only in AC circuits, not in DC circuits' (p. 12-49). Plain resistance opposes ALL current; impedance is resistance and reactance ADDED together. Reactance is specifically the AC-only, coil-or-cap part.

questions.q: Worksheet #13 — Which statement best defines a FIXED CAPACITOR?
options: a capacitor with a constant capacitance value that cannot be adjusted
a capacitor that stores no charge until it is manually set
a capacitor whose value is changed by moving its plates
questions.short: Fixed capacitor — one permanent, unchangeable value.
questions.expl: A fixed capacitor is manufactured at one set capacitance and stays there — mica, ceramic, electrolytic, oil, and polyester film are all fixed types, 'further divided according to the type of dielectric used.' The one you CAN change by moving plates is the variable (tuning) capacitor — that's exactly what makes it variable.

questions.q: Worksheet #14 — Which statement best defines a capacitor's WORKING VOLTAGE?
options: the peak voltage the AC source reaches on each cycle
the maximum voltage the capacitor can safely handle in normal operation
the exact voltage at which the capacitor stores the most charge
questions.short: Working voltage = the max SAFE operating voltage.
questions.expl: The working voltage 'specifies the maximum DC voltage that can be applied without the risk of damage to the device.' It's a safety ceiling, not a sweet spot and not a property of the source. The rule of thumb: 'the capacitor should be selected so that its working voltage is at least 50 percent greater than the highest voltage to be applied.' Stay under the ceiling with margin and the dielectric survives.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-51 (Voltage Rating of a Capacitor)

questions.q: Worksheet #15 — The FARAD is the basic unit of—
questions.expl: 'The basic unit of capacitance is the farad and is given by the letter f. By definition, one farad is one coulomb of charge stored with one volt across the plates of the capacitor.' Inductance is measured in HENRIES and reactance in OHMS — three different quantities, three different units. One farad is huge, so real parts read in microfarads (µF) and picofarads (pF).

questions.q: Worksheet #16 — Which statement best describes a VARIABLE CAPACITOR?
options: one whose capacitance can be adjusted, typically by moving one set of plates relative to the other
one sealed at a single capacitance that never changes
one that must be replaced to obtain a different capacitance
questions.short: Variable cap — move the plates, change the capacitance.
questions.expl: Sliding one plate set in or out of mesh changes how much plate area faces across the gap, and since capacitance is directly proportional to plate area (Factor #1), the value tracks the knob. That's why they're the 'tuning capacitors' of radio circuits (100–500 pF). A part that never changes is a fixed capacitor.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-53 (Variable Capacitors); p. 12-51 (Factors Affecting Capacitance)

questions.q: Worksheet #17 — CAPACITIVE REACTANCE is best defined as—
options: the opposition to current in a DC circuit caused by resistors
the opposition to current in an AC circuit caused by capacitors
the opposition to current in an AC circuit caused by inductors
questions.short: Capacitive reactance (Xc) — AC opposition from capacitors.
questions.expl: As a capacitor charges and discharges on AC it builds an opposing voltage that limits the current — measured in ohms as Xc = 1/(2πfC). Coils give INDUCTIVE reactance (XL); resistors give resistance, which acts in DC too. Reactance of either kind is an AC-only effect.

questions.q: Worksheet #18 — A DIELECTRIC is best described as—
options: a conductor that carries charge from one plate to the other
a semiconductor that lets charge flow one way only
an insulator (nonconductor) placed between the plates of a capacitor
questions.short: Dielectric = the insulator between the plates.
questions.expl: 'Two parallel plates separated by a nonconductor called a dielectric.' Its job is to INSULATE — hold the plates apart so opposite charges can face each other without shorting. If it conducted, the plates would neutralize and store nothing. Every dielectric has a breakdown limit; exceed the working voltage and it arcs through.

questions.q: Worksheet #19 — The RC TIME CONSTANT is defined as the time for a capacitor's voltage to reach about—
questions.expl: 'The time in the formula is the time required to charge to 63 percent of the voltage of the source' — the FAA's rounding of the exact 63.2% (1 − 1/e) your worksheet uses. It reaches ~99% (essentially full) only after FIVE time constants, so one τ is nowhere near 100%, and it's well past the halfway 50% mark. τ = R × C.

questions.q: Worksheet #20 — INDUCTIVE REACTANCE is best defined as—
options: the opposition to alternating current caused by the electric field of a capacitor
the opposition to alternating current caused by the magnetic field of an inductor
the opposition to direct current caused by the resistance of a coil's wire
questions.short: Inductive reactance (XL) — AC opposition from a coil's magnetic field.
questions.expl: 'The effects of the magnetic fields are a continuously inducted voltage opposition to the current in the circuit. This opposition is called inductive reactance, symbolized by XL.' It comes from the coil's collapsing/building MAGNETIC field, not a capacitor's electric field, and it exists only in AC — the coil's plain wire resistance is what opposes DC.

questions.q: A capacitor of 20 µF charges through a 10 kΩ resistor. The RC time constant (τ) of the circuit is—
questions.expl: τ = R × C, but the formula only speaks BASE units — ohms and FARADS. Hop the capacitor down the ladder first: 20 µF, µ→base is 6 hops left, = 0.000020 F. Now multiply: 10,000 × 0.000020 = 0.2 second. After that one τ the cap is ~63% charged; five of them (1.0 s) gets it to ~99%. Forgetting the µF→F hop is what produces the 200-second monster.

questions.q: Find the capacitive reactance of an 80 µF capacitor at 60 cps (the handbook's own sample problem). Xc = 1/(2πfC) equals about—
questions.expl: Straight from p. 12-54: 'First, the capacitance, 80 µF, is changed to farads by dividing 80 by 1,000,000... This quotient equals 0.000080 farad.' Then Xc = 1/(6.28 × 60 × 0.000080) = 33.2 ohms. The whole problem hinges on the µF→F hop (6 places) — skip it and your answer is off by a factor of a million, which is exactly where 33,200 comes from.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-54 (Xc sample problem, 80 µF / 60 cps)

questions.q: In the formula Xc = 1/(2πfC), if the frequency INCREASES, the capacitive reactance—
questions.short: Xc is INVERSE to frequency — freq up, Xc down.
questions.expl: Frequency sits in the DENOMINATOR of Xc = 1/(2πfC), so raising it shrinks Xc: at high frequency the capacitor barely opposes the current (it passes AC easily); at low frequency it opposes a lot; at DC (f = 0) it blocks completely. 'A good capacitor blocks DC and passes the effects of pulsing DC or AC' (p. 12-50). This is the opposite behavior from an inductor.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-54 (Xc = 1/(2πfC)); p. 12-50 (blocks DC, passes AC)

questions.q: In the formula XL = 2πfL, if the frequency INCREASES, the inductive reactance—
questions.short: XL is DIRECT with frequency — freq up, XL up.
questions.expl: 'The inductive reactance of a component is directly proportional to the inductance... and the applied frequency. By increasing either the inductance or applied frequency, the inductive reactance likewise increases.' Frequency multiplies in the NUMERATOR of XL = 2πfL, the mirror image of the capacitor: a coil passes low frequencies (and DC) easily but chokes high frequencies. Memory pair — coil chokes fast AC, cap passes fast AC.

questions.q: An old service manual calls a component a 'condenser.' On a modern schematic you would find this same part labeled a—
questions.short: Condenser = the old name for a capacitor.
questions.expl: Same part, older word. The FAA handbook itself does it — its capacitive-reactance sample problem reads 'the capacitance of a condenser is 80 µF' (p. 12-54). So a 'condenser' stores charge between plates just like any capacitor. An inductor is a coil and a resistor is a current-limiter — neither is a condenser.

questions.q: A capacitor's rating that says the dielectric will physically fail (arc through) if exceeded is its BREAKDOWN voltage. How does it relate to the WORKING voltage a technician selects?
options: the working voltage and breakdown voltage are the same number, used interchangeably
the working voltage is chosen with margin — at least 50% above the highest voltage to be applied — so the capacitor never reaches breakdown
the working voltage is set higher than the breakdown voltage for extra safety
questions.short: Pick working V ≥ 50% above the applied — safely below breakdown.
questions.expl: 'If the voltage applied across the plates is too great, the dielectric breaks down and arcing occurs' — that's breakdown. To stay clear of it, 'the capacitor should be selected so that its working voltage is at least 50 percent greater than the highest voltage to be applied.' The FAA lists 'breakdown voltage, working voltage, or simply the voltage rating' together as the maximum-safe number, but the design habit is to leave a 50% cushion, never to run a cap AT its limit — and you can't exceed the breakdown, so a working V set above it makes no sense.

questions.q: You need a large capacitance (hundreds of µF) in a small can for a DC power-supply filter, and the part is marked with '+' and '−' leads. Which type is it?
questions.short: Electrolytic — big µF, small size, polarized (+/−), DC only.
questions.expl: 'Electrolytic capacitors provide large capacitance in small physical sizes. Their values range from 1 to about 1,500 microfarads. Unlike the other types, electrolytic capacitors are generally polarized, with the positive lead marked +... and should only be subjected to direct voltage.' The '+/−' marking is the giveaway. Mica is a small, stable, non-polarized part (≤ ~0.05 µF); a variable cap is a tiny tunable radio part (100–500 pF).

questions.q: Why is there NO continuous current THROUGH a good capacitor on a steady DC circuit, even though current flows in the wires while it charges?
options: the dielectric is an insulator, so charge builds on the plates but cannot cross the gap between them
the plates are too far apart for electrons to travel between them at any voltage
the capacitor converts the DC into heat until the current stops
questions.short: The dielectric insulates — charge parks on the plates, none crosses.
questions.expl: 'There can be no continuous movement of DC through a capacitor. A good capacitor blocks DC and passes the effects of pulsing DC or AC.' Current flows in the external wires only WHILE the plates are charging or discharging; once charged to the source voltage, it stops — 'even though the circuit is broken by the gap between the capacitor plates.' The dielectric's insulating job is the whole reason: it lets opposite charges face each other without a path across.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, p. 12-50 (Capacitors in Direct Current; blocks DC)

questions.q: A capacitor is marked 1 µF. Expressed in picofarads, that is—
questions.short: µ→p is 6 hops right: 1 µF = 1,000,000 pF.
questions.expl: The two common capacitor units bracket the farad: microfarad (µF) = 10⁻⁶ F and picofarad (pF) = 10⁻¹² F. From µ to p is six decimal places — hop the point six places RIGHT (smaller bucket, so MORE of them): 1 µF → 1,000,000 pF. Going the other way, 1,500 pF would be 0.0015 µF. Keep the ladder handy: it's the same hop that trips people on Xc and τ problems.

questions.q: About how many time constants must pass before a charging capacitor reaches essentially full charge (~99% of source voltage)?
questions.expl: 'The time required to bring the charge to about 99 percent of the source voltage is approximately 5 τ.' One τ gets you only to ~63% (the worksheet's 63.2%); the curve keeps flattening — ~86% at 2τ, ~95% at 3τ, ~98% at 4τ, ~99% at 5τ. The '63' in '63 percent' is a percentage, not a count of time constants, which is the trap in the 63-time-constants answer.

questions.q: 1. A resistor is banded Red-Violet-Orange-Gold. What is its value and tolerance?
questions.expl: Read the first two bands as digits: Red = 2, Violet = 7, giving 27. The third band, Orange = 3, is the multiplier — add 3 zeros (×10^3). So 27 becomes 27,000 Ω. Gold in the fourth band means ±5% tolerance. Wrong multiplier would give 2,700 (only 2 zeros) or 270,000 (4 zeros); silver would be ±10%.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (resistor color code / color band decoding, pp. 12-24-12-25, Fig. 12-49)

questions.q: 2. A resistor is banded Brown-Black-Red-Gold. What is its value and tolerance?
questions.expl: Brown = 1 and Black = 0 give the two digits 10. The third band, Red = 2, adds 2 zeros, so 10 becomes 1,000 Ω (1 kΩ). Gold means ±5%. One zero would give 100 Ω; three zeros would give 10,000 Ω; silver would make it ±10%.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (resistor color code / color band decoding, pp. 12-24-12-25, Fig. 12-49)

questions.q: 3. A resistor is banded Yellow-Violet-Brown-Gold. What is its value and tolerance?
questions.expl: Yellow = 4 and Violet = 7 give 47. The third band, Brown = 1, adds just 1 zero, so 47 becomes 470 Ω. Gold is ±5%. Adding no zeros would give 47 Ω; adding two zeros would give 4,700 Ω; silver would be ±10%.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (resistor color code / color band decoding, pp. 12-24-12-25, Fig. 12-49)

questions.q: 4. A resistor is banded Red-Red-Red-Silver. What is its value and tolerance?
questions.expl: The first two Reds give digits 2 and 2 = 22. The third band, Red = 2, adds 2 zeros, so 22 becomes 2,200 Ω (2.2 kΩ). Silver in the fourth band means ±10%. Gold would be ±5%; one zero would give 220 Ω; three zeros would give 22,000 Ω.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (resistor color code / color band decoding, pp. 12-24-12-25, Fig. 12-49)

questions.q: 5. A resistor is banded Brown-Black-Orange-Gold. What is its value and tolerance?
questions.expl: Brown = 1 and Black = 0 give 10. The third band, Orange = 3, adds 3 zeros, so 10 becomes 10,000 Ω (10 kΩ). Gold is ±5%. Two zeros would give 1,000 Ω; four zeros would give 100,000 Ω; silver would be ±10%.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (resistor color code / color band decoding, pp. 12-24-12-25, Fig. 12-49)

questions.q: 6. A resistor is banded Green-Blue-Brown-Gold. What is its value and tolerance?
questions.expl: Green = 5 and Blue = 6 give 56. The third band, Brown = 1, adds 1 zero, so 56 becomes 560 Ω. Gold is ±5%. Two zeros would give 5,600 Ω; no zeros would give 56 Ω. Reading the digit bands in the wrong order (6 then 5) would wrongly give 650.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (resistor color code / color band decoding, pp. 12-24-12-25, Fig. 12-49)

questions.q: 7. A resistor is banded Orange-Orange-Brown-Silver. What is its value and tolerance?
questions.expl: The two Orange bands give digits 3 and 3 = 33. The third band, Brown = 1, adds 1 zero, so 33 becomes 330 Ω. Silver in the fourth band means ±10%. Gold would be ±5%; two zeros would give 3,300 Ω; no zeros would give 33 Ω.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (resistor color code / color band decoding, pp. 12-24-12-25, Fig. 12-49)

questions.q: 8. A resistor is banded Blue-Gray-Red-Gold. What is its value and tolerance?
questions.expl: Blue = 6 and Gray = 8 give 68. The third band, Red = 2, adds 2 zeros, so 68 becomes 6,800 Ω (6.8 kΩ). Gold is ±5%. One zero would give 680 Ω; three zeros would give 68,000 Ω. Swapping the digit order (8 then 6) would wrongly give 8,600.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (resistor color code / color band decoding, pp. 12-24-12-25, Fig. 12-49)

questions.q: 9. A resistor is banded Yellow-Violet-Orange-Gold. What is its value and tolerance?
questions.expl: Yellow = 4 and Violet = 7 give 47. The third band, Orange = 3, adds 3 zeros, so 47 becomes 47,000 Ω (47 kΩ). Gold is ±5%. Two zeros would give 4,700 Ω; four zeros would give 470,000 Ω; silver would be ±10%.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (resistor color code / color band decoding, pp. 12-24-12-25, Fig. 12-49)

questions.q: 10. A resistor is banded Brown-Black-Yellow-Gold. What is its value and tolerance?
questions.expl: Brown = 1 and Black = 0 give 10. The third band, Yellow = 4, adds 4 zeros, so 10 becomes 100,000 Ω (100 kΩ). Gold is ±5%. Three zeros would give 10,000 Ω; five zeros would give 1,000,000 Ω; silver would be ±10%.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (resistor color code / color band decoding, pp. 12-24-12-25, Fig. 12-49)

questions.q: 11. A resistor is banded Brown-Black-Green-Silver. What is its value and tolerance?
questions.expl: Brown = 1 and Black = 0 give 10. The third band, Green = 5, adds 5 zeros, so 10 becomes 1,000,000 Ω (1 MΩ). Silver means ±10%. Four zeros would give 100,000 Ω; six zeros would give 10,000,000 Ω; gold would be ±5%.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (resistor color code / color band decoding, pp. 12-24-12-25, Fig. 12-49)

questions.q: 12. A resistor is banded Red-Red-Brown-Gold. What is its value and tolerance?
questions.expl: The two Red bands give 2 and 2 = 22. The third band, Brown = 1, adds 1 zero, so 22 becomes 220 Ω. Gold is ±5%. Two zeros would give 2,200 Ω; no zeros would give 22 Ω; silver would be ±10%.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (resistor color code / color band decoding, pp. 12-24-12-25, Fig. 12-49)

questions.q: 13. A resistor is banded Green-Blue-Red-Gold. What is its value and tolerance?
questions.expl: Green = 5 and Blue = 6 give 56. The third band, Red = 2, adds 2 zeros, so 56 becomes 5,600 Ω (5.6 kΩ). Gold is ±5%. One zero would give 560 Ω; three zeros would give 56,000 Ω. Reversing the digits (6 then 5) would wrongly give 6,500.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (resistor color code / color band decoding, pp. 12-24-12-25, Fig. 12-49)

questions.q: 14. A resistor is banded Orange-White-Black-Gold. What is its value and tolerance?
questions.expl: Orange = 3 and White = 9 give 39. The third band, Black = 0, is the multiplier — Black means ADD ZERO zeros, so the value stays 39 Ω. This is the classic trap: a black third band does not make it 390. Gold is ±5%. Swapping digits would wrongly give 93.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (resistor color code / color band decoding, pp. 12-24-12-25, Fig. 12-49)

questions.q: 15. A resistor is banded Brown-Green-Red-Silver. What is its value and tolerance?
questions.expl: Brown = 1 and Green = 5 give 15. The third band, Red = 2, adds 2 zeros, so 15 becomes 1,500 Ω (1.5 kΩ). Silver means ±10%. One zero would give 150 Ω; three zeros would give 15,000 Ω; gold would be ±5%.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (resistor color code / color band decoding, pp. 12-24-12-25, Fig. 12-49)

questions.q: 16. A resistor is banded Gray-Red-Red-Gold. What is its value and tolerance?
questions.expl: Gray = 8 and Red = 2 give 82. The third band, Red = 2, adds 2 zeros, so 82 becomes 8,200 Ω (8.2 kΩ). Gold is ±5%. One zero would give 820 Ω; three zeros would give 82,000 Ω. Reading the digit bands in the wrong order (2 then 8) would wrongly give 2,800.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (resistor color code / color band decoding, pp. 12-24-12-25, Fig. 12-49)

questions.q: 17. A resistor is banded Blue-Gray-Brown-Gold. What is its value and tolerance?
questions.expl: Blue = 6 and Gray = 8 give 68. The third band, Brown = 1, adds 1 zero, so 68 becomes 680 Ω. Gold is ±5%. Two zeros would give 6,800 Ω; no zeros would give 68 Ω. Swapping the digit order (8 then 6) would wrongly give 860.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (resistor color code / color band decoding, pp. 12-24-12-25, Fig. 12-49)

questions.q: 18. A resistor is banded Orange-Orange-Orange-Silver. What is its value and tolerance?
questions.expl: The first two Orange bands give 3 and 3 = 33. The third band, Orange = 3, adds 3 zeros, so 33 becomes 33,000 Ω (33 kΩ). Silver means ±10%. Two zeros would give 3,300 Ω; four zeros would give 330,000 Ω; gold would be ±5%.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (resistor color code / color band decoding, pp. 12-24-12-25, Fig. 12-49)

questions.q: 19. A resistor is banded Brown-Green-Black-Gold. What is its value and tolerance?
questions.expl: Brown = 1 and Green = 5 give 15. The third band, Black = 0, is the multiplier — Black means add ZERO zeros, so the value stays 15 Ω. A black third band never scales the value up. Gold is ±5%. Treating Black as one zero would wrongly give 150; swapping digits would give 51.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (resistor color code / color band decoding, pp. 12-24-12-25, Fig. 12-49)

questions.q: 20. A resistor has only three bands — Red-Red-Brown — and NO fourth band. What is its value and tolerance?
questions.expl: The two Red bands give 2 and 2 = 22, and the third band, Brown = 1, adds 1 zero, so the value is 220 Ω. Because there is no fourth (tolerance) band, the tolerance is understood to be ±20%. Gold would have meant ±5% and silver ±10%, but there is no band at all here.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (resistor color code / color band decoding, pp. 12-24-12-25, Fig. 12-49)

questions.q: 21. Which band sequence marks a 1,000 Ω (1 kΩ) ±5% resistor?
questions.expl: 1,000 Ω is 10 followed by 2 zeros, so the digits are Brown (1) and Black (0), and the multiplier is Red (2) for 2 zeros. Gold gives the ±5% tolerance. Brown third band would be only 1 zero (100 Ω); Orange would be 3 zeros (10,000 Ω); silver would make it ±10%.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (resistor color code / color band decoding, pp. 12-24-12-25, Fig. 12-49)

questions.q: 22. Which band sequence marks a 4,700 Ω (4.7 kΩ) ±5% resistor?
questions.expl: 4,700 Ω is 47 followed by 2 zeros. The digits 4 and 7 are Yellow and Violet, and 2 zeros is the Red multiplier. Gold is ±5%. A Brown third band would give 470 Ω; Orange would give 47,000 Ω; Green-Blue-Red would be 5,600 Ω (wrong digits).
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (resistor color code / color band decoding, pp. 12-24-12-25, Fig. 12-49)

questions.q: 23. Which band sequence marks a 330 Ω ±10% resistor?
questions.expl: 330 Ω is 33 followed by 1 zero. The digits 3 and 3 are both Orange, and 1 zero is the Brown multiplier. Silver gives the ±10% tolerance. Gold would be ±5%; a Red third band would give 3,300 Ω; a Black third band would give 33 Ω.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (resistor color code / color band decoding, pp. 12-24-12-25, Fig. 12-49)

questions.q: 24. Which band sequence marks a 100,000 Ω (100 kΩ) ±5% resistor?
questions.expl: 100,000 Ω is 10 followed by 4 zeros. The digits are Brown (1) and Black (0), and 4 zeros is the Yellow multiplier. Gold is ±5%. Green third band would be 5 zeros (1 MΩ); Orange would be 3 zeros (10,000 Ω); silver would make it ±10%.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (resistor color code / color band decoding, pp. 12-24-12-25, Fig. 12-49)

questions.q: 25. Which band sequence marks a 2,700 Ω (2.7 kΩ) ±5% resistor?
questions.expl: 2,700 Ω is 27 followed by 2 zeros. The digits 2 and 7 are Red and Violet, and 2 zeros is the Red multiplier. Gold is ±5%. An Orange third band would give 27,000 Ω; Brown would give 270 Ω; Red-Green would be digits 2 and 5 (2,500 Ω).
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (resistor color code / color band decoding, pp. 12-24-12-25, Fig. 12-49)

questions.q: 26. Which band sequence marks a 470,000 Ω (470 kΩ) ±10% resistor?
questions.expl: 470,000 Ω is 47 followed by 4 zeros. The digits 4 and 7 are Yellow and Violet, and 4 zeros is the Yellow multiplier. Silver gives ±10%. Gold would be ±5%; an Orange third band would give 47,000 Ω; a Green third band would give 4,700,000 Ω (4.7 MΩ).
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (resistor color code / color band decoding, pp. 12-24-12-25, Fig. 12-49)

questions.q: 27. On a standard 4-band resistor, which band indicates the tolerance?
questions.expl: On a 4-band resistor the bands are, in order: first digit, second digit, multiplier (number of zeros), and tolerance. The tolerance is always the fourth band — the last one — read as Gold = ±5%, Silver = ±10%. The first and second bands are the significant digits, and the third band is the multiplier.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (resistor color code / color band decoding, pp. 12-24-12-25, Fig. 12-49)

questions.q: 28. A resistor has three color bands and no fourth band. What is its tolerance?
questions.expl: When there is no fourth (tolerance) band, the tolerance is understood to be ±20% — the widest standard tolerance. A gold fourth band would mean ±5% and silver would mean ±10%, but with no band at all the value can be 20% higher or lower than marked.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (resistor color code / color band decoding, pp. 12-24-12-25, Fig. 12-49)

questions.q: 29. What is the function of the third band on a standard 4-band resistor?
options: It is the first significant digit
It is the tolerance of the resistor
It is the multiplier — the number of zeros to add after the first two digits (×10^n)
It indicates the resistor's power (wattage) rating
questions.short: The multiplier — number of zeros to add.
questions.expl: The third band is the multiplier: it tells you how many zeros to append to the two digits from the first and second bands (equivalently, multiply by 10 raised to that number). For example, a Red third band (2) adds two zeros. Tolerance is the fourth band, and the color code does not encode wattage at all.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (resistor color code / color band decoding, pp. 12-24-12-25, Fig. 12-49)

questions.q: 30. In the resistor color code, what tolerance do gold and silver tolerance bands represent?
questions.expl: In the fourth (tolerance) band, Gold means ±5% and Silver means ±10%. If there is no band at all, the tolerance is ±20%. Do not mix them up — gold is the tighter (better) ±5% tolerance, silver is the looser ±10%.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12 (resistor color code / color band decoding, pp. 12-24-12-25, Fig. 12-49)

questions.q: What is the most common type of primary-cell battery?
questions.expl: The study guide states the dry cell is the most common type of primary-cell battery, and its characteristics are similar to those of an electrolytic cell.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: Which statement best describes a PRIMARY cell?
options: Its energy-releasing chemical reaction is not reversible, so it cannot be recharged
It produces alternating current instead of direct current
Its chemical reaction is fully reversible, so it recharges normally
It must be kept in a liquid electrolyte bath at all times
questions.short: Non-reversible reaction — it cannot be recharged
questions.expl: A primary cell such as the dry cell is non-rechargeable; the chemical reaction that releases its energy is not reversible. A secondary cell is the reversible (rechargeable) type.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: A secondary cell is best defined as an electrolytic cell in which the energy-releasing electrochemical reaction is what?
questions.expl: The study guide defines a secondary cell as any electrolytic cell in which the electrochemical reaction that releases energy is reversible — that is what allows it to be recharged.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: Which pair correctly matches cell type to its rechargeability?
options: Neither primary nor secondary can be recharged
Both primary and secondary are rechargeable
questions.expl: A primary cell (dry cell) has a non-reversible reaction and is not recharged; a secondary cell has a reversible reaction and can be recharged.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: The dry cell is described as being similar in its characteristics to which kind of cell?
questions.expl: The study guide notes the dry cell is the most common primary cell and is similar in its characteristics to that of an electrolytic cell.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: Voltage (potential difference) is measured in what unit?
questions.expl: Voltage, or potential difference, measures electrical potential and is expressed in volts.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: Electric current — the rate of electron flow — is measured in what unit?
questions.expl: Current is the rate of electron flow and is measured in amperes. The coulomb measures quantity of charge, not the rate at which it flows.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: Resistance — the opposition to current flow — is measured in what unit?
questions.expl: Resistance is the opposition to current flow and is measured in ohms. The siemens is its reciprocal (conductance).
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance. What unit measures conductance?
questions.expl: Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance and is measured in siemens. Resistance itself is measured in ohms.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: Which unit measures capacitance — the ability to store electrical charge?
questions.expl: Capacitance is the ability to store electrical charge and is measured in farads. Inductance (energy stored in a magnetic field) is measured in henrys.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: Inductance — the storing of energy in a magnetic field — is measured in what unit?
questions.expl: Inductance stores energy in a magnetic field and is measured in henrys. The farad measures capacitance (stored charge).
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: Charge — the quantity of electricity — is measured in what unit?
questions.expl: Charge is the quantity of electricity and is measured in coulombs. The ampere measures the rate at which that charge flows.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: Impedance — AC resistance that also includes reactance — is measured in what unit?
questions.expl: Impedance is AC resistance including reactance and, like plain resistance, is measured in ohms.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: Frequency — the rate of oscillation — is measured in what unit?
questions.expl: Frequency is the rate of oscillation and is measured in hertz. Do not confuse it with the henry, which measures inductance.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: Both plain resistance AND impedance are expressed in the same unit. Which unit is it?
questions.expl: Resistance is opposition to current flow and impedance is AC resistance including reactance — both are measured in ohms.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: The siemens is the unit of conductance. Conductance has what relationship to resistance?
options: It is the reciprocal of resistance
It is the square of resistance
questions.short: It is the reciprocal of resistance
questions.expl: Conductance (siemens) is defined as the reciprocal of resistance (ohms) — the greater the resistance, the smaller the conductance.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: The SI prefix 'kilo' (k) represents which power of ten?
questions.expl: Kilo means 10³, or one thousand — for example 1 kV = 1,000 V.

questions.q: The SI prefix 'mega' (M) represents which power of ten?
questions.expl: Mega means 10⁶, or one million — for example 1 MHz = 1,000,000 Hz.

questions.q: The SI prefix 'milli' (m) represents which power of ten?
questions.expl: Milli means 10⁻³, or one thousandth — for example 1 mA = 0.001 A.

questions.q: The SI prefix 'micro' (µ) represents which power of ten?
questions.expl: Micro means 10⁻⁶, or one millionth — for example 1 µF = 0.000001 F.

questions.q: The SI prefix 'nano' (n) represents which power of ten?
questions.expl: Nano means 10⁻⁹ — for example 1 nH = 0.000000001 H.

questions.q: The SI prefix 'pico' (p) represents which power of ten?
questions.expl: Pico means 10⁻¹² — for example 1 pF = 0.000000000001 F.

questions.q: Convert: 1 kV is equal to how many volts?
questions.expl: The prefix kilo means 10³, so 1 kV = 1,000 V.

questions.q: Convert: 1 MHz is equal to how many hertz?
questions.expl: The prefix mega means 10⁶, so 1 MHz = 1,000,000 Hz.

questions.q: Convert: 1 mA is equal to how many amperes?
questions.expl: The prefix milli means 10⁻³, so 1 mA = 0.001 A.

questions.q: Convert: 1 µF is equal to how many farads?
questions.expl: The prefix micro means 10⁻⁶, so 1 µF = 0.000001 F.

questions.q: Convert: 1 pF is equal to how many farads?
questions.expl: The prefix pico means 10⁻¹², so 1 pF = 0.000000000001 F.

questions.q: According to generator theory, voltage is induced in a conductor when what happens?
options: Lines of magnetic force are cut by the conductor passing through them
A chemical reaction occurs inside the conductor
The conductor is held perfectly still inside the magnet
The conductor is heated above its melting point
questions.short: Magnetic lines of force are cut by the conductor
questions.expl: When lines of magnetic force are cut by a conductor passing through them, a voltage is induced in that conductor — the basis of all generator operation.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: The strength of the induced voltage in a generator depends upon which two factors?
options: The speed of the conductor and the strength of the magnetic field
The length of the shaft and the type of bearing grease
The color of the wire and the outside air temperature
The battery voltage and the number of fuses
questions.expl: The induced-voltage strength depends on how fast the conductor moves and how strong the magnetic field is — faster motion and a stronger field both raise the induced voltage.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: What are the three major parts (assemblies) of a DC generator?
options: A stator, an inverter, and a heat sink
A field frame (yoke), a rotating armature, and a brush assembly
A slip ring, a rectifier, and a capacitor bank
A carburetor, a magneto, and a spark plug
questions.short: Field frame (yoke), armature, and brush assembly
questions.expl: All DC generators share the same general construction: a field frame or yoke, a rotating armature, and a brush assembly.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: How many basic types of DC generators are there, and what are they?
options: Two: series wound and parallel wound only
Four: series, shunt, compound, and squirrel-cage
Three: series wound, shunt wound, and compound (shunt-series) wound
questions.short: Three: series, shunt, and compound (shunt-series) wound
questions.expl: There are three types of DC generators — series wound, shunt wound, and shunt-series (compound) wound. The type depends on how the field winding relates to the external circuit.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: What determines whether a DC generator is series, shunt, or compound wound?
options: The size of the cooling fan
The voltage of the aircraft battery
The relationship of the field winding to the external circuit
questions.short: The relationship of the field winding to the external circuit
questions.expl: The difference among the three DC-generator types depends on how the field winding is connected in relation to the external circuit.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: An AC generator and a DC generator induce voltage identically in the rotating loop. What determines whether it is called an AC or a DC generator?
options: How the current is taken from the loop — slip rings give AC, a commutator gives DC
The number of field poles used
Whether the magnets are natural or electromagnets
questions.short: Slip rings produce AC; a commutator produces DC
questions.expl: The generating method is identical; if the current is taken off by slip rings it is alternating current (an alternator), and if it is collected by a commutator it is direct current (a DC generator).
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: When current is collected from the rotating loop by a COMMUTATOR, the output is what?
questions.expl: A commutator collects the current as direct current, so the machine is a DC generator. Slip rings instead would collect alternating current.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: A DC motor is a rotating machine that transforms energy in which direction?
options: DC electrical energy into mechanical energy
AC electrical energy into chemical energy
Mechanical energy into DC electrical energy
questions.short: DC electrical energy into mechanical energy
questions.expl: A DC motor transforms DC electrical energy into mechanical energy. A generator does the reverse — it turns mechanical energy into electrical energy.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: A DC motor consists of which two principal parts?
options: A slip ring and a rectifier
A field assembly and an armature assembly
questions.short: A field assembly and an armature assembly
questions.expl: A DC motor's two principal parts are the field assembly and the armature assembly.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: What are the major parts of a practical DC motor?
options: Piston, cylinder, valve, and spark plug
Slip ring, commutator, diode, and capacitor
Armature assembly, field assembly, brush assembly, and end frame
questions.short: Armature, field, brush assembly, and end frame
questions.expl: The major parts of a practical DC motor are the armature assembly, the field assembly, the brush assembly, and the end frame.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: What are the three basic types of DC motors?
options: Series motors, shunt motors, and compound motors
questions.expl: There are three basic types of DC motors: series motors, shunt motors, and compound motors.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: In a SERIES DC motor, how is the field winding connected relative to the armature?
options: Through a set of slip rings only
In parallel (shunt) with the armature winding
In series with the armature winding
questions.short: In series with the armature winding
questions.expl: In a series motor the field windings — relatively few turns of heavy wire — are connected in series with the armature winding, so all current flows through both.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: How does a SERIES DC motor behave as its load changes?
options: Its speed varies greatly — high speed at light load, low speed at heavy load
It stops turning whenever any load is applied
It always runs at one fixed high speed
Its speed stays exactly constant no matter the load
questions.short: Speed varies greatly with load (fast light, slow heavy)
questions.expl: A series motor's speed depends heavily on load: any change in load brings a substantial change in speed. It runs fast under a light load and slow under a heavy load.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: The field windings of a series motor are described as consisting of what?
options: Relatively few turns of heavy wire
Many turns of very fine wire
A single loop of aluminum foil
No wire at all — permanent magnets only
questions.short: Relatively few turns of heavy wire
questions.expl: A series motor's field windings consist of relatively few turns of heavy wire connected in series with the armature.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: In a SHUNT DC motor, how is the field winding connected, and how does speed respond to load?
options: Connected in parallel (shunt); speed varies very little with load
Connected in series; speed varies greatly with load
Connected to the battery only; speed doubles under load
Connected through slip rings; motor cannot run under load
questions.short: In parallel; speed stays nearly constant
questions.expl: In a shunt motor the field winding is connected in parallel (shunt) with the armature. Field current is constant, so speed varies very little with load; removing all load raises speed only slightly.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: Why is the current through the field of a SHUNT motor essentially constant?
options: The field winding is connected directly across the power supply
The field is powered by a separate battery each second
The field winding carries the full armature current
The field winding has almost zero resistance
questions.short: Its field is connected directly across the power supply
questions.expl: In a shunt motor the field winding is connected directly across the power supply, so the current through the field is constant — giving nearly constant speed.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: A COMPOUND DC motor is best described as what?
options: A motor that runs only on alternating current
A motor with no field winding at all
A combination of the series and shunt motors, with both a shunt and a series field winding
A motor identical to a squirrel-cage induction motor
questions.short: A combination of series and shunt — it has both windings
questions.expl: The compound motor combines the series and shunt motors; it has two field windings — a shunt winding and a series winding — and is used whenever the combined characteristics of both are desired.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: In a compound motor, the series winding may aid the shunt winding or oppose it. What are these two arrangements called?
questions.expl: Like the compound generator, the compound motor's series winding may either aid the shunt winding (cumulative compound) or oppose it (differential compound).
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: How is the direction of rotation of a DC motor reversed?
options: By reversing current in BOTH the armature and field at the same time
By reversing the direction of current flow in EITHER the armature OR the field windings
By adding more brushes to the commutator
questions.short: Reverse current in either the armature OR the field (not both)
questions.expl: Reversing the current in either the armature or the field reverses the motor's rotation, because it reverses the magnetism of that member. Reversing both at once would cancel out and leave rotation unchanged.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: A motor that reverses direction using two field windings wound in opposite directions on the same pole is called what?
questions.expl: One method of reversing rotation uses two field windings wound in opposite directions on the same pole; this arrangement is called a split field motor.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: What are the two general types of AC motors used in aircraft systems?
questions.expl: The two general types of AC motors used in aircraft systems are induction motors and synchronous motors.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: Which is a stated ADVANTAGE of AC motors over comparable DC motors?
options: They use no brushes or commutators, so brush sparking is avoided and maintenance is low
They never need any electrical power source
They produce far more torque at zero speed
They can run directly from a dry-cell battery
questions.short: No brushes/commutators — no sparking, low maintenance
questions.expl: AC motors are generally less expensive than comparable DC motors, and because they use no brushes or commutators, sparking at the brushes is avoided; they are reliable and need little maintenance.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: The speed of rotation of an AC motor depends upon which two things?
options: The number of poles and the frequency of the electrical power source
The number of slip rings and the shaft length
The battery voltage and the brush pressure
The wire color and the ambient temperature
questions.short: Number of poles and supply frequency
questions.expl: The speed of an AC motor depends on the number of poles and the frequency of the electrical source: rpm = (120 × frequency) ÷ number of poles.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: Using rpm = (120 × frequency) ÷ number of poles, what is the speed of a 4-pole AC motor on 60 Hz power?
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: Using rpm = (120 × frequency) ÷ number of poles, what is the speed of a 2-pole AC motor on 400 Hz aircraft power?
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: Using rpm = (120 × frequency) ÷ number of poles, what is the speed of a 6-pole AC motor on 60 Hz power?
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: The three-phase AC induction motor is also known by what name?
questions.expl: The three-phase AC induction motor is also called a squirrel-cage motor.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: How does a SYNCHRONOUS motor differ from an induction motor in how it develops torque?
options: It develops torque only from brush friction
Its torque does NOT depend on inducing currents in the rotor
Its torque depends entirely on inducing rotor currents
It develops torque without any magnetic field
questions.short: Its torque does not depend on induced rotor currents
questions.expl: Like the induction motor, the synchronous motor uses a rotating magnetic field; unlike it, the torque developed does not depend on the induction of currents in the rotor.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: Both the induction motor and the synchronous motor make use of what?
questions.expl: Both principal AC motor types use a rotating magnetic field; the difference is that the synchronous motor's torque does not rely on induced rotor currents.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: An electrical generator that produces alternating current is referred to as what?
questions.expl: A generator that produces alternating current is an AC generator; combining 'alternating' and 'generator' gives the term alternator, which the handbook uses interchangeably with AC generator.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: What is the major difference between an alternator and a DC generator?
options: The method of connection to the external circuit — slip rings versus a commutator
The alternator runs on batteries and the DC generator does not
One converts chemical energy and the other converts light energy
The alternator has no rotor and the DC generator has no armature
questions.expl: The major difference is the connection to the external circuit: the alternator connects through slip rings, while the DC generator connects through a commutator.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: In a three-phase alternator, the voltage induced in each of the three windings is how many degrees out of phase with the other two?
questions.expl: A three-phase (polyphase) alternator has three single-phase windings spaced so that the voltage induced in each winding is 120° out of phase with the voltages in the other two windings.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: A three-phase, or polyphase, circuit is used in most aircraft alternators instead of what?
options: A DC generator with a commutator
questions.expl: Most aircraft alternators use a three-phase (polyphase) circuit rather than a single-phase or two-phase alternator.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: A BRUSHLESS alternator consists of which three parts?
options: A dry cell, a wet cell, and a rectifier
A commutator, a brush, and a slip ring
A pilot exciter, an exciter, and the main generator system
A shunt field, a series field, and an armature
questions.short: Pilot exciter, exciter, and main generator
questions.expl: A brushless alternator consists of a pilot exciter, an exciter, and the main generator system.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: Why is the brushless alternator design considered more efficient, especially at altitude?
options: It uses twice as many brushes for redundancy
It has no brushes to wear down or to arc at high altitudes
It eliminates the need for any magnetic field
It runs only on direct current
questions.short: No brushes to wear or arc at high altitude
questions.expl: The brushless design is more efficient because there are no brushes to wear down or to arc at high altitudes.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: The frequency of an alternator's output voltage depends upon which two factors?
options: The number of slip rings and the length of the shaft
The color of the windings and the battery voltage
The speed of rotation of the rotor and the number of poles
The brush pressure and the oil temperature
questions.short: Rotor speed and number of poles
questions.expl: Alternator frequency depends on rotor speed and pole count: the faster the speed the higher the frequency, and the more poles on the rotor the higher the frequency for a given speed.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: For a given alternator, increasing the ROTOR SPEED has what effect on output frequency?
options: The frequency stays exactly the same
questions.expl: The faster the rotor speed, the higher the frequency; the lower the speed, the lower the frequency.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: A starter-generator on a turbine-powered aircraft performs which dual role?
options: It only generates and can never start the engine
It acts as a fuel pump during start and a hydraulic pump in flight
It acts as a starter during engine start, then acts as a generator once the engine is online
It acts as a battery charger only, never as a starter
questions.short: Starter during start, generator once the engine is running
questions.expl: Many turbine-powered aircraft use a starter-generator that acts like a starter during engine start and, once the engine is online, acts like a generator.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: A three-unit regulator used on many light-aircraft generator systems contains which three units?
options: A rectifier, an inverter, and a capacitor
A pilot exciter, an exciter, and a main generator
A voltage regulator, a current limiter, and a reverse-current cut-out
A shunt field, a series field, and a commutator
questions.short: Voltage regulator, current limiter, reverse-current cut-out
questions.expl: The three-unit regulator includes a voltage regulator, a current limiter (current regulator), and a reverse-current cut-out.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: In a three-unit regulator, what is the job of the reverse-current cut-out (the third unit)?
options: It limits the maximum output current
It compares sampled voltage to a reference
It disconnects the battery from the generator
questions.short: It disconnects the battery from the generator
questions.expl: The third unit is a reverse-current cut-out that disconnects the battery from the generator (to prevent the battery from discharging back through the generator).
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: In a three-unit regulator, the SECOND unit is a current regulator whose purpose is to do what?
options: Reverse the direction of the generator
Limit the output current of the generator
questions.expl: The second of the three units is a current regulator (current limiter) that limits the output current of the generator.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: On what kind of aircraft is a Generator Control Unit (GCU) more commonly found?
questions.expl: The GCU is more commonly found on turbine-powered aircraft, where it handles regulation, sensing, and protection of the DC generation system.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: The most basic GCU performs functions related to which three areas of the DC generation system?
questions.expl: The most basic GCU performs a number of functions related to the regulation, sensing, and protection of the DC generation system.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: What is described as the most basic function of a GCU?
questions.expl: The most basic of the GCU functions is voltage regulation.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: How does the GCU's overvoltage protection system work?
options: It compares the sampled voltage to a reference voltage
It counts the number of alternator poles
questions.short: It compares sampled voltage to a reference voltage
questions.expl: Like the voltage-regulation feature, the overvoltage protection system compares the sampled voltage to a reference voltage.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: What does the paralleling feature of a GCU allow?
options: The battery to be charged twice as fast by lightning
The alternator to skip its exciter stage
A single generator to run backwards as a motor
Two or more GCU/generator systems to work together, sharing the effort of supplying current
questions.short: Two or more generator systems to share the electrical load
questions.expl: The paralleling feature lets two or more GCU/generator systems work in a shared effort to provide current to the aircraft electrical system.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: Over-excitation protection addresses which failure situation?
options: The exciter loses all of its poles
A GCU in a paralleled system fails and one generator becomes overexcited, trying to carry more than its share of the load
questions.short: A failed GCU lets one generator become overexcited and overload
questions.expl: When a GCU in a paralleled system fails, one generator can become overexcited and try to carry more than its share of the load, if not all of it — over-excitation protection guards against this.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: Differential voltage protection requires that before the generator line contactor is closed, the generator voltage must be what?
options: At least double the load-bus voltage
Within a close tolerance of the load bus
questions.short: Within a close tolerance of the load bus
questions.expl: When the GCU allows the logic output to close the generator line contactor, differential voltage protection requires the generator voltage to be within a close tolerance of the load bus.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide

questions.q: Reverse-current sensing detects what condition?
options: The starter has finished cranking the engine
The battery is fully charged and disconnects itself
The generator can no longer maintain the required voltage and begins to draw current instead of providing it
questions.short: The generator draws current instead of supplying it
questions.expl: If the generator is unable to maintain the required voltage level, it eventually begins to draw current instead of providing it — reverse-current sensing detects this.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch.12 (Electricity & Electronics); Block 4 Study Guide
