Is in phase with the voltage
questions.expl: In a circuit with only capacitance, the current leads the applied voltage by 90 degrees (one-fourth cycle). In a circuit with only inductance, current lags voltage by 90 degrees.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: Capacitive reactance (XC), measured in ohms, is found with the formula XC = 1 / (2 pi f C). As frequency INCREASES, XC:
questions.expl: XC = 1/(2 pi f C) is inversely proportional to frequency — as frequency rises, capacitive reactance DECREASES (opposite of inductive reactance).
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: When capacitors are connected in SERIES, their total capacitive reactance is found by:
questions.expl: When capacitors are connected in series, the total reactance equals the SUM of the individual reactances (Xct = Xc1 + Xc2 + ...). Note this is opposite to how their capacitance combines.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: Faraday's Law (the Law of Electromagnetic Induction) states the induced emf in a closed loop of wire is proportional to:
options: The rate of change of the magnetic flux through the coil
questions.short: Rate of change of magnetic flux
questions.expl: Faraday's Law: the induced emf in a closed loop of wire is proportional to the rate of change of the magnetic flux through a coil of wire.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: The property of a coil to oppose any CHANGE in current through it is called:
questions.expl: The primary aspect of a coil's operation is its property to oppose any change in current through it; this property is called inductance (symbol L).
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: In a series RL circuit, the current increases to what percentage of full value in 1 time constant after the circuit is closed?
questions.expl: In a series RL circuit, current increases to 63 percent of full value in 1 time constant, and reaches 99 percent after the 5th time constant — like an RC charging curve.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: As a general rule, the inductance of a coil varies as:
options: The square of the number of turns
The square root of the turns
questions.short: The square of the number of turns
questions.expl: Doubling the number of turns produces a field twice as strong for the same current, but as a general rule the inductance varies as the SQUARE of the number of turns.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: Doubling the LENGTH of a coil while keeping the same number of turns does what to the inductance?
questions.expl: Doubling the length of a coil, while keeping the same number of turns, halves the value of inductance.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: Lenz's Law (1833), which gives the direction of the induced emf, states the induced emf always opposes the:
questions.expl: Lenz's Law: the induced emf always acts in such a direction that the current it drives produces a magnetic field which OPPOSES the change in magnetic flux.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: The basic unit of inductance is the:
questions.expl: The henry (H) is the basic unit of inductance. A circuit has one henry when current changing at one ampere per second induces one volt.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: When inductors are connected in SERIES, the total inductance is:
options: The sum of the individual inductors
questions.expl: When inductors are connected in series, the total inductance LT is the SUM of the individual inductors: LT = L1 + L2 + ... + LN (like resistors in series).
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: When inductors are connected in PARALLEL, the total inductance is:
questions.expl: When inductors are connected in parallel, the total inductance is less than the smallest inductance (uses the reciprocal formula, like resistors in parallel).
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: Inductive reactance, the opposition an inductor offers to AC, is symbolized XL and measured in:
questions.expl: Inductive reactance (XL) is measured in ohms, just as resistance is. Inductance itself is measured in henries.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: Inductive reactance is calculated with XL = 2 pi f L. As frequency INCREASES, XL:
questions.expl: XL = 2 pi f L is directly proportional to frequency and inductance — raise the frequency and inductive reactance rises (opposite of XC).
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: In the handbook example, an inductance of 0.146 H at 60 cps gives an inductive reactance (XL = 2 pi f L) of approximately:
questions.expl: XL = 6.28 x 60 x 0.146 = 55 ohms. This is the handbook's worked example.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: In AC series circuits, inductive reactances are combined how?
questions.expl: In AC series circuits, inductive reactances are added like resistances in series; total reactance equals the sum of the individual reactances.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: The combined total opposition to current flow in an AC circuit, made up of resistance and reactance, is called:
questions.expl: The combined effects of resistance, inductive reactance, and capacitive reactance make up the total opposition called impedance (Z), measured in ohms.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: Ohm's Law for an AC circuit is written as:
questions.expl: For AC, Ohm's Law uses impedance: I = E/Z. When the circuit is resistance only, Z = R and it is the same as the DC form.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: For a series AC circuit with resistance and inductance, impedance is found by:
questions.expl: Resistance and reactance act at right angles, so by the Pythagorean theorem Z = sqrt(R^2 + XL^2). Substitute XC for circuits with capacitance.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: In the handbook example with R = 6 ohms and XL = 8 ohms, the impedance Z is:
questions.expl: Z = sqrt(6^2 + 8^2) = sqrt(36 + 64) = sqrt(100) = 10 ohms. This is the handbook's worked example.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: A series AC circuit has 10 ohms resistance and 13 ohms capacitive reactance. Using Z = sqrt(R^2 + XC^2), the impedance is approximately:
questions.expl: Z = sqrt(10^2 + 13^2) = sqrt(100 + 169) = sqrt(269) = ~16.4 ohms. This is the handbook's worked example.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: When a circuit contains resistance, inductance, AND capacitance, the reactances are combined by:
options: Subtracting the smaller reactance from the larger (X = XL - XC)
questions.expl: Because their effects are exactly opposite, inductive and capacitive reactance are combined by subtraction (smaller from larger): then Z = sqrt(R^2 + (XL - XC)^2).
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: For a series RLC circuit with R = 4 ohms, XL = 10 ohms, XC = 7 ohms, the impedance Z is:
questions.expl: Z = sqrt(R^2 + (XL - XC)^2) = sqrt(4^2 + (10-7)^2) = sqrt(16 + 9) = sqrt(25) = 5 ohms. Handbook worked example.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: At the particular frequency where inductive reactance equals capacitive reactance and they cancel, the circuit is said to be:
questions.expl: At the resonant frequency, XL = XC; since they are opposite, they cancel, leaving only resistance to oppose current. The circuit is 'in resonance'.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: In an AC circuit, the power actually consumed by the resistance portion (the working power, indicated by a wattmeter) is called:
questions.expl: True power (symbol P, measured in watts) is the working power consumed by the resistance, indicated by a wattmeter in the circuit.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: The power consumed by the ENTIRE AC circuit (both resistance and reactance), measured in volt-amps, is called:
questions.expl: Apparent power (symbol S, measured in volt-amps) is the power consumed by the entire circuit, including resistance and reactance — the product of effective voltage and current.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: The ratio of true power to apparent power, usually expressed as a percent, is called the:
questions.expl: Power factor (PF) is the ratio of true power to apparent power, usually expressed in percent: PF = (watts / volt-amperes) x 100.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: A 220-volt AC motor draws 50 amperes; a wattmeter reads 9,350 watts. What is the apparent power?
questions.expl: Apparent power = volts x amperes = 220 x 50 = 11,000 watts (volt-amperes). This is the handbook's worked example.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: For that 220-volt motor (true power 9,350 W, apparent power 11,000 VA), the power factor is:
questions.expl: PF = (9,350 / 11,000) x 100 = 85 percent. This is the handbook's worked example.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: True power equals apparent power ONLY when the AC circuit is made up of:
questions.expl: Only when the AC circuit is pure resistance is apparent power equal to true power. With reactance present, current and voltage are out of phase and true power is less.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: A transformer changes electrical energy from one voltage to another by means of:
questions.expl: A transformer's two coils are not electrically connected; an alternating voltage on one coil creates a voltage in the other by mutual induction.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: Why can a transformer NOT be used with pure (steady) DC voltage?
options: Transformers only pass AC current directly
Only a varying voltage creates the varying magnetic field needed for mutual induction
questions.short: Pure DC produces no varying field
questions.expl: A transformer needs a varying magnetic field for mutual induction. Pure DC produces a steady field, so only AC (or pulsating DC) can be used.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: The three basic parts of a transformer are an iron core, a primary winding, and a:
questions.expl: A transformer has three basic parts: an iron core (low-reluctance flux path), a primary winding (receives source energy), and a secondary winding (receives energy by induction).
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: The factor that determines whether a transformer is step-up or step-down is the:
questions.expl: The turns ratio — primary turns to secondary turns — determines step-up vs. step-down. The voltage ratio equals the turns ratio in an ideal transformer.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: A step-down transformer with a 5-to-1 turns ratio, fed with 10 volts on the primary, produces what secondary voltage?
questions.expl: Voltage ratio = turns ratio. A 5:1 step-down with 10 V on the primary gives 10/5 = 2 V on the secondary. Handbook example.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: A transformer has a 1-to-4 turns ratio (step-up). If 10 volts are applied to the primary, what is the secondary output?
questions.expl: Voltage ratio = turns ratio. With a 1:4 step-up and 10 V primary, secondary = 10 x 4 = 40 V. Handbook example.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: If a transformer steps UP the voltage, it steps DOWN the:
questions.expl: If a transformer steps up voltage, it steps down current by the same ratio, because the power (I x E) of the secondary equals that of the primary minus losses.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: A transformer's primary develops 10,000 lines of force but only 9,000 cut the secondary. The transformer efficiency (coefficient of coupling) is:
questions.expl: 9,000 / 10,000 = 0.9, so the coefficient of coupling is 0.9 and the transformer is 90 percent efficient.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: No transformer is 100 percent efficient because some of the magnetic flux escapes the magnetic circuit. This lost flux is called:
questions.expl: A certain amount of magnetic flux, called leakage flux, leaks out of the magnetic circuit; thus no transformer is 100 percent efficient (though iron-core types approach it).
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: Current transformers are connected how in the circuit, and voltage transformers how?
options: Current transformers in parallel; voltage transformers in series
Current transformers in series; voltage transformer primaries in parallel
questions.expl: Voltage transformer primaries are connected in PARALLEL across the supply voltage; current transformer primaries are connected in SERIES in the primary circuit.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: The 'iron' losses in a transformer are of two types: eddy current loss and:
questions.expl: Iron losses are hysteresis loss (energy to re-magnetize the core each cycle) and eddy current loss (currents induced in the core). Copper loss is a separate conductor loss.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: To reduce eddy current losses in a transformer, the core is made of:
questions.expl: To reduce eddy current losses, transformer cores are made of laminations coated with insulation, which reduces the circulation of induced currents.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: The basic DC meter movement (used in the ammeter, voltmeter, and ohmmeter) that deflects a pointer in proportion to current through a coil is the:
questions.expl: The d'Arsonval meter movement is the basic DC current-measuring device used in the ammeter, voltmeter, and ohmmeter; the pointer deflects in proportion to coil current.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: The amount of current required to drive a meter movement to full-scale deflection is called the meter's:
questions.expl: Current sensitivity is the amount of current required to drive the movement to full-scale deflection (e.g., a 1 mA movement needs 1 mA for full scale).
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: To extend an ammeter's range so it can read currents larger than the movement allows, a resistor is added that bypasses the excess current. This is called a:
questions.expl: A shunt resistor is added in parallel to bypass current exceeding the movement's limit, extending the ammeter's range.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: How is an AMMETER connected to measure current in a circuit?
options: In series with the element being measured
questions.expl: Always connect an ammeter in SERIES with the element whose current is to be measured. NEVER connect an ammeter across a voltage source — its very low resistance allows excessive current.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: Why must an ammeter NEVER be connected directly across a source of voltage such as a battery?
options: Its very low resistance allows excessive current that can damage it
questions.expl: The ammeter's resistance is extremely low; connected across a voltage source, even a volt or so causes very high current to flow through the meter, damaging it.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: The most accurate ammeter readings are obtained at approximately what point on the scale?
questions.expl: The most accurate readings are obtained at approximately half-scale deflection; start with the highest range and work down.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: To extend a VOLTMETER's range, a resistor in series with the movement that drops excess voltage is added; this is called the:
questions.expl: For a voltmeter, a series multiplier resistor (RM) drops any excess voltage above what the movement needs for full-scale deflection.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: Voltmeter sensitivity is defined in terms of:
questions.expl: Voltmeter sensitivity is defined in terms of resistance per volt (ohms/volt). A 50 microamp movement has a sensitivity of 20k ohms/volt.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: How is a VOLTMETER connected to measure the voltage across a component?
questions.expl: Voltmeters are connected in PARALLEL — across the two points being measured. (Ammeter = series; voltmeter = parallel. A classic exam trap.)
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: To prevent shunting (drawing off current and changing the reading) when measuring voltage, a technician should use a voltmeter with:
questions.expl: A low-resistance voltmeter draws off significant current and lowers the circuit's effective resistance. Use a HIGH-resistance voltmeter to prevent shunting.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: The function of the ohmmeter is to measure resistance; unlike the ammeter and voltmeter, it contains its own:
questions.expl: The ohmmeter is self-excited — it contains a battery and a variable resistor in series with the movement to produce current through the resistance being measured.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: On an ohmmeter, when the leads are OPEN (not connected), the pointer indicates:
questions.expl: When the ohmmeter leads are open, the meter indicates infinite resistance (an open circuit). When the leads are shorted, it reads zero.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: The ohmmeter scale, where values decrease from left to right, is often called a:
questions.expl: Because the ohmmeter values decrease from left to right, the scale is often called a back-off scale; it is nonlinear (more compressed toward the left).
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: A high-range ohmmeter containing a hand-operated generator, used to measure insulation resistance with a high 'breakdown' voltage, is a:
questions.expl: The megger (megohmmeter) is a high-range ohmmeter with a hand-operated generator, used to measure insulation resistance, ground, continuity, and short circuits at high potential.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: The chief advantage of the megger over an ordinary ohmmeter is its capacity to measure resistance with a high potential, or:
questions.expl: The megger's chief advantage is its capacity to measure resistance with a high potential, or 'breakdown' voltage, ensuring insulation will not short or leak under electrical stress.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: A standard d'Arsonval (DC) meter connected in an AC circuit reads:
options: Zero (the average of the AC cycle)
questions.expl: A DC d'Arsonval meter in an AC circuit reads zero, because the current reverses too rapidly for the coil to follow, so it assumes an average position (zero).
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: To measure AC with a d'Arsonval movement, additional circuitry is required that converts AC to DC. This device is a:
questions.expl: For AC measurements, additional circuitry with a rectifier (half-wave or full-wave) converts AC to DC so the movement can respond.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: A meter movement that can measure either AC or DC using two concentric iron vanes (one fixed, one movable) inside a solenoid, relying on repulsion, is the:
questions.expl: The moving iron vane meter uses repulsion between two concentric iron vanes inside a solenoid; it depends on induced magnetism and works on AC or DC.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: Electric power is measured by means of a wattmeter, which has two elements (one for current, one for voltage) and is usually of which type?
questions.expl: Because power is the product of current and voltage, a wattmeter needs two elements and is usually of the electrodynamometer type; it can measure AC or DC power.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: The instrument used to view and quantify waveform characteristics (phase, amplitude, duration), typically using a cathode-ray tube, is the:
questions.expl: The oscilloscope makes it possible to see and quantify waveform characteristics such as phase relationships, amplitudes, and durations, usually using a CRT.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: The combined analog instrument that includes the voltmeter, ammeter, and ohmmeter is commonly called a multimeter or:
questions.expl: The combined voltmeter/ammeter/ohmmeter is called a multimeter or a VOM (volt-ohm-milliammeter). Digital versions are the DMM and DVM.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: Compared with older analog meters, digital multimeters (DMM) and digital voltmeters (DVM) offer greater accuracy and:
options: No need for a power source
questions.expl: The DVM/DMM offers greater accuracy, less ambiguity, and higher input resistance, which gives it less of a loading effect on a circuit.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: The two most common materials used for semiconductors, each having four valence electrons, are germanium and:
questions.expl: The two most common semiconductor materials are germanium and silicon; each atom has four valence electrons. Silicon is preferred for its wider temperature range.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: The very stable bond in which two silicon atoms each share one electron equally is called a:
questions.expl: Two silicon atoms share electrons equally in a covalent bond, which is very stable and holds the atoms together tightly.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: The process of adding small amounts of impurities to a semiconductor material to increase its current flow is called:
questions.expl: Doping is the process by which small amounts of additives (impurities) are added to a semiconductor to increase current flow by adding electrons or holes.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: A semiconductor doped with a donor impurity (such as phosphorus or arsenic) that produces an EXCESS of electrons is called:
questions.expl: An N-type semiconductor is doped with a donor impurity, producing an excess of electrons; the electrons are the majority current carriers.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: A semiconductor doped with an acceptor impurity (such as boron or aluminum) that creates 'holes' is called:
questions.expl: A P-type semiconductor is doped with an acceptor impurity having only three valence electrons; this creates holes, which act as positive charges (the majority carrier).
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: A two-element semiconductor device that uses the rectifying properties of a PN junction to permit current flow in one direction only is the:
questions.expl: The semiconductor diode (PN junction diode) is a two-element device that converts AC into DC by permitting current flow in one direction only.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: The region around a PN junction that lacks free electrons and holes is called the:
questions.expl: The area around the junction barrier lacks (is depleted of) free electrons and holes and is called the depletion region; the electrostatic field there is the barrier.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: A semiconductor diode allows current to flow easily in which condition?
questions.expl: A forward-biased diode (negative source to N-type, positive source to P-type) conducts easily. Reverse bias blocks current. This one-way action makes a diode a rectifier.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: In a FORWARD biased diode, the negative voltage source connects to the N-type material and the positive source connects to the:
questions.expl: In a forward biased PN junction, the negative source connects to N-type and the positive source connects to P-type material, allowing current to flow easily.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: When a diode is REVERSE biased, the most noticeable effect is that the depletion zone becomes:
questions.expl: When reverse biased, holes and electrons move away from the junction, widening the depletion zone and preventing current flow by the majority carriers.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: A device that transforms AC into DC by limiting or regulating the direction of current flow is a:
questions.expl: A rectifier transforms AC into DC by limiting/regulating current direction. The two methods discussed are the half-wave rectifier and the full-wave rectifier.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: A rectifier that produces output from only one half (e.g., the positive swing) of each AC cycle is a:
questions.expl: The half-wave rectifier reproduces the input minus the negative voltage swing — it uses only one half of each cycle.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: A full-wave bridge rectifier uses how many diodes, with the output being a continuous sequence of pulses?
questions.expl: The full-wave bridge rectifier uses four diodes (D1-D4). During each half cycle, two diodes conduct so current passes through the load in the same direction both alternations.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: A diode designed to break down (conduct) at a specific reverse-bias voltage and act as a voltage regulator is a:
questions.expl: Zener (breakdown) diodes conduct when reverse-bias voltage reaches a designed value, then behave like a constant voltage source — functioning as a voltage regulator.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: In a forward-biased diode where energy is dissipated as LIGHT rather than heat, the device is a:
questions.expl: In an LED, the energy released as electrons fall into holes is dissipated as light. Advantages over incandescent lamps: longer life, lower voltage, faster operation, less heat.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: A variable-capacitance diode whose capacitance is controlled by the reverse voltage applied is a:
questions.expl: The varactor (varicap) is a variable-capacitance diode; the reverse voltage applied controls its capacitance. It often replaces mechanically tuned capacitors.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: A three-terminal device used primarily to amplify signals and control current is the:
questions.expl: The transistor is a three-terminal device used primarily to amplify signals and control current within a circuit.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: The three regions of a transistor are the collector, the emitter, and the:
questions.expl: A transistor's three regions are the collector (moderately doped), the emitter (heavily doped), and the base (significantly less doped and thinnest).
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: Which transistor region is HEAVILY doped?
questions.expl: The emitter is heavily doped, the collector is moderately doped, and the base is significantly less doped (and thinnest).
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: Transistors are classified as either NPN or PNP according to:
options: The arrangement of their N and P materials
questions.short: Arrangement of N and P materials
questions.expl: Transistors are classified NPN or PNP according to the arrangement of their N and P materials. NPN has P sandwiched between two N regions; PNP is the opposite.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: On a transistor schematic symbol, how are NPN and PNP distinguished?
options: By the direction of the arrow on the emitter
By the thickness of the base line
By the color of the symbol
questions.expl: The arrow is on the emitter. Arrow pointing IN = PNP; arrow pointing OUT = NPN.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: To use a transistor as an amplifier, the emitter-base junction is biased in the forward direction (low resistance) and the collector-base junction is:
questions.expl: For amplification, the emitter-base junction is forward biased (low resistance) and the collector-base junction is reverse biased (high resistance), producing power gain.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: In a PNP transistor, the majority current carriers are:
questions.expl: In a PNP transistor the majority carriers are holes (the opposite of the NPN, where electrons are the majority carriers). To bias a PNP, the bias network polarity is reversed.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: The name 'transistor' is a combination of which two words?
questions.expl: Because the device transfers current from a low-resistance path to a high-resistance one, its name combines 'transfer' and 'resistor' — transistor.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: A transistor design with only ONE PN junction that is a VOLTAGE-controlled device (rather than current-controlled) is the:
questions.expl: The field-effect transistor (FET) has only one PN junction and is a voltage-controlled device, unlike the bipolar transistor which has two junctions and is current-controlled.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: The transistor configuration that provides the best combination of voltage and current gain and is the only one giving a 180-degree phase reversal is the:
questions.expl: The common-emitter (CE) configuration provides good gains for voltage, current, and power, and is the only configuration that provides a 180-degree phase reversal.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: A logic gate whose output is HIGH only when ALL of its inputs are high is the:
questions.expl: The AND gate output is high only when all inputs are high. If any input is low, the output is low — it determines when conditions are met at the same time.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: A logic gate whose output is HIGH when ANY ONE (or more) of its inputs is high is the:
questions.expl: The OR gate output is high whenever any one of its inputs is high; the output is low only when no input is high.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: A logic gate (also called a NOT gate) that converts one logic state into its opposite is the:
questions.expl: The inverter (NOT gate) converts one logic state into the opposite — a 1 to a 0 or a 0 to a 1.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: A NAND gate produces a LOW output only when:
questions.expl: NAND = NOT-AND (AND with inverted output). The NAND output is low only when all inputs are high; if any input is low, the output is high.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: Replacing the slip rings of a basic AC generator with two half-cylinders (a commutator) produces a:
questions.expl: Replacing the slip rings with a commutator (two half cylinders) makes a basic DC generator; the commutator action produces a DC voltage.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: The rotating parts of a DC generator — the coil and commutator together — are called the:
questions.expl: The rotating coil and commutator of a DC generator are together called the armature.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: Which DC motor has its field windings connected in SERIES with the armature, producing HIGH starting torque (used as an aircraft engine starter)?
questions.expl: In a series motor the field windings are in series with the armature; the large starting current produces high starting torque — its principal advantage. Used as engine starters and for gear/flap operation.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: What is the danger if a SERIES motor has its load removed entirely?
options: It may overspeed until the armature flies apart
questions.short: It may overspeed and fly apart
questions.expl: A series motor runs at high speed under light load; if the load is removed entirely, the motor may operate at such a high speed that the armature flies apart.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: A DC motor whose field winding is connected in PARALLEL (shunt) with the armature, giving fairly constant speed, is a:
questions.expl: In a shunt motor the field winding is connected in parallel (shunt) with the armature; starting torque is less than a series motor's, but speed is more constant.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: A DC motor that combines a series winding and a shunt winding in the field is a:
questions.expl: The compound motor combines series and shunt motors; it has both a shunt winding and a series winding in the field. Its starting torque is higher than a shunt but lower than a series motor.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: When a DC motor's armature rotates in the magnetic field, a voltage is induced that opposes the applied voltage. This is called:
questions.expl: The voltage induced in the armature windings as it rotates is the counter (back) emf, opposite in direction to the applied voltage. It limits the armature current.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: As a DC motor's armature speed INCREASES, the counter emf increases and the current through the armature:
questions.expl: The faster the armature rotates, the greater the counter emf; counter emf opposes the applied voltage, so armature current decreases as speed increases. A motor draws high current on starting.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: An AC-series motor is a single-phase motor that resembles a DC motor in that it has brushes and a commutator, and it can operate on:
questions.expl: The AC-series motor resembles a DC motor (brushes and commutator) and operates on either AC or DC circuits. Modifications (laminations, compensating winding) make it work well on AC.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: The frequency of an alternator's output voltage depends on the number of poles and the:
options: Speed of rotation of the rotor
questions.expl: Alternator frequency depends on the number of poles and the speed of rotation: the faster the speed (or the more poles), the higher the frequency.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: A device used to convert a portion of the aircraft's DC power to AC (mainly for instruments, radio, radar, lighting) is an:
questions.expl: An inverter converts DC power to AC, used mainly for instruments, radio, radar, lighting, and accessories — usually at 400 cps.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: Aircraft inverters are usually built to supply AC current at a frequency of:
questions.expl: Inverters are usually built to supply current at a frequency of 400 cps. Some provide more than one voltage (e.g., 26 V AC and 115 V AC).
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: The two basic types of inverters are the rotary inverter and the:
questions.expl: The two basic types of inverters are the rotary and the static (solid-state). Static inverters have no moving parts, are smaller, lighter, and more efficient.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: The binary number system is a base-2 system that uses which digits?
questions.expl: Binary has only two digits, 0 and 1 — matching a switch or transistor that is either OFF (0) or ON (1). That is why aircraft digital electronics are built on binary.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: In the binary number system, the place values of the digits are based on:
questions.expl: Binary is a Base-2 system: reading right to left, the place values are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128 — each place doubles.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: Using the handbook's method, the binary number 10110011 converts to what decimal number?
questions.expl: Add the place values holding a 1: 128 + 32 + 16 + 2 + 1 = 179. (Ignore the places holding a 0.) This is the handbook's own worked example.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: The decimal number 233 expressed as an 8-bit binary number is:
questions.expl: Subtract place values from the top down: 233-128=105 (1), 105-64=41 (1), 41-32=9 (1), 16 doesn't fit (0), 9-8=1 (1), 4 and 2 don't fit (00), 1-1=0 (1) -> 11101001. Handbook worked example.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: A logic gate whose output is HIGH only when ALL of its inputs are LOW is the:
questions.expl: The NOR gate is an OR with an inverted output: any high input drives the output low; only all-low inputs give a high output — the exact opposite of the OR gate.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: The logic gate that produces a 1 output only when exactly ONE of its two inputs is 1 (both inputs at 1 give a 0) is the:
questions.expl: The exclusive OR is a modified OR gate: 1 output when ONLY one input is 1. When both inputs are 1, the output stays 0 — that's what makes it 'exclusive.'
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: The logic gate that produces a 1 output when all inputs are 1s AND ALSO when all inputs are 0s is the:
questions.expl: The X-NOR is an X-OR with an inverted output: it outputs 1 when the inputs MATCH (both 1 or both 0). Think of it as an 'equality detector.'
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: Compared to circuits built from discrete components, integrated circuits (ICs) have the advantage of being:
options: Smaller, more reliable, and less power-hungry
questions.short: Smaller, more reliable, and less power-hungry
questions.expl: The IC packs all the logic functions onto one chip: smaller, consumes less power, very reliable, and inexpensive. (They are NOT ESD-immune — quite the opposite.)
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: The output voltage of a DC generator is controlled by varying the:
questions.expl: A rheostat in the field circuit sets the field current: more field resistance means less field current, a weaker magnetic field, and lower output voltage. Less resistance means a stronger field and higher voltage.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: In a vibrating-type voltage regulator, when the generator terminal voltage rises above the critical value, the solenoid opens the contact points, which:
options: Disconnects the armature from the load
Shorts the field winding directly to ground
Reinserts the field rheostat, reducing field current and terminal voltage
questions.short: Reinserts the field rheostat, reducing field current and terminal voltage
questions.expl: The contacts rapidly vibrate open/closed: closed shorts out the field rheostat (voltage rises); open reinserts it (voltage falls). The rapid cycle holds the average voltage steady from no load to full load.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: Vibrating-type regulators cannot be used with generators that require high field current, because the contacts pit and burn. Heavy-duty generator systems instead use a:
questions.expl: High field current arcs across vibrating contacts and destroys them. The carbon pile regulator varies resistance through a stack of carbon disks instead — no contacts to burn.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: The three units of a three-unit regulator used on many light aircraft are a voltage regulator, a current limiter, and a:
questions.expl: Three-unit regulator = (1) voltage regulator, (2) current regulator/limiter to cap generator output current, (3) reverse current cut-out to disconnect the battery from the generator.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: If the battery is not disconnected when generator voltage falls below battery voltage, the battery discharges through the generator armature and drives the generator like a motor. This action is called:
questions.expl: That is exactly what the reverse current cut-out prevents: without it, the battery would 'motor' the generator and discharge itself in a short time.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: Series-wound DC generators are never employed as airplane generators because they have:
options: Very poor voltage regulation under changing load
questions.short: Very poor voltage regulation under changing load
questions.expl: In a series generator the load current IS the field current, so output voltage swings up and down with load. Airplane generators use shunt or compound field connections instead.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: Per the RIGHT-hand motor rule, when the index finger points in the direction of the magnetic field and the second finger points in the direction of current flow, the thumb indicates:
options: The direction the current-carrying wire moves
The polarity of the induced emf
The north pole of the field
questions.short: The direction the current-carrying wire moves
questions.expl: Right hand = MOTOR rule (index = Field, second finger = Current, thumb = Motion of the wire). The left-hand rules cover conductors, coils, and generators.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: The three types of DC generators are series wound, shunt wound, and:
questions.expl: The type depends on how the field winding relates to the external circuit: in series with the load, in parallel (shunt), or both (compound).
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: The two general types of AC motors used in aircraft systems are:
questions.expl: Either type may be single-, two-, or three-phase. Three-phase induction motors drive big loads (starters, flaps, landing gear, hydraulic pumps); synchronous motors run at constant speed (flux gate compasses, prop synchronizers).
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: Because of the shape of its rotor, the three-phase AC induction motor is also called a:
questions.expl: The rotor's longitudinal bars joined by end rings look like a squirrel cage. Voltage is induced in the bars by the rotating stator field — no brushes or slip rings needed.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: With a 60-cycle supply, the rotating magnetic field of a 2-pole induction motor stator makes 60 revolutions per second (3,600 rpm). This speed is known as the:
questions.expl: The stator's rotating field turns at synchronous speed, set by supply frequency and number of poles.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: An induction motor's rotor always turns slightly SLOWER than the rotating stator field. This speed difference — needed so the field keeps cutting the rotor bars and inducing current — is called:
questions.expl: If the rotor ever matched field speed, no lines of force would be cut, no emf induced, no rotor current, and no torque — so the rotor must 'slip' behind the field.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: The amount of torque developed in a motor coil depends on the strength of the magnetic field, the number of turns in the coil, and:
options: The gauge of the supply wire
The position of the coil in the field
The direction of the earth's field
questions.short: The position of the coil in the field
questions.expl: Torque is zero when the coil plane is parallel to the flux lines and 100 percent when it cuts them at right angles — which is why a DC motor needs a commutator to keep torque alive.
sources: Ch.12 General — Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics

questions.q: A drawing that shows the principle of operation of a system — locating components relative to each other with standard symbols, but NOT their size, shape, or physical location — is a—
questions.short: Schematic = how it works, symbols only.
questions.expl: A schematic diagram is the troubleshooting/training drawing: it shows how a system operates by placing symbols for each component in relation to one another, ignoring real size, shape, and location. A wiring diagram instead shows the actual wires and their identification codes; an installation diagram shows where each component physically sits in the aircraft.

questions.q: A drawing that shows the actual electrical wiring and circuitry of every appliance and device on the aircraft, with each wire coded for identification, is a—
questions.short: Wiring diagram = the real wires, coded.
questions.expl: A wiring diagram maps the real electrical wiring — every device and its connecting, identification-coded wires. A schematic shows only the principle of operation in symbols; a block diagram simplifies a complex system into labeled rectangles connected by lines.

questions.q: A phase relationship can exist between any two sine waves. In a single circuit fed by one alternator, the phase relationship is most fundamentally measured between—
questions.short: Phase is between voltage and current.
questions.expl: In a circuit fed by one alternator there must be a certain phase relationship between the voltage and the current for the circuit to work efficiently. Phase can also be compared between the voltages/currents of two alternators or between two circuits — but the basic pair is voltage versus current. Resistance/power and frequency/wavelength are not 'sine waves' being compared for phase.

questions.q: As a generator armature turns, the voltage it produces at exactly 90 degrees of rotation is the—
questions.expl: The instantaneous voltage climbs from zero at 0° to its largest value at 90° — that is the peak (maximum) value; it swings to the opposite peak at 270°. The effective (RMS) value is smaller (0.707 × peak), and the voltage is only zero at 0°, 180°, and 360°.

questions.q: The induced voltage or current flowing at any single instant during a cycle — any one point on the sine wave — is the—
questions.short: Instantaneous = value at any one point.
questions.expl: An instantaneous value is simply the voltage or current at one moment during the cycle; the whole sine wave is a series of these values. The peak is the single largest instantaneous value (at 90°/270°), and the effective (RMS) value is the DC-equivalent heating value, 0.707 × peak.

questions.q: The effective value of AC — the value AC voltmeters read, equal to the DC voltage that produces the same heating — is also called the—
questions.expl: The effective value is the root-mean-square (RMS) value — a measure of the sine wave's heating effect, equal to the DC voltage that dissipates the same heat. It equals 0.707 times the peak. (Turned around, peak = 1.41 × RMS, which is why 110 V house AC peaks near 155 V.)

questions.q: The Greek letter lambda (λ) in the study of AC waveforms indicates—
questions.expl: Lambda (λ) stands for wavelength — the distance a waveform travels during one period (one complete cycle), measured from a point on one wave to the matching point on the next. Frequency is cycles per second; impedance is total opposition to AC and carries the symbol Z.

questions.q: Electromagnetic induction — the basis of every generator — is best defined as—
options: producing a magnetic field by a steady voltage
producing a voltage in a conductor by a changing magnetic field
storing charge on two plates separated by a dielectric
questions.expl: Faraday's Law of electromagnetic induction: a changing magnetic field through a coil induces a voltage (EMF) proportional to how fast the flux changes — move a magnet through a coil and a voltage appears. Storing charge on plates is a capacitor's job, not induction.

questions.q: Ohm's law states that the current in a circuit is—
options: independent of both voltage and resistance
directly proportional to both voltage and resistance
directly proportional to voltage and inversely proportional to resistance (E = I × R)
questions.short: E = I × R; more voltage → more current, more resistance → less current.
questions.expl: Ohm's law ties the three together linearly: E = I × R, or I = E ÷ R. Raise the voltage and current rises; raise the resistance and current falls. That inverse tie to resistance is exactly why the 'directly proportional to resistance' option is wrong.

questions.q: The three types of DC generators, classified by how the field winding connects to the load, are—
questions.expl: DC generators are series-wound (field in series with the load), shunt-wound (field in parallel with the load), or compound-wound (both, a shunt-series combination). The classification is purely about how the field winding ties to the external circuit.

questions.q: Which 'wound' type of DC generator is NEVER employed as an airplane generator, because its output voltage swings wildly with the load?
questions.short: Series-wound = terrible regulation → not used on aircraft.
questions.expl: In a series-wound generator the field carries the full load current, so more load means more field, more EMF, and a runaway output voltage — very poor regulation. Because of that it is never used as an airplane generator; aircraft use shunt- or compound-wound fields, which hold voltage far steadier.

questions.q: The three major parts of a DC generator are the field frame (yoke), the brush assembly, and the—
questions.expl: A DC generator is built from the field frame (yoke) that completes the magnetic circuit and supports everything, the rotating armature whose coils cut the field to induce voltage, and the brush assembly riding the commutator. The commutator on that armature is what flips the induced AC into DC. A stationary stator winding belongs to an alternator, not a DC generator.

questions.q: Within a DC generator, the job of the field frame (yoke) is to—
options: complete the magnetic circuit between the poles and mechanically support the generator
carry the load current out to the external circuit
rectify the AC output into DC
questions.expl: The field frame (yoke) is the foundation of the generator: it completes the magnetic circuit between the poles and acts as the mechanical support for the other parts. Turning the induced AC into DC is the commutator's job, and carrying current to the load is done by the brushes.

questions.q: The two major components of an aircraft DC alternator are the—
options: stator (stationary armature winding) and rotor (rotating field winding)
questions.expl: Aircraft alternators are the revolving-field, stationary-armature type: the stator is the stationary armature winding that feeds the load, and the rotor is the rotating field winding. Keeping the armature stationary avoids sliding contacts in the heavy load circuit. Commutators/brushes belong to DC generators.

questions.q: A GCU (Generator Control Unit) on an aircraft is used to—
options: convert AC bus power directly into hydraulic pressure
store emergency charge like a backup battery
regulate, sense, and protect the generating system (voltage regulation, overvoltage, paralleling, reverse-current)
questions.expl: The GCU manages the DC generating system: it holds the output voltage at reference, trips on overvoltage, shares load when generators are paralleled, controls the line contactor by differential voltage, and pulls a failing generator off the bus on reverse current. It is a control unit, not a power converter or a battery.

questions.q: 'Paralleling' on a twin-engine aircraft refers to—
options: two or more generator systems sharing the electrical load equally on the bus
wiring the two batteries in parallel to raise voltage
running two hydraulic pumps off one engine
questions.short: Paralleling = generators share the load evenly.
questions.expl: Paralleling lets two or more generator/GCU systems work together, each carrying its fair share of current to the aircraft bus; the GCU compares the busses and equalizes the load sharing. (Wiring batteries in parallel raises capacity, not voltage — and that's a different topic entirely.)

questions.q: On a large aircraft, the constant 400 Hz output frequency of an AC alternator is ensured by a—
options: full-wave bridge rectifier on the output
constant-speed drive (CSD) between the engine and the alternator
voltage regulator on the field winding
questions.short: CSD holds alternator speed constant → 400 Hz.
questions.expl: Output frequency depends on rotor speed, but engine rpm varies — so a constant-speed drive (a hydraulic transmission) is placed between the engine and the alternator to hold the alternator's speed constant, keeping the frequency at 400 Hz. (A CSD and alternator combined in one unit is an integrated drive generator, IDG.) A regulator controls voltage, not frequency; a rectifier makes DC.

questions.q: On large aircraft, electrical power distribution is controlled by two line-replaceable units: the Generator Control Unit (GCU) and the—
questions.short: GCU + BPCU control large-aircraft electrical power.
questions.expl: The GCU regulates and protects each generator, and the Bus Power Control Unit (BPCU) manages the bus-tie contactors and switches power between sources across the busses. The CSD regulates alternator speed (frequency), and the RAT is an emergency backup power source — neither is the power-distribution controller.

questions.q: The two main materials used to make semiconductors are—
questions.expl: Silicon and germanium are the two semiconductor materials — each atom shares four valence electrons in covalent bonds. Silicon is preferred today for its wider temperature range. Copper/aluminum are conductors, and carbon/zinc belong to the old dry-cell battery.

questions.q: You turn pure silicon into a useful (conducting) semiconductor by—
options: heating it until the covalent bonds melt
doping it — adding a small impurity to create N-type (extra electrons) or P-type (holes) material
coating its surface with tin plating
questions.short: Doping = add impurity → N-type or P-type.
questions.expl: Pure silicon is nearly an insulator because all its valence electrons are locked in covalent bonds. Doping adds a trace impurity: a donor (phosphorus, arsenic, antimony) gives extra electrons for N-type; an acceptor (boron, aluminum, gallium) leaves holes for P-type. Now the crystal conducts. Tin plating is for copper wire, not silicon.

questions.q: The diode used in almost all voltage regulation — it breaks down at a set reverse-bias voltage and then holds that voltage constant — is the—
questions.expl: A zener ('breakdown') diode conducts once the reverse voltage reaches its rated value and then behaves like a constant-voltage source — perfect for voltage regulation. An LED radiates light when forward-biased; a Schottky diode is a fast, low-drop switching diode.

questions.q: A full-wave rectifier built from four diodes, so that both halves of the AC cycle are converted to DC, is known as a—
questions.expl: The four-diode full-wave arrangement is the bridge rectifier — it flips the negative half of the cycle up so both halves feed the load as DC. A half-wave rectifier passes only one half of the cycle; a dry-disk rectifier is an older junction type (copper-oxide, selenium).

questions.q: A spring-loaded switch that makes contact only while it is held — a momentary-contact switch — is a—
questions.expl: A pushbutton switch is spring-loaded and designed for momentary contact, so it completes the circuit only while pressed. A rotary selector opens one circuit and closes another as it turns; a DIP switch is a bank of tiny slide/rocker switches inside equipment.

questions.q: A magnetically operated switch — where the coil's field pulls an iron core to complete the circuit — is commonly described as a—
questions.expl: When a coil is energized it pulls a spring-loaded iron core to the center, completing a circuit — that device is the solenoid, also called a solenoid switch or relay. A rheostat and a potentiometer are variable resistors, not switches.

questions.q: The key difference between a relay and a solenoid is that—
options: a relay switches contacts (small current controls a larger one); a solenoid produces mechanical motion / handles heavy current
a relay works on AC only and a solenoid on DC only
a relay stores charge and a solenoid stores magnetic flux permanently
questions.short: Relay = light switching; solenoid = motion / heavy current.
questions.expl: A relay is an electromechanical switch: a small coil current opens or closes light-duty contacts to control a bigger circuit. A solenoid uses its coil to physically pull an iron plunger, producing linear motion — used to actuate a mechanism or make a heavy-duty contactor (battery/starter). It's about switching versus motion, not AC-versus-DC.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12, Page 12-33 relay; Page 12-15 solenoid

questions.q: Which of these is a set of THREE valid circuit-protection devices?
options: fuse, circuit breaker, and current limiter
questions.expl: Circuit-protection devices open the circuit before excess current does damage: a fuse melts a metal link (one-time), a circuit breaker trips and resets, and a current limiter is a heavy-duty slow-blow fuse for high-capacity circuits. Capacitors, resistors, relays, solenoids, and rectifiers are circuit components, not protection devices.

questions.q: A heavy-duty protective device used in high-capacity circuits to guard against a direct short, essentially a slow-blow fuse, is a—
questions.expl: A current limiter is the heavy, high-capacity fuse used where big currents flow — it tolerates brief surges but opens on a hard short. A thermocouple generates a small voltage from heat (temperature sensing); a commutator is part of a DC generator.

questions.q: The two conductor materials most commonly used for aircraft wire are—
questions.expl: Aircraft wire is made of copper or aluminum — aluminum being chosen on large aircraft to save weight. Silver and gold are excellent conductors but too costly for general wiring; iron and nickel are poor conductors by comparison.

questions.q: Bare copper wire is protected from surface oxidation by—
options: wrapping it in cotton lacing tape
coating (plating) it with tin, silver, or nickel
questions.expl: A thin tin, silver, or nickel plating seals the copper from oxygen so it can't form an oxide film — and it keeps the wire easy to solder. Anodizing is an aluminum treatment, not a copper one; lacing tape ties bundles together but doesn't stop oxidation.

questions.q: A 'flooded' or 'wet' battery is one that—
options: is completely sealed and never needs servicing
uses a dry paste electrolyte like a flashlight cell
has free liquid electrolyte covering the plates and must be vented and serviced (watered)
questions.expl: A flooded (wet) battery holds free liquid electrolyte over its plates and must be vented, with water and specific gravity checked in service. That's the opposite of a sealed (SLA) battery, which needs no watering, and of a dry cell, which uses a paste electrolyte and isn't rechargeable.

questions.q: The electrolyte in a nickel-cadmium battery is potassium hydroxide (an alkali). The electrolyte in a lead-acid battery is—
questions.short: Lead-acid = sulfuric acid; ni-cad = potassium hydroxide.
questions.expl: Lead-acid cells use sulfuric acid and water — an acid — while nickel-cadmium cells use potassium hydroxide, an alkali. They're chemical opposites, which is exactly why they need opposite spill neutralizers and must never be serviced in the same area. Pure water carries no charge.
questions.cite: FAA-H-8083-30B, Ch. 12, Page 12-91 KOH; Page 12-87 sulfuric acid

questions.q: Nickel-cadmium battery life can be extended to five years or more by performing—
options: a hydrometer specific-gravity check each week
scheduled deep-cycle (reconditioning) maintenance — full discharge, then recharge
topping off the acid with fresh sulfuric acid
questions.expl: A ni-cad slowly develops 'voltage depression' (falsely called memory) that hides real capacity. A scheduled deep cycle — fully discharging each cell, then recharging — clears it and restores capacity, stretching service life. A hydrometer is useless on a ni-cad, and a ni-cad holds no sulfuric acid to top off.

questions.q: The state of charge of a nickel-cadmium battery is determined by—
options: measuring the color of the electrolyte
reading electrolyte specific gravity with a hydrometer
a measured discharge (capacity test) on the bench
questions.short: Ni-cad charge = measured discharge, not SG.
questions.expl: A ni-cad's specific gravity barely changes and its voltage stays nearly flat, so neither reveals its charge — the only reliable way is to discharge it on the bench and measure the energy delivered. The hydrometer trick works on lead-acid only.

questions.q: Which type of wire can be severely damaged on the INSIDE with no evidence of damage on the outside?
questions.expl: Coaxial cable can be crushed, kinked, or over-bent so its center conductor or dielectric is ruined inside while the outer jacket looks perfect — 'severely damaged on the inside without any evidence of damage on the outside.' That's why coax is never stepped on, dropped on, or bent tighter than its allowable radius.

questions.q: The minimum bend radius for a wire group or bundle must be at least—
options: 2 times the diameter of the smallest wire
10 times the outside diameter of the largest wire in the bundle
exactly equal to the bundle diameter
questions.short: Bundle bend radius ≥ 10× largest wire OD.
questions.expl: A wire bundle must not be bent tighter than 10 times the outside diameter of its largest wire; at breakouts or where it reverses direction it may go to 6 times if properly supported (and RF cable no tighter than 6×). Bending sharper strains and cracks insulation.

questions.q: The primary purpose of conduit around aircraft wiring is—
options: to increase the current-carrying capacity of the wires
to identify the circuit by color code
mechanical protection of the wires or cables
questions.expl: Conduit — metallic or nonmetallic, rigid or flexible — is there to physically protect the wire bundle from abrasion and damage. It does nothing for current capacity, and it isn't a color-coding scheme; wires are identified by printed codes, sleeves, or tape.

questions.q: Wires are identified in an aircraft by which set of methods?
options: printing the code directly on the wire, printed identification sleeves, and identification tape
the size of the terminal lug crimped on each end
color of the insulation only, nothing else
questions.expl: Wire identification uses the code marked (hot-stamped/printed) directly on the wire, printed identification sleeves slid over the wire, or identification tape — repeated at each end and along the run. Terminal-lug size is about the wire gauge, not its circuit identity.

questions.q: SWAMP areas of an aircraft, for wiring purposes, are—
options: Severe Wind And Moisture Problem areas — wheel wells, near flaps, wing folds, and pylons
Standard Wiring And Maintenance Panels inside the cabin
questions.short: SWAMP = severe wind & moisture (wheel wells, flaps, pylons).
questions.expl: SWAMP stands for Severe Wind And Moisture Problem — harsh exterior spots like wheel wells, areas near wing flaps, wing folds, and pylons. Wire there needs special moisture-resistant construction, so it's often hard to substitute. It has nothing to do with cabin panels or the avionics bay.

questions.q: The maximum number of terminal lugs permitted on any one stud is—
options: four (or three lugs plus a bus bar)
questions.short: No more than 4 lugs per stud.
questions.expl: No more than four terminal lugs — or three lugs plus a bus bar — may be attached to a single stud; the bus bar counts toward the four. Stacking more crowds the joint and invites loose, high-resistance connections that overheat.

questions.q: Wire-bundle clamps are installed to aircraft assemblies mainly to—
options: support the bundle and prevent movement and chafing against structure
questions.expl: Cushioned clamps fastened to structure with hardware hold the bundle securely at intervals, keeping it from vibrating, shifting, or chafing on the airframe, and relieving strain. They're mechanical supports, not electrical devices — they don't change voltage or protect the circuit.

questions.q: Grounding, in an aircraft electrical system, is—
options: applying a metallic braid to eliminate stray radio energy
electrically connecting conductive objects to structure (or a return path) to safely complete a normal or fault circuit
connecting two metal parts to equalize static and lightning
questions.short: Grounding = the current return path to structure.
questions.expl: Grounding connects conductive objects to a conductive structure or return path so a normal or fault circuit is safely completed — it provides the current return. Applying a braid to kill stray energy is shielding; tying metal parts together for static/lightning is bonding.

questions.q: Bonding, in an aircraft electrical system, is—
options: completing the normal current return path to ground
adding a dielectric between two charged plates
providing a low-impedance connection between metal parts and structure (RF return, reduce EMI, conduct static/lightning)
questions.short: Bonding = low-impedance ties between metal parts.
questions.expl: Bonding puts metallic parts and the airframe at the same potential through low-impedance connections — giving radio-frequency return paths, cutting EMI, and safely draining static charges and lightning currents. Completing the current return is grounding; a dielectric between plates describes a capacitor.

questions.q: Shielding of aircraft wiring is—
options: applying a metallic covering over wiring to eliminate interference from stray electromagnetic energy
torque-striping a fastener to show it has been tightened
the space left below battery plates for sediment
questions.short: Shielding = grounded metallic braid kills EMI.
questions.expl: Shielding wraps a metallic braid or foil around a wire and grounds it, so stray electromagnetic energy is drained away instead of inducing noise in the conductor. Torque striping is a fastener-inspection mark; sediment space is a battery-case feature — neither is shielding.

questions.q: EMI and RFI, in avionics, stand for—
options: Engine Monitoring Instrument and Radio Frequency Indicator
Electromagnetic Interference and Radio-Frequency Interference — unwanted voltages induced by stray fields
Emergency Master Interlock and Remote Fault Isolation
questions.short: EMI/RFI = interference induced by stray fields.
questions.expl: EMI is Electromagnetic Interference — high-frequency voltages induced in a wire or component by stray electromagnetic (radio-wave) fields — and RFI is that interference specifically in the radio-frequency band. Both cause system errors and are fought with shielding, bonding, and grounding.

questions.q: A 'glass cockpit' refers to a flight deck that—
options: has an all-acrylic canopy for better visibility
displays flight and navigation information on electronic flat-panel screens instead of individual mechanical gauges
questions.expl: A glass cockpit (glass flight deck) presents flight, engine, and navigation data on solid-state flat-panel screens — an EFIS-based panel — replacing rows of individual mechanical instruments. It has nothing to do with the canopy material, and it's the modern alternative to vacuum-gyro analog gauges.

questions.q: To send useful information through the atmosphere, radio transmitters and receivers manipulate the—
questions.expl: A plain radio wave carries no information — it is a carrier wave. Transmitters add the voice or data by modulating (altering) that carrier's amplitude or frequency; the receiver demodulates it to recover the signal. They manipulate the carrier wave, not the atmosphere or the airframe.

questions.q: Radio waves that bounce (refract) off the ionosphere layer of the atmosphere, extending range far beyond line-of-sight, are—
questions.short: Sky waves (HF) bounce off the ionosphere.
questions.expl: High-frequency (HF, roughly 2–25 MHz) sky waves refract off the ionosphere and return to earth well past the horizon, which is why transoceanic aircraft use HF radios. Ground waves follow the earth's curvature; space waves (VHF and up) travel only line-of-sight and do not refract.

questions.q: Ground waves are radio waves that—
options: refract off the ionosphere back to earth
travel only in a straight line of sight
follow the curvature of the earth from transmitter to receiver (VLF/LF/MF)
questions.short: Ground waves hug the earth's curve.
questions.expl: Ground waves are the low-frequency band (VLF/LF/MF) that follow the earth's curvature from the broadcast antenna to the receiver — good for long-distance work like ADF and LORAN. Refracting off the ionosphere is the sky wave's trait; line-of-sight only is the space wave's.

questions.q: Which lists the frequency ranges of ground, sky, and space waves correctly?
options: ground ≈ 3 kHz–3 MHz (VLF/LF/MF); sky ≈ 2–25 MHz (HF); space = VHF/UHF/SHF (30 MHz–30 GHz)
ground = VHF; sky = UHF; space = VLF
all three are the same VHF band, 30–300 MHz
questions.short: Ground = low kHz-MHz; sky = HF; space = VHF & up.
questions.expl: Ground waves live in the low bands (VLF/LF/MF, about 3 kHz–3 MHz), sky waves in HF (about 2–25 MHz), and space waves above HF — VHF (30–300 MHz), UHF (300 MHz–3 GHz), and SHF (3–30 GHz). Most aircraft comm/nav gear rides space waves, which are line-of-sight.

questions.q: AM, in reference to modulation, means the information is carried by varying the carrier wave's—
options: amplitude (its height), while frequency stays constant
questions.expl: Amplitude modulation impresses the signal on the carrier by varying its amplitude (height) while the frequency is held steady — the method used by aircraft VHF communication radios. Varying the frequency instead would be FM.

questions.q: On the study guide, 'PM' in reference to modulation is best given as—
options: Power Modulation — varying transmitter output power
Phase Modulation — varying the carrier's phase (timing) with amplitude constant — while noting some courses mean Pulse Modulation (timed bursts, as DME/transponders use)
questions.short: PM = Phase Modulation (or Pulse Modulation — confirm).
questions.expl: The 8083 series defines only AM and FM by name, so 'PM' is ambiguous: Phase Modulation varies the carrier's phase/timing with amplitude held constant (a close cousin of FM), while some avionics courses use 'PM' for Pulse Modulation — sending the carrier in short timed bursts, the method DME, transponders, and radar use. Neither 'power' nor 'polarity' modulation is a standard term. Confirm which meaning your instructor grades.

questions.q: Aircraft antennas are frequently mounted at a slight angle (canted) in order to—
questions.expl: Many antennas are canted — tilted at a slight angle — for better reception of the signal. The small angle is about signal pickup, not drag reduction or de-icing.

questions.q: One of the OLDEST and most useful navigational aids, still in wide use, is the—
questions.expl: The handbook names the very-high-frequency omnidirectional range (VOR) as one of the oldest and most useful navigational aids — built after WWII and still flown today on the Victor airway network. GPS is far newer, and TCAS is a collision-avoidance system, not a navigation aid.

questions.q: If an aircraft has no dedicated VOR gauge (OBS/CDI), the VOR information is instead displayed on—
options: an RMI, HSI, EFIS display, or EADI
questions.short: VOR info moves to RMI / HSI / EFIS / EADI.
questions.expl: As panels evolved, VOR course and bearing information was integrated into other displays — the radio magnetic indicator (RMI), the HSI, an EFIS display, or the EADI — rather than a stand-alone VOR gauge. The transponder head and marker lights do entirely different jobs.

questions.q: DME, in reference to aircraft navigation, is—
options: Distance Measuring Equipment — it shows the distance from the aircraft to the ground station
Directional Magnetic Equipment — a backup compass
Dual Mode Encoder — an altitude reporter
questions.expl: DME (Distance Measuring Equipment) calculates and displays the slant distance from the aircraft to the DME/VORTAC ground station, and can also give groundspeed and time-to-station. It operates in the UHF band (962–1213 MHz). It is not a compass or an altitude encoder.

questions.q: Pairing a VOR bearing with a co-located DME lets a pilot—
options: fix the aircraft's exact position (a bearing plus a distance)
questions.short: VOR bearing + DME distance = a position fix.
questions.expl: The VOR gives the bearing to the station and the co-located DME gives the distance to it — together a bearing and a range pin down the aircraft's exact location. That's why VOR/DME and VORTAC stations are so useful. It has nothing to do with engine monitoring or weather broadcasts.

questions.q: An ILS (Instrument Landing System) guides an aircraft to the runway in poor visibility using three radio elements: a localizer, marker beacons, and a—
options: glideslope (for vertical guidance down the correct descent angle)
questions.expl: The ILS combines a localizer (horizontal guidance to the runway centerline), a glideslope (vertical guidance down the ~3° descent path), and marker beacons (distance from the runway). A transponder and a radio altimeter are separate systems, not part of the ILS itself.

questions.q: Within the ILS, horizontal guidance to the runway centerline is provided by the localizer, and vertical guidance is provided by the—
questions.expl: The localizer keeps you lined up left-to-right on the centerline; the glideslope brings you down the correct vertical descent angle. Marker beacons only mark distance from the runway, and a compass locator is an NDB that helps you intercept the approach — neither gives vertical guidance.

questions.q: The purpose of a marker beacon in an ILS is to—
options: transmit the aircraft's altitude to ATC
indicate the aircraft's position/distance along the glidepath to the runway
questions.expl: A marker beacon transmits a narrow upward 75 MHz signal that lights a cockpit light and sounds a tone as the aircraft passes over it, marking its position/distance along the approach (outer = blue/400 Hz, middle = amber/1300 Hz, inner = white/3000 Hz). The glideslope gives the descent angle; the transponder reports altitude.

questions.q: RNAV (Area Navigation) allows an aircraft to—
options: detect nearby traffic and issue evasive commands
land automatically with no pilot input
fly a direct point-to-point route using computed waypoints, not just over ground navaids
questions.expl: Area navigation lets the aircraft fly direct between computed waypoints — defined by VOR radial/distance pairs or by GPS/INS/FMS — instead of zig-zagging station to station. It is a routing method, not an autoland system or a collision-avoidance system.

questions.q: WAAS (Wide Area Augmentation System) improves navigation by—
options: correcting GPS signals (via ground stations and satellites) to sharpen accuracy to about 1–3 meters
replacing GPS with ground-based VOR stations
questions.short: WAAS = corrections that sharpen GPS to ~1–3 m.
questions.expl: WAAS uses about 25 surveyed ground stations that measure GPS errors and, through geostationary satellites, broadcast corrections to WAAS-enabled receivers — tightening accuracy to roughly 1–3 meters and enabling precision approaches. It augments GPS, it doesn't replace it or jam anything.

questions.q: An IRS (Inertial Reference System) determines position by—
options: receiving corrections from WAAS ground stations
using self-contained accelerometers and gyros from a known start point, with NO ground/radio signals
questions.short: IRS = self-contained inertial, no outside signals.
questions.expl: An inertial reference system (a modern INS) continuously computes position, velocity, and attitude from its own accelerometers and gyros, starting from a known initialized point — needing no ground station or radio input at all. That self-contained trait is the whole point; WAAS and VOR both rely on outside signals.

questions.q: The component used to locate personnel after a crash — triggered by the excessive G-forces of impact — is the—
questions.expl: The ELT carries a built-in G-force (impact) sensor aligned with the aircraft's longitudinal axis; a crash trips it and it transmits a distress/location signal (406 MHz, with 121.5 MHz for homing) so search and rescue can find the site and its occupants. A CVR records audio; a radio altimeter measures height.

questions.q: For onboard collision-avoidance systems, the transponder mode type used is—
questions.expl: Mode S ('mode select') is a data-packet protocol also used by onboard collision-avoidance systems; TCAS interrogates other aircraft with Mode C and Mode S at 1030 MHz and gets 1090 MHz replies.
