Mode 3/A returns only an identity code, and there's no civilian collision-avoidance 'Mode 1.'

questions.q: A TCAS TA (Traffic Advisory)—
options: is issued only by TCAS II
alerts the pilot to nearby traffic to aid visual acquisition, with no evasive command; issued by TCAS I and II
commands a specific vertical evasive maneuver
questions.short: TA = 'traffic's out there, look for it' — no command.
questions.expl: A Traffic Advisory simply warns the pilot of an intruder nearby so they can see and avoid it — no maneuver is commanded — and it's issued by both TCAS I and TCAS II. TCAS I identifies traffic within about a 35–40 mile range and is mandated on aircraft with 10–30 seats; a TA fires roughly 25–48 seconds before projected contact. Commanding an evasive maneuver is the RA's job.

questions.q: A TCAS RA (Resolution Advisory)—
options: is issued by both TCAS I and II as a visual-only alert
tells ATC to reroute the intruder aircraft
is issued only by TCAS II and commands a specific vertical evasive maneuver (e.g., CLIMB/DESCEND)
questions.short: RA = TCAS II vertical evasive command.
questions.expl: A Resolution Advisory is issued only by TCAS II when a collision is imminent; it aurally commands a specific vertical maneuver (CLIMB or DESCEND), coordinated so the other TCAS II aircraft is told to go the opposite way. Pilots must follow an RA even over an ATC instruction. TCAS II is required above 30 seats or 15,000 kg, with the RA firing ~within 35 seconds of contact.

questions.q: A transponder must be inspected and tested every 24 calendar months, and that requirement comes from which part of 14 CFR?
options: Part 91 (§91.413) — tested per Part 43, Appendix F
questions.short: Transponder check: every 24 mo., 14 CFR Part 91.
questions.expl: 14 CFR §91.413 (Part 91) requires transponders in controlled airspace to be inspected and tested every 24 calendar months, done in accordance with Part 43, Appendix F. Part 65 covers mechanic certificates and Part 21 covers product/parts certification — neither drives the transponder check.

questions.q: EGPWS stands for, and does, the following:
options: Engine Ground Power Warning System — warns of low APU power
Enhanced Ground Proximity Warning System — adds a terrain database and GPS for forward-looking terrain alerts
Electronic Glideslope Path Warning System — an ILS backup
questions.expl: The enhanced ground proximity warning system builds on GPWS by adding a terrain/obstacle database and GPS position, giving the crew earlier forward-looking warnings of dangerous terrain — the modern defense against controlled flight into terrain. It has nothing to do with APU power or the glideslope.

questions.q: An HSI (Horizontal Situation Indicator) is an instrument that—
options: shows only engine RPM and temperatures
combines the heading indicator with VOR/ILS course-deviation information in one display
questions.short: HSI = heading + course deviation in one gauge.
questions.expl: The HSI merges the heading indicator (compass card) with VOR/ILS course-deviation (and glideslope) information, showing the aircraft's position relative to a selected course on a single face — reducing pilot workload. It's a navigation display, not an engine gauge or an altimeter.

questions.q: An EFIS (Electronic Flight Instrument System) is—
options: a system that displays flight-instrument information on electronic screens (PFD and navigation display)
questions.short: EFIS = flight instruments on electronic screens.
questions.expl: EFIS presents the flight instruments on electronic CRT/LCD screens — the primary flight display and the navigation display — replacing individual mechanical gauges. It's the heart of the glass cockpit, not an engine controller or a floatation system.

questions.q: An EADI (Electronic Attitude Director Indicator) displays—
options: aircraft attitude plus flight-director command guidance on a screen
distance to the next DME station
questions.expl: The EADI is the electronic version of the attitude director indicator: it shows the aircraft's attitude (pitch and bank) together with flight-director command bars and related guidance on a screen. Outside air temperature and DME distance are shown elsewhere.

questions.q: The acronym RAT, in aircraft systems, stands for—
options: Ram Air Turbine — an emergency air-driven turbine for backup power
questions.expl: A Ram Air Turbine deploys into the slipstream to drive an emergency generator and/or hydraulic pump, providing backup power when the normal generators fail. It is not a radio tuner or a rudder sensor.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “AC” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: AC stands for Alternating Current — electrical current that periodically reverses direction (rises and falls as a sine wave); the aircraft power that lets transformers work and that 400-Hz systems use.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “DC” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: DC stands for Direct Current — electrical current that flows in one direction only; battery power and the output of a rectified/generator system.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “EMF” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: EMF stands for Electromotive Force — the electrical 'pressure' (voltage) produced by a source that pushes current through a circuit; measured in volts.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “CEMF” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: CEMF stands for Counter-Electromotive Force — the induced 'back voltage' created in a coil/inductor that opposes the change in current that produced it (also called back-EMF).

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “PD” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: PD stands for Potential Difference — the difference in electrical potential between two points — the voltage that drives current from one point to the other.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “RMS” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: RMS stands for Root-Mean-Square — the effective (heating) value of an AC waveform — the DC voltage that would produce the same heat; equals 0.707 x peak.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “PF” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: PF stands for Power Factor — the ratio of true power to apparent power in an AC circuit (the cosine of the phase angle between voltage and current).

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “TP” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: TP stands for True Power — the real power actually consumed by the resistive part of an AC circuit, measured in watts.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “AP” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: AP stands for Apparent Power — the product of AC voltage and current (volt-amperes) before power factor is applied — includes both true and reactive power.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “VA” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: VA stands for Volt-Ampere — the unit of apparent power in an AC circuit (voltage times current, without accounting for power factor).

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “XL” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: XL stands for Inductive Reactance — the opposition an inductor (coil) offers to alternating current; it increases as frequency increases.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “XC” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: XC stands for Capacitive Reactance — the opposition a capacitor offers to alternating current; it decreases as frequency increases.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “Z” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: Z stands for Impedance — the total opposition to alternating current — the combination of resistance and reactance (XL and XC) in an AC circuit.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “R” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: R stands for Resistance — opposition to current flow, measured in ohms; the symbol R in electrical formulas.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “L” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: L stands for Inductance — the property of a coil that opposes any change in current, measured in henries; the symbol L in electrical formulas.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “C” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: C stands for Capacitance — the ability of a component to store electric charge, measured in farads; the symbol C in electrical formulas.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “Hz” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: Hz stands for Hertz — the unit of frequency — one cycle per second; aircraft AC systems commonly run at 400 Hz.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “LED” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: LED stands for Light-Emitting Diode — a diode that emits light when forward-biased; used in indicators and modern lighting.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “SCR” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: SCR stands for Silicon-Controlled Rectifier — a gate-triggered solid-state switch/rectifier that conducts once its gate is pulsed and stays on until current stops.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “FET” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: FET stands for Field-Effect Transistor — a voltage-controlled transistor whose output current is set by the voltage on its gate.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “JFET” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: JFET stands for Junction Field-Effect Transistor — a field-effect transistor that uses a reverse-biased P-N junction as its control gate.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “UJT” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: UJT stands for Unijunction Transistor — a three-terminal switching device used mainly in timing and trigger circuits (e.g., firing an SCR).

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “NPN” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: NPN stands for Negative-Positive-Negative (transistor) — a bipolar transistor with a P-type base between two N-type layers; its emitter arrow points OUT.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “PNP” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: PNP stands for Positive-Negative-Positive (transistor) — a bipolar transistor with an N-type base between two P-type layers; its emitter arrow points IN toward the base.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “GCU” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: GCU stands for Generator Control Unit — the box that regulates a generator/alternator's voltage and provides its protection (over-voltage, reverse-current, etc.).

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “BPCU” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: BPCU stands for Bus Power Control Unit — on large aircraft, the unit that manages and switches the electrical busses and external/APU power onto them.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “GPU” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: GPU stands for Ground Power Unit — an external power cart plugged in on the ground to supply the aircraft's electrical needs with engines off.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “APU” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: APU stands for Auxiliary Power Unit — a small onboard turbine that supplies electrical (and often pneumatic) power on the ground and as backup in flight.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “CSD” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: CSD stands for Constant-Speed Drive — a drive that holds the alternator at a constant rpm regardless of engine speed so it produces a steady 400-Hz output.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “IDG” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: IDG stands for Integrated Drive Generator — a constant-speed drive and alternator built into one single unit.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “RAT” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: RAT stands for Ram Air Turbine — an emergency wind-driven turbine that drops into the airstream to power a generator/hydraulic pump if normal power fails.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “TRU” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: TRU stands for Transformer Rectifier Unit — a unit that steps AC down and rectifies it to DC to supply the DC busses on an AC-primary aircraft.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “VR” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: VR stands for Voltage Regulator — a device that holds a generator/alternator's output voltage constant as load and speed change.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “Ni-Cd” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: Ni-Cd stands for Nickel-Cadmium (battery) — a rechargeable battery using nickel and cadmium plates in a potassium-hydroxide electrolyte; tolerates heavy loads and wide temperatures.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “Ni-MH” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: Ni-MH stands for Nickel-Metal-Hydride (battery) — a rechargeable battery similar to Ni-Cd but using a hydrogen-absorbing alloy for higher capacity.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “Li-ion” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: Li-ion stands for Lithium-Ion (battery) — a lightweight, high-energy-density rechargeable battery used in some modern aircraft (with strict thermal management).

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “VRLA” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: VRLA stands for Valve-Regulated Lead-Acid (battery) — a sealed lead-acid battery with a pressure-relief valve so it needs no electrolyte servicing.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “SLA” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: SLA stands for Sealed Lead-Acid (battery) — a lead-acid battery in a sealed case that requires no water/electrolyte servicing; increasingly used over flooded and Ni-Cd types.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “Ah” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: Ah stands for Ampere-Hour — a battery's capacity rating — the current it can deliver over time (e.g., 40 Ah supplies its rated current for the rated period).

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “SG” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: SG stands for Specific Gravity — the ratio of the electrolyte's weight to that of water; measured with a hydrometer to judge a lead-acid battery's state of charge.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “AWG” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: AWG stands for American Wire Gauge — the standard numbering system for wire size — a larger AWG number means a smaller (thinner) wire.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “SWAMP” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.short: SWAMP = Severe Wind And Moisture Problems (areas).
questions.expl: SWAMP stands for Severe Wind And Moisture Problems (areas) — aircraft zones with a harsh wind/moisture environment (wheel wells, wing-flap areas, wing folds, pylons) that demand extra wiring protection.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “LRU” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: LRU stands for Line-Replaceable Unit — a modular black-box unit designed to be removed and replaced quickly on the flight line without shop-level teardown.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “ESD” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: ESD stands for Electrostatic Discharge — a sudden flow of static electricity between two objects; it can silently destroy sensitive avionics components.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “FOD” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: FOD stands for Foreign Object Damage/Debris — damage (or the loose debris that causes it) from stray objects — e.g., a dropped tool or hardware left in a bay.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “EMI” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: EMI stands for Electromagnetic Interference — unwanted voltages induced in a wire or component by stray electromagnetic (radio-wave) fields; fought with shielding and bonding.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “RFI” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: RFI stands for Radio-Frequency Interference — electromagnetic interference specifically in the radio-frequency band that can disrupt communication/navigation systems.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “RF” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: RF stands for Radio Frequency — the range of electromagnetic frequencies used for radio transmission (roughly a few kHz up to hundreds of GHz).

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “KVL” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: KVL stands for Kirchhoff's Voltage Law — the rule that the sum of the voltage drops around any closed loop equals the source voltage (voltages around a loop sum to zero).

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “KCL” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: KCL stands for Kirchhoff's Current Law — the rule that the current into any junction equals the current out of it (currents at a node sum to zero).

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “RPM” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: RPM stands for Revolutions Per Minute — the rotational speed of a shaft; the CSD holds alternator RPM constant to keep frequency at 400 Hz.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “CT” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: CT stands for Current Transformer — a transformer that surrounds a conductor to sense the current flowing in it (used for load metering and protection).

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “CB” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: CB stands for Circuit Breaker — a resettable protective device that trips open on overcurrent and can be reset by hand — protecting the wiring, not the device.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “BNC” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: BNC stands for Bayonet Neill-Concelman (connector) — a quick bayonet-locking coaxial connector, the most widely used coax connector for avionics antenna/RF cables.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “NAND” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: NAND stands for NOT-AND (logic gate) — a logic gate whose output is the inverse of AND — LOW only when all inputs are HIGH.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “NOR” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: NOR stands for NOT-OR (logic gate) — a logic gate whose output is the inverse of OR — HIGH only when all inputs are LOW.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “XOR” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: XOR stands for Exclusive-OR (logic gate) — a logic gate whose output is HIGH only when its inputs differ from each other.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “XNOR” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: XNOR stands for Exclusive-NOR (logic gate) — a logic gate whose output is HIGH only when its inputs are the same (the inverse of XOR).

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “VOR” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: VOR stands for VHF Omnidirectional Range — a ground-based navigation aid that lets a receiver determine its bearing to/from the station using VHF radio (108-117.95 MHz).

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “VHF” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: VHF stands for Very High Frequency — the 30-300 MHz radio band; the primary band for aviation voice communication and for VOR navigation.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “UHF” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: UHF stands for Ultra High Frequency — the 300 MHz-3 GHz radio band; used by DME and military/transponder equipment.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “HF” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: HF stands for High Frequency — the 3-30 MHz radio band; travels long distances (used for over-ocean communication) but is prone to atmospheric noise.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “LF” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: LF stands for Low Frequency — the roughly 30-300 kHz radio band; long wavelengths used by some beacons (needs long antennas).

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “MF” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: MF stands for Medium Frequency — the roughly 300 kHz-3 MHz radio band; used by non-directional beacons and AM broadcast.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “VLF” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: VLF stands for Very Low Frequency — the roughly 3-30 kHz radio band; very long wavelengths, historically used by some long-range/nav systems.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “SHF” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: SHF stands for Super High Frequency — the 3-30 GHz radio band; used by radar and satellite links.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “ADF” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: ADF stands for Automatic Direction Finder — a receiver that automatically points to a non-directional beacon (NDB), giving the bearing to that station.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “NDB” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: NDB stands for Non-Directional Beacon — a ground transmitter that radiates equally in all directions; an ADF onboard uses it to find a bearing.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “RMI” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
options: Navigation System with Timing And Ranging
questions.expl: RMI stands for Radio Magnetic Indicator — a cockpit instrument that combines a compass card with pointers showing bearing to VOR/ADF stations.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “ILS” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: ILS stands for Instrument Landing System — a precision approach aid that gives the pilot both horizontal (localizer) and vertical (glideslope) guidance to a runway.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “LOC” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: LOC stands for Localizer — the part of an ILS that provides horizontal (left/right of centerline) guidance to the runway.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “GS” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: GS stands for Glideslope — the part of an ILS that provides vertical (descent-angle) guidance to the runway.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “DME” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: DME stands for Distance Measuring Equipment — a system that measures the aircraft's slant distance to a ground station and displays distance, speed, and time.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “TACAN” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: TACAN stands for Tactical Air Navigation — a military navigation system that combines VOR-like bearing with DME distance in one UHF system.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “VORTAC” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: VORTAC stands for VOR + TACAN (co-located facility) — a single ground station that houses both a VOR and a TACAN, so civil and military aircraft share the location (VOR bearing + DME distance).

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “TVOR” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
options: Traffic Alert and Collision Avoidance System
questions.expl: TVOR stands for Terminal VOR — a lower-power VOR located at or near an airport to serve traffic in the terminal area.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “RNAV” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: RNAV stands for Area Navigation — navigation that lets an aircraft fly any desired path (direct routes/waypoints), not just leg-to-leg between ground stations.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “GPS” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
options: Navigation System with Timing And Ranging
questions.expl: GPS stands for Global Positioning System — satellite navigation using the NAVSTAR constellation to fix the aircraft's position anywhere on earth.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “WAAS” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: WAAS stands for Wide Area Augmentation System — a network of ground stations and satellites that corrects GPS signals for greater accuracy and integrity.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “LAAS” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: LAAS stands for Local Area Augmentation System — an airport-based augmentation that boosts GPS accuracy near a specific field for precision approaches.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “GNSS” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: GNSS stands for Global Navigation Satellite System — the general term for any satellite-based positioning system (GPS is the U.S. example).

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “NAVSTAR” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
options: Navigation System with Timing And Ranging
questions.short: NAVSTAR = Navigation System with Timing And Ranging.
questions.expl: NAVSTAR stands for Navigation System with Timing And Ranging — the name of the U.S. satellite constellation that provides GPS.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “INS” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: INS stands for Inertial Navigation System — a self-contained system that tracks position from a known start using accelerometers and gyros — no outside signal needed.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “IRS” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: IRS stands for Inertial Reference System — a modern strapdown inertial system (using laser/fiber gyros) that supplies position, attitude, and heading data.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “IRU” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: IRU stands for Inertial Reference Unit — the sensor box (gyros/accelerometers) at the heart of an inertial reference system.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “AHRS” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.short: AHRS = Attitude Heading and Reference System.
questions.expl: AHRS stands for Attitude Heading and Reference System — a solid-state system that supplies attitude and heading to glass-cockpit displays, replacing spinning gyros.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “ELT” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: ELT stands for Emergency Locator Transmitter — a crash-activated beacon that transmits a distress signal so search-and-rescue can find a downed aircraft.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “LORAN” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.short: LORAN = Long Range Aid to Navigation.
questions.expl: LORAN stands for Long Range Aid to Navigation — an older ground-tower-pulse navigation system (no longer supported in the U.S.) that located aircraft within a tower network.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “TCAS” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
options: Traffic Alert and Collision Avoidance System
questions.short: TCAS = Traffic Alert and Collision Avoidance System.
questions.expl: TCAS stands for Traffic Alert and Collision Avoidance System — an onboard system that interrogates other aircraft transponders and warns of traffic conflicts, issuing avoidance guidance.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “ACAS” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
options: Traffic Alert and Collision Avoidance System
questions.expl: ACAS stands for Airborne Collision Avoidance System — the international/ICAO term for a collision-avoidance system (TCAS is the common implementation).

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “TA” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: TA stands for Traffic Advisory — a TCAS alert that tells the crew where nearby conflicting traffic is, so they can look for it.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “RA” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: RA stands for Resolution Advisory — a TCAS alert that commands a vertical maneuver (climb/descend) to resolve a collision threat.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “ADS-B” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: ADS-B stands for Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast — a system that broadcasts the aircraft's GPS position and status so ATC and other aircraft can see it (ADS-B OUT and IN).

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “Mode C” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: Mode C stands for Transponder altitude-reporting mode — a transponder mode that automatically reports the aircraft's pressure altitude to ATC along with its code.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “Mode S” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: Mode S stands for Transponder Selective (data-link) mode — a transponder mode that allows selective, addressed interrogation and data exchange (the basis of ADS-B and TCAS coordination).

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “ATC” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: ATC stands for Air Traffic Control — the ground service that separates and sequences aircraft; radios and transponders link the aircraft to it.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “SSB” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: SSB stands for Single Side Band — a bandwidth-efficient AM technique that transmits only one sideband of the modulated carrier (used on HF radios).

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “AM” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: AM stands for Amplitude Modulation — encoding information by varying the amplitude (strength) of the carrier wave; simple and long-range but prone to static.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “FM” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: FM stands for Frequency Modulation — encoding information by varying the frequency of the carrier while amplitude stays constant; largely immune to static noise.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “PM” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: PM stands for Phase Modulation — encoding information by varying the phase of the carrier wave. (Note: in aviation 'PM' can also mean Pulse Modulation, used by DME/transponders/radar.)

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “MB” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: MB stands for Marker Beacon — a low-power vertical-fan transmitter along an ILS that tells the pilot the distance remaining to the runway.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “NAV” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: NAV stands for Navigation (radio) — the cockpit label for the navigation radio/receiver (e.g., NAV 1 / NAV 2 selecting VOR/ILS frequencies).

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “COMM” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: COMM stands for Communication (radio) — the cockpit label for the voice communication radio/transceiver (e.g., COMM 1 / COMM 2).

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “FCC” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: FCC stands for Federal Communications Commission — the U.S. agency that assigns and controls radio-frequency usage.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “BITE” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: BITE stands for Built-In Test Equipment — self-monitoring circuitry inside an avionics unit that reports its own faults to speed troubleshooting.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “RADAR” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: RADAR stands for Radio Detection And Ranging — a system that transmits radio pulses and times their echoes to detect the range/bearing of objects (traffic, weather, terrain).

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “WX radar” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: WX radar stands for Weather Radar — airborne radar that detects precipitation and storm cells ahead so the crew can avoid weather.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “FMS” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: FMS stands for Flight Management System — an integrated system that automates navigation, performance, and flight-plan management using its computer and displays.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “FMC” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: FMC stands for Flight Management Computer — the central computer of the flight management system that does the navigation and performance calculations.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “CDU” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: CDU stands for Control Display Unit — the keypad-and-screen crew interface used to enter data into and read back from the flight management system.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “EFIS” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: EFIS stands for Electronic Flight Instrument System — the system that replaces individual mechanical gauges with computer-driven flat-panel displays (the glass cockpit).

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “EADI” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: EADI stands for Electronic Attitude Director Indicator — an electronic display that shows aircraft attitude plus flight-director command bars and other situational data on one screen.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “EHSI” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: EHSI stands for Electronic Horizontal Situation Indicator — an electronic evolution of the HSI showing heading, course, and navigation data on a screen.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “ADI” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
options: Engine Indicating and Crew Alerting System
questions.expl: ADI stands for Attitude Director Indicator — an attitude indicator that also displays flight-director steering commands.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “HSI” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: HSI stands for Horizontal Situation Indicator — an instrument that merges the heading indicator with VOR/ILS course guidance into one display.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “FDI” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: FDI stands for Flight Director Indicator — the instrument that displays the flight director's command bars showing the pilot the attitude to fly.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “FD” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
options: Engine Indicating and Crew Alerting System
questions.expl: FD stands for Flight Director — a system that computes and displays the attitude needed to fly a selected flight path — an autopilot's brain without the servos.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “CDI” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: CDI stands for Course Deviation Indicator — the needle/display that shows how far left or right of the selected VOR/localizer course the aircraft is.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “OBS” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: OBS stands for Omni-Bearing Selector — the knob a pilot uses to select the desired VOR radial/course to fly to or from the station.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “ECAM” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: ECAM stands for Electronic Centralized Aircraft Monitor — an Airbus-style system that automatically monitors aircraft systems and alerts the crew (with cues) when a fault occurs.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “EICAS” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
options: Engine Indicating and Crew Alerting System
questions.short: EICAS = Engine Indicating and Crew Alerting System.
questions.expl: EICAS stands for Engine Indicating and Crew Alerting System — a Boeing-style system that displays engine parameters and crew alerts/warnings on centralized screens.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “PFD” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: PFD stands for Primary Flight Display — the main glass-cockpit screen that combines attitude, airspeed, altitude, heading, and vertical speed for the pilot.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “MFD” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: MFD stands for Multi-Function Display — a flat-panel screen that can show navigation, weather, engine, or system pages selectable by the crew.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “CRT” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: CRT stands for Cathode-Ray Tube — the older display technology used in early glass-cockpit screens before flat LCDs.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “LCD” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: LCD stands for Liquid-Crystal Display — the flat-panel screen technology used in modern glass cockpits, replacing bulky CRTs.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “AFCS” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: AFCS stands for Automatic Flight Control System — an integrated autopilot with many related functions combined into a single system (attitude, heading, nav, glideslope).

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “SAS” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: SAS stands for Stability Augmentation System — a system (common on helicopters) that makes small automatic control inputs to stabilize the aircraft and reduce pilot workload.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “GPWS” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: GPWS stands for Ground Proximity Warning System — a system that warns the crew when the aircraft is dangerously close to terrain.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “EGPWS” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
options: Engine Indicating and Crew Alerting System
questions.short: EGPWS = Enhanced Ground Proximity Warning System.
questions.expl: EGPWS stands for Enhanced Ground Proximity Warning System — a GPWS upgraded with a terrain database and GPS position for earlier, look-ahead terrain warnings.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “TAWS” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.short: TAWS = Terrain Awareness and Warning System.
questions.expl: TAWS stands for Terrain Awareness and Warning System — the FAA term for the modern terrain-warning system (the certified successor to GPWS/EGPWS).

questions.q: What does the abbreviation “AGL” stand for (in Block 6 systems)?
questions.expl: AGL stands for Above Ground Level — altitude measured from the terrain directly below the aircraft (as opposed to above sea level).

questions.q: Which abbreviation stands for “Electromotive Force”?
questions.expl: Electromotive Force is abbreviated EMF — the electrical 'pressure' (voltage) produced by a source that pushes current through a circuit; measured in volts.

questions.q: Which abbreviation stands for “Counter-Electromotive Force”?
questions.expl: Counter-Electromotive Force is abbreviated CEMF — the induced 'back voltage' created in a coil/inductor that opposes the change in current that produced it (also called back-EMF).

questions.q: Which abbreviation stands for “Power Factor”?
questions.expl: Power Factor is abbreviated PF — the ratio of true power to apparent power in an AC circuit (the cosine of the phase angle between voltage and current).

questions.q: Which abbreviation stands for “Inductive Reactance”?
questions.expl: Inductive Reactance is abbreviated XL — the opposition an inductor (coil) offers to alternating current; it increases as frequency increases.

questions.q: Which abbreviation stands for “Capacitive Reactance”?
questions.expl: Capacitive Reactance is abbreviated XC — the opposition a capacitor offers to alternating current; it decreases as frequency increases.

questions.q: Which abbreviation stands for “Impedance”?
questions.expl: Impedance is abbreviated Z — the total opposition to alternating current — the combination of resistance and reactance (XL and XC) in an AC circuit.

questions.q: Which abbreviation stands for “Generator Control Unit”?
questions.expl: Generator Control Unit is abbreviated GCU — the box that regulates a generator/alternator's voltage and provides its protection (over-voltage, reverse-current, etc.).

questions.q: Which abbreviation stands for “Constant-Speed Drive”?
questions.expl: Constant-Speed Drive is abbreviated CSD — a drive that holds the alternator at a constant rpm regardless of engine speed so it produces a steady 400-Hz output.

questions.q: Which abbreviation stands for “Integrated Drive Generator”?
questions.expl: Integrated Drive Generator is abbreviated IDG — a constant-speed drive and alternator built into one single unit.

questions.q: Which abbreviation stands for “Nickel-Cadmium (battery)”?
questions.expl: Nickel-Cadmium (battery) is abbreviated Ni-Cd — a rechargeable battery using nickel and cadmium plates in a potassium-hydroxide electrolyte; tolerates heavy loads and wide temperatures.

questions.q: Which abbreviation stands for “American Wire Gauge”?
questions.expl: American Wire Gauge is abbreviated AWG — the standard numbering system for wire size — a larger AWG number means a smaller (thinner) wire.

questions.q: Which abbreviation stands for “Severe Wind And Moisture Problems (areas)”?
questions.short: Severe Wind And Moisture Problems (areas) = SWAMP.
questions.expl: Severe Wind And Moisture Problems (areas) is abbreviated SWAMP — aircraft zones with a harsh wind/moisture environment (wheel wells, wing-flap areas, wing folds, pylons) that demand extra wiring protection.

questions.q: Which abbreviation stands for “Line-Replaceable Unit”?
questions.expl: Line-Replaceable Unit is abbreviated LRU — a modular black-box unit designed to be removed and replaced quickly on the flight line without shop-level teardown.

questions.q: Which abbreviation stands for “Electrostatic Discharge”?
questions.expl: Electrostatic Discharge is abbreviated ESD — a sudden flow of static electricity between two objects; it can silently destroy sensitive avionics components.

questions.q: Which abbreviation stands for “VHF Omnidirectional Range”?
questions.expl: VHF Omnidirectional Range is abbreviated VOR — a ground-based navigation aid that lets a receiver determine its bearing to/from the station using VHF radio (108-117.95 MHz).

questions.q: Which abbreviation stands for “Instrument Landing System”?
questions.expl: Instrument Landing System is abbreviated ILS — a precision approach aid that gives the pilot both horizontal (localizer) and vertical (glideslope) guidance to a runway.

questions.q: Which abbreviation stands for “Distance Measuring Equipment”?
questions.expl: Distance Measuring Equipment is abbreviated DME — a system that measures the aircraft's slant distance to a ground station and displays distance, speed, and time.

questions.q: Which abbreviation stands for “Area Navigation”?
questions.expl: Area Navigation is abbreviated RNAV — navigation that lets an aircraft fly any desired path (direct routes/waypoints), not just leg-to-leg between ground stations.

questions.q: Which abbreviation stands for “Global Positioning System”?
questions.expl: Global Positioning System is abbreviated GPS — satellite navigation using the NAVSTAR constellation to fix the aircraft's position anywhere on earth.

questions.q: Which abbreviation stands for “Wide Area Augmentation System”?
questions.expl: Wide Area Augmentation System is abbreviated WAAS — a network of ground stations and satellites that corrects GPS signals for greater accuracy and integrity.

questions.q: Which abbreviation stands for “Inertial Navigation System”?
questions.expl: Inertial Navigation System is abbreviated INS — a self-contained system that tracks position from a known start using accelerometers and gyros — no outside signal needed.

questions.q: Which abbreviation stands for “Inertial Reference System”?
questions.expl: Inertial Reference System is abbreviated IRS — a modern strapdown inertial system (using laser/fiber gyros) that supplies position, attitude, and heading data.

questions.q: Which abbreviation stands for “Emergency Locator Transmitter”?
questions.expl: Emergency Locator Transmitter is abbreviated ELT — a crash-activated beacon that transmits a distress signal so search-and-rescue can find a downed aircraft.

questions.q: Which abbreviation stands for “Traffic Alert and Collision Avoidance System”?
questions.short: Traffic Alert and Collision Avoidance System = TCAS.
questions.expl: Traffic Alert and Collision Avoidance System is abbreviated TCAS — an onboard system that interrogates other aircraft transponders and warns of traffic conflicts, issuing avoidance guidance.

questions.q: Which abbreviation stands for “Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast”?
questions.expl: Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast is abbreviated ADS-B — a system that broadcasts the aircraft's GPS position and status so ATC and other aircraft can see it (ADS-B OUT and IN).

questions.q: Which abbreviation stands for “Electronic Flight Instrument System”?
questions.expl: Electronic Flight Instrument System is abbreviated EFIS — the system that replaces individual mechanical gauges with computer-driven flat-panel displays (the glass cockpit).

questions.q: Which abbreviation stands for “Electronic Attitude Director Indicator”?
questions.expl: Electronic Attitude Director Indicator is abbreviated EADI — an electronic display that shows aircraft attitude plus flight-director command bars and other situational data on one screen.

questions.q: Which abbreviation stands for “Automatic Flight Control System”?
questions.expl: Automatic Flight Control System is abbreviated AFCS — an integrated autopilot with many related functions combined into a single system (attitude, heading, nav, glideslope).

questions.q: In a series circuit, which quantity is the SAME at every point in the circuit?
questions.expl: A series circuit has only one path, so the same current flows through every part. Voltage drops differ; current does not.

questions.q: Three resistors of 1 kΩ, 3 kΩ, and 5 kΩ are connected in series. What is the total resistance?
questions.expl: Series: the pinches simply add. One operation per line: 1 k + 3 k = 4 k, then 4 k + 5 k = 9 kΩ. Keys: 1 + 3 = → 4 + 5 = → 9. Sanity: a series total always comes out bigger than the biggest single resistor.

questions.q: In a parallel circuit, which quantity is the SAME across every branch?
questions.expl: Every branch connects across the same two source terminals, so each branch sees the same voltage. The branch currents differ.

questions.q: Compared to the smallest branch resistor, the total resistance of a parallel circuit is always:
options: Equal to the sum of all branches
questions.expl: Adding a parallel path gives current another road, lowering total resistance. The result is always less than the smallest individual branch — the opposite of series.

questions.q: Two resistors of 500 Ω and 400 Ω are connected in parallel. Using product-over-sum, what is the total resistance?
questions.expl: Product-over-sum, one operation per line: product 500 × 400 = 200,000; sum 500 + 400 = 900; divide 200,000 ÷ 900 = 222.2 Ω. Keys: 500 × 400 = → 200000, then 500 + 400 = → 900, then 200000 ÷ 900 = → 222.2. Sanity: a parallel total must land below the smaller branch (400 Ω) — 222.2 does.

questions.q: Two 60 Ω resistors are connected in parallel. What is the total resistance?
questions.expl: Equal resistors in parallel: value ÷ number of branches. 60 ÷ 2 = 30 Ω. Keys: 60 ÷ 2 = → 30. Sanity: below the smallest branch (60 Ω), as parallel always is.

questions.q: The correct product-over-sum formula for two resistors in parallel is:
questions.expl: Total resistance for two parallel resistors equals the product of the two divided by their sum: (R1×R2)/(R1+R2).

questions.q: In a series circuit, the individual voltage drops across the resistors must add up to:
questions.expl: Each resistor uses a share of the push; the shares add back to the applied source voltage (this is Kirchhoff's Voltage Law).

questions.q: A 12 V source feeds two series resistors: R1 = 100 Ω and R2 = 300 Ω. What is the voltage drop across R2?
questions.expl: Three little moves, one operation each: total resistance 100 + 300 = 400 Ω. Current: I = E ÷ R = 12 ÷ 400 = 0.03 A. Drop across R2: E = I × R = 0.03 × 300 = 9 V. Keys: 100 + 300 = → 400, then 12 ÷ 400 = → 0.03, then 0.03 × 300 = → 9. Sanity: R2 is 3/4 of the pinch, so it takes 3/4 of the 12 V.

questions.q: A device that uses series resistors to obtain more than one voltage from a single power source is called a:
questions.expl: A voltage divider is a series resistor string with taps; different voltages appear between the taps because the source voltage divides among the resistors.

questions.q: Kirchhoff's Voltage Law states that around any closed loop, the source voltage minus all the voltage drops equals:
questions.expl: KVL: applied voltage minus the sum of all drops equals zero — every bit of the source's push is used up by the loads around the loop.

questions.q: A 100 V source feeds four series resistors. Three drops are 2 V, 10 V, and 20 V. By Kirchhoff's Voltage Law, the fourth drop is:
questions.expl: The missing drop is the leftover push. Add the known drops one at a time: 2 + 10 = 12, then 12 + 20 = 32. Leftover: 100 − 32 = 68 V. Keys: 2 + 10 = → 12 + 20 = → 32, then 100 − 32 = → 68. Check: 2 + 10 + 20 + 68 = 100 — every volt accounted for.

questions.q: Kirchhoff's Current Law states that the current flowing into a junction (node):
options: Equals the current flowing out of it
Is greater than the current out
questions.expl: At any junction, current in equals current out — nothing accumulates. For parallel branches this gives It = I1 + I2 + I3.

questions.q: 75 mA flows into a node. Two branches leaving carry 30 mA and 20 mA. By Kirchhoff's Current Law, the third branch carries:
questions.expl: Cars in = cars out. Add the known outs: 30 + 20 = 50 mA. The missing branch carries the leftover: 75 − 50 = 25 mA. Keys: 30 + 20 = → 50, then 75 − 50 = → 25. Check: 30 + 25 + 20 = 75 — matches what flowed in.

questions.q: In a parallel circuit, the total current drawn from the source equals:
options: The sum of all branch currents
The same current in every branch
questions.expl: The source current splits among the branches and rejoins, so It = I1 + I2 + I3 (Kirchhoff's Current Law applied to a parallel circuit).

questions.q: To solve a series-parallel circuit, the FIRST step is usually to:
options: Reduce each parallel group to its single equivalent resistor
questions.expl: Solve the parallel groups first and replace each with one equivalent resistor; the circuit then collapses into a simple series circuit you can sum.

questions.q: R1 = 1 kΩ is in series with a parallel pair (2 kΩ and 3 kΩ). What is the total resistance of the circuit?
questions.expl: Collapse the parallel pair first, working in kΩ: product 2 × 3 = 6; sum 2 + 3 = 5; divide 6 ÷ 5 = 1.2 kΩ. Now it's plain series: 1 + 1.2 = 2.2 kΩ. Keys: 2 × 3 = → 6, then 2 + 3 = → 5, then 6 ÷ 5 = → 1.2, then 1 + 1.2 = → 2.2. Sanity: the pair collapsed below its smaller branch (2 kΩ).

questions.q: An OPEN circuit is best described as:
options: A break or incomplete path so no current flows
A path with exactly the rated resistance
questions.expl: An open is an incomplete path for current — a break, blown fuse, or burned-open part — so no current flows in that path.

questions.q: A SHORT circuit is best described as:
options: An unwanted low-resistance path that lets current bypass the load
questions.expl: A short allows current to flow across a part that should insulate, bypassing the load. It causes excessive current and rapid heating.

questions.q: What is the typical symptom of a SHORT circuit in terms of current?
options: Excessive current that can blow a fuse or breaker
questions.expl: A short is a near-zero-resistance shortcut, so current spikes and generates heat quickly — this is what trips circuit protection.

questions.q: A voltmeter placed across a suspected break in an energized circuit reads the FULL source voltage. This indicates:
options: A blown branch resistor in parallel
questions.expl: With an open, no current flows, so no voltage is dropped elsewhere — the entire source voltage appears across the break.

questions.q: With power removed, an ohmmeter across a component reads infinite (∞) ohms. The component is:
questions.expl: Infinite resistance means no complete path — an open. A short would read near 0 Ω.

questions.q: Which fault can occur in a resistor or fuse WITHOUT any visible sign of damage?
questions.expl: The NCATT guide notes a resistor or fuse can open with no visible damage, so a meter/continuity check is needed to confirm it.

questions.q: Which meter is used to find a circuit problem with the power REMOVED from the circuit?
questions.expl: The ohmmeter measures resistance and runs continuity checks with power off. The voltmeter and ammeter are used with power on.

questions.q: Which meter is used to find a circuit problem with the power ON, and is a good first check for input voltage?
questions.expl: The voltmeter works on a live circuit; checking that input voltage is even present is a recommended starting point.

questions.q: A continuity check is performed to verify:
options: That a complete electrical path exists between two points
The peak value of an AC waveform
questions.expl: A continuity check confirms a complete path exists between two points; it is usually done with an ohmmeter or voltmeter, testing at each terminal.

questions.q: Which single instrument combines a voltmeter, ammeter, and ohmmeter and is the most versatile tool the technician uses?
questions.expl: A multimeter contains a voltmeter, ammeter, and ohmmeter, measuring voltage, current, and resistance — the most versatile electrical instrument.

questions.q: In the troubleshooting process, the recommended FIRST action is to:
options: Isolate the problem by asking how and when it occurs
Start replacing components one by one
Apply maximum voltage to the circuit
questions.expl: The NCATT process begins by isolating the problem — is it intermittent, worse during taxi/takeoff/cruise/landing, weather-related — before touching parts.

questions.q: When narrowing down where a fault is along a wire run, the efficient measurement strategy is to:
options: Measure at the middle, decide which half holds the fault, then split again
Test every single terminal in order from the source
questions.expl: Measuring at the midpoint and discarding the good half each time corners the fault in a few moves instead of testing every point.

questions.q: Direct current (DC) differs from alternating current (AC) in that DC:
options: Flows constantly in one direction with constant polarity
questions.expl: DC flows constantly in one direction with constant polarity; AC reverses direction at regular intervals, tracing a sine wave.

questions.q: The number of complete AC cycles that occur each second is called the:
questions.expl: Frequency is cycles per second, measured in hertz (Hz). The time for one cycle is the period.

questions.q: If an aircraft AC system operates at 400 Hz, the period of one cycle is:
questions.expl: Period and frequency are reciprocals — the '1 ÷' flip: period = 1 ÷ 400 = 0.0025 s. Keys: 1 ÷ 400 = → 0.0025. To read that in milliseconds, hop the decimal 3 places right: 0.0025 s → 2.5 ms.

questions.q: One reason aircraft use AC rather than DC for many systems is that AC voltage:
options: Can be easily stepped up or down with transformers
questions.expl: AC can be raised or lowered by transformers, transmits over distance more easily, and AC motors are smaller, lighter, and brushless.

questions.q: What is the primary job of a resistor in a circuit?
options: To oppose (limit) the amount of current flow
questions.expl: A resistor's general use is to limit the amount of current flow.

questions.q: In the standard resistor color code, what digit does BLACK represent?
questions.expl: Black is the very first color in the 0-9 sequence, so Black = 0. Then Brown=1, Red=2, and so on up to White=9.

questions.q: What digit does the color WHITE represent?
questions.expl: White is the highest digit, 9, at the end of the 0-9 color sequence.

questions.q: Reading from the end toward the center of a 4-band resistor, what does the THIRD band represent?
options: The multiplier (number of zeros to add)
questions.expl: Band 3 tells how many zeros to add to the first two digits.

questions.q: On a standard 4-band resistor, what does the FOURTH band indicate?
questions.expl: The fourth band gives the percentage tolerance; no fourth band means +/-20%.

questions.q: A GOLD tolerance band means the resistor is accurate to within:
questions.expl: Gold in the fourth (tolerance) slot = +/-5%. Learn the three-step ladder: gold 5%, silver 10%, no band at all 20%.

questions.q: A SILVER tolerance band means the resistor tolerance is:
questions.expl: Silver in the tolerance slot = +/-10%. Same ladder every time: gold 5%, silver 10%, no fourth band 20%.

questions.q: A resistor has NO fourth (tolerance) band. What tolerance is understood?
questions.expl: If there is no fourth band, the tolerance is understood to be 20 percent.

questions.q: Decode Brown-Black-Red-Gold. What is the value and tolerance?
questions.expl: Step ladder: Brown=1, Black=0 -> digits '10'. Red = 2 zeros, added one at a time: 10 -> 100 -> 1,000 ohms. Gold = +/-5%. Range: 1,000 x 0.05 = 50; 1,000 - 50 = 950; 1,000 + 50 = 1,050.

questions.q: Decode Yellow-Violet-Orange-Silver.
Decode Green-Blue-Brown-Gold.
questions.expl: Step ladder: Green=5, Blue=6 -> digits '56'. Brown = 1 zero: 56 -> 560 ohms. Gold = +/-5%. Range: 560 x 0.05 = 28; 560 - 28 = 532; 560 + 28 = 588.

questions.q: Decode Red-Red-Red-Gold.
questions.expl: Step ladder: Red=2, Red=2 -> digits '22'. Red = 2 zeros, one at a time: 22 -> 220 -> 2,200 ohms (2.2 k). Gold = +/-5%.

questions.q: Decode Brown-Green-Green-Silver.
questions.expl: Step ladder: Brown=1, Green=5 -> digits '15'. Green = 5 zeros, one at a time: 15 -> 150 -> 1,500 -> 15,000 -> 150,000 -> 1,500,000 ohms. Hop the decimal 6 places left and that is 1.5 M ohms. Silver = +/-10%.

questions.q: What is the correct order of the first five color-code colors (digits 0 through 4)?
questions.expl: 0=Black, 1=Brown, 2=Red, 3=Orange, 4=Yellow.

questions.q: Which color represents the digit 5?
questions.expl: Green=5. (Blue=6, Yellow=4, Violet=7.)

questions.q: Which color represents the digit 7?
questions.expl: Violet=7. A common confusion is Blue=6 vs Violet=7.

questions.q: A resistor's first two bands are Blue then Gray. What two digits is that?
questions.expl: Blue=6, Gray=8 -> '68'.

questions.q: Which resistor type is built from finely ground carbon/graphite mixed with an insulating filler and binder, pressed into a rod?
questions.expl: Carbon composition uses graphite + filler + binder; graphite amount sets the resistance.

questions.q: Which resistor type typically handles LARGE current and has HIGH power ratings, built by winding resistance wire on a porcelain rod?
questions.expl: Wirewound: resistance wire wound on a porcelain (ceramic) rod. All that wire and ceramic sheds heat well, so it handles large currents and high power ratings.

questions.q: A film resistor is made by:
options: Winding wire on a ceramic rod
Pressing graphite and filler into a rod
Depositing a thin resistive material evenly on a ceramic rod
questions.short: Thin film deposited on a ceramic rod.
questions.expl: Film resistors deposit resistive material (graphite, nickel-chromium, etc.) on a ceramic rod.

questions.q: What is the difference between a rheostat and a potentiometer?
options: A rheostat has 3 terminals; a potentiometer has 2
A rheostat varies current (2 terminals); a potentiometer varies voltage (3 terminals)
A rheostat is temperature-sensitive; a potentiometer is light-sensitive
questions.short: Rheostat varies current; potentiometer varies voltage.
questions.expl: Rheostat = 2-terminal, varies current. Potentiometer = 3-terminal (wiper), varies voltage.

questions.q: A thermistor is a variable resistor that responds to:
questions.expl: A thermistor is temperature-sensitive with a negative temperature coefficient.

questions.q: Before measuring a resistor's value with an ohmmeter, you must:
questions.expl: An ohmmeter uses its own internal battery; circuit power must be off or it damages the meter and gives false reads.

questions.q: When testing a resistor in-circuit, why should you disconnect (isolate) at least one lead?
options: So parallel components don't provide a sneak path that falsifies the reading
To increase the voltage across it
Because the ohmmeter needs two batteries
questions.expl: Other components in parallel give the meter a second path, reading lower than the resistor alone; lifting a lead isolates it.

questions.q: An ohmmeter across an isolated resistor reads INFINITE (OL). The resistor is:
questions.expl: Infinite resistance means a broken path with no continuity = an open resistor.

questions.q: An ohmmeter across an isolated resistor reads 0 ohms. The resistor is:
questions.expl: Zero ohms means current passes where it should be opposed = a shorted resistor.

questions.q: The NCATT guide says an OPEN resistor is a fault caused by:
options: A foreign metal bridging two traces
An incomplete path for current from one terminal to another
questions.expl: An open is an incomplete path for current; it can occur with no visible signs of damage.

questions.q: The NCATT guide describes a SHORTED resistor as a fault that:
options: Allows current to flow across a part of the circuit that should act as an insulator
questions.short: Current flows where it should be blocked.
questions.expl: A short allows current across a portion that should insulate; often from foreign material or close traces.

questions.q: A resistor marked Brown-Black-Red-Gold (1,000 ohms +/-5%) measures 1,180 ohms after isolation. It is:
questions.expl: One line at a time: wiggle room 1,000 x 0.05 = 50. Low end 1,000 - 50 = 950. High end 1,000 + 50 = 1,050. The meter reads 1,180, which is above 1,050 (by 1,180 - 1,050 = 130), so it is out of tolerance. Keys: 1000 x 0.05 = -> 50; 1000 + 50 = -> 1050.

questions.q: A 470 ohm +/-10% resistor is within tolerance if it measures between:
questions.expl: One line at a time: 10% = 0.10, so wiggle room = 470 x 0.10 = 47 (10% of anything is one decimal hop left). Low end: 470 - 47 = 423. High end: 470 + 47 = 517. Keys: 470 x 0.10 = -> 47; 470 - 47 = -> 423; 470 + 47 = -> 517.

questions.q: You need a 330 ohm +/-5% resistor. Which color bands?
questions.expl: Backward steps: digits 3,3 = Orange, Orange. Count the zeros one at a time: 33 -> 330 is 1 zero = x10 = Brown. Tolerance +/-5% = Gold. Check by decoding your own answer: Orange-Orange-Brown-Gold -> '33' + 1 zero -> 330 ohms +/-5%. Round trip matches.

questions.q: What does a resistor's POWER RATING (in watts) tell you?
options: The maximum heat it can dissipate without being damaged
questions.expl: The power rating is the most heat (watts) the resistor can shed without overheating; P = I-squared x R.

questions.q: Three resistors of 100, 220, and 330 ohms are in SERIES. The total resistance is:
questions.expl: Series: pinches add, one operation per line: 100 + 220 = 320; then 320 + 330 = 650 ohms. Keys: 100 + 220 = -> 320 + 330 = -> 650. Sanity: bigger than the biggest single resistor (330), as series always is.

questions.q: Two 100 ohm resistors are connected in PARALLEL. The total resistance is:
questions.expl: Equal-pair shortcut: 100 / 2 = 50 ohms. Long way (product-over-sum), one operation per line: 100 x 100 = 10,000; 100 + 100 = 200; 10,000 / 200 = 50. Both roads land on 50 — below the smallest branch, as parallel must be.

questions.q: On a color-banded resistor, the body (base) color of the resistor:
options: Has nothing to do with the resistance value
questions.expl: The body/base color has nothing to do with the color code and is never the same as a value band.

questions.q: The first color band of a standard 4-band resistor is never which colors?
questions.expl: The first (and second) digit band is never gold or silver in color.

questions.q: What does an inductor oppose, and where does it store energy?
options: A change in current; stored in a magnetic field
A change in voltage; stored in an electric field
A change in resistance; stored as heat
A change in frequency; stored in the dielectric
questions.expl: An inductor opposes a CHANGE in current and stores energy in a magnetic field. (The capacitor is the voltage/electric-field one.)

questions.q: What is the basic unit of inductance?
questions.expl: The henry (H) is the unit of inductance: 1 H when current changing 1 A/sec induces 1 V.

questions.q: Which change INCREASES a coil's inductance?
options: Stretching the coil to twice its length
Removing the iron core and using air
questions.expl: More turns increases inductance (it varies as the square of the turns). Longer coil, air core, and smaller area all DECREASE inductance.

questions.q: Doubling the number of turns on a coil (same current) changes the inductance by about what factor?
questions.expl: Inductance varies as the SQUARE of the number of turns, so doubling turns gives roughly 4x the inductance.

questions.q: Three inductors are connected in SERIES. How do you find total inductance?
options: Add them: LT = L1 + L2 + L3
questions.expl: Inductors in series add directly, just like resistors in series: LT = L1 + L2 + L3.

questions.q: The formula for inductive reactance is:
questions.expl: Inductive reactance XL = 2πfL, measured in ohms. (The 1/(2πf...) form is capacitive reactance.)

questions.q: As frequency increases, inductive reactance (XL):
questions.expl: XL = 2πfL, so higher frequency means higher inductive reactance. (Capacitive reactance does the opposite.)
sources: AET Academy M6 — Power Supplies & Filters

questions.q: Find XL for L = 0.146 H at 60 cps.
questions.expl: Ladder: knowns L = 0.146 H, f = 60 Hz. Formula XL = 2πfL (2π is always 6.28). One operation per line: 6.28 × 60 = 376.8, then 376.8 × 0.146 = 55.01, round ≈ 55 ohms. Keys: 6.28 × 60 = → 376.8 × 0.146 = → 55.01.

questions.q: With 110 V across an inductor whose XL = 55 ohms, the current is:
questions.expl: Reactance slots into Ohm's law exactly where R goes: I = E / XL. Plug: 110 ÷ 55. One operation: 110 ÷ 55 = 2 → 2 amperes. Sanity: 55 ohms of fight against a 110 V push = a modest 2 A. Makes sense.

questions.q: In the memory aid 'ELI the ICE man,' the 'ELI' part means:
options: Current leads voltage in an inductor
Voltage equals current in an inductor
Voltage (E) leads current (I) in an inductor (L)
questions.short: ELI: E leads I in L
questions.expl: ELI reads in the order things happen: in an inductor (L), voltage (E) leads current (I). The coil is slow to let current build, so the push arrives first and the flow lags behind.

questions.q: In a purely inductive AC circuit, the current:
options: Is exactly in phase with voltage
questions.expl: Inductance causes the current to lag the applied voltage by 90 degrees (ELI).

questions.q: What does a capacitor oppose, and where does it store energy?
options: A change in current; in a magnetic field
A change in frequency; as heat
A change in voltage; in an electric (electrostatic) field
questions.expl: A capacitor opposes a CHANGE in voltage and stores energy in an electric (electrostatic) field between its plates.

questions.q: A capacitor is basically constructed of:
options: A coil of many turns of wire
Two parallel plates separated by a dielectric
An iron core with two windings
questions.expl: A capacitor is two parallel plates separated by an insulator called the dielectric.

questions.q: The basic unit of capacitance is the farad, defined as:
options: 1 coulomb of charge stored at 1 volt
questions.expl: One farad is one coulomb of charge stored with one volt across the plates.

questions.q: One microfarad (µF) equals:
questions.expl: A microfarad is 10^-6 farad; a picofarad (pF) is 10^-12 farad.

questions.q: Which change INCREASES capacitance?
options: Using a dielectric with a lower K
questions.expl: Closer plate spacing increases capacitance. Larger plate area and a higher-K dielectric also increase it.

questions.q: How do capacitors combine when connected in PARALLEL?
options: They simply add: CT = C1 + C2 + C3
The total is the smallest value
questions.expl: Capacitors in parallel ADD directly (effective plate area increases) - the OPPOSITE of resistors in parallel.

questions.q: C1 = 330 µF and C2 = 220 µF are wired in parallel. Total capacitance?
questions.expl: Parallel balloons just add: 330 + 220 = 550 µF. Both values are already in µF, so no hops needed — the answer stays in µF. Sanity: two caps together hold more than either alone.

questions.q: Capacitors connected in SERIES are calculated:
options: By the reciprocal rule, like resistors in parallel
The same as inductors in series
questions.expl: Capacitors in series use the reciprocal rule (1/CT = 1/C1 + 1/C2 ...), like resistors in parallel; total is less than the smallest.

questions.q: The formula for capacitive reactance is:
questions.expl: Capacitive reactance XC = 1/(2πfC), in ohms.

questions.q: As frequency increases, capacitive reactance (XC):
questions.expl: Because XC = 1/(2πfC), higher frequency means LOWER capacitive reactance - opposite of inductive reactance.
sources: AET Academy M6 — Power Supplies & Filters

questions.q: Find XC for C = 200 µF (0.000200 F) at 60 cps.
The 'ICE' half of 'ELI the ICE man' means:
options: Voltage leads current in a capacitor
Current equals voltage in a capacitor
Current (I) leads voltage (E) in a capacitor (C)
questions.short: ICE: I leads E in C
questions.expl: ICE reads in order: in a capacitor (C), current (I) leads voltage (E). Charge has to flow IN before the voltage across the plates can rise - flow first, pressure second.

questions.q: In a purely capacitive AC circuit, the current:
questions.expl: In a capacitive circuit the current reaches maximum ahead of voltage - it leads by 90 degrees (ICE).

questions.q: The RC time constant is the time for the capacitor voltage to reach what percent of the applied voltage?
questions.expl: One time constant (τ = R × C) is the time to reach 63.2% of applied voltage; ~5 time constants for full charge.

questions.q: For R = 10,000 ohms and C = 100 µF (0.0001 F), the time constant (τ = RC) is:
questions.expl: Hop first: 100 µF → F: hop 6 left → 0.000100. Then one operation: 10,000 × 0.000100 = 1 → 1 second. Handy check: ohms × farads always comes out in seconds. Full charge takes about 5 × 1 = 5 seconds.

questions.q: Before handling or testing a capacitor, you should always:
options: Discharge it (short the leads through a resistor)
questions.expl: A charged capacitor can hold a dangerous voltage; always discharge it before handling or testing.

questions.q: You test a capacitor with an ohmmeter. A GOOD capacitor will:
options: Read a steady mid-scale resistance forever
Momentarily read low, then climb to high/infinite
questions.expl: A good cap charges (brief low reading) and then the reading rises toward high/infinite as charging current stops.

questions.q: An ohmmeter on a capacitor reads 0 ohms and never changes. The capacitor is:
questions.expl: A reading stuck at 0 ohms means the plates are touching - the capacitor is shorted; its electrical qualities are gone.

questions.q: An ohmmeter on a capacitor reads infinite immediately with NO initial charging dip. This indicates:
questions.expl: No momentary charging current (no dip) means the cap never charges - it is open.

questions.q: Electrolytic capacitors are POLARIZED, which means:
options: They only work on DC of any polarity
They must be installed observing + and - polarity
questions.expl: Electrolytic caps have marked + and - leads and must be installed with correct polarity or the dielectric breaks down.

questions.q: By what process does energy cross from a transformer's primary to its secondary?
options: Mutual induction (a shared changing magnetic field)
questions.expl: The windings are not electrically connected; the changing magnetic field of the primary induces voltage in the secondary by mutual induction.

questions.q: A transformer will NOT operate on:
questions.expl: A transformer needs a CHANGING voltage to create a changing magnetic field. Pure steady DC produces no change, so no transformation.

questions.q: The transformer turns-ratio relationship is:
questions.expl: Voltage divides in proportion to turns: Vp/Vs = Np/Ns. Memory tip: primary sits on top of BOTH fractions, so the ratio can't get flipped on you.

questions.q: A transformer with MORE turns on the secondary than the primary is a:
questions.expl: More secondary turns gives a higher secondary voltage - a step-UP transformer.

questions.q: If a transformer steps the voltage UP, what happens to the current?
options: It steps up by the same ratio
It steps down by the same ratio
questions.expl: Current is inverse to voltage (power in ≈ power out). Step voltage up = step current down by the same ratio.

questions.q: Primary = 240 V on 100 turns; secondary = 25 turns. Secondary voltage?
questions.expl: Say the turns fraction out loud first: 25 ÷ 100 = 0.25 (the secondary has a quarter of the turns). Then one operation: 240 × 0.25 = 60 → 60 V. Fewer secondary turns = step-DOWN.

questions.q: Primary = 10 V on 50 turns; secondary = 500 turns. Secondary voltage?
questions.expl: Say the turns fraction out loud first: 500 ÷ 50 = 10, so this transformer says "multiply by 10." Then one operation: 10 × 10 = 100 → 100 V (a 1:10 step-up). The secondary current drops to 1/10 of the primary.

questions.q: A 4:1 step-up transformer is fed 10 V at 4 A on the primary. The secondary output is:
questions.expl: Voltage steps UP 4×: 10 × 4 = 40 V. Current steps DOWN 4×: 4 ÷ 4 = 1 A. Power check, one operation per line: 10 × 4 = 40 W in; 40 × 1 = 40 W out — the same. No free power, ever.

questions.q: You check a transformer winding with an ohmmeter and it reads INFINITE ohms. The winding is:
questions.expl: A healthy winding shows continuity (low resistance). Infinite ohms means an open winding - the wire is broken.

questions.q: A transformer secondary that is OPEN will produce what output voltage with power on the primary?
questions.expl: An open secondary has no coupling action, so the fault shows as zero volts output.

questions.q: When checking for SHORTED turns, the affected winding's resistance will typically read:
questions.expl: Shorted turns bypass part of the winding, so its measured resistance reads lower than the normal specified value (and it overheats).

questions.q: A resistance check between a transformer's primary winding and its core should read:
options: The same as the winding resistance
questions.expl: Windings must be insulated from the core and each other, so that reading should be infinite. A low reading means insulation breakdown.

questions.q: The safest way to verify a transformer's ratio is correct is to:
options: Apply DC and measure resistance only
Leave the current-transformer secondary open under load
Apply safe AC and compare secondary/primary voltage to the rated turns ratio
questions.short: Compare V ratio to N ratio
questions.expl: Apply safe AC and compare the measured Vs/Vp to the rated Ns/Np. Never leave a current-transformer secondary open while energized.

questions.q: A semiconductor's electrical behavior places it where compared to other materials?
options: It is between a conductor and an insulator
It is a perfect insulator like glass
It has no electrons in its outer shell
It is a better conductor than copper
questions.expl: A semiconductor conducts better than an insulator but worse than a true conductor; its usefulness is that we can control when it conducts.

questions.q: Which two elements are the common semiconductor materials?
questions.expl: Silicon (Si) is the most common semiconductor; germanium (Ge) is the other. Boron and phosphorus are doping impurities, not the base material.

questions.q: What is doping?
options: Coating the crystal with copper oxide
Adding small amounts of impurities to increase current flow
Removing all free electrons from the crystal
questions.expl: Doping adds impurities that contribute either extra electrons or extra holes, creating N-type or P-type material.

questions.q: An N-type semiconductor's majority current carriers are:
questions.expl: N-type is doped with 5-electron (donor) impurities, leaving an excess of electrons as the majority carrier.

questions.q: A P-type semiconductor's majority current carriers are:
questions.expl: P-type is doped with 3-electron (acceptor) impurities, leaving 'holes' (missing electrons) as the majority carrier.

questions.q: A 'hole' in a semiconductor is best described as:
options: A physical crack in the crystal
An empty place where an electron would go, which acts like a positive charge
An extra electron that bonds to silicon
questions.short: An empty electron position acting positive
questions.expl: A hole is the absence of an electron; as electrons shift to fill holes, the hole appears to move as a positive charge.

questions.q: How many PN junctions does a basic diode have?
questions.expl: A diode is a single PN junction formed by joining P-type and N-type material. The '1N' prefix on diode part numbers means one junction.

questions.q: The fundamental job of a diode is to:
options: Store electric charge like a capacitor
Allow current to flow in one direction only
questions.expl: A diode is a one-way valve; it conducts when forward biased and blocks when reverse biased, which lets it rectify AC into DC.

questions.q: To FORWARD bias a diode, you connect:
options: Positive to the P side, negative to the N side
Both terminals to the same polarity
Nothing; a diode needs no bias
Positive to the N side, negative to the P side
questions.short: Positive to P, negative to N
questions.expl: Forward bias puts positive on the P (anode) and negative on the N (cathode), shrinking the barrier so current flows.

questions.q: A diode connected positive-to-N and negative-to-P is:
questions.expl: Positive to N / negative to P widens the depletion region and blocks current (only tiny leakage). This is reverse bias.

questions.q: Approximately what forward voltage drop does a SILICON diode have?
questions.expl: A silicon PN junction turns on at about 0.7 V; germanium is about 0.3 V.

questions.q: Approximately what forward voltage drop does a GERMANIUM diode have?
questions.expl: Germanium turns on at roughly 0.3 V, lower than silicon's 0.7 V.

questions.q: A PN-junction diode offers maximum resistance when it is:
questions.expl: Forward bias = very little resistance; reverse bias = maximum resistance (essentially blocks current).

questions.q: When a diode is reverse biased, the depletion region:
questions.expl: Reverse bias pulls carriers away from the junction, widening the depletion region and blocking current.

questions.q: The marked band (or dot) on a diode body indicates which terminal?
questions.expl: Manufacturers mark the cathode (N side) with a band, dot, colored stripe, or the letter 'k'.

questions.q: What is the primary function of a Zener diode?
options: Store energy in a magnetic field
questions.expl: A Zener operates in reverse breakdown and holds a constant voltage, acting as a voltage regulator.

questions.q: In what bias condition is a Zener diode normally operated?
questions.expl: Unlike an ordinary diode, the Zener is run in reverse at its rated breakdown voltage, where it conducts and regulates.

questions.q: A Zener diode behaves like what once its rated reverse voltage is reached?
questions.expl: At breakdown the Zener conducts and clamps the voltage, behaving like a constant-voltage source for regulation.

questions.q: An LED produces light when it is:
questions.expl: In a forward-biased LED, electrons falling into holes release energy as light instead of heat.

questions.q: Compared to an incandescent lamp, an LED offers all of these advantages EXCEPT:
questions.short: It does NOT produce more heat
questions.expl: LEDs produce LESS heat, not more; they also have longer life, lower voltage, and faster switching.

questions.q: How many terminals does a transistor have?
questions.expl: A transistor is a three-terminal device: emitter, base, and collector.

questions.q: The three terminals of a bipolar transistor are:
questions.expl: Emitter (heavily doped), base (thin, lightly doped control layer), and collector (moderately doped).

questions.q: The two primary functions of a transistor are to:
